items.title: Zoe Kleinman: How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions
items.summary: Zoe Kleinman explains how the man who built Nvidia from the ground up lost everything in a matter of days.

scraped.title: Zoe Kleinman: How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions
scraped.description: Zoe Kleinman explains how the man who built Nvidia from the ground up lost everything in a matter of days.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: Zoe Kleinman: How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions
scraped.body_text:
If I'd told you this time last week that Jensen Huang was about to leave Nvidia, you would not have believed me.

The man who co-founded this enormously successful AI chip company, working tirelessly to build it from the ground up and steering it through some disastrous times with endless energy and ruthless determination, has ultimately been undone by his own love life.

It's an extraordinary tale and a strangely old fashioned one for a tech firm with its sights set on the future.

It spawned a plethora of viral memes, seeing Huang as the man caught by the Coldplay kiss-cam with a married colleague , or singing along to George Michael's classic hit about betrayal, Careless Whisper.

Both were ironically AI-generated using the very tech he was helping to build.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang quits in wake of affair with suspected Chinese spy, as firm's stocks plunge

This week I met two Silicon Valley execs and I asked them how they were processing the news - "in memes", was the response.

But they didn't seem to think Huang would be forced out by his alleged adultery.

The stakes were too high, they said, the entire AI industry relies too heavily on Nvidia chips to break a winning formula.

In as many words, "the Valley" was on his side.

But that was before rumours of a second affair surfaced, this time with a colleague, and the board decided he had gone too far.

His behaviour suddenly cast him in a different light: a man who could make bad decisions and cover them up.

Huang always made a point of standing out from the crowd.

During the coronavirus lockdowns, he streamed keynote speeches from his kitchen (which gained internet fame in its own right, but were later revealed to have been AI-generated).

He is rarely seen without a leather jacket – he has joked that he only owns one suit, and he borrows his daughter's partner's tie.

Huang rubbed shoulders with the elite, with a network including Donald Trump, Elon Musk and King Charles.

The last time I saw him was at St James' Palace last year, where he was receiving the prestigious Queen's Prize for Engineering.

I was told he would not talk to the press - but he wandered over by himself and we spent about 10 minutes having a chat while press officers hovered nervously in the background. He was articulate and optimistic about the progress of AI and the UK's role in it.

For many people, Huang was Nvidia. He had as many as 200 people directly reporting to him.

He expected high standards – in his book about its inner workings, the Nvidia Way, author Tae Kim wrote the office hours were long.

Huang's feedback could be both brutal and public, and he thought nothing of pointing out individuals' mistakes in all-staff meetings.

Now it is his own shortcomings which are on very public display, and he has been forced into a brutal ending of his own career.

Colette Kress, who takes over for now, will be a familiar face internally and that must feel reassuring to some at Nvidia.

She's worked at the firm for 13 years and for those who follow the firm's considerable finances, she is often present on earnings calls. She is a billionaire in her own right and a high-flying tech exec.

But she's not an engineer and Nvidia's products are highly technical.

She will have to convince investors that it is business as usual for Nvidia, that the innovation for which it is renowned can continue at its existing pace, and that the top talent won't leave with Huang.

A wobbly Nvidia would be bad news for the entire AI industry because its ever-advancing chips drive the most powerful AI models, and it's also regarded as something of a central bank, loaning money to other firms.

As for Huang himself, we assume for now that the investigation into his relationship with the woman accused of being a Chinese spy will continue, and the results of that may well determine what he does next.

He probably won't be short of offers despite his conduct – and I expect Nvidia's rivals can't believe their luck that their formidable rival has taken himself out of the game. Elon Musk has already said it would be "an honour" to work with him at SpaceX.

It's important though to remember that even if Huang turns out not to have betrayed his company or his country, he still betrayed his wife of 41 years, Lori Huang.

And for her, it's not a story of tech, temptation and trillion-dollar-valuations.

It's a painfully personal matter.

The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal

Who is Nvidia's interim CEO Colette Kress - and who could take over permanently?

items.title: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drone in Gulf of Finland
items.summary: The attack is thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have attacked a Russian ship in an open stretch of the Baltic Sea.

scraped.title: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drone in Gulf of Finland
scraped.description: The attack is thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have attacked a Russian ship in an open stretch of the Baltic Sea.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drone in Gulf of Finland
scraped.body_text:
The Naro-Fominsk is believed to have headed back to port in St Petersburg after the attack

Finnish officials have confirmed that a Russian warship was attacked in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, although little is known about the strike.

Ukraine's SBU security service said it targeted the ship Naro-Fominsk as part of a broader drone operation against Russia's Ust-Luga oil export depot on the Baltic coast.

The attack, thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have attacked a Russian ship in an area of the Baltic Sea open to civilian maritime traffic, has raised questions about whether Ukraine could expand its strikes.

Helsinki has been one of Kyiv's closest European allies, and Finnish officials have described the incident as a direct result of Russia's continued full-scale war.

Finland's military has given few details of the incident, but it appears to have taken place in a narrow stretch some distance from the Finnish coast.

The country's Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen was adamant that the situation in the Baltic Sea remained stable and safe and that there was no threat of any kind to marine traffic.

Defence officials are understood to have stressed to Kyiv that the Gulf is a relatively narrow waterway used by oil tankers and civilian vessels, and is also home to subsea data cables.

Ukraine's SBU described the Russian ship as a Buyan-M type small corvette that carried Kalibr and Oniks cruise missiles. There were also unconfirmed reports of Russian combat helicopters being destroyed.

Martin Herem, the defence minister of Estonia, which borders the Gulf, told public broadcaster ERR that the ship was hit at about 05:30 (03:30 GMT) on Wednesday but did not say how it was attacked: "We know that smoke came from the ship afterwards. The ship itself went back towards St Petersburg."

The extent of casualties or damage sustained by the Russian navy ship remains unclear, and Moscow rarely gives such details.

"The Baltic Sea fleet has been untouched up to this point but there seemingly was a window of opportunity for Ukraine and they understandably tried to use it," said military analyst Emil Kastehelmi, co-founder of the Black Bird monitoring group.

Russian and Ukrainian vessels have been repeatedly targeted in the Black Sea since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, but even though the latest strike on a ship in the Baltic is unprecedented, Kastehelmi told the BBC he did not consider it a serious escalation.

Ukrainian drones are regularly launched into Russia from northern Ukraine. Several storage tanks at the Ust-Luga terminal are thought to have been hit overnight on Wednesday and fires at the port were visible over the border in Estonia.

Herem said Ukrainian drones attacked the Ust-Luga region from midnight until about 06:00, mostly flying close to the Estonian border but still in Russian airspace.

He added that one drone had entered Estonian airspace briefly from Latvia and then headed towards Russia.

Nato aircraft based in the Baltic states were in the air at the time, but Herem said it had not been considered safe for them to destroy the drones.

Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesman Heorhiy Tykhyy said late on Wednesday that Moscow's allegations that Kyiv had used the airspace of the Baltic states to attack Russia were "baseless", although he acknowledged "incidents might occur when Russia diverts drones from its airspace using electronic warfare".

items.title: Microsoft users report outages amid tech giant 'connectivity issues'
items.summary: Users worldwide report issues after tech giant says its infrastructure has been hit by "elevated load"

scraped.title: Microsoft outage sees Teams, Outlook and Copilot suffer 'connectivity issues'
scraped.description: Users worldwide report issues after tech giant says its infrastructure has been hit by "elevated load"
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: Microsoft users report outages amid tech giant 'connectivity issues'
scraped.body_text:
Microsoft says it is working to tackle "connectivity problems" after users worldwide reported outages on Thursday.

Services including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's AI software Copilot were affected.

The tech giant said a part of its infrastructure was experiencing "elevated load", which was likely contributing to connectivity errors.

While the issue was originally reported in the US, Microsoft said the connectivity problems could affect users "in any region".

At around 18:30 GMT on Thursday evening, monitoring website Downdetector showed a spike in UK users reporting issues with Microsoft products.

Similarly for the US, the monitoring site suggested there had been over 131,000 reports of Microsoft Outlook problems at 18:15 GMT.

"We determined the elevated load isn't driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure," Microsoft said in a statement.

In a further update issued at 19:50 GMT, Microsoft said it was "testing a configuration" to fix the problem, which was "causing servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable".

All affected servers had been restarted, it added.

scraped.author: https://www.theguardian.com/profile/rachel-savage
scraped.h1: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story
scraped.body_text:
After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-written’

The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.

Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter , which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.

Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara said the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated.

The Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement : “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.”

She said: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation.

“Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama said. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.”

Kundizeza, who had strongly denied using generative AI to write the story, said he was “relieved” that the allegations had been dismissed after the investigation. “It was not necessary in the first place, I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey,” he said.

Vara’s article prompted outrage online, with many claiming that Black writers, and Africans in particular, were being unfairly singled out by allegations of the use of AI.

Associated Press contributed to this report

items.title: 'Punch in the gut': Homes sales fall to their lowest in 16 years
items.summary: Existing homes sales in October declined 8.8% from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors. Existing homes sales in October declined 8.8% from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors.(Image credit: Mario Tama)

scraped.title: 'Punch in the gut': Homes sales fall to their lowest in 16 years
scraped.description: Existing homes sales in October declined 8.8% from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors.
scraped.h1: 'Punch in the gut': Homes sales fall to their lowest in 16 years
scraped.body_text:
By

Stephan Bisaha

Home sales fell to their lowest since 2010, a new report shows, in large part due to high mortgage rates. Mario Tama/Getty Images hide caption

The housing market has finally broken out of the stagnant holding pattern it's been stuck in for more than four years – just not in the right direction.

Existing home sales in October fell to 3.75 million, making an 8.8% decline in sales from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors. The last time sales were this low was 16 years ago.

"It was a punch in the gut," said Joel Berner, senior economist at Realtor.com . "We expected to see a soft month but not the softest month since 2010."

The drop is mainly due to high mortgage rates.

In October, the average rate for a 30-year fixed rate mortgage hit as high as 7.40%, the highest since 2023. Rates have gone down a bit since then, but are still well above where they were a year ago.

Higher inflation and bond yields have driven up mortgage rates, but some of this housing slowdown was by design.

The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate in September to increase the cost of borrowing, including home mortgages. Fewer home sales and other purchases mean less economic activity, which the Fed wants in order to reach its goal of lowering inflation.

Policymakers at the Fed have signaled another rate hike could come in December, which could further slow down the housing market.

"It might seem like kicking the housing market while it's down right now for the Fed to continue a rate raising cycle but in the long run getting inflation under control is really the goal," Berner said.

By

NPR Staff

A view of the site where a building collapsed in Brooklyn, New York on Wednesday. Yuki Iwamura/AP hide caption

The New York City Fire Department reported Thursday that more victims had been found after a three-story residential building in the Flatbush neighborhood of Brooklyn collapsed a day earlier.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani said six people had been declared dead at the scene. Two others died in a hospital. 18 other people were injured in the building collapse.

Search efforts are continuing with more than 250 firefighters and emergency workers deployed to the site, according to city officials.

First responders rescue a person after a building collapsed in Brooklyn, New York on Wednesday. Ryan Murphy/AP hide caption

First responders navigate a collapsed building in Brooklyn, New York on Wednesday. Kena Betancur/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

A construction worker embraces a child at the scene of a partial building collapse on Wednesday. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images hide caption

Onlookers watch as emergency personnel respond to the scene of a partial building collapse on Wednesday in the Flatbush neighborhood of Brooklyn, New York. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images hide caption

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks during a press conference after a building collapsed in Brooklyn on Wednesday. Kena Betancur/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

New York City Public Advocate Jumaane Williams consoles a man after his pregnant wife was rescued from the rubble at the scene of a partial building collapse on Wednesday. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images hide caption

Members of the New York City Fire Department work at the scene one day after a building collapsed in Brooklyn. Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

A resident from a building watches as cleanup begins at the scene of a partial building collapse on Thursday in the Flatbush neighborhood of Brooklyn, New York. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images hide caption

A drone flies over the site of a building that collapsed the previous day in Brooklyn, New York on Thursday. Yuki Iwamura/AP hide caption

An excavator cleans up debris at the scene of a partial building collapse on Thursday in Flatbush, Brooklyn. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images hide caption

scraped.title: Democrats want to stop Trump's arch, golf course and more. What are their options?
scraped.description: As Trump's arch and other projects make their way through the courts, many critics are looking to Congress to stop them. Democrats have a few tools, including funding and oversight.
scraped.h1: Democrats want to stop Trump's arch, golf course and more. What are their options?
scraped.body_text:
By

Rachel Treisman

President Trump signed the final steel beam at the White House ballroom the day after the midterm elections. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images hide caption

President Trump's efforts to remake Washington, D.C., have dominated his second term, even after his party's resounding midterm defeat.

He started his election week at the scandal-plagued Reflecting Pool and ended it with an order declaring his gilded Oval Office a national monument to "make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space."

That proclamation, like any executive order, could be undone by a future president. But many of Trump's construction projects are changing D.C. in more permanent ways.

His administration has already downed hundreds of trees at East Potomac Park and demolished the East Wing of the White House to make space for a ballroom — which he called "the safest place in Washington" as he showed it to reporters the day after the midterms.

Trump has taken a uniquely unilateral approach to construction , packing regulatory commissions with his allies and bypassing Congress entirely. Most of his projects — from the triumphal arch to the Kennedy Center — are now playing out in court .

Critics accuse the Trump administration of skirting federal laws and misleading judges in its effort to progress as quickly as possible before the end of his term.

Democrats have vowed to use their soon-to-be congressional majority to push back on what they describe as Trump's "vanity projects."

When asked about that, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR in an email that "no other president has done more to beautify our Nation's interior than President Trump." He cited park cleanups, the Reflecting Pool and the White House helipad and ballroom as examples, and said Democrats "should work with President Trump to make our nation's capital beautiful again."

Rep. Jared Huffman, center, poses with activists protesting Trump's triumphal arch at Memorial Circle in May. He will soon become the chair of the committee with legislative and oversight authority over public lands. Andrew Harnik/Getty Imags hide caption

Rep. Jared Huffman, D.-Calif., told NPR in an interview that the Trump administration has "played this game of Catch Me If You Can, where they roll ahead with the bulldozers and the tree cutters … and they wait for courts to shut them down." He says a Democrat-led Congress will fight back.

"There's no way that we could look away while these sacred, iconic places are being permanently changed in ways that violate the law and could have really terrible lasting impacts," said Huffman, the top Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, which has a legislative purview over public lands and national parks.

Huffman says blocking Trump's construction projects — and holding people accountable for potential wrongdoing — will be a top priority when he leads the committee. Earlier this week, he sent letters ordering dozens of administration officials and private companies to preserve their records for a future investigation.

"Whether it is the arch or … or the East Potomac golf course or any number of other examples around the United States capital, that is federal land, and we have a direct statutory responsibility to either authorize those changes or to stop them if they're proceeding without the proper authorization," Huffman said.

What would that actually look like? Democrats have many tools at their disposal, from legislation to lawsuits. But experts say only two are likely to succeed: funding and oversight.

Trump made a final pre-Midterm Day pitch to voters from the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, whose renovations took months longer than anticipated due to algae blooms and peeling paint. Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

Congress could — at least in theory — pass laws to block specific projects from moving ahead. Some Democratic lawmakers have already introduced bills to protect the Kennedy Center from demolition and prohibit the construction of an arch at Memorial Circle.

But Trump has promised to " veto everything ," and Democrats won't have a big enough majority to override him on their own.

"Legislation in principle is the cleanest way of doing it, but it's also not achievable," said David Super, who teaches administrative and constitutional law at Georgetown. "So what they're likely to do is cut off funds."

The Constitution says that the federal government may spend money only if is appropriated by Congress. But Trump has neither sought nor received congressional authorization for projects like the arch and the White House ballroom — he maintains he doesn't need it.

Rep. Chellie Pingree of Maine is one of many who disagree. She's the top Democrat on the House committee that oversees funding for the Interior Department.

"Certainly Congress should have been involved, because we have the power of the purse," Pingree told NPR. "That is our ultimate tool. And Republicans have refused to use that. But we can use that in very many ways to block him or to use it for leverage."

Pingree says a Democratic majority will be able to write appropriations bills with clear language from the outset about where money can and can't be spent — and potentially take the president to court if he doesn't follow it.

Super expects Congress would prevail in such a challenge, because it has clear-cut authority over federal funds.

For example, he noted that some of Trump's D.C.-area beautification projects have been funded at least in part by diverted national park entrance fees . Congress could "cap how much money can be used in the greater Washington area, and force the money to be used in the Everglades and Yosemite and Great Smoky Mountains," he said.

Congress will have to make some appropriations decisions in the coming weeks, since it needs to pass a short-term funding bill by Dec. 11 to avoid a government shutdown. Democrats could use that opportunity to try to limit funding for at least one of Trump's construction projects.

Huffman has proposed language that would prevent Trump from using federal funds for the East Potomac golf course renovations, limiting them instead to repairs of the park's crumbling seawall. Pingree said she will join him in fighting to negotiate that into next month's bill.

On one October Saturday, the Trump administration cut down some 430 trees at East Potomac Park, where the president wants to develop a municipal golf course into a championship-level course. Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images hide caption

"Whether or not the president will sign that with that in there, I don't know yet," she said. "But certainly those are the most … immediate crisis points … People want the president to stop cutting down the trees on the golf course and stop trying to take that over, and they want to make sure that no shovel goes into the ground on building the arch."

Earlier this year Pingree introduced an amendment that would have outright blocked construction of the arch; it failed along party lines. She wonders whether any Republicans might vote differently after the midterms, given the message Americans sent at the polls.

"They want the president to be focused on the issues they're dealing with: the cost of health care, the cost of food, the cost of gasoline," she said. "And if every time the president gives a speech, he's either standing in front of the Reflecting Pool, which he spent millions of dollars on, or showing you the new marble choices he's putting into the ballroom, it just makes a lot of people mad."

Pingree said she's been surprised to hear how strongly people feel about these projects – even people well outside D.C. And she agrees with them that potential corruption and misuse of taxpayer dollars are worth fighting: "After the first of the year, we will use every tool in our toolbox."

Lawmakers and experts acknowledge that not every project is reversible, or potentially even worth the fight. Huffman suggested he will focus on bigger projects, and ones that are moving too fast for courts to adequately rein in.

"Are we going to throw all of our efforts at stopping the gilding of every statue in Washington, D.C.? Probably not," said Huffman. "But these are iconic places that we're talking about, with permanent damage that we need to engage on to try to prevent."

Even so, Democrats could decide that certain construction projects are "the price they pay for other priorities," said Claire Leavitt, a professor of government at Smith College. Voters made clear they want lawmakers to focus on ending the Iran war and making life more affordable, big asks that may take a lot of political capital.

"And that's not corruption or Democrats not doing their job," Leavitt said. "It's just the natural trade-offs of dealing with who you're dealing with, and understanding that what matters to Trump more than anything seems to be building the arch, building the ballroom … remaking the Kennedy Center."

Whether or not these projects move forward, Congress can provide a fuller public accounting of how they came to be — in the hopes of preventing more in the future.

"They can gavel in hearings. They have agenda-setting power," Leavitt said. "They determine what the public hearing roster is. They decide which witnesses to invite. And that means they have a unique opportunity to draw negative public attention to the Trump administration."

Work on the White House ballroom is moving quickly. Andrew Harnik/Getty Images hide caption

That may be easier said than done, especially with an administration that has pointedly refused to comply with congressional oversight and is now warning Democrats that their future investigations could constitute criminality. Huffman was coy when asked how he is preparing to handle such challenges.

"We are going to have to have a strategy and a plan to do these things that prior Congresses have never imagined they would have to do," he said.

One investigative priority, lawmakers say, will be following the money — especially when it comes to donations for the ballroom and other projects. Leavitt says that focus has an added benefit: Private companies and individuals are likely more willing to testify than a member of the administration.

Another example: Congress could subpoena for information about the decision-making processes of the Kennedy Center board and the physical state of the building, which trustees say must be closed for two years of repairs. And it can put that information in the Congressional — and therefore historical — Record.

"Both the current public can make its judgments, and history can make its judgments," Leavitt said.

Leavitt said oversight can often lead to policy change in the longer term. For example: The committee investigating the Jan. 6 insurrection didn't stop Trump from eventually pardoning Capitol rioters , but it did lead Congress to pass an electoral reform act .

"The frustrating part about congressional oversight is Congress can draw attention to a problem, and they can demand accountability for something that's already been done," Leavitt said. "But it's very hard for Congress to stop something from happening that the president is determined to do."

Super agrees that Democrats are playing a long game. He expects to see more bipartisan support after Trump leaves office for preventing future presidents from following his playbook.

"The process in the past has been built on trust, and President Trump certainly broke that trust in numerous ways," he said. "Laws can be written so that we don't depend on trust, we depend on law. And I'm guessing we're going to do that."

items.title: The loss of Dan Hicks hits hard, Lindsey Vonn has a couple screws loose & Mullen's radical playoff idea
items.summary: Lindsey Vonn underwent a total ACL replacement in a five-hour surgery, her ninth operation since February, as legendary Dan Hicks is mourned at 64. scraped.title: The loss of Dan Hicks hits hard, Lindsey Vonn has a couple screws loose & Mullen's radical playoff idea
scraped.description: Sports broadcaster Dan Hicks, known for golf and Olympics calls, has died at 64. Lindsey Vonn also undergoes total ACL replacement surgery after her leg injury.
scraped.author: Zach Dean
scraped.h1: The loss of Dan Hicks hits hard, Lindsey Vonn has a couple screws loose & Mullen's radical playoff idea
scraped.body_text:
The selection committee has officially traded credibility for drama, ranking manufactured television narratives instead of actual on-field resumes.

'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday-Friday on OutKick.com .

Over the hump and safely into the second half of the week. We made it. We're here.

We've got Thursday Night Football tonight. We've got college football all weekend — and we don't have a ton of those left, so I'd suggest not missing a single second.

We're two weeks out from Thanksgiving. The weather is starting to turn, even down here in Florida. We're supposed to stay in the 60s all Saturday. Do you know the last time that happened?

March.

March!

Yeah, it's been a while. We gutted it all summer in the 90s. We stayed the course in September and October when it rained every single day. This weekend, the grind finally pays off.

Let's roll.

MASSIVE COLLEGE FOOTBALL BRAWL LEAVES 23 PLAYERS SUSPENDED

Tiger Woods is interviewed by NBC's Dan Hicks after winning the TOUR Championship on Sept. 23, 2018, at East Lake Golf Club in Atlanta, Ga. It was Woods' 80th career PGA win. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

Welcome to a Thursday Nightcaps — the one where we pay tribute to legendary broadcaster Dan Hicks, who died today at 64.

Just brutal. What a terrible, terrible loss.

I've also got Lindsey Vonn going back under the knife to get a new ACL, Dan Mullen offering up maybe the smartest idea I've ever heard, and I downloaded the "Back When" app last night after talking about it in yesterday's class ...

Spoiler alert: It's the most incredible thing I've ever seen. I spent two hours on it last night. I was in a trance. I was mesmerized. I may never watch 2026 TV again.

OK, grab you whatever drink you'd like — pour it out for Dan Hicks — and settle in a Thursday 'Cap.

Before we officially get this class started, I need to talk about Dan Hicks. The legendary sports broadcaster, most known for his work in golf and the Olympics, died today at 64.

How? I don't know. They're calling it an "acute illness." Whatever the reason, it's beyond sad. Hicks was a legend. We grew up with him calling some of the golf's biggest moments. You may not have realize it, but I can promise you that you've heard a Dan Hicks call.

SPORTS WORLD REACTS TO DAN HICKS' DEATH

Dan Hicks poses for a photo during the NBC Golf Channel Broadcast during the third round of THE PLAYERS Championship at Stadium Course at TPC Sawgrass on March 11, 2023 in Ponte Vedra Beach, Florida. (Photo by Ben Jared/PGA TOUR via Getty Images) (Ben Jared/PGA TOUR via Getty Images)

Doesn't have to be golf, either. He famously called the Men’s Olympic 4x100m Freestyle Relay in Beijing in 2008. He called NFL playoff games . He called Notre Dame games.

His most famous call, in my mind? Tiger's long putt at the 2008 US Open.

"Expect anything different?!"

I've watched that putt a billion times. I watched it live with my dad on Father's Day when I was 15. I still get chills to this day.

It was an iconic sports moment, and Hicks gave us an all-time call. I expected nothing different.

Hicks was our comfort food on the weekend of a major tournament. You knew when you heard Dan's voice, something big was happening. You also knew he was going to nail it.

Amazingly enough, he called a Notre Dame game just last month:

Just shocking. When I saw the news this morning, I was stunned. Everyone was.

Nobody did it better than Dan Hicks. Sundays in the spring and summer won't be the same. Saturdays on NBC won't be, either.

What a gut-punch.

OK, let's try our best to transition to something a little lighter on this Thursday, although it's still not great. Lindsey Vonn spent all day yesterday back on the operating table as she continues her recovery from last February's devastating leg injury.

The latest? A total ACL replacement.

Check out what they took OUT of Lindsey's LEG:

Lordy. First of all, I had no clue they could just ... give you a new ACL. Is that normal? I assume so, but I had no idea.

"Surgery went well!" Vonn wrote in a separate Instagram post , which featured some more behind-the-scenes footage from her operation.

WARNING: Some of the pics ain't for the squeamish.

"It took over 5 hours to remove all of the plates and screws from my leg and replace my ACL," she continued. "I am home from the hospital now and thankful to be on the final road to a full recovery."

Lindsey Vonn attends the Opening Night and USTA Foundation Gala at the 2026 U.S. Open at USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center on Aug. 30, 2026, in New York, N.Y. (Variety via Getty Images)

This was Vonn's ninth surgery since February, by the way. What a warrior. What a patriot. She'll be back upright in no time. Can't wait.

OK, let's rapid-fire this Thursday class into a big Thursday night of FOOTBALL. First up? There's been a ton of CFP talk this week with the expansion to 24 teams becoming official starting next year.

Best I can tell, nobody likes it. At all. UNLV coach Dan Mullen did, however, propose a radical idea involving the G6 teams that I'm 100000% on board with.

Take a look:

I think it's brilliant. Have the four best G6 teams play two de-facto play-in games the weekend before the playoffs begin. Start the first one at noon, followed by Army-Navy at 3:30, and the final game at 8.

Pretty sound plan, if you ask me.

Thoughts? First impressions? I love it. I doubt the P4 teams will ever allow TWO G6 teams in the dance, but that's not my problem. You want some actual stakes at the end of an increasingly meaningless season? There they are.

I'm all in.

Next? Yesterday I talked about this new app on Roku called "Back When." Essentially, it's an app that transports your TV back to the 1990s (or '80s) and has actual shows — and commercials — airing as if it's happening in real time.

I got an email from Eric P. last night saying that not only was this app legit, it was as good as advertised.

Naturally, I had to find out for myself ...

back when app (Screenshot)

Braves-Dodgers. (Screenshot)

I was hooked right off the bat. I found an old Braves-Dodgers game with Lasorda in the dugout and Glavine on the mound, and a Pittsburgh-West Virginia game on ESPN from 2000. Just two random channels on this app, and THAT's what they were playing.

Both were complete with commercials from the actual telecast, too. The first commercial during the WVU game? The classic Bowflex commercial that I'm quite certain anyone my age has burned in their brain:

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

I was hooked. I couldn't stop scrolling through the channels. I also found an old episode of Still Standing on ABC Family (now Freeform), an old episode of Roseanne and an episode of Cheers from NBC's Saturday night lineup in 1985.

I've never been more in on an app. I never want to go back to today's television. We had it so much better back then, it's not even funny.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

What a pleasure it was to be transported back to the '90s for a few hours.

OK, that's it for today. Good class, everyone. Let's have a big Thursday night of FOOTBALL, and end the week strong tomorrow.

See you then.

Zach Dean is a writer for OutKick.

items.title: Drake Maye tells reporters they don't know 'what they're talking about' during Germany press conference
items.summary: Drake Maye called out the media in Munich over reports about Rhamondre Stevenson's injury status ahead of the Patriots-Lions game in Germany. The New England Patriots landed in Munich, Germany on Thursday for Sunday's game against the Detroit Lions and then made quarterback Drake Maye available to reporters to discuss all things international NFL games, and this trip, and the game.And Maye took the opportunity in front of the German and American reporters to tell them what he thinks of them —...

scraped.title: Drake Maye tells reporters they don't know 'what they're talking about' during Germany press conference
scraped.description: Drake Maye called out the media in Munich, saying reporters don't know what they're talking about regarding Rhamondre Stevenson's injury ahead of the Patriots-Lions game.
scraped.author: Armando Salguero
scraped.h1: Drake Maye tells reporters they don't know 'what they're talking about' during Germany press conference
scraped.body_text:
The Green Bay Packers beat the New England Patriots 45-27, and the Patriots fell to 5-4. Nick Wright, Kevin Wildes, and Danny Parkins discuss the biggest concerns for the Patriots and Drake Maye, if the Packers are Super Bowl contenders, and the Patrick Mahomes injury scare during the Kansas City Chiefs’ win over the New York Jets.

The New England Patriots landed in Munich, Germany on Thursday for Sunday's game against the Detroit Lions and then made quarterback Drake Maye available to reporters to discuss all things international NFL games, and this trip, and the game.

And Maye took the opportunity in front of the German and American reporters to tell them what he thinks of them — which apparently is not much, sometimes.

It began with a mundane question about running back Rhamondre Stevenson being present for the team's practice and working off to the side during the portion of drills open to reporters.

NFL OWNERS APPROVE RECORD 10 INTERNATIONAL GAMES FOR 2027 WITH SIGHTS ON MORE EXPANSION ABROAD

"I think that's just, speaks to, you know, first off, the media not really knowing 100 percent what they're talking about a lot of the time," Maye said.

Hey now.

PATRIOTS' DRAKE MAYE SAYS HE'S 'A LITTLE BIT SKEPTICAL' US LANDED ON MOON, NASA RESPONDS

Just for the sake of context, this is where we remind everyone that Drake Maye is salt of the Earth kind of people. Nice. Polite.

He's competitive, yes, but not with that Tom Brady-grab-opponents-by-the-throat mentality. And yet, there he was in Munich grabbing the media by the proverbial throat with his opinion of them.

So where did this come from?

First, it shows that recent reports of Stevenson's injury status obviously bothered Maye. One local Boston outlet reported Stevenson is expected to miss multiple weeks with a plantaris tendon injury behind one of this knees, an injury he suffered in Sunday's blowout loss to the Green Bay Packers.

PATRIOTS LOSE AJ BROWN TO INJURY AGAIN, RULE OUT OTHER OFFENSIVE PLAYERS AHEAD OF MATCHUP WITH DIVISION RIVAL

That report apparently struck a nerve with Maye.

"He's a guy that wants to be out there, you know, wants to be back for his team and that's what we're in the midst of trying to make a run here and win a big one before the bye," Maye said. "So this is a time for players, a lot of the players on this team that are trying to get out there, play with teammates and knowing that he's a great player, help us out."

Maybe the report about Stevenson rubbed Maye the wrong way because it suggested the running back is not going to contribute through the bye when, in fact, he's trying to do the opposite.

But this begs more context. Again, Maye is a good person. He wasn't angry with reporters when he slammed them. He even shared his FIFA thoughts and said maybe Harry Kane's experience under great pressure could help him transition to being an NFL kicker as the star has suggested he wants to do.

But Maye, in only his third NFL season, is perhaps also showing the wear of having an inconsistent season as the followup to last year's trip to the Super Bowl. That inconsistency has made him the target of criticism.

And the Patriots have been at the epicenter of media attention — much of it negative – this year that perhaps also has affected how Maye views the coverage of his team.

NEW VIDEO SHOWS MIKE VRABEL AND DIANNA RUSSINI ON PRIVATE BOATING TRIP DURING HER PREGNANCY

Remember, the coverage of the relationship between coach Mike Vrabel and reporter Dianna Russini was seemingly nonstop for months and was admittedly exhausting at times.

The Patriots apparent Super Bowl hangover has also been a constant topic of discussion and frustration because for whatever reasons, including injuries, the team that lost only three regular-season games last season is 5-4 now and the schedule doesn't promise to get easier.

It's impossible to know if Maye was letting the frustration over all that rough coverage slip into one moment of a press conference.

But it raised eyebrows.

And maybe, with Stevenson trying to play on Sunday counter to a report, Maye had a point.

FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

Armando Salguero is OutKick's Senior NFL Writer.

items.summary: Democrats say Howard Lutnick, Stephen Miller, Tom Homan and Marco Rubio could face impeachment efforts and congressional hearings in January. scraped.title: The top Trump officials Democrats admit are on their hit list for investigations in the new Congress
scraped.description: House Democrats signal impeachment efforts and congressional investigations targeting Stephen Miller, Tom Homan, Howard Lutnick and Marco Rubio in Trump's administration.
scraped.author: Pedro Rodriguez-Aparicio
scraped.h1: The top Trump officials Democrats admit are on their hit list for investigations in the new Congress
scraped.body_text:
This material may not be published, broadcast, rewritten, or redistributed. ©2026 FOX News Network, LLC. All rights reserved. Quotes displayed in real-time or delayed by at least 15 minutes. Market data provided by Factset . Powered and implemented by FactSet Digital Solutions . Legal Statement . Mutual Fund and ETF data provided by LSEG .

Congressional Democrats tell Fox News Digital that members of the administration, including Lutnick, Rubio, Homan and Miller could be on their chopping block in the 120th Congress

Democrats are sharing their growing list of senior officials and advisors in President Donald Trump's administration who could face impeachment efforts and congressional investigations when they take control of Congress in January.

Left-wing lawmakers are signaling that their oversight ambitions extend well beyond War Secretary Pete Hegseth after Tuesday's failed impeachment effort.

Top House and Senate Democrats told Fox News Digital they are considering investigations, congressional hearings and potential impeachment proceedings targeting senior administration officials, including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio , White House adviser Stephen Miller and border czar Tom Homan.

‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH

Incoming House Oversight Committee leader Rep. Robert Garcia warned that Democrats could investigate President Donald Trump's pardons as well as allies of the president. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

"Our job of accountability doesn't change, we are going to hold everyone accountable that needs to be held accountable," Sen. Ruben Gallego , D-Ariz., told Fox News Digital when asked about possible action against Miller and Homan. "Especially if we've seen the violations and any kind of gross abuses."

Gallego acknowledged that the details of any potential efforts to remove the officials "remain to be seen."

Miller and Homan did not respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., who introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth in April, echoed Gallego's remarks, signaling support for further accountability efforts in the House.

HEGSETH COULD FACE NEW IMPEACHMENT PUSH OVER UKRAINE AID, LAWMAKERS WARN

Rep. Adelita Grijalva, D-Ariz., also expressed support for increased congressional scrutiny, arguing that voters sent a message during the midterm elections.

"What we heard from the American people on Tuesday (midterms) was to put an end to the corruption," Grijalva told Fox News Digital.

"We're looking at the executive in the White House making hand over fist millions of dollars while in office," she continued.

Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., demanded that the Trump administration refund billions in tariff revenue following President Donald Trump's stinging Supreme Court loss. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., the current vice chair of the House Democratic Caucus and a candidate to lead the conference in January, also backed discussions about potential investigations into Miller and Homan.

Lieu told Fox News Digital that, if elected caucus chairman, he intends to discuss with Democratic leadership how to proceed with congressional hearings, investigations and possible impeachment proceedings targeting the two officials.

The California Democrat also called for an investigation into Lutnick over allegations involving NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese intelligence operative.

NVIDIA SPY CASE EXPOSES HOW FOREIGN AGENTS TARGET AMERICA’S CORPORATE ELITE: 'HE IS COMPROMISED'

"Howard Lutnick needs to be investigated over his role in Jensen Huang and the Chinese spy, we're going to have an investigation into those allegations, that's completely unacceptable," Lieu told Fox News Digital.

Lieu alleged that Lutnick knew about the reported relationship but failed to investigate or take action.

Lutnick did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

President Donald Trump attends a Cabinet meeting in the Cabinet Room at the White House in Washington on May 27, 2026. (Jacquelyn Martin/AP)

Rep. Ro Khanna , D-Calif., a vice chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus and member of the House Select Committee on China , also supported investigating Lutnick and did not rule out scrutinizing Rubio's potential involvement.

DEMOCRATS RALLY BEHIND GOP LAWMAKER'S HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT PUSH, SIGNAL MORE TO COME IN JANUARY

"I think we need transparency," Khanna told Fox News Digital. "I think we need to understand what they (Rubio and Lutnick) knew."

"Rubio knew about the Chinese spy, and then got invited to the China trip," Khanna continued. "We need to get to the bottom of this."

Howard Lutnick, US commerce secretary, in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, DC, US, on Wednesday, Aug. 6, 2025 (Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Rubio did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

The lawmakers' remarks signal that Democrats could use their congressional majorities to expand oversight of Trump's administration, although no findings of wrongdoing involving the named officials have been established in the allegations presented.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

While the House can impeach federal civil officers by a simple majority, conviction and removal require a two-thirds vote in the Senate.

Republicans, meanwhile, accused Democrats of pursuing politically motivated impeachment proceedings against Trump administration officials.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital following Tuesday's vote that he was "not surprised" by Democrats' interest in impeaching Hegseth.

Mast argued that Democrats were determined to impeach "anyone who was appointed by the president," regardless of whether evidence supported the allegations.

items.title: Who is Colette Kress, Nvidia’s new interim CEO?
items.summary: For 13 years, Colette Kress helped manage the company’s transformation from a graphics-chip maker into the company at the center of the AI boom. Nvidia's Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress.

scraped.title: Who is Colette Kress, Nvidia’s new interim CEO?
scraped.description: For 13 years, Colette Kress helped manage the company’s transformation from a graphics-chip maker into the company at the center of the AI boom.
scraped.h1: Who is Colette Kress, Nvidia’s new interim CEO?
scraped.body_text:
For You

Settings

news Alerts

There are no new alerts at this time

For 13 years, Colette Kress helped manage the company’s transformation from a graphics-chip maker into the company at the center of the artificial intelligence boom. Now, she’s being asked to lead it through one of the most turbulent moments in its history.

Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, was named interim CEO Thursday following the abrupt resignation of Jensen Huang, who co-founded the company and led it for 33 years. Huang’s departure comes amid revelations of extramarital relationships with an alleged Chinese spy and one of his own reports.

“We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead,” Kress said in a press release. “Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.”

“I believe deeply in this company and in its future. More than anything, I believe in each of you, in our customers and partners and in the vital role we play every day in the global economy,” Kress said in an email to staff following her appointment, acknowledging the “extraordinarily difficult period” for the company.

Kress joined the company in September 2013 after tenures at Cisco and Microsoft, where she also held finance positions. She has helped see Nvidia through its transition from a video game-focused processor manufacturer to an AI-chip powerhouse.

“Having worked with Colette at Cisco, I know she understands what it takes to lead through major market transitions, build strong teams, and execute at scale,” said John Chambers, former Cisco executive chairman and CEO. “Nvidia is at a critical moment, not just for the company, but for the future of AI and America’s technology leadership. I really believe Colette’s ability to step in as interim CEO. She is an amazing leader.”

Chambers, who himself has moved from a CFO to a CEO role in the past, said that despite the uncertainty a leadership change creates, he does not believe it will fundamentally alter the company’s trajectory.

“Every company goes through near death experiences,” Chambers said. “Nvidia is no different. It will be a challenging next year, I think they will continue to be a leading force in the AI landscape.”

Kress and Huang worked closely together. Huang long leaned on Kress during financial conferences and the company’s earnings calls to debrief the investing public about the latest developments with the company’s operations.

The company’s release noted its planned earnings call will go ahead on Nov. 17. Kress is expected to lead it, five days after taking on the new role.

As Nvidia grew its business to focus on AI, Kress has been instrumental in managing financial relationships. Under her watch, the company has invested heavily into the technology sector, including Intel, Nokia and a partnership with OpenAI.

In the past, Kress has noted that the inability to sell to China would affect the industry in the long run, a stance echoing Huang’s. “If you are unable to sell products to them, it will have an impact,” she said in an interview to Israeli publication Globes .

In a November 2025 earnings call, Kress told investors the company is not expecting data center compute revenue from China.

“Sizable purchase orders never materialized in the quarter due to geopolitical issues and the increasingly competitive market in China,” Kress told investors, according to a transcript of the call. “While we were disappointed in the current state that prevents us from shipping more competitive Data Center compute products to China, we are committed to continued engagement with the U.S. and China governments and will continue to advocate for America’s ability to compete around the world.”

Kress’ tenure at Nvidia has been lucrative. Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index named her as one of two new Nvidia executives whose net worth exceeded $1 billion last year , largely based on the company stock she holds.

Nvidia shares dipped Thursday following the announcement of Huang’s resignation and Kress’ new position.

The crisis comes at a pivotal moment for AI development in the U.S. as outfits like Anthropic and OpenAI rely on Nvidia’s dominant chip technology. Kress’ role will be to see the company through the crisis and again cast it as a reliable player in the global markets.

That may be difficult, as both investors and lawmakers are probing Nvidia for details of the alleged spy plot. Huang has agreed to brief Congress on his relationship as well as the company’s security protocols.

“Jensen Huang’s decision to resign from NVIDIA does not absolve him, other executives, or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said in a statement Thursday. “They still owe Congress answers.”

Jane Lytvynenko is a senior technology reporter for NBC News.

items.summary: An X account associated with D.C. shooting suspect Matt Lambert was filled with complaints about mold, rodents and disrepair in his unit in the condo building.

scraped.title: Social media account linked to D.C. shooter complained of disrepair, invoked man who killed healthcare CEO
scraped.description: An X account associated with D.C. shooting suspect Matt Lambert was filled with complaints about mold, rodents and disrepair in his unit in the condo building.
scraped.h1: Social media account linked to D.C. shooter complained of disrepair, invoked man who killed healthcare CEO
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

November 12, 2026 / 3:42 PM EST / CBS News

The gunman who opened fire at a gym in a luxury condo building in Washington, D.C., Thursday morning had been complaining about mold and water problems in his apartment in the building. Multiple law enforcement sources have identified him as Dr. Matt Lambert.

Police said he shot and killed himself in his apartment after killing at least one person and wounding four others in what law enforcement sources said was a targeted attack.

Three firearms were recovered from his apartment, according to law enforcement sources in Washington.

An account on X under the name @OfMiceandMold has served as a repository for complaints about the alleged disrepair of the apartment where Lambert lived.

In dozens of X posts, he vented his frustration with the Metropole Condominiums' building contractors, EJF Real Estate Services, and his allegations they failed to address problems with his unit. CBS News has reached out to EJF Real Estate Services for comment.

Lambert, who was 52 and ran a D.C.-based healthcare consultancy, had purchased the condo in September 2016 for $1,095,000, according to D.C. tax records. Court documents show he owned a penthouse unit in the building.

Before the shooting, he posted what he claimed was an engineering report that investigated mold and water issues in his building. "My manifesto is an engineering report," he wrote.

At one point, he appeared to invoke Luigi Mangione , who shot and killed UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson in 2024. On Oct. 1, he wrote, "After months of 'Luigi' tactics (delay, deny, defend) by the HOA, we were finally able to submit an independent engineering report into the record," and said he would share the engineering report on X "when the time is right." Mangione had written "delay, deny, defend" on the bullets he used in the shooting.

In a social media post from April 28, he wrote: "If you're looking for the building manager, I would check the gym."

Lambert sued the Metropole Condominium Association, listing his grievances and alleging damages of more than $290,000 as of May.

The Metropole Condominium Association and EJF denied causing the damage and said any damage was caused by third parties beyond their control and that Lambert failed to limit his losses.

The Metropole Condominium Association and EJF did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Police said he carried out the shooting inside the Vida Fitness center on the ground floor of the building, which caters to the building's residents.

One woman said she was on a treadmill in the gym when she heard the shots fired. She described having to evacuate past the scene where one victim was killed.

"There was no way of getting out of the gym other than going past that scene." she said.

"It was like chaos. It was horrific, honestly."

A witness who was about 20 feet from the shooting told CBS News that he lived directly below Lambert, and described him as being increasingly upset at HOA meetings. He said Lambert used to invite people into his apartment to show them how bad it was. The witness called the building a "tight-knit community" with 99 units.

The witness said that during the shooting and standoff with police, his girlfriend barricaded herself in the apartment, which is now under an inch of water from the response to a fire at the scene.

Logan Circle is a vibrant neighborhood in Washington, D.C., gentrified in the 2010s, with historic architecture and some of the most popular restaurants and bars in the city.

Lambert was the founder and CEO of MLEM, a healthcare and technology consultancy, according to his Linkedin profile. He obtained his undergraduate and medical degree at Marshall University in West Virginia, and completed his residency at West Virginia University, according to his profile

items.title: Huang's exit rocks Nvidia and creates openings for rivals
items.summary: Huang was a visionary leader with deep relationships in the complex world of tech. Losing him will hurt Nvidia, according to Wall Street analysts.

scraped.title: Jensen Huang's exit rocks Nvidia and creates openings for rivals
scraped.description: Huang was a visionary leader with deep relationships in the complex world of tech. Losing him will hurt Nvidia, according to Wall Street analysts.
scraped.h1: Jensen Huang's exit rocks Nvidia and creates openings for rivals
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

November 12, 2026 / 3:38 PM EST / CBS News

The abrupt resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang raises questions about the strategic direction of the world's most important chipmaker and opens the door to competitors at a pivotal moment for the growing artificial intelligence business, according to technology industry experts.

"He has really created the AI revolution," Yorkville Ives and Co. tech analyst Dan Ives told CBS News. "There is no way to sugarcoat it. It's a gut punch to the industry that had so much confidence in and praise for him."

Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia effective immediately following a scandal involving an alleged spy, the company's board of directors announced Thursday. Nvidia on Thursday appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as its interim CEO, as the company launches a search for a permanent chief executive .

Yet Huang's long-range strategic vision, unique qualities as a leader and deep connections in the tech world will be hard to replace, Ives emphasized. "The biggest fear of any competitors, as well as China, is Jensen," he said. "You take him out, and it levels the playing field for domestic chipmakers and other players globally."

Nvidia controls roughly 90% of the market for graphics processing units, critical components for training and deploying AI models. That dominance will not suddenly evaporate because Huang is no longer at the helm, with the company's product development roadmap already anchored to a new family of chips and strong global demand for its tech, according to Ives.

"They are roughly 2-3 years ahead of the nearest competitor, and the demand trajectory the next few years is not changing because Jensen is gone," he told investors in a research note, describing Nvidia as the "clear leader in GPU chips for the AI revolution."

Cody Acree, an equity research analyst at StoneX, said the business and operational impact of Huang's ouster on Nvidia is likely to be limited over the next year or two. "Everything is already designed, planned, booked, and scheduled for production and delivery well into 2028," he told CBS News.

Yet Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, possessed other abilities that even top execs could find hard to match, according to the company's followers. Tech analysts point to his sense of timing and ability to strike partnerships and other deals, a key skill in building a global corporate powerhouse in the deeply interconnected world of tech.

"Our concern ... is that without Huang, Nvidia loses the creative, relationship-driven dealmaking that has underpinned its market leadership over the last two years," William Blair & Co. tech analyst Sebastien Naji said in a report.

Huang was especially creative in fueling demand for Nvidia's products by financing some of its major customers, including a February deal to invest $30 billion in ChatGPT developer OpenAI, which buys Nvidia GPUs and other hardware.

"He was equally central on the supply side, securing leading allocations of memory, wafers, and optics through prepayments, multiyear purchase agreements, and equity stakes in suppliers," Naji said. "While existing contracts will survive a CEO change, what's at risk is the next round of deals, and with it Nvidia's ability to defend its share into 2027 and beyond."

Over the longer term, Huang's departure could help other AI gear manufacturers, such as AMD and Broadcom, gain ground on Nvidia, according to tech analysts.

"This presents an opportunity for some of Nvidia's competitors to take a bigger share of the market than they were planning to over the next few years," Naji said. "That happens anytime a company is distracted by an investigation, or succession planning, and takes their eye off the ball in terms of a product roadmap in a competitive space."

Edited by Megan Cerullo

scraped.title: Hegseth awards medal to soldier who reprimanded his group at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
scraped.description: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth awarded a medal to the service member who reprimanded his group for making noise at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier​.
scraped.h1: Hegseth awards medal to soldier who reprimanded his group at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

Updated on: November 12, 2026 / 3:02 PM EST / CBS News

Washington — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth awarded a medal on Thursday to the service member who reprimanded his group for making noise at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Veterans Day.

Hegseth posted a series of photos on X with the soldier, Spc. Thomas Iglesias, and other members of the unit who guard the tomb at Arlington National Cemetery around the clock. One of the photos showed Hegseth pinning a medal to Iglesias' chest.

"We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist," Hegseth wrote. "Carry on Patriots."

We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist. Carry on Patriots. pic.twitter.com/Uk6ek6oOso

A Pentagon official said Hegseth "welcomed the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, the Old Guard, to the Pentagon where he proudly awarded Specialist Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026."

Iglesias was guarding the tomb following a Veterans Day event that included Hegseth, President Trump and other administration officials. Footage showed Hegseth, his wife, his chief of staff and other aides posing for photos near the tomb. Someone laughed, and Iglesias shouted: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."

In the aftermath, Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told CBS News: "The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored-and will always honor-the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe. While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."

Soldiers reminding visitors to maintain decorum at the tomb is not uncommon. One member of the regiment that guards the tomb said in an Army interview in 2022 that sentinels react to the crowd two or three times per day.

Charlie D'Agata and Joe Walsh contributed to this report.

scraped.title: Outlook outage: Microsoft reports 'issues' with Teams and email
scraped.description: Microsoft is reporting "issues" with users accessing Outlook and Teams.
scraped.author: ABC News
scraped.h1: Outlook outage: Microsoft reports 'issues' with Teams and email
scraped.body_text:
The company posted about the disruptions on social media.

Microsoft reported issues with users' Exchange Online mailboxes and an issue with Microsoft Teams, according to posts on social media Thursday.

"We're investigating reports of users experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas," the company wrote , after first reporting "users experiencing issues when accessing or using Microsoft Teams functionality in North America."

The company initially said the issues involving Exchange Online mailboxes could be due to infrastructure "experiencing elevated load across multiple regions."

Microsoft later clarified, "We determined the elevated load isn't driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure."

Regarding the issues with Microsoft Teams, the company followed up shortly after first reporting the issue, writing, "Our mitigative actions have successfully restored service health and functionality."

Downdetector , which monitors outages, reported issues with both Microsoft Teams and Outlook, among other products on Thursday.

Regarding the issues affecting Exchange Online mailboxes, the company added, "we've confirmed the issue may affect Microsoft 365 service connectivity for users in any region."

The company continued to provide updates on the potential fix to the mailbox issue on Thursday, and added, "We're aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact. We've paused all deployments, we're moving additional traffic off the affected infrastructure, and we're restarting affected servers to return them to service."

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

items.title: Timeline of the stunning fall of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
items.summary: While the depths of the scandal have yet to be disclosed, here is a timeline indicating who knew what and when about Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

scraped.title: Timeline of the stunning fall of powerful Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
scraped.description: While the depths of the scandal have yet to be disclosed, here is a timeline indicating who knew what and when about Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
scraped.author: ABC News
scraped.h1: Timeline of the stunning fall of powerful Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
scraped.body_text:
Huang resigned after two extramarital affairs surfaced, one with an alleged spy.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's stunning resignation from the tech company he co-founded in 1993 comes amid investigations by federal authorities and his own board of directors into allegations that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Huang, 63, had become a trusted ally of President Donald Trump and an adviser to the president on AI technology, visiting the White House for events more than a half-dozen times between January 2025 and October 2026. This year, he has traveled with Trump on a state visit to China and joined the president during a state visit to Great Britain.

A timeline pieced together by ABC News indicates that Huang and Chinese businesswoman and alleged spy Alice Huang (no relation) have known each other since at least 2024, and that Trump had been briefed twice over the past year on the relationship by intelligence officials and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

June 7, 2024 -- The first known photo of Jensen Huang and Alice Huang emerges of them sitting next to each other at Computex Taipei, the world's largest AI exhibition.

Jan. 31, 2025 -- President Donald Trump meets Jensen Huang for the first time during a meeting at the White House.

May 22, 2025 -- Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are captured on video by Taiwanese news outlet TVBS leaving a restaurant together in Taipei.

Fall of 2025 -- Trump is briefed on U.S. intelligence that Jensen Huang is having an affair with a woman believed to be working for Chinese intelligence, a U.S. official and sources briefed on the matter told ABC News. The president does not take any action at the time, the official and sources said.

Dec. 8, 2025 – Trump publicly announces a major policy change that would allow Nvidia to sell H200 AI chips to China in exchange for the U.S. receiving a 25% cut on the sales.

March 25, 2026 -- Trump appoints Jensen Huang as one of 13 members of the newly established President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.

April 28, 2026 -- Jensen Huang and his wife of more than 40 years, Lori, are guests at the state visit and state dinner honoring Britain's King Charles.

Spring 2026 -- A classified memo is drafted that warns top administration officials that Jensen Huang has a close relationship with a woman that U.S. intelligence officials believe to be a Chinese spy, sources familiar with the matter told ABC News, confirming reporting in The New York Times.

May 12, 2026 -- Secretary of State Marco Rubio shares intelligence with President Trump on Air Force One showing Jensen Huang is in a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy, a U.S. official and two sources familiar with the matter have told ABC News. This is the second known time that Trump had been warned about the suspected espionage plot, sources with knowledge of the situation tell ABC News.

Trump's briefing from Rubio, first reported in The New York Times, came shortly before Huang joined the president on a state visit to China, according to the U.S. official and sources. Huang was initially not listed among the CEOs joining Trump's China trip, but he joined the president's entourage in Alaska after news reports noted his absence. Trump later posted on his Truth Social platform that Huang was on Air Force One with him.

Sept. 24, 2026 -- Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori, attend a state dinner at the White House hosted by Trump during Chinese Leader Xi Jinping's state visit to the United States.

Oct. 8, 2026 -- Huang attends the "Golden Age of American Innovation" summit at U.S. Institute of Peace in Washington, D.C., where Trump honors him with a National Medal for Science and Technology and Innovation.

Oct. 29, 2026 -- The New York Times reports that Huang and Alice Huang, an executive at the Singaporean tech company Megaspeed, had a "close relationship."

Oct. 31, 2026 -- The Wall Street Journal reports that intelligence officials in the U.S., Singapore and Taiwan had reason to believe that Alice Huang might be a Chinese spy.

Nov. 8, 2026 -- Jensen Huang releases a memo to colleagues acknowledging "I was unfaithful to my wife." He goes on to say, "I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it." He also apologizes to his colleagues, the Nvidia board, partners and shareholders, saying, "My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility."

Nvidia's board of directors announces it is launching an independent investigation into allegations that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort." The board says that while it "has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information."

Nov. 9, 2026 -- Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun tells reporters, "The claim regarding a so-called Chinese spy is completely groundless and pure slander."

That same day, President Trump tells reporters he has spoken to Jensen Huang on the phone. "He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy," Trump says at a press briefing.

Nov. 10, 2026 -- The Republican chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Rep. Brian Mast, tells ABC News he's prepared to subpoena Jensen Huang if he does not respond to a request from several House Republicans for a closed-door briefing on Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

Nov. 11, 2026 -- The New York Times reports that Huang allegedly had a second extramarital relationship with an Nvidia executive who reports to him. The Wall Street Journal reports that Nvidia's Board of Directors is reportedly planning to oust Jensen Huang as the company's CEO.

Nov. 12, 2026 -- Nvidia announces Jensen Huang has resigned as the company's CEO and that Colette Kress, executive vice president and CFO of Nvidia, has been appointed the company's interim CEO as the board initiates a search for a permanent replacement for Huang.

24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

Qatar Under-17 World Cup is on despite US pull out

The Under-17 World Cup in Qatar will kick off as scheduled next week despite the United States’ decision to withdraw its team from the tournament. US Soccer pulled out citing safety concerns, but FIFA boss Gianni Infantino says teams and fans will be safe in the host country.

items.title: Regional security dominates European talks in Dublin amid hybrid attacks
items.summary: European nations discuss security collaboration and an envoy for Ukraine peace talks during the summit in Ireland.

scraped.title: Regional security dominates European talks in Dublin amid hybrid attacks
scraped.description: European nations discuss security collaboration and an envoy for Ukraine peace talks during the summit in Ireland.
scraped.author: Al Jazeera Staff
scraped.h1: Regional security dominates European talks in Dublin amid hybrid attacks
scraped.body_text:
European nations discuss security collaboration and an envoy for Ukraine peace talks during the summit in Ireland.

Save

Share

Leaders from more than 40 European countries have gathered in Dublin for a summit dominated by the growing number of hybrid attacks across the continent.

The biannual European Political Community (EPC), a regional group established in 2022 after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine , brought together heads of state and government officials on Thursday to discuss the region’s fragile security, amid a new United States-backed effort to revive talks between Russia and Ukraine to end the war.

The gathering comes after a series of hoaxes and cyberattacks that have recently targeted supermarkets, blood banks, passenger airlines, schools and media outlets in Europe.

Earlier on Thursday, more than 3,700 Italian schools received hoax bomb warnings , a day after 6,300 schools were affected by a similar widespread alert .

The Republic of Ireland’s Prime Minister Micheal Martin, known as the taoiseach, said those responsible for the attacks seek to “create confusion, sow division and weaken public confidence in our democratic systems”.

“We will not allow them to succeed. We will continue to use forums like this to share our experiences, learn from one another and to work together to protect our democracies,” he told reporters.

European officials have accused Russia of being behind the disruptive attacks on key infrastructure that fall below the threshold of war. Russia has denied allegations of involvement in the recent threats.

A major topic of conversation was Europe’s quest for an envoy to represent it in peace talks after calls from Washington and Kyiv. It remains unclear who will be named as European representative.

Earlier on Thursday, US envoy Steve Witkoff said Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed to let European representatives join the next round of Ukraine discussions following a meeting in Moscow .

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham pledged his “complete support” to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and said he would push for European representation in the US-brokered talks.

Burnham co-chaired a group meeting on Ukraine with Zelenskyy at the summit.

The EPC comes at a moment of growing political tensions in Europe, and a week after the US midterm elections that saw extensive losses for US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party.

While populist leaders have recently been ousted in Serbia and in Hungary , the far right is still on the rise in Europe and has made recent gains in regional elections in Germany. Voters will cast their ballots in the months ahead in the continent’s biggest countries, including Spain, France, Italy and Poland.

Meanwhile, two people were arrested during a protest organised by “Mothers Against Genocide” over Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in Dublin’s city centre, while the EPC was ongoing.

Those taking part in demonstrations carried Palestine flags and Irish tricolours and banners, including one calling for a boycott of Israel.
