items.title: Pete Hegseth honors soldier who scolded him at Arlington cemetery
items.summary: The soldier had reprimanded the US Defense Secretary and his group after they were heard talking and laughing at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. The site is one of the most solemn military memorials in the US.

scraped.title: US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth honors soldier who scolded him at Arlington cemetery in viral clip
scraped.description: The soldier had reprimanded the US Defense Secretary and his group after they were heard talking and laughing at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. The site is one of the most solemn military memorials in the US.
scraped.h1: Pete Hegseth honors soldier who scolded him at Arlington cemetery
scraped.body_text:
The soldier had reprimanded the US Defense Secretary and his group after they were heard talking and laughing at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. The site is one of the most solemn military memorials in the US.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has awarded a soldier who reprimanded him and his entourage for laughing at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Wednesday.

Hegseth posted photos on his X account on Thursday that show him giving the Joint Service Commendation Medal to Specialist Thomas Iglesias "for the execution of his duties."

"We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist," Hegseth said alongside the photos.

The Joint Service Commendation Medal is seen as one of the US military's top awards and is not usually given to junior enlisted service members.

In footage that was widely shared on social media, Iglesias was seen forcefully reprimanding Hegseth and a group that included his wife and some of his staffers, who were heard talking and laughing while taking photos on the steps in front of the tomb.

Iglesias shouted: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times!"

Soon after the video emerged, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell praised Iglesias for "correctly and respectfully" reminding Hegseth and his party to "maintain decorum."

The public reprimand comes the same week that the under-fire defense secretary survived an impeachment attempt over his handling of the war with Iran.

US President Donald Trump pointed to the war as a major factor behind his Republican Party's stunning defeats in midterm elections last week.

In his first press conference in months on Tuesday, Hegseth slammed the impeachment attempt as a "farce, a stunt" and "sabotage."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The tomb at Arlington National Cemetery outside Washington D.C. is considered of the most solemn military monuments in the US.

It is the burial site of US military personnel killed during World War I, World War II and the Korean War. It also features an empty site to honor missing soldiers from the Vietnam War.

Since 1948, the tomb has been guarded around the clock by a soldier from the US Army's 3rd Infantry Regiment, which is known as "The Old Guard," according to the cemetery's website.

items.title: Nigeria: Axe-wielding men attack opposition campaign rally in Lagos
items.summary: A group of men armed with axes, clubs and machetes have reportedly attacked an opposition rally in the run-up to presidential elections. Journalists were also attacked as victims pointed fingers at the ruling APC party.

scraped.title: Nigeria: Axe-wielding men attack opposition candidate Peter Obi presidential campaign in Lagos
scraped.description: A group of men armed with axes, clubs and machetes have reportedly attacked an opposition rally in the run-up to presidential elections. Journalists were also attacked as victims pointed fingers at the ruling APC party.
scraped.h1: Nigeria: Axe-wielding men attack opposition campaign rally in Lagos
scraped.body_text:
A group of men armed with axes, clubs and machetes have reportedly attacked an opposition rally in the run-up to presidential elections. Journalists were also attacked as victims pointed fingers at the ruling APC party.

A group of armed men rushed a campaign event in Nigeria on Thursday, attacking journalists and supporters of opposition candidate Peter Obi at a political rally two months before the country's January 16, 2027, presidential election .

Videos uploaded to social media captured the mid-morning incident, showing men armed with axes, clubs and machetes barging into an event center in Lagos, where they attacked supporters of Nigerian Democratic Congress (NDC) candidate Obi.

Supporters, who vowed they would not be intimidated, blamed the attack on the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC). APC spokesman Felix Morka rejected the claim, citing a lack of evidence.

The NDC has also accused the APC of being behind the forced cancellation of several of its campaign events, claiming the government of President Bola Tinubu is pressuring venue owners to turn them away.

Here, too, the government has denied the accusations.

Violence is a regular feature of Nigeria's elections and is often carried out by individuals colloquially referred to as "thugs."

Eyewitnesses on Thursday said the attackers, "came into the hall, [and] broke all the entrance doors and the glass walls."

"The NDC guys repelled them, chased them out of the hall into the road," one eyewitness added.

After that, the two groups engaged in pitched street battles for over an hour before police arrived on the scene and began firing tear gas to disperse them.

Security officials on the scene said they had not been on site to protect participants when the violence broke out because they had not been notified of the event.

A local journalist attacked in the melee described being hit with an axe as well as being punched and kicked before thugs made off with all of his equipment.

"I tried to resist, so they started attacking me" said Sam Adebanjo of the online out TheCable .

"I eventually yielded and surrendered the devices when one of them kept shouting, 'Leave the camera — do you want them to kill you?'"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Oil-rich Nigeria, Africa's most populous country, ranked 112 out of 180 countries in the Reporters Without Borders 2026 World Press Freedom Index.

January's election will pit President Bola Tinubu, who is seeking his second term in office: against Obi, who placed third in the country's 2023 election ; and Atiku Abubakar, who was runner-up in 2023.

Abubakar is facing legal challenges to his candidacy and accuses Tinubu's government of trying to push him out of the way with lawfare, a charge the APC also denies.

items.title: Czechia braces for massive protest as anger over government's public media reform plans boils
items.summary: A fast-tracked bill on public media funding reform has sparked strikes, rallies and fears for the independence of public broadcasting in Czechia. A massive protest is due to take place in Prague on November 15.

scraped.title: Czechia braces for massive protest as anger over government's public media reform plans boils
scraped.description: A fast-tracked bill on public media funding reform has sparked strikes, rallies and fears for the independence of public broadcasting in Czechia. A massive protest is due to take place in Prague on November 15.
scraped.h1: Czechia braces for massive protest against public media reform plans
scraped.body_text:
A fast-tracked bill on public media funding reform has sparked strikes, rallies and fears for the independence of public broadcasting in Czechia. A massive protest is due to take place in Prague on November 15.

Hundreds of thousands of people are expected to rally in Prague this weekend to protest the Czech government's bid to ram a bill to reform public media funding through parliament in a surprise overnight session late last month.

The populist coalition of Prime Minister Andrej Babis fast-tracked the first of three readings of the legislation, which culminated in a vote of approval at 04:36 a.m. on October 24.

The bill has already provoked numerous demonstrations and strikes across the country, but Sunday's gathering in the capital's Letna Park is likely to be by far the largest to date.

Under the government's proposal, the license fee model that currently funds Czech Television (CT) and Czech Radio (CRo) would be scrapped, and the broadcasters would be funded directly from the state budget.

The three parties in the coalition — Babis's centrist ANO, the far-right SPD, and radical conservative Motorists, whose voter bases tend to be less affluent — insist that the license fee is an unfair tax.

The parties argue that the new arrangement, which would see funding for CT and CRo cut by around 15% in the first year, would make the two more efficient. They also point out that several other European Union states have made similar changes.

Critics have angrily dismissed these justifications.

Opposition parties, civil society organizations and international watchdogs accuse the government of seeking to undermine the independence of the broadcasters, whose critical reporting has long irked ANO and the SPD in particular.

Analysts point out that while models in other EU states include guarantees of long-term financial stability and editorial independence, the Czech government proposal offers neither.

CT and CRo have warned that the reduced budget included in the bill will mean programming- and staff cuts .

When the first publication of the proposed bill was met with protests over the summer, Vaclav Stetka of the European New School of Digital Studies told DW that such "dramatic budget cuts represent an act of cultural vandalism."

There has also been condemnation of the restriction of the parliamentary debate amid the fast-tracking of the bill.

"The confrontational approach, the attempts to limit parliamentary debate and the government's rhetoric towards journalists and critics have all contributed to the public backlash," Otto Eibl, political scientist at Masaryk University in Czechia 's second city Brno, told DW.

The backlash was immediate. Crowds picketed parliament through the night as the government pushed through the first reading of the bill.

Since then, multiple rallies have taken place in cities and towns across the country. Many of these protests were led by students and joined by unions, Churches and representatives of educational and cultural institutions.

CT and CRo staff called a strike in early November, disrupting the country's TV and radio schedules.

Sunday's protest is set to up the ante.

It will take place two days before the anniversary of the start of the Velvet Revolution, which ultimately brought down communism in what was then Czechoslovakia in 1989.

The civil society group Million Moments for Democracy, which is organizing Sunday's rally, brought an estimated 300,000 onto the streets to protest during Babis's first term as prime minister in 2019 and more than 200,000 earlier this year .

The government's sudden bid to push through the proposal reflects impatience to deliver on a core pledge made ahead of the October 2025 election, as well as the longstanding ambition of the prime minister, who was stymied in his attempt to engineer control of CT's governing council during his first term in power in 2017–21.

Vaclav Stetka notes that repeated assaults on public media by Czech governments past and present reflect a particular political culture across Europe's post-communist states.

"The political elite has never accepted the independence of public media," he asserted.

In Czechia, however, the public broadcasters have earned special status as cornerstones of democracy .

That standing was forged in what became known as the "Czech TV crisis" of 2000–01, when an occupation of CT's studios by staff and mass protests forced the government of the day to back down on a bid to wrest control.

"The fight over the public service media has become a symbol of the defense of liberal democratic values and institutions," Eibl said.

As anger has swelled, the government has sought to calm the situation. Babis has said that a new proposal, which would see public media funding moved off budget and editorial independence guaranteed, would be drawn up and made available for a full and open debate.

However, critics remain unimpressed, noting a lack of any detail and the fact that other members of the government appear determined to remain on course.

Million Moments for Democracy has insisted the pressure must continue.

"Words are worth nothing," the group said. "While people stand up for independent media, the government continues to act as if it owns the country."

With little sign that the opposition will dissipate, the government faces a choice.

It has the parliamentary majority it needs to push the bill through and defeat any likely vetoes from the upper house Senate and President Petr Pavel .

But this could come at a cost.

Polls suggest political support for the government has been weakened and could diminish further if the protests expand to include growing frustrations over the cost of living and housing, as happened recently with student-led protests in France and other European countries .

"The real risk for the government is that the media issue becomes a lightning rod for broader dissatisfaction," said Martin Vokalek of the Prague-based EUROPEUM Institute for European Policy.

Babis is aware of the danger.

The PM announced that he will not attend the Velvet Revolution anniversary celebrations on November 17, which are hugely symbolic, in the hope that his absence might "calm the tense situation."

However, there's little concern that the Czech protests could descend into violence.

Analysts note that the anger in Czechia remains tightly focused on the public media proposal and continues to be expressed in a similar way to the seismic events of the country's modern history.

"I would not expect French-style scenes," Vokalek told DW, noting that the same "large, peaceful and civic Czech protest culture," which gave the Velvet Revolution and 1993's Velvet Divorce from Slovakia their name, is still strong.
scraped.lead_paragraph: A fast-tracked bill on public media funding reform has sparked strikes, rallies and fears for the independence of public broadcasting in Czechia. A massive protest is due to take place in Prague on November 15.

items.title: U.S. army guard receives medal from Hegseth after scolding him at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
items.summary: U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth has given a top award to the service member who scolded him and his staff at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier following a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery.

scraped.title: U.S. army guard receives medal from Hegseth after scolding him at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier | CBC News
scraped.description: U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth has given a top award to the service member who scolded him and his staff at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier following a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery.
scraped.h1: U.S. army guard receives medal from Hegseth after scolding him at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
scraped.body_text:
Hegseth delegation appears to be rebuked at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier

U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth has given a top award to the service member who scolded him and his staff at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier following a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery.

Hegseth welcomed to the Pentagon the army unit that guards the tomb and awarded Specialist Thomas Iglesias with the Joint Service Commendation Medal "for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Nov. 11, 2026," the Pentagon said.

On social media, Hegseth posted photos Thursday that show him pinning the award and shaking hands with a soldier. His post says: "We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist."

We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist. Carry on Patriots. https://t.co/Uk6ek6oOso

Iglesias reprimanded Hegseth and a group of his staffers when a loud laugh was heard after they took photos at the site following a ceremony that included U.S. President Donald Trump and Vice- President JD Vance.

Video showed Hegseth taking photos on the empty steps in front of the tomb on Wednesday with his wife, Jennifer, chief of staff Ricky Buria, deputy chief of staff Patrick Weaver and senior adviser Tami Radabaugh.

Joining lawsuit, Kennedy family members say Trump's arch would be 'denigration' of JFK, RFK plots at Arlington

The tomb is considered to be one of the most solemn and revered war memorials in the U.S., being the final resting place of unidentified soldiers from the First World War, the Second World War and the Korean War. It has been guarded around the clock regardless of weather conditions by a soldier from the Army's 3rd Infantry Regiment, also known as "The Old Guard," since 1948.

The Joint Service Commendation Medal is considered to be one of the higher awards in the military and is not typically issued to junior enlisted service members.

Republicans block impeachment push against Hegseth

Sean Parnell, the Pentagon's top spokesperson, said soon after video of the reprimand emerged that the soldier "correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."

The scolding drew attention once more to the embattled war secretary, who had survived an attempt to open impeachment proceedings . The effort was led by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie and backed by Democrats, though 11 missed the vote as other Republicans rejected the effort.

While Hegseth's critics were not successful in Tuesday's vote, Republicans may have only delayed a bid to impeach him. With Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate in January, those efforts are likely to be renewed.

Hegseth rebuked the move Tuesday in his first news conference in months, arguing that he had committed none of the high crimes required in the U.S. Constitution for his removal and framing the effort as an indictment against the nation's service members and their successes.

"This is not patriotism," Hegseth argued. "This is sabotage."

items.title: Israeli strike on a Gaza hospital kills 6 people, including surgeon, health authorities say
items.summary: An Israeli airstrike on southern Gaza's main hospital overnight killed at least six Palestinians, including a surgeon and a teenage boy, medics said, the latest Israeli attack to undermine a year-old ceasefire in the war-shattered territory.

scraped.title: Israeli strike on a Gaza hospital kills 6 people, including surgeon, health authorities say | CBC News
scraped.description: An Israeli airstrike on southern Gaza's main hospital overnight killed at least six Palestinians, including a surgeon and a teenage boy, medics said, the latest Israeli attack to undermine a year-old ceasefire in the war-shattered territory.
scraped.h1: Israeli strike on a Gaza hospital kills 6 people, including surgeon, health authorities say
scraped.body_text:
Israeli airstrike on Gaza hospital kills 6, officials say

An Israeli airstrike on southern Gaza's main hospital overnight killed at least six Palestinians, including a surgeon and a teenage boy, medics said, the latest Israeli attack to undermine a year-old ceasefire in the war-shattered territory.

The strike hit a building containing surgery wards at Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis. Israel's military said it targeted a senior Hamas commander and accused the militants of using the hospital complex to plan attacks, which the group denied.

Medics and witnesses said two missiles crashed through the roof of the five-storey building, causing extensive damage. The surgery department, which serves half of Gaza's two million people, was knocked out of service. At least 20 others were wounded.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, which oversees the ceasefire agreement and a broader peace plan, called on both Israel and Hamas to honour the deal, in a rare response to an individual attack.

Ayman Abu Obeid, a doctor who was injured in the attack, said he was on an overnight shift in the hospital when an explosion ripped through the room where he and others were sleeping.

"All of a sudden, the world turned upside down. It went dark all at once," he said from a hospital bed. Near him, piles of mangled furniture and medical equipment could be seen covered in dust from blown-out concrete. Torn wires hung down from the ceiling.

Among those killed was Rezik Abushira, a surgeon who was featured in a 2026 documentary, American Doctor , working alongside three visiting U.S. doctors who help provide medical care for Palestinians in Gaza. The dead also included a 13-year-old boy, according to Gaza's Education Ministry.

Commenting on the vehicle strike, the Israeli military said it hit a Hamas militant, without giving further details. It did not comment on the two other incidents.

Nasser Medical Complex director Dr. Ahmed Al-Farra said that the strike occurred without any prior warning or evacuation notice. The Israeli military claimed it had held "warning conversations" with Gaza health officials before Thursday's strike regarding militant use of hospitals. It said it made clear that "if the activity was not halted, it would act to remove the threats posed by it."

"What sin did the hospital that is treating children, the elderly and women commit to get targeted?" Khalil Shaheen told CBC News outside of Nasser Hospital.

"All the countries in the world are watching us. This is wrong. The hospital is full of sick people," Maryam Abu Hatab told CBC News on Thursday. "We're afraid to even come to the hospital now."

A projectile lies next to remains from another projectile inside Nasser Hospital following an Israeli airstrike in Khan Younis, in the southern Gaza Strip on Thursday. (Ramadan Abed/Reuters)

Since the start of the Gaza war, Israel's military has struck the Nasser Hospital complex at least seven times, Al-Farra and other hospital officials say.

"This will not stop. They will continue targeting Nasser Medical Complex," Al-Farra said at a news conference Thursday, adding that Gaza's already devastated health-care system is now in a much more dire situation as a result of the attack.

Al-Farra said only one of two projectiles targeting the hospital had detonated, adding that if the second one had also gone off, hospital officials would be dealing with a "massacre."

Meanwhile, four more Palestinians were killed later on Thursday in separate incidents. Two were killed and several were wounded in an Israeli airstrike on a car in Gaza City, and one other person was killed by Israeli gunfire in central Gaza's Bureij refugee camp, medics said. A fourth person was killed in an airstrike near a cemetery in Jabalia, north of the enclave, taking Thursday's death toll to at least 10.

Hospitals are protected under international humanitarian law and attacking them is a war crime.

Medical facilities can lose that protected status if they are used for military purposes "to commit acts harmful to the enemy." But the Geneva Conventions, passed in 1949, say there must be a warning with a reasonable period of time before any attack, and that the attack must be proportional to the military threat and take care to avoid civilian casualties.

Medical organizations and rights groups also have criticized Israel's restrictions on medical aid and equipment entering Gaza as a violation of international law. The Israeli military says it allows aid to enter Gaza but bars some "dual use" items it asserts could be used for military purposes.

"Gaza's health facilities are lifelines for its people. They must be protected. They must never be militarized or attacked," said World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus in a statement.

Doctors from Nasser Hospital attend the funeral of Dr. Rezik Abushira, who was killed in an Israeli strike at Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, according to the Gaza health ministry, during his funeral in Khan Younis, southern Gaza strip, November 12, 2026. REUTERS/Ramadan Abed (Ramadan Abed/Reuters)

Francesca Albanese, the UN special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territories, says Israel's attack on Nasser hospital is going to be a "blow," to Gaza's health infrastructure.

"Nasser hospital is one of the last functioning parts … of the devastated health system in Gaza," Albanese told CBC News from Tunis on Thursday.

"We have proof for three years that Israel has intentionally, systematically — and in a widespread fashion destroyed the health infrastructure so i wouldn't assume that this is because Hamas is there."

Camps destroyed in 2 Israeli military strikes on Gaza City

In a statement, Israel's military said it targeted a person named Muhammad Abu Ismail, describing him as "the commander of Hamas' Khan Younis Brigade." The military said he and other militants "were hiding inside the Nasser Hospital."

The military accused the militants of "turning the Nasser Hospital compound into a headquarters and operating from there."

Hamas rejected the military's claim that it had used the hospital as a base for operations. It did not immediately provide comment on whether a leader from the group had been targeted, injured or killed in the strike.

Woman, 3 children killed in Gaza after sand embankment collapses onto tents

In August 2025, the hospital was hit by a double-tap Israeli attack that killed at least 20 people, including journalists and health workers.

An October 2025 ceasefire halted major fighting but has failed to halt Israeli attacks or secure Hamas's disarmament. At least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire went into effect, according to Gaza's Health Ministry. The Israeli military says five Israeli soldiers have been killed during the same period.

With files from CBC's Mohamed El Saife, Saša Petricic, Sara Jabakhanji and The Associated Press

scraped.description: Travel from Canada to the U.S. dropped amid President Donald Trump's threats and trade war. While many Canadians view the Democratic Party's midterm election victory as an 'encouraging' sign, they say it's too soon to visit the U.S. again amid continued distrust.
scraped.h1: Will U.S. travel pick up after midterm 'blue wave'? Not so fast, say these Canadians
scraped.body_text:
John May had low expectations ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

But he was glad to see the Democratic Party take control of both chambers of Congress in a Nov. 3 vote that many observers have described as a resounding rebuke of U.S. President Donald Trump .

"It's encouraging, isn't it? To see that there's finally some common sense coming around down there," said the 73-year-old from Manotick, Ont., an Ottawa suburb.

How will Republicans and Democrats move forward after midterms?

Americans in Canada hope midterm results will help mend ties between both countries

May, who stopped travelling to the United States last year amid Trump's repeated threats against Canada, said he and his wife Patti aren't ready to go south of the border again just yet though.

The couple had spent winters in Florida for more than a decade before May said the atmosphere turned "toxic" as Trump mocked Canadian leaders and pushed to turn Canada into the "51st state."

"We'd like to, but we're not feeling like we want to go back yet," May told CBC News.

"I think we've got to wait until they've got a different president down there and a whole different attitude," he said. "Things haven't changed enough. We'll need a couple more years, I think."

John and Patti May pose for a photo in Key West, Fla., in February 2024. (Submitted by John May)

Many Canadians, including those with relatives or business interests south of the border, have continued to travel to the U.S. amid Trump's threats and the trade war with Canada.

But data shows travel to the U.S. has dropped alongside the strained relationship.

According to Statistics Canada , return border crossings from the U.S. fell by about 25 per cent in 2025 compared with the previous year.

There has been a slight increase in 2026: A total of 1.9 million return trips by car and air from the U.S. were reported in October, marking the seventh consecutive month of year-over-year growth and a three per cent increase from October 2025, Statistics Canada reported .

But when compared with October 2024, return trips by car were down 29 per cent while those by air were down 19.6 per cent.

Elbows up or down? Windsorites are mixed on returning to the U.S. post-midterms

It's too soon to say whether the midterms will lead to a major increase in Canadian travel south.

McKenzie McMillan, a travel consultant and co-owner of The Travel Group in Vancouver, said that, anecdotally, there may be some "softening" around U.S. travel.

"But it hasn't really translated at this point into new bookings, or a real change in the overall sentiment to avoid the United States," McMillan said. "We are still hearing overall that travellers are looking to alternative destinations for their winter travel and beyond."

Spokespersons for Air Canada and Porter Airlines also told CBC this week that it was too early to say whether the midterms have had an effect on travel. Air Transat said it did not have sufficient data to identify a trend.

What the U.S. midterm results could mean for border cities

But the midterms may help ease the negative feelings that some Canadians have had.

Marja Vermeer, a 67-year-old from Strathroy, Ont., said the vote results, coupled with messages over the past two years from Americans rejecting the Trump administration's attacks against Canada, make her more open to visiting the U.S.

"Especially to the states where they voted Democrat, I think they're ... a bit more comfortable and a bit more welcoming," she said.

Jill Ellis-Worthington, 65, of London, Ont., also said the midterms made a recent trip to the U.S. more palatable.

Ellis-Worthington — who is originally from the U.S. but has been living in Canada since age 25 — said she went to her home country this month to deal with issues at a Texas property she owns. It was her first visit since 2024, and one she had put off for as long as possible.

Windsor residents not ready to return to U.S. despite Democratic midterm wins

How the Democrats' midterm wave shows a path back to the presidency

"There's just so much chaos and so much denial of everything that is America going on now with the government, so I just didn't want to support that in any way," she told CBC.

"I think there are a lot of people who feel great relief [after the midterms] and feel that there might be some light on the horizon."

Ellis-Worthington said Americans had been "nothing but friendly, gracious [and] hospitable" during her trip. But she acknowledged that some Canadians likely won't be going back soon, despite last week's vote. "And some won't ever go back, I don’t think."

The Peace Bridge U.S.-Canada border crossing is seen on March 20 in Buffalo, N.Y. (Yuki Iwamura/The Associated Press)

Indeed, the new Congress doesn't take office until January, and many observers say the Trump administration's policies — including an immigration crackdown that has led to the detention of several Canadian citizens in recent months — continue to fuel distrust.

Mary Thurber, who lives in Lake Country in B.C.'s Okanagan Valley, said she has avoided going to the U.S. for several reasons.

"It's a combination of anger at their policies and disgust with some of the treatment of their own citizens, and frankly, a little bit of fear," said Thurber, 70. "And do I want to support the economy of ... an administration that is actively attacking my country?"

But she said visiting the U.S. is now "an active discussion" in her home after the midterms.

"My husband sometimes says, 'I know! Let's only go to the blue states,'" she said with a laugh. "And I'm like, 'Yeah but that doesn't quite deal with the fact that their president is still actively attacking us.'"

Thurber said she doesn't know when she might feel comfortable going back, adding she expects the Trump administration's policies to have a lasting impact. "That's a hard one," she said.

Senior writer

Jillian Kestler-D'Amours is a senior writer at CBC based in Montreal. You can reach her at jillian.kestler-d.amours@cbc.ca.

scraped.h1: Labor puts permanent freeze on emergency services tax for farmers
scraped.body_text:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

ABC Rural

Topic: State and Territory Elections

CFA volunteers and farmers made their feelings known during numerous protests. ( ABC News: Joseph Dunstan )

Victorian Labor has promised to permanently freeze the emergency services tax rate imposed on farmland.

The Emergency Services and Volunteers Fund has been wildly unpopular with farmers, who had been facing large rate hikes.

The Coalition and One Nation have committed to scrap the fund altogether.

Victorian Labor will permanently freeze the contentious Emergency Services and Volunteers Fund (ESVF) levy charged on farmland if it wins re-election this month.

The new tax to fund fire and emergency services prompted a backlash from farmers and Country Fire Authority volunteers who labelled it unfair and unaffordable, with some facing rate increases of tens of thousands of dollars.

Just before the ESVF came into effect in July last year, the government announced a temporary backdown , capping the rate charged on farmland at 28.7 per cent.

It later extended the freeze for two years.

The Coalition and One Nation have already promised to scrap the ESVF.

Farmers who volunteer with the CFA threatened in May 2025 to resign in protest over the ESVF. ( ABC Rural: Warwick Long )

Agriculture Minister Michaela Settle told the Victorian Country Hour on Thursday the freeze would stay.

"It’s 28.7 per cent and staying there."

Ms Settle said the cap maintained the rate charged under the old Fire Services levy.

"When the Coalition talk about axing the tax, they're talking about axing the CFA rebate, they're talking about axing funding for the SES," she said.

Michaela Settle says Labor will freeze the charge on farmland. ( ABC Rural: Jane McNaughton. )

Victorian Farmers Federation president Ryan Milgate welcomed Labor's promised rate freeze.

"This is the first time we've heard any sort of announcement or guarantee about this. I was pleasantly surprised" he said.

"It's a major change of what we've been hearing in the past and a significant relief to all Victorian farmers."

Mr Milgate said the ESVF was calculated on the capital increased value of farmland.

"There's still devil in the detail in making sure that we're not paying for things that we shouldn't be."

"We also want to ensure that our emergency services, primarily the CFA, is adequately funded and we have the resourcing that we need."

Ryan Milgate has welcomed Labor's decision, but he does not think it will sway votes. ( ABC Rural: Annie Brown )

Although Mr Milgate welcomed Labor's commitment, he said it was unlikely to sway many regional Victorian votes in the coming state election.

"In May last year we had four or 5,000 people in front of Parliament House exercising their displeasure that the Labor government was going to raise this emergency services levy."

"But the reality is this is a big policy shift from what we've seen and I'm kind of surprised Labor haven't been leveraging a bit more off this, to be honest."

Emma Kealy says Labor's emergency services tax is not fair. ( Supplied: Emma Kealy )

If elected, the Coalition plans to dump the ESVF in its first 100 days of government, restoring the former Fire Services Property Levy model.

Opposition Agriculture Spokesperson Emma Kealy said Labor’s "unfair tax" needed to go.

Mr Kealy criticised Labor's decision to consider the rate hike on farmers in the first place.

"It was so cruel for that to be rolled out on farmers on the eve of the horrible drought that many areas were experiencing," she said.

"This is why Labor is in trouble in regional areas."

items.title: Victorian woman aims to grow 300,000 snails for restaurants
items.summary: French expat Coralie Schaff aims to house 300,000 snails at her Otways property to supply restaurants. Coralie Schaff grew up in France and now has a snail farm in the Otways in south-west Victoria.

scraped.title: Victorian woman aims to grow 300,000 snails for restaurants
scraped.description: French expat Coralie Schaff aims to house 300,000 snails at her Otways property to supply restaurants.
scraped.author: https://www.abc.net.au/news/tamsyn-buckle/106432138
scraped.h1: French expat aims to farm 300,000 snails in Victoria's Otways
scraped.body_text:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

By Tamsyn Buckle

ABC South West Vic

Topic: Agriculture

Coralie Schaff grew up in France and now has a snail farm in the Otways in south-west Victoria. ( ABC South West Victoria: Tamsyn Buckle )

French expat Coralie Schaff is heading down the slow and steady trail on her way to becoming a snail farmer in south-west Victoria.

Ms Schaff aims to grow her commercial farm to 300,000 snails to supply restaurants.

A so-called "snail consultant" says there is a niche but potentially successful market for snails in Australia.

Growing up in France, Coralie Schaff often went snail hunting with her father and siblings.

She now does the same thing with her six-year-old son in Victoria's Otway Ranges.

But instead of covering the snails they find in garlic butter, she adds them into a custom-made pen that 3,000 other snails already call home.

"I want to grow the pens to be able to, at capacity, have close to 300,000 snails," Ms Schaff said.

She has set out to start a commercial snail farm, which, according to her research, will be the only one of its kind in Australia.

"As of today, all of the snails eaten in Australia are imported, so there is a market that we can fill," Ms Schaff said.

Coralie Schaff’s neighbours collect snails from their garden and offer them to her. ( ABC South West Victoria: Tamsyn Buckle )

The idea came about after she and her husband purchased 21 hectares of land in the green hills of Beech Forest.

Looking for a unique way to utilise the property, she went to France in April last year to visit some snail farms and was convinced it was a viable option.

"I really enjoyed it and so I came back and I was like, 'This is what I want to do,'" she said.

Delayed by an unseasonably cold summer and a black slug invasion, her snails started breeding early this year.

Ms Schaff plans to eventually sell to local restaurants, go to French festivals in Geelong, and create a farmgate experience where visitors can stop by and enjoy a snail or two.

But the first step is building up her snail numbers before she can start selling them.

Going between her home in Geelong and her new endeavour, she spends her time at the farm collecting buckets of garden snails from neighbours, perfecting her feeding methods and ensuring birds do not get into her carefully constructed pen.

Mesh covers the snail pens on Coralie Schaff's farm to protect the snails from birds. ( ABC South West Victoria: Tamsyn Buckle )

Snails prefer moderate temperatures and lots of rainfall, making the Otways an ideal location.

"It's very similar to the climate in France where a lot of the snail farms are," she said.

Ms Schaff is not the first person to notice how well-suited the area is to the niche type of agriculture.

A road-side sign would welcome visitors to Simpson Snails. ( Supplied: The Bawden Crew )

Helene Hawes started a snail farm with her husband in Simpson in 2014, about an hour's drive from Ms Schaff's farm.

"Simpson is slap bang in the middle of dairy country, so it's lovely rolling green hills and good rainfall," Ms Hawes said.

The couple moved from Queensland to start Simpson Snails, and before long were selling snails to restaurants and welcoming tourist buses to their farm.

But keeping up with demand from restaurants in Melbourne ordering 1,500 snails a week became more than they bargained for.

"I said to my husband, 'Look, we're going to have to employ people. I'm going to have to be sitting behind a computer,'" she said.

Helene Hawes closed Simpson Snails in 2017 to relocate back to Queensland. ( Supplied: Helene Hawes )

"That's not what we did this for."

The pair sold the farm and relocated back to Queensland nine years ago.

Victoria Howe ran into a similar issue after starting a snail farm in Yanmah in southern Western Australia with her husband in 2021.

Victoria Howe has become a self-proclaimed "snail consultant" following her own experiences. ( Supplied: Victoria Howe )

"We just grew too big too quickly and then we weren't able to supply the demand," Ms Howe said.

They supplied snails to nearby restaurants and installed a large greenhouse to boost breeding, but after four years of farming they decided to close.

"It was that awful cycle that I think small businesses find themselves in: that you need more people to run the business, but then you don't have the finances to pay for them," Ms Howe said.

"We were kind of waiting for these snails to grow to sell, to make the money."

The snail pen has a wooden structure for snails to seek shade. ( ABC South West Victoria: Tamsyn Buckle )

Their snails sold for between $125 and $180 per kilogram, depending on their size.

Ms Howe is now a self-described "snail consultant," using her experience to guide others.

"I would often get and still do weekly emails from people wanting to start snail farms," she said.

Unlike in Europe, where snail farming practices are passed down through generations, reliable information customised to Australian conditions is hard to find.

"It was essentially farming, but it was still sort of a very niche product, and I didn't have anyone to turn to," Ms Howe said.

This has also been a challenge for Ms Schaff, but she has a secret weapon.

Carolie Schaff keeps a folder of snail farming research dating back decades. ( ABC South West Victoria: Tamsyn Buckle )

In a manilla folder labelled "Snail Farming Info", she has research that dates back decades and has crossed oceans.

It was passed on to her from a former snail farmer in the Yarra Valley, who first received it from another retired farmer in New South Wales.

Armed with this expertise, Ms Schaff said she hoped to one day see her snails used in snail stews, sausages, pâté and even skincare.

But for now, she is happy taking things at a fittingly slow pace.

"Sometimes you fail, but you just learn and then you start again," she said.

Backstory

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

live

By Dannielle Maguire

By Fergus Gregg

Topic: Technology

By Dannielle Maguire

Great question!

The company has been giving updates on Microsoft's Service Health Status website.

Earlier, it said the outage was linked to " a large number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable , which is shifting load onto the remaining infrastructure".

We're not exactly sure why those servers are unavailable, but Microsoft's team is working on it.

Here's what the company said in its latest update a few minutes ago.

"While we haven't identified any recent changes that correlate with the start of impact, our investigation indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component on the affected servers that's responsible for processing them.

"We're deploying a targeted change to bypass this component on a subset of servers to validate whether this restores availability, and we've taken steps to prevent additional servers from being removed from service while we work to return the affected servers to service.

"We're also investigating why affected servers are experiencing elevated processor usage while handling requests."

By Fergus Gregg

AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic confirmed they've been affected by the widespread Microsoft outage.

ChatGPT creators, OpenAI, said it was investigating an issue with Microsoft connectors as tools were not working as expected.

Anthropic said it had identified an issue with an upstream provider affecting its Microsoft 365 connector.

Microsoft says it's working to mitigate the outage and is restarting the affected servers.

Reporting with Reuters

By Dannielle Maguire

Good morning, thanks for joining us today.

If you're one of the many people having troubles accessing your Outlook emails this morning, you're not alone!

Microsoft, the company behind the email platform many people around the world rely on, is having a major outage at the moment.

Microsoft confirmed the outage was affecting Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other platforms.

"We're aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact," the company said.

"We're investigating what's causing these servers to become unavailable while we work to safely return them to service."

Buckle up, we'll bring you more updates as they come to hand.

Over the last hour or so, reports have come in from around the world that people can’t access their Outlook email, either through the web or apps. Microsoft has acknowledged the issue from its Microsoft 365 Status account , saying that “We’ve determined a portion of infrastructure is experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors.”

There were also some reports of problems with Teams, but some of the people reporting issues say Teams is still working now.

Now, as of 3:30PM ET, Microsoft says :

While we haven’t identified any recent changes that correlate with the start of impact, our investigation indicates the failed health checks may originate from a specific component on the affected servers that’s responsible for processing them.

We’re deploying a targeted change to bypass this component on a subset of servers to validate whether this restores availability, and we’ve taken steps to prevent additional servers from being removed from service while we work to return the affected servers to service. We’re also investigating why affected servers are experiencing elevated processor usage while handling requests.

But it’s still unclear how long it will take before access is restored, or if that will fix all of the issues people are seeing. On DownDetector , reports of issues with Outlook started to spike just before 1PM ET, and they have not completely gone away yet. It’s also probably not the best sign that we’re struggling to consistently load Microsoft’s own status pages to check on progress. If there are any more details, we will update this article.

Update, 3:42PM ET: Added latest status update from Microsoft.

This is Optimizer , a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. We’ll be taking a break next week and will be back on November 25th. Opt in for Optimizer here .

The SS Jeremiah O’Brien is a World War II Liberty ship. The hulking vessel was built in 56 days. It made 11 trips to Normandy, France, to supply the Allied powers in the fight against German U-boats. Last week, it was the site of a black-tie peptide party thrown by a trio of Gen Z venture capitalists.

Roughly 150 people attended the event, where four types of peptide samples were provided to guests — no injections. One was a topical cream with GHK-Cu, while the other three were dissolvable sublingual strips from peptide startup Afterglow. GHK-Cu is a popular skincare ingredient, but it’s unclear how well sublingual peptide strips work. The topic of the night wasn’t just the state of peptides. The venue was a deliberate reference to American industrial prowess — and why the pharmaceutical supply chain ought to be centered in the United States.

The timing couldn’t have been more pointed.

Sourcing is one of the biggest question marks with gray-market peptides — something the US Department of Health and Human Services is trying to address with its recent interim policy decision allowing certain unapproved peptides for compounding.

The decision is a controversial one. FDA career scientists haven’t endorsed it, though to the average person it might seem like they have. In fact, at a public hearing in July, FDA scientists categorically stated that there wasn’t enough evidence proving safety or efficacy for the experimental peptides in question. Some industry experts have cautioned that the HHS’s decision threatens the current clinical trial framework . By circumventing gold-standard clinical trials, it arguably allows telehealth providers and compounding pharmacies to bypass the approval process and create a parallel, dubiously regulated market.

But for the party’s organizers Roxana Grunenwald, Yuva Krishnapillai, and Elia Ahmadi — all three are from Haus Fund, a biotech accelerator — this was an opportunity to make the case for American peptides. Hence the party on a wartime cargo ship, where guests left with stickers and hats emblazoned with “My Peptides Are Made in America.”

Listening to the three speak, they wouldn’t strike you as typical hooah patriots or MAHA activists — though there’s some overlap in their talking points. They’re venture capitalists promoting a certain viewpoint that’s trending in Silicon Valley right now. But it’s not just them making this argument. Hims & Hers — one of the most recognizable telehealth brands right now — is also hopping on the American peptide bandwagon.

The push for American manufacturing is a thorny one. Last year, President Donald Trump’s tariff policies also reignited the American manufacturing argument, though the reality is it’s difficult to return to “made in America” after decades spent shaping the country into a services-based economy.

Pharmaceuticals have also globalized. According to the US Pharmacopeia, 51 percent of all US prescription active pharmaceutical ingredients (API) comes from India and the European Union. China accounts for 10 percent. But when it comes to gray-market peptides, there’s a reason they’re commonly referred to as “Chinese peptides.” The vast majority of these research chemicals sold online come from Chinese manufacturers.

“Right now, Americans are buying consumer peptides from gray-market sellers in China. And that concerns me because American consumers have little recourse if something goes wrong,” Ahmadi said in response to a panel question. “This is not a blanket criticism of China. This is not a criticism of Chinese people. America needs to be able to make its own medicines.”

“I think this is a really good first step in solving the gray market problem,” Krishnapillai tells me, referring to the HHS’s interim decision. While building industrial infrastructure is a lengthy, complicated, and expensive process, he argues that this decision opens the door for compounding pharmacies to build a supply chain that adheres to US consumer safety laws. That in turn could give the FDA more insight into how to more effectively regulate the market. “The FDA [will be] able to see from a bird’s-eye view a lot more clarity, which will allow for structure to be built out and eventually a new path to API classification,” he adds.

“We’re taking the stance that if people will be purchasing these peptides and taking them, sometimes even injecting, we want them to be American peptides,” adds Grunenwald. “We want them to be both compounded, produced, and verified on American soil.”

“The hardware industry — semiconductors, the compute industry, electronics — have all recognized that the reliance on China for critical minerals is a huge issue. That’s very clear. The bio industry has not yet had that same pushback and the same epiphany about our reliance on Chinese APIs. We aim to bring this onshore. It’ll take a lot of money and a lot of time, but it’s not impossible,” says Grunenwald.

For Ahmadi, onshoring peptides back to America is also a matter of regulatory consistency.

“That made-in-America stamp is really only the beginning,” he says. “If we don’t have our own domestic production, we won’t be able to enforce our own regulations. Our markets are always going to be flooded by foreign imports and we won’t be able to have accountability to American consumers. So, we see this as the first step in a larger conversation to have America set the global standard for quality and safety in this new space.”

Broadly speaking, these points have some merit. Several gray-market peptide users I’ve spoken with for an upcoming story stated that the mere act of importing “research drugs” and worrying about customs was a significant source of anxiety. That said, cost is another major reason why my sources tell me they opted to seek Chinese suppliers. It’s too soon to tell, but American-made peptides will likely be more expensive. That’s because an end-to-end US supply chain for these drugs is no easy feat.

Even so, for some, that extra expense is worth it if it means signaling a higher-quality product.

“We purchased an API manufacturing facility in California recently … Our intention is to leverage that capability to provide US-made API, and as a result, US-made product through the whole supply chain,” says Dr. Anant Vinjamoori, chief medical officer at Hims & Hers. The company purchased the facility last year , though it does partner with other companies globally to deliver compounded medications outside the US.

But in this particular case, Vinjamoori is also specifically referring to Peptides Plus, a forthcoming service from Hims & Hers announced in the wake of the HHS interim policy. In a blog announcing Peptides Plus, Hims & Hers CEO Andrew Dudum writes that the company “spent years building the infrastructure we need in our very own U.S.-based peptide manufacturing facility.” At launch, the company plans to provide access to “Sermorelin, Glutathione, B12, NAD+, and L-carnitine, with BPC-157 and TB-500 to follow when allowable.” Notably, some of these substances, like vitamin B12 and NAD+, aren’t peptides at all. Meanwhile, sermorelin and glutathione are already legal. All of these, with the exception of BPC-157 and TB-500, are currently available through legal pathways.

“I think it’s important not just to be able to say, ‘Oh, this is US made,’ but because it gives us direct oversight into the whole process,” says Vinjamoori, who says that he had prescribed peptides to patients in the past before the Biden administration moved certain research peptides to the no-compounding list.

“Even then, there was inconsistency between compounding pharmacies. Everyone knew this,” he says, noting that doctors would individually recommend pharmacies based on what they were prescribing. “That to me, is still not ideal. That’s why we really felt it was worth making this investment — and to be clear, this is not easy.”

When asked about how this might affect Peptide Plus pricing, Vinjamoori demurred, stating that the company would have more to share in “due time.”

There are yet many unknowns with regard to the HHS decision and how it’ll impact the peptide economy at large. The decision is most notably an interim policy. It’s not necessarily a permanent or lasting change. It was also made before the midterm elections, so who can say how the policy winds will shift concerning tariffs and whether the zeal for “made in America” will fizzle as a result.

But for now, it’s more than likely that you’ll start seeing some vendors touting that their peptides are proudly made in America. It’s entirely possible that they might imply that makes their product “safer.” That might be true with regard to sourcing and, to a degree, accountability. But it’s not the whole story. After all, in peptide America, sourcing is only part of the problem.

Scientists are getting tired of amateurs parachuting into their fields and making ‘discoveries’ with AI.﻿

Scientists are getting tired of amateurs parachuting into their fields and making ‘discoveries’ with AI.﻿

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

See All by Robert Hart

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

See All by Robert Hart

Armed with a team of AI agents, Google researcher Pietro Miotti claimed earlier this week to have discovered a potentially unmapped Maya site in Mexico. There was just one problem: The site had already been discovered and was published in an academic journal last year. The incident, which sparked criticism among archeologists online, underscores a growing tension in science as amateurs wielding increasingly powerful AI tools parachute into specialist fields, often without the expertise needed to understand what they are looking at.

Local communities are often already well aware of sites in their area.

Miotti said the idea to use AI to search for archeological sites came to him while traveling in Peru, when he began wondering what historic explorers might do with access to modern technology. He settled on lidar, a laser-based mapping technology that can produce detailed three-dimensional images of the environment, and set a team of 48 AI agents to comb through NASA lidar data for signs of undocumented sites. As “Peru isn’t well covered” by public lidar data, Miotti wrote, he shifted his focus to the Maya region.

The agents flagged numerous promising locations, including “one major village [that] doesn’t seem to have been registered” in existing records. Miotti, who described the research to The Verge as a personal side project done without any Google compute or resources, said he then reached out to Mexico’s National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) to check whether the apparent discovery was already known, including through unpublished research. Using the agents to translate his correspondence into Spanish, Miotti said INAH told him it had no record of a registered site at that location.

“It took less than 72 hours to go from a random thought while traveling to an official reply from the Mexican government. This is by far the best time ever to be alive,” Miotti wrote on his blog.

Miotti stressed that he is not an archeologist and emphasized that the finding would need to be verified with fieldwork. Nevertheless, he hailed it as proof that “we’re on the brink of a revolution across every science” and called for the “entire planet” to be mapped with lidar so AI agents could “help us find the rest.” Had he been an archaeologist familiar with the region, however, Miotti might have spotted a problem: The site was already known, and had been documented in an academic journal more than a year earlier.

“I didn’t expect it to get this much attention.”

Archeologists were quick to point out the oversight on social media. In a series of posts on Bluesky, Sarah Parcak, an archeology professor at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, stressed the importance of carefully checking findings against existing research. “This is why we have peer review,” Parcak wrote, adding that just because the Mexican government doesn’t have something in its database doesn’t mean it is unknown or unmapped. Other archeologists echoed her criticism, slamming the project for spreading misinformation and taking credit away from archeologists, who have been using advanced digital tools in their work for decades.

“This was a personal project that I was excited to share,” Miotti told The Verge . “I didn’t expect it to get this much attention.” He added that as a non-archaeologist, he had not realized a site not being registered wasn’t the same as it not having been mapped, adding that expert knowledge “is needed to verify what the agents find.” He also addressed the limits of his AI tools: “My agents and I missed it. Archaeologists rightly don’t publish the coordinates of sites, so checking whether a site is already known means comparing images against figures in papers, not searching a database. That’s much harder for agents, and it’s something these tools need to get better at. When people pointed it out, I updated the post and the blog as soon as I could to credit their work.”

Nevertheless, Miotti said this was an example of how agents could be used to help experts sort through large amounts of data. He said he has been encouraged by the archaeologists and PhD students that he said were reaching out to him “excited about the workflow and wanting to know how it works and whether it could help with their own survey data.”

“Our ‘problem’ is not discovering new sites,” Elizabeth Graham, a professor of Mesoamerican archaeology at University College London, told The Verge . “Most of us working in the Maya area know about tons of sites not explored or excavated or mapped, most of these found on foot,” she said. Graham also critiqued the use of the word “discover,” noting that local communities are often already well aware of sites in their area.

While she credited Miotti with doing a decent job of using AI to map the mounds from lidar data — “the interpretation of lidar data can be tricky” — Graham argued the bigger obstacle is funding for research. “The fact is, there just isn’t the funding to excavate or map sites as there was in the past, so in a way it doesn’t matter how many more are ‘discovered.’”

“Just spotting something does not add much to our knowledge.”

The controversy reflects a broader problem with AI in science, perhaps most visible with OpenAI’s recent advances in mathematics . While AI tools are increasingly capable of producing genuinely impressive results, they don’t always engage with the existing research those findings build upon. The result can be claimed breakthroughs that have, as is the case here, already been made by someone else, or a general failure to credit earlier work. Even when the findings are actually new, they can lack context a specialist would bring. Ultimately, amateur use of AI tools often ends up shifting the burden of establishing what has actually been found and why it matters to actual experts, work that would ordinarily be part of making a scientific discovery in the first place.

Ivan Šprajc, a professor of archaeology at the Research Centre of the Slovenian Academy of Sciences and Arts in Ljubljana and a coauthor of the paper documenting the site, told The Verge he wasn’t particularly impressed by the agents’ work. Archeologists have been using lidar and “other sophisticated remote sensing tools for quite some time,” he said, adding that “just spotting something does not add much to our knowledge.” He told The Verge that while it is commendable that Miotti checked in with INAH, doing so is “not sufficient” as the institution does not have access to all possible information. “The fact that INAH has no official knowledge of a particular cluster of archaeological features does not necessarily mean that it has not been spotted or even explored by archaeologists.”

Šprajc said that he worries the growing use of AI tools by amateurs could overwhelm archeologists with claims of new discoveries. “Just today I have received an email from another AI ‘discoverer,’ so I am a little bit concerned about being flooded by this kind of message,” he said. He also raised another potential risk of amateurs publicizing the locations of archeological sites: attracting looters. “But as long as these findings do not lead to looting, I don’t see a major problem,” he added.

scraped.description: A livestream Ars discussion is happening on November 17 at 1 pm Eastern Time.
scraped.h1: Ars Live: What drone attacks on data centers mean for modern life in the cloud
scraped.body_text:
A livestream Ars discussion is happening on November 17 at 1 pm Eastern Time.

Drone and missile strikes have inflicted unprecedented damage on data centers in Eastern Europe and the Middle East this year, disrupting cloud services for millions of people and permanently deleting some Amazon Web Services customer data. This trend represents a new concern for Big Tech companies—but also for governments and everyone else who depends on common digital services in modern life.

To explore what this all means for modern society’s reliance on cloud resilience, I will be hosting a live conversation titled “Drone attacks and data centers: New Risks for Big Tech” on Tuesday, November 17 at 1 pm ET with Joseph Jarnecki , a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK defense and security think tank. He leads RUSI’s work on how cloud services factor into national security and defense, along with tech sovereignty efforts.

Jarnecki has done extensive research on how Ukraine strengthened its cloud resilience with Western partners despite facing both cyberattacks and kinetic attacks at the start of the full-scale Russian invasion, and explored what that means for NATO and European governments’ cloud adoption plans.

This year, Jarnecki has written about Iran’s drone and missile strikes on Amazon data centers in the Middle East during the US-Israeli war with Iran, and the broader implications for governments and Big Tech. He has also commented on the impacts of Russia and Ukraine exchanging strikes on each other’s data centers.

For more background on the data center attacks that have transpired so far in 2026, you can see my previous Ars coverage of how the Iranian strikes left Amazon with months of repairs , and caused enough damage to result in the permanent loss of some AWS customer data.

I’ve also covered why Russia was not ready for the data center war it started with Ukraine, with the systematic Russian strike campaign targeting Ukraine’s data centers provoking Ukrainian counterstrikes that damaged Russian government data centers and AI data centers owned by the Russian tech giant Yandex .

My conversation with Jarnecki will explore why data centers have become much more prominent military targets, whether defending or hardening data centers against drones and missiles is a realistic option, how cloud resiliency can be improved in wartime conditions, and the choices governments and cloud providers face in deploying data centers during an era of growing geopolitical risks.

You can watch the discussion live on YouTube on November 17 at 1 pm ET. We will also be fielding a few audience questions.

scraped.description: N-Gage exclusive Shadowkey gets an AI-coded glow-up with plenty of new features.
scraped.h1: The Elder Scrolls’ most obscure adventure gets a 4K PC makeover
scraped.body_text:
N-Gage exclusive Shadowkey gets an AI-coded glow-up with plenty of new features.

So, you think you’re an Elder Scrolls superfan? You say you’ve been there since The Elder Scrolls Arena on MS-DOS and have logged hundreds of hours in The Elder Scrolls Online ? You say you’ve bought all of the roughly 5,000 re-releases and remasters of Skyrim that have been made available in the last 15 years?

Tell me, then: What do you think of The Elder Scrolls Travels: Shadowkey ?

What’s that? You’ve never played Shadowkey ? You weren’t there day one back in 2004, Nokia N-Gage in hand , ready to experience the game’s 176 x 208 resolution mobile hack-and-slash RPG combat for yourself? And you call yourself a real Elder Scrolls fan?

Well, don’t worry. Now you can fill in this crucial gap in your history without even having to track down functional, decades-old N-Gage hardware. That’s thanks to Shadowkey: Reforged , a free fan-made PC port that pairs updated art with the original game files and scripts for an upscaled, 4K experience that runs natively on PC, no N-Gage or emulator needed.

Moving from a pre-iPhone mobile game to a modern PC obviously comes with major graphical upgrades, powered by a completely rewritten PC graphics engine. What was once a cramped portrait orientation on the N-Gage has now been expanded for a 16:9 monitor standard that displays at up to 120 fps (though the game’s logic still matches the original game’s 25 fps). In addition to newly retextured character and environmental models, the new port also sports small touches like bloom lighting, rippling water, and an upgraded interface with sharper text rendering than was possible on an ancient mobile phone.

Using the original game files (which you can obtain from an easy-to-find legitimate copy of the game , of course) means that Reforged ‘s quests, dialogue, and game rules are “worked out from the original program,” as the game’s website puts it. That said, the game’s “Modern” mode adds a few touches like smarter enemy AI, fall damage, searchable containers, and a fast travel system that are missing from the original game (and from Reforged ‘s more authentic “Classic” mode). The Modern mode also includes some welcome quality-of-life improvements like controller rumble, a smoother on-screen interface, and “better death poses.”

Those with a disposition against vibe-coded clones and ports should know that Reforged author Dan Whelan writes that he used “AI to assist with coding and building the engine, and with debugging,” as well as for the creation of “most of the modern, higher resolution artwork.” But those who are OK with this AI assistance should be happy to see the project moved from its first playable version in late October to a full-featured “release day” build for Windows, Mac, and Android that came out Wednesday. Whelan has been releasing daily updates to the project and seems set to continue, if the current “Version 0.2.9” designation is any indication.

The inherent limitations of 2000s-era N-Gage game development (which helped earn the original release some middling review scores ) are still pretty apparent in even this Reforged remake. Still, it’s nice that Elder Scrolls completionists can now experience one of the series’ least-played releases. At the very least, it’s something to tinker with as we all continue the long wait for Elder Scrolls VI .

scraped.title: Google rolls out Gemini 4 Hydrogen, finally replacing 3.8 Flash
scraped.description: Gemini 4 Hydrogen isn't getting a slow, security-conscious release like Carbon and Argon.
scraped.h1: Google rolls out Gemini 4 Hydrogen, finally replacing 3.8 Flash
scraped.body_text:
Gemini 4 Hydrogen isn’t getting a slow, security-conscious release like Carbon and Argon.

Google is continuing its elemental AI naming scheme with the new Gemini 4 Hydrogen . These names are less descriptive than the Pro/Flash monikers of earlier releases, but Hydrogen’s purpose is clear: It replaces the faster, more economical Flash models most people in Google’s ecosystem use.

With Google’s recent Argon and Carbon releases, the rollout was staged and began with cybersecurity researchers. Even when general availability began, Google restricted access to users paying for its most expensive AI subscription. The limits for Hydrogen are much more relaxed, with access beginning immediately. This model has replaced Gemini 3.8 Flash across the company’s products.

Google claims that Hydrogen represents a major improvement versus the previous Flash model. It runs in one of four thinking levels (low, medium, high, and the new xhigh), and even in high mode, it’s 2.5 times faster than Flash 3.8. Plus, it reduces “fabricated claims” by more than 5x, according to Google’s analysis. Users will also see gains in code generation, with Hydrogen more than tripling 3.8 Flash’s score in Terminal-Bench. In some cases, Hydrogen even trades blows with Argon. It managed a score of 54 in the popular Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with xhigh mode versus 50 for Argon.

Google believes Hydrogen will be a key part of how developers work with agentic coding tools. While it still positions Argon and Carbon as the best for long-horizon tasks and security, Hydrogen’s speed makes it ideal for generating simpler code and running tests without blowing through token budgets.

Hydrogen is also being integrated with Google Search , which the company says is the biggest update to its AI-powered search tools ever. The new model should better handle long, multipart questions, and the responses in both AI Overviews and AI Mode will have more visual elements. The company also claims Hydrogen’s fan-out search has been tuned to link to more sources, but we’ve heard that from Google before.

Everyone will reportedly get access to Hydrogen in search, but it’s a bit more restricted in the Gemini app and AI Studio. The new model is live for AI Pro and Ultra subscribers, but AI Plus and free users are still stuck with the old 3.5 Flash-Lite model. Developers can plug into Hydrogen via the API at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens, which is unchanged from 3.8 Flash. Carbon and Argon are currently $2/$10, but they will go up to $4/$20 starting next month.

Nvidia founder Jensen Huang was having a separate affair with an employee that has not been previously reported, Reuters reported on Thursday .

Huang stepped down as CEO and board member for the company earlier today, in the wake of news of extramarital affairs with accused spy Alice Huang and Nvidia VP of Health Care Kimberly Powell. CFO Colette Kress has stepped in as interim CEO , but no permanent successor has been named.

Reuters is withholding the name of the new employee linked to Huang, but says she is an employee of Nvidia.

Huang has been called before Congress to testify about the national security implications of his relationship with Alice Huang in the coming weeks — but it’s unclear how much more will be revealed before the hearings take place. Already, his abrupt fall from grace is expected to have significant repercussions for the industry at large.

Google Search is getting better at understanding complicated questions, including those with multiple parts, highly specific requests, or confusing typos. The updates are coming via the company’s newly released Gemini 4 Hydrogen model, which Google claims is its “biggest model improvement to Search yet.”

While Google’s frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon, are best at deep reasoning for hard problems, Hydrogen is designed for fast execution across a variety of agentic workflows, or tasks in which an AI carries out multiple steps on its own, the company explained in an announcement.

The idea behind the model’s release is that using the most powerful model isn’t always needed — sometimes a faster, cheaper, and reasonably smart one will do. Google says Hydrogen completes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash, its previous fast model, but it’s still pretty smart, even beating the more powerful Gemini 4 Argon on one broad intelligence benchmark, the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , at its default high thinking level.

In Search, Hydrogen brings several improvements, including a better understanding of user intent, the ability to offer more helpful links and visual responses, and better answers across the different languages supported by Google’s AI Mode.

In terms of intent, Google says Hydrogen can handle more nuanced and complicated questions more quickly. This means people can ask their questions in their natural train of thought, including those that have multiple parts or that include highly specific requests. Hydrogen is also better at navigating hard-to-understand typos, Google says. Because of its improvements and better ability to follow instructions and call the right tools, Hydrogen is able to more precisely address each part of a user’s question.

Its advanced reasoning also improves Search’s fan-out technique, which breaks down a single user’s prompt into multiple subqueries. This allows people to discover websites related to the query that they may have otherwise missed, the blog post explains.

The addition of Hydrogen to Search will also mean more images, structured responses, comparison tables, and custom tools will appear as visual responses to users’ queries in AI Mode.

Google also says Hydrogen can work on its own for everyday work in areas like writing code, running tests, or verifying code changes, or it can be paired with Carbon and Argon in workflows that combine several models.

The model offers four thinking levels: low, medium, high (default), and a new, extra-high tier (“xhigh”), all of which are designed to complete tasks faster with fewer output tokens.

On multi-step tasks like deep research, data analysis, and broad codebase navigation, Hydrogen ranks No. 5 on Agent Arena’s benchmarks, the company pointed out.

In addition to Search, Gemini 4 Hydrogen is coming to all tiers of Google’s AI Studio, the Gemini API, the Gemini App, and the paid AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google’s Antigravity development platform.

Google says the Hydrogen update is rolling out to all Search users globally.
