Nectar , an AI-powered operating system for marketing, is launching a new AI agent designed to take a lot of the manual work out of influencer marketing, from finding the right creators to contacting them, managing partnerships, and tracking results.

Founded by sisters Misbah and Farah Uraizee, both former Meta employees, Nectar came out of stealth last year and uses AI agents to help brands manage social media, customer conversations, content moderation, creator partnerships, and competitor research.

Announced Thursday, its new “Creator Agent” can search for creators, check their content and brand partnerships, send personalized messages, coordinate collaborations, and monitor how campaigns perform. Instead of having marketing teams spend weeks scrolling through social media, building spreadsheets, and sending individual DMs, Nectar wants its agent to handle much of that work automatically.

Nectar joins other companies introducing agentic AI assistants designed to automate influencer outreach, including Aspire and GRIN . The launch also comes as more brands turn to creators to reach customers. U.S. spending on creator advertising is expected to reach $44 billion in 2026, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau . As companies work with hundreds or even thousands of creators, keeping track of relationships and measuring results can get pretty difficult.

Nectar says its Creator Agent searches more than 300 million creator profiles to find potential partners, including smaller creators who may not yet have a large following but are gaining traction. The system analyzes videos to understand what creators post about, how their content fits a brand, and whether their previous partnerships are appropriate. It also checks brand safety by reviewing content in context rather than simply searching for specific keywords.

Nectar then creates ranked lists of recommendations and adds new matches as creators become more popular.

Once it finds a potential match, the agent can draft and send messages in a brand’s voice, create custom landing pages to collect creator information, and help manage contracts, product gifting, and shipping details. It also remembers previous conversations and interactions, so brands can keep track of relationships without relying on spreadsheets.

“Brands can share voice guidelines in any format, and Nectar picks up the rest from their history,” CEO Misbah Uraizee tells TechCrunch. “On top of that sits a set of proprietary guardrails that keep every draft on tone and in context. Nectar understands what is being said in a video, reads the tone of the conversation, and knows the difference between a quote post on X and a TikTok comment section. A brand should not sound identical in both, and with Nectar it doesn’t.”

Another feature looks for personal milestones in creators’ lives, such as an engagement, a new baby, or completing a marathon. The agent can then suggest a personalized message or gift, helping brands build relationships that feel less like one-off advertising deals.

Creator Agent is available today globally and covers Instagram creators and TikTokers.

The company plans to make the agent available through its Model Context Protocol (MCP), allowing teams to use it through AI assistants such as Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot, as well as their own custom-built agents.

This past May, Nectar raised a $30 million Series A round led by Menlo Ventures and its Anthology Fund, which is a joint initiative launched with Anthropic.

items.title: Alice Huang tied to Nvidia’s biggest Chinese competitor
items.summary: The woman with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had a relationship also owned stakes in companies that provided computing power to Huawei, a key Nvidia competitor.

scraped.title: Alice Huang tied to Nvidia’s biggest Chinese competitor
scraped.description: The woman with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had a relationship also owned stakes in companies that provided computing power to Huawei, a key Nvidia competitor.
scraped.author: Eamon Javers,Paige Tortorelli
scraped.h1: Alice Huang tied to Nvidia’s biggest Chinese competitor
scraped.body_text:
In this article

Alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang may have simultaneously owned stakes in businesses in China that benefited Nvidia's biggest competitor in China, Huawei, while she was in business with Nvidia and also reportedly having a romantic affair with its ousted CEO Jensen Huang .

The connection between Alice Huang and Huawei was first discovered by analysts at private intelligence firm Tesari. The firm exclusively shared its findings with CNBC. Tesari provides intelligence research to private companies and the U.S. government.

This previously unreported entanglement was first uncovered by the research firm which uses artificial intelligence to collect evidence and specializes in national security investigations around the world. The connections may raise questions about Alice Huang's intent and conduct in her relationship with the CEO and whether Jensen Huang knew his romantic partner was closely connected with his competition. Jensen Huang has acknowledged having an affair, though the precise timing of his relationship with Alice Huang is unknown.

The mysterious saga of Alice Huang involves a tangle of interlocking corporations and transactions that show her connection to entities that ultimately provided computing power to Huawei in China.

Huawei is known as a Chinese government "state champion" in the technology and telecommunications sectors, meaning it receives enormous financial support from the government in Beijing so it can lower prices and undercut global competitors. It is considered a key part of the Chinese government's push for global technical dominance and is closely linked to the Chinese Communist Party.

Businesses connected to Alice Huang were linked with supplying Nvidia computing power to Huawei, according to documents reviewed by CNBC, around the same time she and Jensen Huang were first publicly seen together in December 2023.

In 2024, Nvidia said Huawei was a top competitor , specifically in artificial intelligence chips including graphics processing units, central processing units and networking chips.

"This activity, which surfaced through our analysis of Alice's network, warrants a national security and [technology] counterproliferation investigation," said Brian Andersen, Tesari's vice president for national security applications and a former supervisory special agent with Homeland Security Investigations.

If the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry Security and Homeland Security Investigations found evidence that anyone transferred "controlled equipment" to Huawei without authorization, potential charges might include include export-control violations, conspiracy and smuggling, Andersen said.

The connection between Alice Huang and Huawei is so convoluted that analysts at Tesari told CNBC that based on their previous investigative experience, they suspect it was designed to deliberately obscure the relationship.

Nvidia and Huawei did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment. Jensen Huang did not respond to a voicemail left on a mobile phone. Alice Huang could not be reached.

According to Chinese corporate records and media reports compiled by Tesari and provided to CNBC, Alice Huang, whose Chinese name is Huang Le and who according to documents at the time was based in Hong Kong, in 2019 sold a cloud business she owned called Osmanthus to a Chinese gaming company called 7Road. A subsidiary of 7Road, which was based in Singapore, was spun off as "Megaspeed" in 2023 . Megaspeed would go on to become a key Nvidia customer, helping facilitate at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese firms, The Information reported Tuesday.

As early as 2016, Alice Huang had also become a co-owner of a financial firm known as Shanghai Hexi , which heavily invests in tech and data centers.In 2021, Hexi in turn acquired 27 percent of a company called Shanghai Century Longteng, a data center developer, which Hexi held until 2024 . That firm owned a controlling 50.1 percent stake in a data center facility called Shenzhen Yifeng Technology Co., Ltd. in mainland China.

The key customer of that data center was Huawei Cloud , the Shenzhen, China-based subsidiary of Huawei Technologies.

In addition, Alice Huang's firm Hexi guaranteed the loans required to finance the Shenzhen data center, which did business with Huawei.

Hexi did not immediately respond to a message via its LinkedIn page sent outside of normal business hours.

CNBC translated corporate records and Chinese news articles in Mandarin that Tesari provided.

It's not clear if the Shenzhen data center was able to acquire Nvidia GPUs, but its majority owner began purchasing the chips in 2023 . That company is known as Zhejiang Century Huatong Group and is a business partner of Alice Huang's Hexi through their joint ownership of Century Longteng.

That made Alice Huang a part owner of a data center providing computing power to Huawei. And that was happening at around the same time the first known sightings came of Alice Huang and Jensen Huang in public together.

And that raises the question of why Huawei, which has access to Chinese made chips, would need to rent computing power from an outside entity.

Hexi exited its stake in the data center development company in 2024, but individuals within Alice Huang's network are still connected to the Shenzhen data center. Her husband Kang Wei is a longtime business associate who founded Hexi, where Alice Huang previously held an executive role. In 2022, Kang became an executive of Century Longteng, which owns the controlling stake in the Shenzhen data center and he also attended the company's signing of the Huawei agreement.

scraped.title: Jensen Huang is out and Nvidia stock is down—what market pros say about buying dips
scraped.description: Nvidia stock fell 5% on Thursday following the departure of CEO Jensen Huang. Some see it as a signal to sell, others an opportunity to buy.
scraped.author: Ryan Ermey
scraped.h1: Jensen Huang is out and Nvidia stock is down—what market pros say about buying dips
scraped.body_text:
Related Stories

Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned as the firm's president and CEO, the company announced Thursday. Investors reacted negatively to the news. By 2:30 p.m., shares of the chipmaking giant were down more than 5%, and now sit 31% below their high on October 6.

It's easy to see why Huang's departure, which comes amid revelations of his romantic ties to a woman believed by the U.S. intelligence community to be a Chinese spy , has investors feeling queasy. The company Huang co-founded 33 years ago — and whose chips have powered the artificial intelligence boom — has grown into the firm currently valued at about $4 trillion under his leadership.

"The premise here is that there is no successor to a generational founder," says Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of the Founders 100 ETF, which invests in founder-led companies. "It's that they're one of one, and what they bring from a vision, execution and grit standpoint is not replaceable."

While some investors are exiting Nvidia positions based on that premise — Monaghan's fund must, per its prospectus — others will see the slip in Nvidia's price as an opportunity to buy a great stock on proverbial sale , he says.

Looking purely at the numbers, the opportunity to buy a stock with Nvidia's prodigious projected growth at its current depressed price "happens once a decade, maybe once in a career as an investor," he says.

In investing parlance, the latter group of investors is " buying the dip " — investing in an asset after a decline in its value in anticipation of a bounceback. Whether it's a prudent strategy for you with Nvidia or any other stock requires some examination, investing experts say — not only of the stock in question, but your own portfolio strategy.

When an investment you own or are interested in declines, your first move is to examine your reason for buying or holding it, says Tom Hainlin, national investment strategist at U.S. Bank Asset Management.

Ask yourself if whatever caused the slide has changed your investment narrative, he says. "Has it changed why I bought the stock or why I'm investing in the market?"

If you own a diversified portfolio and the broad U.S. stock market has declined, buying dips is a relatively straightforward decision, investing pros say. Because the stock market has historically trended upward, each downdraft has offered investors an opportunity to add an appreciating asset at a discount.

"If you have a solid, long-term investment, it's always attractive to buy the dip because you always get a new high," Jeff Buchbinder, chief equity strategist with LPL Financial, told Make It in August. "In the history of the S&P 500, every dip has been attractive because you eventually made new highs."

Individual stocks have no such track record, meaning that a major slide should prompt you to re-examine the thesis behind any given investment, Hainlin says. That analysis is twofold. On one hand, you should rethink the position any one stock occupies in your portfolio. If it's a large enough chunk that a pullback is keeping you up at night, it might be worth paring the position back to put things more in line with your tolerance for risk, he says.

And whether you own the stock or are thinking about buying, a dip is a good time to evaluate your outlook for that investment. If you plan to hold a particular stock for the long term, for instance, you'll have to weigh whether the short-term bad news could have a lasting impact on the firm's profitability.

"Did Nvidia's prospects change as a result of [Huang's resignation]? There's no definitive answer for that," he says.

Monaghan says that, based on historical data, there may be reason to worry. His fund's fact sheet cites data from consultancy Bain & Company showing that founder-led companies vastly outperformed their peers from 1990 through 2014. Even companies that have successfully replaced their founders, such as Apple and Microsoft , have failed to grow as quickly as under original leadership, he says.

Investors will have to weigh the risk that Nvidia will lag without Huang at the helm against the firm's still impressive growth projections — the company will report third-quarter fiscal year earnings results on Nov. 17 — and their long-term belief in the firm's position as a top supplier of microchips that power AI.

"One thing we do know is that AI demand hasn't changed," Hainlin says.

items.title: Nvidia: Ex-prosecutor Joon Kim and Wachtell, Lipton bring big track record to investigation
items.summary: The retention of Wachtell, Lipton for the Nvidia probe comes on the heels of the law firm's investigation for the NBA into the Los Angeles Clippers.

scraped.title: Nvidia: Ex-prosecutor Joon Kim and Wachtell, Lipton bring big track record to investigation
scraped.description: The retention of Wachtell, Lipton for the Nvidia probe comes on the heels of the law firm's investigation for the NBA into the Los Angeles Clippers.
scraped.author: Dan Mangan
scraped.h1: Nvidia: Ex-prosecutor Joon Kim and Wachtell, Lipton bring big track record to investigation
scraped.body_text:
In this article

Joon Kim , the lawyer tapped by artificial intelligence chip giant Nvidia to investigate its former CEO Jensen Huang , and the Big Law firm he works for have a long history of investigating high-profile cases.

Kim, in his career as a top federal prosecutor and as an attorney in private practice, has had in his sights mobster John "The Teflon Don" Gotti's son, former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo , the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp . and other high-profile people and companies.

The law firm that Kim recently joined — Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz — this year conducted an investigation for the NBA of the Los Angeles Clippers and its billionaire owner, Steve Ballmer , which ended with the basketball league imposing stiff sanctions on Ballmer and the Clippers for violating salary cap rules in connection with superstar Kawhi Leonard.

On Tuesday, Nvidia said it had retained Kim, 55, and Wachtell, Lipton to "conduct a thorough and independent investigation" of allegations that its then-CEO Jensen Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort involving his affair with a woman, Alice Huang. U.S. intelligence suspects her of being a spy for China .

Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Thursday morning on the heels of a New York Times report that he had also had an extramarital affair with an Nvidia executive, Kimberly Powell, who reports to him.

That allegation could be added to the list of issues that Kim will be looking into as part of his probe.

Nvidia did not immediately respond when asked if the parameters of the investigation would be affected by the new claim. A spokeswoman for Wachtell, Lipton declined to comment for this article on behalf of the firm and Kim.

Friends and former colleagues of Kim said Nvidia has made a smart decision in retaining him for the job.

"I think he's the ideal person for this role," said Edward Kim, a New York white-collar defense lawyer who worked in the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York with Joon Kim. The two men are not related.

"I think they're going to get a serious, credible investigation. I believe Joon will follow the facts wherever they will lead," Edward Kim said.

The son of a South Korean diplomat, Joon Kim was born in Los Angeles. He attended Phillips Exeter Academy and later Stanford University.

After graduating cum laude from Harvard Law School, he clerked for a federal judge in Manhattan and then worked as an associate at the major law firm Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton starting in the late 1990s. After that, he spent seven years in the SDNY as an assistant U.S. attorney. His tenure as a prosecutor there included four years in the Organized Crime and Terrorism Unit.

The SDNY, by virtue of its location in Manhattan, handles some of the most high-profile criminal investigations in the United States, including cases of major financial crimes, government corruption and organized crime.

During his first stint at the SDNY, Kim investigated and prosecuted crimes that included "racketeering, murder, money laundering, securities fraud, firearms and narcotics offenses, tax evasion, and terrorism," the office has previously said.

Kim's trial wins at the SDNY included obtaining a conviction of Peter Gotti, then-head of the Gambino Mafia family, for conspiring to kill notorious mob turncoat Salvatore "Sammy the Bull" Gravano. Kim and his fellow prosecutors were less successful, however, in prosecuting Peter Gotti's nephew, John Gotti Jr., whose trials ended with several hung juries.

"He could be a very tenacious courtroom advocate," said Chris Conniff, a New York attorney who worked with Kim in the SDNY, and who considers Kim one of his closest friends.

"He's incredibly smart," Conniff said. "I think he's known by everyone in the business as just an outstanding investigator, leaves no stone unturned."

Kim in 2006 returned to Cleary Gottlieb as a partner in the firm's litigation and enforcement group but then went back to the SDNY in 2013. During his second stint there, he served as deputy U.S. attorney, and then served as U.S. attorney from 2017 to 2018.

Kim's elevation to acting U.S. attorney came as a result of President Donald Trump 's firing of then-U.S. Attorney Preet Bharara in March 2017 after Bharara refused the new president's demand that he resign.

"Preet's departure was very unique," and the mood in the SDNY "was shaky" after his ouster, Conniff said.

"Preet was very well-liked and well-respected," said Conniff, who was in private practice at the time that Bharara was fired. "We just lost a very charismatic and effective leader, and in a very dramatic way."

In taking over from Bharara, Kim, "from my external viewpoint, he righted the ship and continued to do the work of the office in the time he was there."

"Joon, I would say, gave people confirmation that it was going to be alright, and it was going to be business as usual," Conniff said.

Kim left the SDNY in April 2018, and began his third stint at Cleary Gottlieb, which he recently left to join Wachtell, Lipton's litigation department.

In March 2021, Kim and another attorney, Anne Clark, a partner at Vladeck, Raskin & Clark, were tapped by New York Attorney General Letitia James to investigate then-Gov. Andrew Cuomo over allegations that he had sexually harassed several women.

"These are serious allegations that demand a rigorous and impartial investigation," Kim said in a statement at the time. "We will act judiciously and follow the facts wherever they lead."

Kim and Clark in August 2021 submitted a 165-page report to James, which concluded that Cuomo had sexually harassed at least 11 women and then retaliated against a former employee who had publicly complained about his behavior. As part of the probe, Kim, Clark and their team interviewed 179 witnesses and reviewed tens of thousands of documents.

Cuomo adamantly denied some of the allegations and said that other claims of alleged misconduct had been mischaracterized or misinterpreted.

A week after the report was publicly released, Cuomo announced that he would resign .

Two years after the Cuomo probe, Kim was retained by the FDIC to conduct an independent review of allegations of sexual harassment and interpersonal misconduct at the agency. As part of the probe, Kim and his team conducted 167 interviews of current and past FDIC employees, and hundreds of additional interviews with individuals who contacted a hotline the team set up for employees to report misconduct claims.

An April 2024 report by Kim and his team found "for far too many employees and for far too long, the FDIC has failed to provide a workplace safe from sexual harassment, discrimination, and other interpersonal misconduct."

More than five years after Cuomo left office, the former governor's spokesman has not forgotten, or forgiven, Kim, whom he accused of writing a report on Cuomo with a predetermined outcome.

Kim was a "hired hack," said the spokesman, Rich Azzopardi.

Azzopardi said Kim "hid evidence" that was exonerating of Cuomo, and accepted at face value "outright lies" from a number of witnesses.

The bad blood between Cuomo's camp and Kim predates the sexual harassment probe.

While working in the SDNY, Kim and Bharara oversaw the investigation that led to the corruption trial of Joseph Percoco, who had been a close aide of Cuomo. The trial took place after both prosecutors had left the office.

Azzopardi cited that prosecution in his scathing remarks about Kim.

Percoco was sentenced to six years in prison after his 2018 conviction for honest-services wire fraud. The conviction was overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court in a unanimous ruling in 2023 — after his release from prison — because the judge's instructions to jurors were too vague.

Azzopardi said that Kim and Bharara were motivated to prosecute Percoco for "their own personal glory" and "to generate headlines for themselves."

Bharara, in a two-word email response about Azzopardi's claim, wrote, "Andrew who?," referring to Cuomo.

Azzopardi said he did not believe there was any other reason for Nvidia's board to retain Kim to investigate the Huang situation other than to reach a predetermined outcome by the board.

"I don't know what the aims of the board are," Azzopardi said.

Kim's friend Conniff, when asked if he expected that the Nvidia investigation would be a whitewash that would serve the board's interests, said, "No."

"I don't think Joon would take an engagement in which he could not provide a fulsome report of what he uncovered during this investigation," Conniff said. "Any company board that is looking to do a good, thorough investigation of potential wrongdoing, Joon's perfect ... for it."

items.summary: A police helicopter crew found William, who has Level 2 autism, lying asleep on a flat rock beside a creek and he was later reunited with his mother.

A 17-year-old who went missing on a camping trip was found alive Thursday after six days lost in eastern Australian woodlands.

The boy, who police identified only as William, was camping with a teenage friend when he disappeared last Friday east of Melbourne, Victoria Police said in a news release .

William was dropped off by his mother for the purposes of camping for the weekend when he walked a short distance to the drop-off location to retrieve further camping equipment, police said.

When William failed to return shortly after, his friend searched the area but found no trace of him, according to police.

“An extensive search of the area was conducted by Victoria Police uniform officers, specialist units and other agencies over the past six days,” police said.

A police helicopter crew found William lying asleep on a flat rock beside a creek, wearing shorts and boots and using towels as blankets.

Police said that he was in good spirits and mostly in good health.

William was later taken to a hospital for his health to be monitored, police said.

After becoming lost, William trekked for days up and down “some very steep terrain,” Acting Police Inspector Jason Benbow said.

He spent the last two days where he was found at the creek, trapped by the steepness of his surrounds two kilometres from the his camp site, Benbow said.

“He woke up to the sound of the helicopter, gave them a thumbs up and they winched him to safety,” Benbow told reporters.

William’s mother told The Associated Press that she’s “over the moon that he’s alive.”

“And he’s never leaving the house again. He’s grounded for life. He’s not going anywhere ever again,” Elizabeth joked.

William’s family said he has Level 2 autism. That requires “substantial support,” according to Autism Speaks .

Someone with Level 2 autism may have deficits in verbal and nonverbal social communication skills, social impairments apparent even with supports in place, limited initiation of social interactions, reduced or abnormal responses to social overtures from others, according to the organization.

The organization says that a person with Level 2 autism may also experience inflexibility of behaviour, difficulty coping with change, or other restricted/repetitive behaviours appear frequently enough to be obvious to the casual observer and interfere with functioning in a variety of contexts.

—With files from The Associated Press

The federal government says Russian hockey players will not be permitted to compete at next month’s world juniors championship in Alberta, even if they already hold valid Canadian visas.

A statement provided Wednesday by Secretary of State for Sport Adam van Koeverden says Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada will take measures to individually assess and prevent Russian and Belarusian athletes and officials from entering Canada to compete.

There are Russians with valid visas playing in the Canadian Hockey League, the umbrella organization for the country’s three top major junior hockey leagues.

Russians and Belarusians were banned from the CHL’s import draft from 2022-24 before being allowed back in. According to the CHL, Russia led this year’s draft with 32 of the 114 players selected.

Wednesday’s statement appears to close the door on Russia’s return to the world juniors following last month’s Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling that the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) must reinstate the country in international hockey.

Norway’s hockey federation said Sunday the IIHF had informed it that Russia would be added to the tournament at Norway’s expense.

Norway qualified for the tournament and has said it still hopes to compete.

The IIHF has not formally announced any changes to the tournament field. Its website continues to list Norway among the 10 participating teams.

Hockey federations from several nations, including Finland, Sweden, Czechia and Norway, have said their teams will refuse to compete against Russian players.

Russia and Belarus have been banned from international hockey competition since Russia invaded Ukraine with Belarusian assistance in 2022.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said last week that Russian and Belarusian athletes could not compete in Canada while representing their countries as long as the war continues.

The government’s earlier position allowed individual athletes to compete as neutrals, leaving open the question of whether a Russian team could participate under a neutral designation.

Van Koeverden clarified Monday that the neutral designation applied to individual athletes, not teams.

The government said its position would not change as long as Russia continues its war in Ukraine with Belarus’s complicity.

The world junior championship begins Dec. 26 in Edmonton and Red Deer.

Russia and Ukraine agreed to a large exchange of prisoners of war, both sides said Wednesday as two days of U.S.-mediated talks concluded with no major breakthrough on ending Moscow’s nearly five-year-old full-scale invasion.

Hopes had been low for any significant development in the first meeting in nine months between the delegations. Russia and Ukraine have from time to time swapped POWs but have remained far apart in their demands for accepting a peace settlement.

U.S. officials say they are determined to revive Washington’s peace efforts that so far have failed to deliver significant results.

Along with postwar security guarantees for both countries, other key hurdles are the fate of Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory and what role European countries will play in an eventual settlement.

The sides last met in February on Russia’s invasion, which analysts and humanitarian organizations say has killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians.

The talks lasted just under two hours Wednesday, after a four-hour session the previous day.

“One of the positives is we agreed that we’re going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we’re going to finalize the numbers tomorrow,” said Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, after the Abu Dhabi talks ended.

Vladimir Medinsky, head of the Russian delegation, and Rustem Umerov, who led Kyiv’s contingent, confirmed the planned POW exchange, although Medinsky noted the agreement was “in principle.”

Alexander Zorin, a deputy chief of the General Staff’s information department who attended the talks, told Russian state TV it would be one of the biggest such swaps since 1,000 soldiers from each side returned home last year.

The latest exchange could take place in the next two or three weeks, he said.

Kushner said he and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff will travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet with President Vladimir Putin, then fly to Dublin, Ireland, to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

The Ukrainian leader gave a muted welcome to the outcome of the talks, saying a proposed prisoner exchange was a positive step. But he said Ukraine will not give in to demands that it cede its territory that has been occupied by Russia in exchange for peace.

Medinsky said he felt the talks helped Moscow and Kyiv edge closer to peace, while Kremlin foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov described them as “substantive and quite useful.”

Umerov said Kyiv’s delegation was expected to meet later Wednesday with representatives of European governments, the European Union and NATO who were in the capital of the United Arab Emirates but did not attend the three-way talks.

Moscow doesn’t want European countries, which are concerned about Russia’s conduct and broader intentions on the continent, involved in the direct negotiations. Kushner said one of the goals of the Moscow meeting is to try to get Europeans added to the talks.

In Dublin, Zelenskyy said it was positive that security advisers and senior officials from European governments, the EU and NATO were in Abu Dhabi, even though they were not a part of the talks.

Despite that. he said there had been a “change in temperature,” with Washington warming to the idea of a European role.

“Ending this war without Europe’s participation would be unjust, and it would be impossible,” Zelenskyy said through an interpreter.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said European representatives could eventually join peace talks but added their current statements “don’t indicate any desire on their part to contribute to movement along the path toward peace.” Moscow complains that Europe is financing and supplying weaponry to Ukraine.

Kushner said both Ukraine and Russia needed clarity on postwar security arrangements. He said European countries, the EU and NATO have to be involved in those discussions to build consensus on next steps.

Ukraine wants to ensure that Moscow doesn’t invade again, and EU officials say any discussions on Europe’s security arrangements could only start after a ceasefire. Many in Europe see the inclusion of Russia in those plans as a concession to Putin, who has described NATO’s eastward expansion as a top security threat to his country. Moscow has demanded that the alliance’s troops be pulled back its troops from Russia’s borders.

Russia’s security concerns were discussed at the talks, Kushner said, adding that Moscow was told it needs to provide different de-escalation proposals acceptable to Europe.

“The reality is, is there’s no trust right now between the sides. And that’s to be expected after a conflict like this,” he said. But he posted on X later that the POW exchange “will reunite families, build trust and create momentum toward peace.”

The context of the negotiations has changed since the February meeting in Geneva. The Trump administration now must reckon with Democrats taking over the U.S. Congress in January following the U.S. midterm elections, and they could demand more support for Ukraine.

Also, Russia’s wartime economy is under heavy strain, and Ukraine is reeling from devastating aerial attacks on its power grid.

Fighting continues on the front line, where little territory has changed hands this year. Both countries are battering each other with long-range missiles and drones.

Three people died and 11 were injured after Russia launched a daytime attack on a market in the southern Odesa region, local authorities said. Residential buildings were damaged, said Oleh Kiper, head of the regional military administration.

Overnight, Russia struck the Zaporizhzhia region in southern Ukraine and the eastern city of Kharkiv, wounding seven civilians and damaging property, Ukrainian officials said.

Russia’s Defense Ministry said it downed 627 Ukrainian drones overnight, 150 of them over the region around St. Petersburg. Regional Gov. Alexander Drozdenko said the drones started a fire at the port of Ust-Luga, a main facility for Russian oil exports, injuring three workers.

Meanwhile, a 49-year-old Indonesian man reportedly was captured on the battlefield in southern Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region after he claimed he was unknowingly recruited to fight for the Russian military.

The Indonesian Embassy in Kyiv was seeking access to the man, who was in Ukrainian custody, according to Yvonne Mewengkang, a spokesperson for the Indonesian Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

According to Ukraine’s “I Want to Live” project that offers Russian troops the opportunity to surrender, the man was taken to occupied Donetsk with no military training and then to the Zaporizhzhia region, where his unit was attacked and he was captured.

The man said he signed what he believed to be a contract to work in construction for one year in Moscow, the group said on Telegram.

Ukrainian and Russian officials had no immediate comment.

— AP reporters Susie Blann in Kyiv, Ukraine, Barry Hatton in Lisbon, Portugal and Edna Tarigan in Jakarta contributed.

scraped.title: HK to gazette bill banning national security offenders from teaching
scraped.description: The Hong Kong government has announced a draft law set to be gazetted this Friday barring people convicted of national security offences from becoming teachers in the city.
scraped.author: James Lee
scraped.h1: Hong Kong to gazette bill barring those with national security convictions from teaching
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

The Hong Kong government has announced a draft law set to be gazetted this Friday barring people convicted of national security offences from becoming teachers in the city.

The Education Bureau said in a Thursday statement that the national security safeguard under the Education (Amendment) Bill 2026, along with a certification requirement, would “ensure that all teachers are fit and proper persons.”

It said it would gazette the bill on Friday “with the aim of enhancing the teacher registration mechanism by imposing practising certificate requirements, and introducing a mechanism to handle matters of teacher registration for persons convicted of offences endangering national security.”

The new system would “elevate society’s recognition of the education profession and raise the social status of teachers,” the statement said. The bill is set to be introduced to the Legislative Council (LegCo) on November 25.

Hong Kong authorities introduced national security-focused curriculum guidelines months after Beijing imposed a national security law in the city in June 2020.

Teachers in local schools must now also pass a test on the city’s mini-constitution and its national security legislation before they can be appointed.

The certification system established under the bill will grant teachers a practising certificate valid for no more than three school years, after which it must be renewed.

See also: Nat. security checks now required for school activities by external organisers to prevent ‘political propaganda’

“Amid the complex and rapidly changing development of our society, the public and parents have increasingly high expectations of teachers’ professionalism,” the statement said.

“The bill meets schools’ actual operational needs, encourages teachers to keep pace with the times and strengthens teacher management, with the ultimate goal of safeguarding the well-being of students,” it continued.

scraped.title: HK police reportedly question churches over Tai Po fire memorial masses
scraped.description: Two Catholic churches have reportedly been questioned by police over plans to hold a one-year anniversary memorial mass for victims of the Tai Po fire.
scraped.author: Hillary Leung
scraped.h1: Hong Kong police reportedly question two Catholic churches over Tai Po fire memorial masses
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

Two Catholic churches have reportedly been questioned by police over plans to hold a one-year anniversary memorial mass for victims of the Tai Po fire.

Immaculate Heart of Mary Church in Tai Po was questioned by police twice after announcing a special service this Sunday to mourn the 168 people killed in the fatal blaze last November, former radio host and local parishioner Antony Yiu said.

The church has since replaced the anniversary mass with a general ceremony for “the brothers and sisters who died in the past year,” according to a Facebook post on Tuesday.

“As a churchgoer, I respect the church’s decision. But I’d like to ask: do police now have the power to dictate who believers pray for?” Yiu wrote .

In a screenshot of the since-deleted social media post, the church had written: “It is almost the one-year anniversary of the Wang Fuk Court fire in Tai Po. The sorrow still lingers.”

“With November being the month of remembrance in the Catholic Church, we pray for the eternal rest of the deceased… we ask God for mercy, compassion and blessing.”

Separately, a church in Wan Chai – Our Lady of Mount Carmel – also planned a memorial mass marking one year since the deadly fire, local media reported citing churchgoers.

The church, however, did not publicise the mass.

On a Commercial Radio show on Tuesday, Our Lady of Mount Carmel parish priest Father Thomas Law said November was a month of remembrance for the Catholic community, and that the church held such a memorial every year.

Asked whether the mass would address victims of the Tai Po fire, Law said that anyone who wished to pray for them might do so, and that there was “no need to add or subtract.” He said he had not been contacted by police.

But hours after the radio segment aired, reporters learned from Law that he had since been questioned by three police officers asking about details of the mass and how many people would attend.

Law said that police did not threaten him, and that they were just concerned and “curious.”

Police said in response to HKFP that officers would “act in accordance with the law based on actual circumstances and maintain communication with organisers where necessary” when handling events.

Secretary for Security Chris Tang said on a television programme last week that he understood the desire of victims’ families to mark the anniversary. He said that as long as they abided by the law , authorities would “definitely assist.”

Asked if police had received applications for memorial events, Tang said only that police would consider factors including the safety of the venue and families’ wishes.

scraped.title: Xi-Trump-Putin summit evokes 1945 Yalta carve-up
scraped.description: A possible China-US-Russia summit has prompted alarm of a modern-day Yalta Conference, with three powerful men carving up the world -- with little regard for Ukraine, Europe and Taiwan or anyone else.
scraped.author: AFP
scraped.h1: Xi-Trump-Putin summit in Shenzhen evokes 1945 Yalta carve-up
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

A possible China-US-Russia summit has prompted alarm of a modern-day Yalta Conference, with three powerful men carving up the world — with little regard for Ukraine, Europe and Taiwan or anyone else.

But apart from an historic photo opportunity, the meeting between Presidents Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin at the November 18-19 APEC summit in Shenzhen will likely achieve little, analysts say.

When then US president Franklin D. Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Yalta in February 1945, they laid out the post-WWII settlement and new territorial boundaries in Europe.

That meeting in Yalta, then in the Soviet Union and now in a part of Ukraine annexed by Russia in 2014, laid out the foundations for the Soviet domination of Eastern Europe and the Cold War.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky has raised alarm that Shenzhen could be a Yalta-like “redistribution of spheres of influence” for the 21st century.

At talks in Abu Dhabi this week — the first since February — Russian negotiators rattled Ukraine and its European supporters by pushing a review of the continent’s security architecture as part of any peace deal, with the US also floating a new framework.

Russia’s delegation chief in Abu Dhabi, Vladimir Medinsky, fanned such fears by questioning the inclusion of Europe in further talks.

The trilateral rankles because it signals “the idea that a few great powers can decide the security and future of other countries over their heads”, according to Tsiporah Fried at the Hudson Institute.

The format alone “would already send a message about who counts, and whose interests can be negotiated by others”, she told AFP.

Beyond the symbolism, however, divergent interests make the creation of a new world order in Shenzhen unlikely.

Even the agenda reportedly remains contentious: Russia has suggested the meeting focus on Ukraine, Trump has pushed for talks on nuclear weapons and the Iran war, and China has remained tight-lipped on both.

“The three parties have vastly different demands, making the management of expectations difficult. There is a high probability that talks could end without a breakthrough,” according to Wang Wen, dean of the Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies at Renmin University in Beijing.

There are also few issues where input from all three leaders could bring progress.

The main points of contention between Beijing and Washington are trade and the AI technology race, for instance.

Beijing — which presents itself as a champion of multilateralism — has repeatedly said that Europe should be part of peace negotiations over Ukraine.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said that in a recent meeting, Xi showed “irritation” when the idea of the trilateral talks covering Ukraine came up.

“He explicitly pointed out that this is a European conflict, in which the Europeans must also be at the table,” Steinmeier told ARD.

On nuclear disarmament, China has long insisted that the US and Russia reduce their own giant nuclear arsenals before it agrees to talks on its own stockpile.

The summit therefore is more likely to produce minor outcomes such as crisis hotlines or some cooperation on counter-terrorism, public health, or climate change, Wang told AFP.

“There is no single enemy to unite all three great powers the way that the fight against Nazi Germany united Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin,” said Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at Australian National University.

“It follows that piecemeal horse-trading is in; a grand bargain is out.”

However, Taiwan — which China claims — will still be watching the meeting closely, Sung said.

“If the Trump administration is open to abandoning one partner (Ukraine) out of convenience, then it can abandon another,” he said.

The Trump administration has sought to reassert US dominance over the “Western hemisphere” — including by capturing Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January — but splitting the world among great powers like it’s 1945 may not guarantee security.

China has opposed the logic of Yalta — the clandestine division of spheres of influence and major powers determining the fate of other nations — “from the very beginning”, according to Renmin University’s Wang.

See also: What the US midterms mean for ties with China

China could allay fears of a second Yalta by using the summit to “emphasise the defence of sovereignty and support for multilateral organisations”, Wang said.

If Beijing uses the meeting to insist on European inclusion in talks regarding the continent’s security, it “could, in fact, open a new window for communication between China and Europe”, he said.

“The original Yalta opened the path to the Korean War and Indochina Wars in addition to various conflicts and insurgencies across Asia, Africa, and Latin America,” said Chong Ja Ian at the National University of Singapore.

Any Yalta 2.0 agreement “will almost certainly run into the same kinds of issues”, Chong said.

Next week, Mumbai will become the stage for one of the world’s boldest climate ideas. The largest ever Earthshot Prize edition will bring together innovators, investors, businesses, policymakers and young people to turn environmental solutions into impact at scale. Five winners will each receive £1 million to accelerate their work.

This year two of the 15 finalists are based in India. As the Prize arrives in Mumbai, India’s growing influence in clean growth and climate innovation will be on full display.

items.title: Japan Faces Economic Fallout From Nvidia Leadership Crisis
items.summary: The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on November 12 following allegations involving a woman suspected of links to Chinese intelligence has raised concerns in Japan over the potential impact on semiconductor investment, financial markets and the yen, as uncertainty surrounding the American AI chipmaker threatens to disrupt the global technology industry. (News On Japan)

scraped.title: Japan Faces Economic Fallout From Nvidia Leadership Crisis
scraped.description: The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on November 12 following allegations involving a woman suspected of links to Chinese intelligence has raised concerns in Japan over the potential impact on semiconductor investment, financial markets and the yen, as uncertainty surrounding the American AI chipmaker threatens to disrupt the global technology industry.
scraped.author: News On Japan
scraped.h1: Japan Faces Economic Fallout From Nvidia Leadership Crisis
scraped.body_text:
TOKYO - The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on November 12 following allegations involving a woman suspected of links to Chinese intelligence has raised concerns in Japan over the potential impact on semiconductor investment, financial markets and the yen, as uncertainty surrounding the American AI chipmaker threatens to disrupt the global technology industry.

Huang, who founded Nvidia in 1993 and built it into a company valued at approximately 5.8 trillion dollars, or more than 900 trillion yen, stepped down as chief executive, president and director. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has been appointed interim CEO while the company searches for a permanent successor. The departure comes as Japan is seeking to strengthen its domestic semiconductor industry and expand investment in artificial intelligence, with Japanese manufacturers and technology companies increasingly tied to the global supply chain for advanced chips. Huang has maintained close connections with Japan's semiconductor industry. During a visit to Tokyo in July, he attended a gathering of semiconductor executives at an izakaya restaurant in the Kanda district, reflecting Nvidia's growing importance to Japanese technology companies. The controversy surrounding Huang involves allegations that he had an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a former television journalist in China and former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, which reportedly purchased billions of dollars worth of advanced Nvidia semiconductors. According to reports, Megaspeed developed data centers in Southeast Asia that were subsequently used by Chinese technology giant Alibaba, raising questions about whether American export restrictions on advanced AI chips had been circumvented. The allegations of espionage and unauthorized disclosure of product information have not been established as fact. The scandal could have wider implications for Japan because of its potential impact on negotiations between the United States and China over semiconductor exports and rare earth supplies. Washington has restricted exports of advanced AI chips to China, while President Donald Trump had reportedly considered relaxing some controls in exchange for greater Chinese cooperation on rare earth exports. However, the allegations involving Nvidia could make such concessions politically difficult, potentially complicating negotiations between the two countries. Rare earth minerals are essential to Japanese manufacturing, particularly in the automotive, electronics and advanced technology industries. Any disruption to supplies could create additional pressure on production costs and supply chains. Tetsuo Kotani, a professor specializing in American politics and international security, warned that the controversy could weaken Washington's negotiating position and make future agreements with Beijing more difficult. The implications for Japan's financial markets could also be significant. AI-related stocks have attracted substantial investment in the United States, and a loss of confidence in Nvidia could trigger a broader correction in technology shares, affecting Japanese investors and semiconductor-related companies. However, a decline in American technology stocks could also have an unexpected benefit for Japan through the foreign exchange market. Large capital flows into US equities have contributed to the yen's weakness, and a reversal of those investments could encourage funds to return to Japan, supporting the Japanese currency. A stronger yen would reduce the cost of imported energy, food and raw materials, potentially easing financial pressure on Japanese households and businesses. Analysts suggested that while investors exposed to American technology stocks could suffer losses, a recovery in the yen could benefit companies and consumers more dependent on domestic economic activity. The scale of any impact remains uncertain, particularly as concerns have already emerged over whether the rapid growth in AI-related investment is sustainable. For Japan, the immediate concern is whether Nvidia's leadership crisis will undermine confidence in the global AI industry at a time when the country is committing substantial resources to semiconductor development and advanced computing. The outcome of US-China negotiations, changes in semiconductor export restrictions and movements in American technology stocks will be key factors determining how far the consequences extend into Japan's economy.

scraped.h1: Japanese Reporter Held in Russia for a Month With No Prospect of Release
scraped.body_text:
MOSCOW - The Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper identified its correspondent detained in Russia on espionage allegations as Yuki Imai on November 12, one month after his arrest by Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB), with no indication of when he might be released.

Imai, a male journalist stationed in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk on Russia's Sakhalin Island, was detained by the FSB on October 13 on suspicion of espionage. The Hokkaido Shimbun announced his identity for the first time on November 12, explaining that Imai had obtained a valid Russian journalist visa and was engaged in routine reporting activities at the time of his detention. The newspaper said it had decided to identify Imai publicly because a month had passed since his detention without any clear prospect of his release, making it necessary to appeal more directly to the public for support. The company emphasized that Imai had been carrying out legitimate journalistic duties in Russia and that his continued detention raised concerns about his safety and rights. The Hokkaido Shimbun said it would continue working closely with relevant authorities and organizations to ensure Imai's safety and protect his rights while making every possible effort to secure his release and return to Japan as soon as possible.

scraped.title: Dangerous Photography Plagues Kyoto
scraped.description: Visitors flocking to a popular autumn foliage destination in Kyoto
scraped.author: News On Japan
scraped.h1: Dangerous Photography Plagues Kyoto's Hot Spot
scraped.body_text:
KYOTO - Visitors flocking to a popular autumn foliage destination in Kyoto's Nishikyo Ward have sparked growing concerns among residents, with photographers repeatedly stepping into the middle of busy roads to capture pictures and drivers illegally parking near bus stops and residential streets.

The tree-lined avenue in Katsurazaka New Town, known for its striking autumn colors, has become a favorite destination for photography enthusiasts. Nearly 360 sweetgum trees, known in Japan as momiji-bafu, line a roughly 2-kilometer stretch of road featuring curves and changes in elevation, creating a picturesque landscape as their leaves turn brilliant shades of red, orange and yellow. While many visitors enjoy the scenery responsibly, others have been engaging in dangerous behavior that disrupts traffic and creates problems for nearby residents. At one point, a man walked into the middle of the road to take photographs despite approaching traffic. A vehicle coming from behind sounded its horn as he continued taking pictures. Other visitors were seen stepping beyond the sidewalk and standing near the center of the roadway to capture photographs from what they considered the best angle. One local resident suggested that the growing popularity of photographs posted on social media was attracting increasing numbers of visitors. "People post pictures on X, and I think more people are coming here after seeing them," the resident said. In another incident, a woman continued posing for photographs even as a motorcycle approached. After the motorcycle passed, she moved farther into the road to resume taking pictures. A passing police patrol car issued a warning over its loudspeaker, telling visitors to return to the sidewalk because standing in the road was dangerous. However, some photographers stepped back onto the roadway shortly after the police vehicle had passed. Asked why they were taking pictures in the road, one visitor explained that the location offered the best view of the autumn foliage. "This is the best position for taking pictures. That's where the scenery looks beautiful," the visitor said. When questioned about the danger of standing in the roadway, the photographer replied, "Well, just for a little while." A foreign visitor who had also been taking photographs from the road acknowledged the potential danger, saying, "It might be a little dangerous." Illegal parking has become another source of frustration for residents. Some visitors have been leaving their vehicles near active bus stops, where parking is prohibited, while others have parked along narrow residential streets, making it difficult for local drivers to enter and exit their neighborhoods. Residents say the additional traffic and improperly parked vehicles have become particularly troublesome during the morning rush. "We try to drive carefully ourselves, but when you're in a hurry in the morning and get held up by illegally parked cars, it wastes valuable time," one resident said. Another resident described being verbally confronted after asking a visitor to behave more responsibly. "I once warned someone here, and they told me to shut up," the resident said. "This really is a residential road that everyone uses. We want people to come here with some sense of responsibility and respect for others." The problems have reportedly increased as photographs of Katsurazaka's autumn scenery spread across social media, drawing more visitors to the neighborhood. With Kyoto entering the peak autumn foliage season, residents are calling on sightseers to respect traffic rules, avoid obstructing roads and remember that the area's scenic streets are also part of a residential community where people live and travel every day.
