scraped.title: Extreme weather risk is scaring big corporations away from poorer countries – that hurts the companies, too
scraped.description: When floods, heat waves and other climate disasters cost companies money, the results can shape their willingness to invest there in the future.
scraped.author: Jonas Gamso
scraped.h1: Extreme weather risk is scaring big corporations away from poorer countries – that hurts the companies, too
scraped.body_text:
Share article

Print article

When multinational companies decide where to build a factory, open a mine or establish a regional office, they have to consider whether the investment will still be profitable years into the future.

Making that decision increasingly means thinking about risks, like whether surrounding roads will flood, worker safety will be compromised by extreme heat in the summer, and clean water will be available.

As climate change increases the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events around the world, these effects can be especially severe in poorer countries that lack the resources to prepare for disasters or recover quickly after they hit.

I study how political and environmental risks affect international business . In my new book, “ Multinational Corporations and Climate Change: Risks, Responsibilities, and Resilience ,” I explore how disaster risk is affecting the ways global companies see these climate-vulnerable markets, and how those views are leading some foreign investors to avoid these developing nations altogether.

Low- and middle-income countries aren’t the only ones that suffer when multinational corporations pass them by. The companies themselves also stand to lose out on business opportunities in emerging markets if they pull away.

Evidence from several studies suggests that multinationals are systematically avoiding investing in the most climate-vulnerable countries. These include my own analysis of 159 countries. Although these studies focus on different samples, they identify the same trend: Countries characterized by greater climate vulnerability received less foreign investment .

The results are not trivial. My book identifies a 12% reduction in foreign direct investment for each 1-point rise in climate vulnerability on a 100-point scale, while holding other relevant factors constant. This vulnerability data measures countries’ exposure to climate hazards as well as their capacity to adapt.

Companies rarely say why they’re avoiding a particular location, but their climate-related concerns occasionally become visible.

For example, Google halted plans to build a US$200 million data center in Chile after an environmental court revoked its construction permit over the likely effects on water supplies and the environment. Similarly, a $1 billion data center proposed in Kenya by Microsoft and the Abu Dhabi-based artificial intelligence company G42 was delayed and ultimately suspended amid concerns about water stress in the area.

Companies have reason to be cautious about climate risks.

One analysis of 71 large publicly traded companies found that firms reporting major flood losses experienced a 5% average decline in shareholder value over the following year, after accounting for broader market movements.

In Vietnam, typhoons and floods caused an estimated $475 million in damage to energy and transportation infrastructure in 2022. Unreliable infrastructure cost companies there about $280 million .

Severe flooding in Thailand in 2011 forced several companies, including Toyota, Nissan and Honda, to temporarily suspend production as factories flooded, shutting down production of parts or vehicles made there.

Costs like those shape where companies choose to invest next.

While climate risk does not stop all investment in climate-vulnerable markets, it does make projects in these nations relatively more expensive, less attractive and more difficult to finance than less risky locations.

For developing countries, less foreign investment means fewer jobs are created . These countries also have fewer opportunities to benefit from exposure to the new technologies that multinationals bring when they invest abroad.

Those results highlight another way climate change is deepening global inequality. It reduces the economic activity that could support future development, while simultaneously damaging physical infrastructure and threatening human health and well-being.

Developing countries are especially vulnerable to the effects of rising global temperatures, whether for their dependence on agricultural markets, geography or relatively fragile infrastructure . A report from the Climate Impact Lab at the University of Chicago projects that 90% of heat-related deaths in the coming decades will take place in low- and middle-income countries. Similarly, a 2022 study found that around 90% of people exposed to flooding live in developing nations.

Yet poor countries have contributed only a tiny fraction of the emissions that are causing climate change, even as they face the brunt of the damage. For example, African countries are responsible for less than 4% of greenhouse gas emissions globally. But they stand to experience the greatest negative effects of climate change.

When a company avoids investing in climate-vulnerable countries, that may reduce its exposure to floods, droughts or extreme heat, but the decision also carries potential costs for the company.

Many of these countries have growing consumer markets, energy resources or critical minerals that multinationals need. Companies that dismiss them as too risky may lose out on promising opportunities.

For example, the Democratic Republic of Congo supplies most of the world’s cobalt , while Indonesia has become the dominant producer of nickel . These countries are highly vulnerable to climate change , which is likely scaring some companies away .

Yet companies with a greater tolerance for risk have established strong positions in those countries’ mineral industries . Thus, more cautious firms may reduce their risk exposure, but they are also surrendering access to important resources and growing markets.

There are ways to help companies overcome their climate-risk avoidance so more investment can pour into these countries:

Foreign aid from wealthy countries can help developing countries shore up their roads, ports, electrical grids and water systems before extreme storms or droughts occur. My 2025 study found that climate-vulnerable countries that received more aid for climate adaptation also received more foreign direct investment than those receiving less aid. The result suggests the funding may reassure companies that climate risks are being addressed.

International development banks can share some of the risks by providing climate risk insurance to multinationals. This would offer a safety net to absorb some of the losses if a covered disruption prevents a project from operating as intended. The World Bank already offers similar coverage against political risk incidents, which has given companies confidence to invest in countries such as Kenya , Mozambique and Nigeria .

Better data can give companies more precise information about climate risks. Many risk scores label entire nations as vulnerable or not, even though exposure varies from one city or project site to another. More detailed information about local flood exposure, water availability, heat, infrastructure and adaptation capabilities would allow companies to limit their avoidance to the riskiest areas, instead of bypassing those countries altogether.

Understanding the local risk, insuring companies against risk and helping countries make their infrastructure more resilient to storms, droughts and heat can help boost investment in ways that benefit the companies and spur economic growth and development in climate-vulnerable countries at the same time.

Associate Professor of International Trade and Global Studies, Arizona State University

scraped.title: Global Warming Remains Unchecked, Experts Warn at UN’s COP31 Climate Summit - Inside Climate News
scraped.description: Current climate and energy policies will have devastating consequences for ecosystems and communities worldwide, new reports show.
scraped.author: By Bob Berwyn
scraped.h1: Global Warming Remains Unchecked, Experts Warn at UN’s COP31 Climate Summit
scraped.body_text:
ANTALYA, Turkey—Amid upbeat green-tech pep talks and notices for happy hours at the annual United Nations COP31 climate change conference on Thursday, two new reports offered a stark reminder of how far the world remains from containing global warming.

Climate Action Tracker , a nonprofit group that analyzes climate policies, found that the planet is still on track to warm nearly 5 degrees Fahrenheit by 2100, a rise that would devastate coral reefs, disrupt agriculture and forests and melt most of the world’s ice. In a separate bulletin, the European Union’s Copernicus climate change service reported that global warming has accelerated significantly since the 2015 Paris climate agreement .

When the Paris agreement was adopted, the average global temperature was projected to surpass the pact’s long-term threshold of 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit above the preindustrial average around 2045. After another decade of global climate summits, warming is now projected to cross that benchmark as soon as 2029, according to Copernicus.

“This striking change suggests that global warming has accelerated in recent years,” the EU scientists wrote. Even without understanding every aspect of the recent rapid global temperature increase, “It is clear that the ever-growing concentrations of greenhouse gases emitted by human activity in the atmosphere remain the main driver of this trend.”

The current level of warming has already triggered deadly and destructive floods, wildfires and catastrophic glacier collapses, said Swedish activist Greta Thunberg , who is attending the U.N. “Conferences of the Parties” climate talks, for the first time since 2021.

“The climate crisis is a matter of life and death,” she said. “The actions from those in power here are completely detached from reality. As we speak, we are losing priceless lives, ecosystems and species that we will never get back.”

Sarah Heck , a climate policy analyst with Climate Analytics , an international climate science and policy institute, said governments have failed to meaningfully improve the outlook for end-of-century warming.

“Our message is a stark one,” Heck said. “Collective government action on climate change has stalled for the fifth consecutive year.” Efforts to speed up the shift away from fossil fuels have been negated by new oil and gas drilling projects and governments that are “delaying, weakening or rolling back their climate policies.”

Even under the most optimistic scenario, assuming full implementation of existing policies and promises, global temperatures would rise 3.4 degrees Fahrenheit above preindustrial levels by 2100, an increase climate scientists consider extremely dangerous .

While there has been progress on developing renewable energy sources, the “brutal truth is that these positive developments have not yet added up to bend the curve fast enough,” said Niklas Höhne , a researcher with The New Climate Institute. Developing new oil and gas projects is a bit like discovering your food is burning and then turning up the stove instead of turning it off, he added.

Getting into the specifics of the current negotiations at COP31 surrounding global renewable goals, he noted that conference co-hosts Turkey and Australia have so far opposed including the word “clean” in connection with electrification targets.

“It’s very hard to understand, and the only explanation I can think of is their interest in fossil fuels,” Höhne said.

Australia is one of the world’s biggest coal exporters, and Turkey is a major coal consumer, with its power sector still highly dependent on the most climate-damaging fossil fuel. Even as they host this year’s climate conference, neither country has offered any specific plans to transition away from fossil fuels.

Bill Hare, the CEO of Climate Analytics, called out wealthy, developed countries for their lack of leadership on climate action, noting that European Union Commission President Ursula von der Leyen failed to mention anything about transitioning away from fossil fuels during her speech this week at COP31.

“Governments … at this COP have a stark choice,” Hare said. If they continue supporting fossil fuels, “it would consign humanity and our ecosystems to insurmountable economic damage and irretrievable loss.”

scraped.author: By Dylan Baddour
scraped.h1: Feds Greenlight Construction of Advanced Nuclear Reactors in Texas
scraped.body_text:
The Nuclear Regulatory Commission this week issued a permit for construction of four next-generation nuclear reactors at a petrochemical complex on the rural Gulf Coast of Texas.

The Long Mott Generating Station, developed by chemical giant Dow and nuclear startup X-energy, is one of two flagship projects selected by the U.S. Energy Department in 2020 for its Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program, intended to kickstart a new era of growth for the nation’s nascent nuclear sector.

“This milestone marks a significant step forward,” Mike Goff, principal deputy assistant secretary for nuclear energy, said in a press release Monday. “The NRC’s approval demonstrates meaningful progress toward deploying advanced reactors.”

The Texas project is at the leading edge of a new generation of reactor designs that could revolutionize the commercial model for atomic energy. They replace the gargantuan construction projects currently required for nuclear power plants with small, modular units that can be produced in factories and then shipped and assembled onsite at industrial installations, from data centers to petrochemical plants.

“We understand that owning a nuclear facility is a different kind of responsibility,” said Kreshka Young, North American business director for energy and climate at Dow, during a public meeting on the project’s construction permits in the town of Port Lavaca in September. “We do not take that lightly.”

Dow plans to install four 80-megawatt reactors by X-energy at its Seadrift Operations complex, on the Gulf Coast between Houston and Corpus Christi. The units won’t require the towering, concrete containment structures characteristic of existing nuclear reactors, nor the 10-mile emergency planning zone, thanks to what scientists describe as revolutionary safety features inherent in new reactor designs.

X-energy CEO J. Clay Sell, a former deputy energy secretary, has described the company’s Xe-100 unit as “physically impossible to melt down.”

Diane Wilson, a retired fourth-generation shrimper from the tiny nearby town of Seadrift and director of San Antonio Bay Waterkeeper, a local environmental organization, remains deeply skeptical. “Frankly, it’s outrageous,” she said. “This is outrageous.”

Spent fuel from the reactors will be stored indefinitely on-site as nuclear waste, she noted, as the U.S. still lacks a permanent national disposal site.

In 2025, Wilson’s organization filed legal challenges to the project’s permit application over safety concerns, which were ultimately dismissed by the NRC. The agency approved Dow’s reactor construction permit after an expedited review under executive orders from President Donald Trump aimed at accelerating the national energy sector.

“We delivered on the 18-month schedule, proving we can do rigorous safety reviews on predictable timelines that move advanced nuclear technology from design to construction,” said NRC Chairman Ho K. Nieh in a press release.

Dow still needs to make a final decision to proceed with the project, the company said in a release . If it does, construction could begin before 2030.

If the project proves successful, it would “provide a pathway other industries can emulate” to install dedicated, onsite power generation, said Martin O’Neal, general counsel for the Nuclear Energy Institute, at the September meeting in Port Lavaca.

The NRC hosted the meeting to take questions and comments from the public on the Long Mott Generating Station.

“The nuclear industry is watching this project very closely,” O’Neal said.

In the last three decades, the U.S. has built just one new nuclear power plant, but federal authorities have pushed in recent years for an industry revival based on new reactor designs. The NRC issued its first permit for construction of an advanced test reactor in 2023 , and its first permit for an advanced commercial reactor in March 2026 .

While typical nuclear reactors use water to cool, advanced designs use alternatives, from molten salt to gas. The Xe-100 uses helium gas. Rather than traditional fuel rods, the Xe-100 uses a pelletized fuel form in a moving bed of pebbles.

“These are new technologies,” said Mehdi Reisi Fard, deputy director of advanced reactors at the NRC, during the public meeting in Port Lavaca in September.

The innovations add up to a feature known as “functional containment,” where the natural resilience and circulation of fuel pebbles prevents the kind of runaway warming that could lead the reactor to meltdown.

Compared with current control systems, functional containment is “less reliant on pumps or human intervention to mitigate anomalies,” Fard explained.

It works thanks to a new kind of pelletized nuclear fuel, called TRISO fuel , which has been developed in Energy Department labs over decades.

“Simply put, TRISO particles cannot melt in a commercial high-temperature reactor,” a DOE webpage says.

The new technology enables developers to skip the big, expensive safety features, like the massive concrete casings, that are required for traditional water-cooled reactors.

“The argument these developers are using is that they don’t need a physical containment because the reactor is so safe,” said Edwin Lyman, director of nuclear power safety with the Union of Concerned Scientists, in an interview earlier this year. “Nuclear designers have been trying to reduce the costs of containment, and one way to do that would be to eliminate it entirely.”

But Lyman doesn’t consider the fuel to be as safe as authorities say.

“It’s just a myth that this fuel is indestructible or meltdown-proof,” he said. “This fuel has vulnerabilities.”

scraped.author: By Dan Gearino
scraped.h1: How Data Center Opponents Won the Election
scraped.body_text:
Data center developers had a rough election, losing 40 of 41 ballot measures nationwide.

The volunteers behind one of those measures celebrated this week at Big Walnut Grill in Sunbury, Ohio, a suburb of Columbus. These were the 20 or so people who gathered signatures, delivered yard signs and knocked on doors to support a referendum to ban large data centers within city limits. They won 79 percent to 21 percent.

The campaign taught them about the power of community organizing, said Alicia Doty, one of the leaders. She lives near the proposed Amazon Web Services data center that inspired the ballot measure.

“We are much stronger together,” she said, in an interview later that evening.

Doty and her neighbors won partly because they were a movement that emerged from genuine community concerns , and if I were a data center developer, I’d be chomping on antacids right now. It is difficult to see how the data center industry—including some of the largest companies in the world—can shake off rejection in so many of the best locations for construction.

Data center opponents are apprehensive about the scale of these projects, their potential emissions and their demands for electricity and water, which could drive up costs and strain supplies for other users. Fears of artificial intelligence also play a role, since the largest data centers provide the computing power for AI systems.

It helped, Doty said, that the people campaigning for data centers hurt their own cause. The most visible local campaign against the referendum was from NetChoice , a trade group whose members include Amazon. NetChoice canvassers and printed materials sought to discredit the ballot measure as funded by “extreme California special interests,” according to a door-hanger distributed in Sunbury. That message didn’t connect with voters.

Pataskala, which is 23 miles from Sunbury, also had a data center referendum. Pataskala voters rejected data centers with a 74 percent to 26 percent vote.

In at least one case, the people handing out materials opposing the ballot measure appear to have gotten their cities mixed up. One piece distributed in Sunbury said, “PATASKALA BEWARE” and then showed a cartoon wolf holding a clipboard. “There is a California wolf at our door.”

The warning about funding from California refers to a $10,000 donation to Conserve Ohio, a statewide organization opposing data centers, from PowerSwitch Action, an Oakland, Calif.-based nonprofit that supports progressive causes. The donation was the largest of $16,356 listed in Conserve Ohio’s most recent report filed with the Ohio Secretary of State.

Conserve Ohio’s average donation was $103. Excluding PowerSwitch’s contribution, the average was $40.

Conserve Ohio provides free legal advice to groups such as the one in Sunbury. I wrote about Conserve Ohio last month, including how it began with a few volunteers in rural Adams and Brown counties.

Austin Baurichter, one of several Conserve Ohio leaders, said it’s ironic that data center developers, largely based on the West Coast, such as Amazon, would criticize his group for accepting a donation from a California organization.

“We are and will continue to be grateful for any donation help we can get from anyone,” he said.

It’s a stretch to say PowerSwitch Action was funding the Sunbury campaign. Doty’s group spent about $5,000 and raised that money largely from group members, she said.

NetChoice didn’t respond to messages seeking comment.

“We appreciate the opportunity to engage with communities on the benefits that our data center investments bring,” said an Amazon spokesperson in an email. “We remain committed to setting a high bar for responsible data center development [and] continuing to engage communities early in our development process.”

Amazon also explained its approach to data centers and responses to common objections in an Oct. 2 blog post .

The Data Center Coalition, a trade group for data center companies, had this statement:

“The data center industry is committed to engaging with residents and local leaders to understand community priorities, towards ensuring that the growth of digital infrastructure meets local standards and delivers clear benefits that communities are seeking,” said Dan Diorio, executive vice president of state policy and government affairs for the Data Center Coalition.

Diorio said communities that indicate they are “closed for business and investment” may lose opportunities, costing them high-wage jobs and tax revenue.

The election was a big win for Conserve Ohio. With a tiny budget, the group has worked with data center opposition campaigns across the state, advising residents how to get measures on their local ballots.

“I was amazed,” said Nikki Gerber, a leader of Conserve Ohio, about the election results. Voters “acted like they want democracy back, and that gave me hope.”

Gerber owns Moondoggie Liveree, an outdoor tourism business. She joined the push against data centers this year after Amazon Web Services proposed building a data center in her county.

Voters in Sprigg Township, which includes the project site, passed a referendum last week to establish zoning regulations that would limit data centers. But Gerber is concerned the referendum, with text revised by township officials, isn’t strong enough.

Gerber is also wary of the potential for state or local officials to find ways to push the project through, despite local opposition. I asked if she’s pleased to see Democrat Amy Acton, former director of the Ohio Department of Health, win the election for governor. Acton has said she supports a “conditional moratorium” on data center development.

“I still don’t have any faith in the government until I see the government do something for us,” Gerber said.

Nationwide, data center opponents won in 40 of the 41 local races where development was on the ballot last week, according to Ballotpedia. Ohio was the epicenter of voting on the issue, with 21 measures, followed by Illinois with four and Maine with three.

The only place data centers won was Harwood, N.D., near Fargo, which rejected a referendum that would have required additional review of proposed development, including data centers. The measure failed on a 24 percent to 76 percent vote. The regional chamber of commerce fought the referendum, saying that taxes would increase with new limits on development, as Fortune reported .

Equity analysts viewed the nationwide results, with local rejection of data centers and the election of candidates who oppose the projects, as potentially harmful to the economy.

Morgan Stanley, the investment bank, said the electoral success of Democrats increases the chances of restrictions on development , which could “split the country into areas that are open to new data centers and those without,” according to the Associated Press. Morgan Stanley identified Acton and Democrat Gina Hinojosa in Texas as incoming governors who could restrict data center development.

If that happens, it would be significant for the industry. Ohio and Texas are among the top U.S. markets for data center development.

Developers may hope that the backlash will lose momentum.

But Doty said the Sunbury campaign was no one-off. Organizers are prepared to challenge any effort to build a data center despite the referendum’s outcome, as well as projects in other industries that they believe are not in the community’s best interests.

“Our group is not going away,” she said.

Other stories about the energy transition to take note of this week:

Senate Advances Permitting Overhaul But Roadblocks Loom: The U.S. Senate has begun debate on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, following a procedural vote on Monday. The 73-25 vote, with most Republicans and some Democrats on the prevailing side, indicates support for the measure, but several Democrats said the bill needs changes before they will vote for it on final passage. The debate has divided groups that are typically allies, with many environmental organizations warning that the legislation will lead to a massive buildout of natural gas power plants, as my colleague Marianne Lavelle and I report for ICN .

Why the World Is Still Running on Fossil Fuels After 30 Years of Climate Talks: The smell of fossil fuels has become a familiar part of the United Nations “Conference of the Parties” climate talks, with airplanes and buses transporting people to the talks, as my colleague Bob Berwyn reports from COP31 in Turkey. He places this year’s event in historical context, recounting decades of stalled efforts and false starts.

Cattle Could Soon Be Grazing Under Solar Panels: Christiana, Tenn., is home to the first commercial-scale solar array with cattle grazing, according to the developer, Silicon Ranch. The new project could be a significant step forward for agrivoltaics, which combines agriculture and solar power, as Julian Spector reports for Canary Media . I wrote about the potential for livestock grazing and solar last year after visiting a project in Kentucky.

Solar Power Poised for Rapid Growth, IEA Reports: Ahead of COP31, the International Energy Agency published its annual renewable energy report, forecasting the addition of 3.6 terawatts of solar power capacity by 2031, as Jonathan Touriño Jacobo reports for PV Tech . To put this in perspective, solar power growth would be the driver of global renewable electricity reaching about 45 percent market share in 2031, up from 33 percent in 2025. More than half of the growth in solar capacity would come from utility-scale projects, while the rest would come from rooftop solar and other customer-owned systems.

scraped.title: This surprise cost could derail your heat pump or EV charger installation. Here’s how to avoid it.
scraped.description: If all goes to plan, I will spend a grand total of zero dollars on an electrification project that could have cost me well over $10,000.
scraped.author: Tik Root
scraped.h1: This surprise cost could derail your heat pump or EV charger installation. Here’s how to avoid it.
scraped.body_text:
We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

Δ

A nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to telling stories of climate solutions and a just future.

Δ

“Electrify everything” has become a mantra in the fight against climate change. Switching a home’s heating, cooling, and other energy-intensive loads from fossil fuels to electricity could drastically reduce planet-warming emissions. But electrification has often run into a major, and expensive, hurdle: upgrading a home’s electric capacity.

A home’s connection to the grid is rated by amperage, or amps, which caps the amount of current it can safely draw at once. The standard for houses built in the last few decades is generally 200 amps. Many older residences, however, have a lower limit because they were constructed when electricity powered little more than the lights, refrigerator, microwave, and perhaps the dryer. Research from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory found that roughly a third of homes in the United States have panel capacity of 100 amps or less. In the Northeast, that share rises to closer to half.

As people install heat pumps, induction stoves, and EV chargers, they can run into a couple of potential issues. Their electric panel may simply run out of slots to install more circuit breakers, in which case the relatively easy fix of adding a subpanel often does the trick. But sometimes homeowners run into a bigger problem, where an electrician says all the new loads will push them past their home’s peak power limits.

Upgrading an electrical service can start at a few thousand dollars and quickly skyrocket, particularly in rural areas or places where power lines run underground. “We’ve seen estimates of $10,000 to $20,000,” said AJ Rossman, an electrical engineer with VEIC, a contractor that runs much of Efficiency Vermont’s state program.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The exact scope of the problem is unclear. There is scant data on how many service upgrades are done each year, let alone those that may have been recommended and never made due to the cost. But the Lawrence Berkeley research suggests there may be thousands, if not millions, of homeowners who are told they need to upsize their service as they electrify.

The good news is, there are workarounds — if you or your electrician know where to look. It’s a lesson my wife and I recently learned.

When we moved into our Burlington, Vermont, home, natural gas powered the furnace, stove, and dryer. We knew we’d eventually want to electrify, so I had our service increased from 150 amps to 200. Because we needed the upgrade as part of other work, the bill wasn’t horrible.

The change allowed us to install an EV charger, switch to heat pumps, get an induction stove, and plan for an electric dryer. We were happy to have a home largely free of fossil fuels.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Then we decided to build an addition.

Our plan for an extra 800 square feet would require two more small heat pumps along with lighting, outlets, and ditching our gas dryer. None of this was much of a concern until our electrician did the math. He determined that the laundry room swap alone would push our theoretical load to around 192 amps. Upgrading to 300 or 400 amp service would require trenching a new underground line and possibly even overhauling the transformer serving our block. It could cost us well over $10,000.

I panicked and started digging for answers. I had heard about a growing array of products designed to help people in my situation. For example, a friend had installed a smart panel that monitors how much electricity each circuit is using to ensure demand does not exceed the home’s capacity. If things get close, the panel shuts off lower-priority breakers as needed, then turns them back on when it’s safe.

This was appealing, but expensive. Converting my panel would have cost around $4,000 in materials alone. Even options that control a few circuits starts at about $2,000. With labor, the outlay seemed almost as staggering as a service upgrade.

I came across a cheaper category of devices called load-sharing switches, or smart splitters. They allow two high-demand appliances to share the same circuit, with just one running at a time. That means only the heavier load counts in a home’s demand calculation. Each switch cost around $800, depending on the brand. The issue was that we would probably need at least two to bring our calculated load below 200 amps. That was certainly an improvement, but it still wasn’t cheap and it left little wiggle room for the future.

There must be a better option, I thought. So, as a last-ditch effort, I called my utility provider, who I assumed may have other customers in a similar position. An advisor immediately asked me a question I had taken for granted: Is your electrician sure you need an upgrade?

When my electrician had calculated how much power my house would need, it appears he used the National Electrical Code’s standard method. Simply put, this approach uses the rated loads of all the electrical items in a home to calculate its theoretical load. Using one of the many online calculators to replicate his work, I arrived at the same conclusion: I was already taking up about 187 amps and the addition would push me to around 227 — beyond the panel’s 220-amp limit.

But Burlington Electric told me there was a lesser-known section of the code that could give me a very different answer. Commonly referred to as Section 220.87, even though it was recently moved to section 120.87 , this method uses a year’s worth of utility data to identify a home’s actual peak demand instead of relying on hypothetical usage. Like 73 percent of residences around the country , my home has a smart meter, so it was relatively easy to request that information from my utility. A spreadsheet arrived the next day.

The file was thousands of rows long, so I put it into TrueLoadapp.com , a tool electricians can use to evaluate a customer’s load using this alternative method. It parsed the data to find my peak, which came on January 20, when my home topped out at just under 62 amps. The code mandates a 25 percent buffer when calculating usage, which bumped me about 77 amps.

Even then I was using less than 40 percent of my service and less than half what the standard method calculated. I then added my new loads the traditional way, and discovered there was more than enough capacity without upgrading my service. I had just saved thousands of dollars

“My mission is to get anybody who is considering any sort of electrification to do this first,” said Jake Marin, the founder of TrueLoad. “There are many, many, many situations where there is nothing wrong with your panel.”

Marin used to work at the VEIC, where he was involved in dozens of panel upgrades and started to wonder whether there was a better approach to the problem. That’s when he found 220.87 and built TrueLoad. “It tends to show that you have a lot more headroom than you actually thought,” he said. “People are spending $10,000 or more that they don’t need to.”

This aligns with the Lawrence Berkely research , which found that only a small fraction of homes actually need an upgrade, especially when using 220.87. “Most electrical panels have headroom for additional load,” said lead author Sean Murphy in a webinar earlier this year. Efficiency Vermont also looked into this issue , with similar results.

“We’re finding it really depends on the electrician,” said Rossman, who co-authored the white paper on the topic. It found that many electricians use rules of thumb in evaluating headroom, and few of those surveyed were aware of 220.87. Even homes with smaller services may have more capacity remaining than homeowners or electricians realize. “For a reasonable household, we are not seeing anything that comes close with the 200 amps,” said Rossman, noting that even fully electric homes utilize a fraction of that. “And it’s rare where you need something with more than 100 amps.”

Whether a load calculation is accepted ultimately rests with local inspectors. Some don’t even require one. Those who do shouldn’t have a problem with 220.87 because it’s been around for decades, said Dean Austin, a senior electrical specialist at National Fire Protection Association. Master electrician Johnathan Quong, who owns New England Electric, has been turning to it for years, when the traditional calculation suggests a home lacks capacity.

“We’ve been able to keep tons of people on 100 amp panels,” said Quong, who added that he’s never had an inspector reject a 220.87 project. The bigger obstacle, he said, may be getting electricians to adopt it. At an industry conference this year where the topic came up, he said he sensed skepticism from colleagues accustomed to traditional calculations.

“It didn’t sound like they knew about it, or didn’t feel like that was acceptable, and they still felt like it was their responsibility to make sure that it was 100 percent safe,” he said. “In my mind, there shouldn’t be any resistance.”

One caveat is that homeowners must get usage data from their utility, and Marin said access varies widely. Some utilities print a home’s peak load on the monthly bill, and TrueLoad has a feature for helping users make requests, but customers can still end up having to dig for that data — and navigating the system isn’t easy even for experts.

“I don’t even know how I would get that data from my own smartmeter,” said Ric O’Connell, executive director of GridLab, a nonprofit focused on supporting a clean grid. A few days later he emailed to say that after “a long time” and a battle with a “really poor” user interface, he obtained his data from Pacific Gas and Electric Company in California. It showed that his home peaked at just 65 amps.

For those who can’t access data, there are a few options. Another section of the code, 220.83 (recently changed to 120.83), allows some loads to be discounted based on the assumption that not everything in a home will be running simultaneously. In certain situations, that method may produce an even lower calculated demand than 220.87, said Jenny Low, director of panel optimization work and electrical reassessments for Build It Green, a nonprofit working to create equitable, healthy, and regenerative neighborhoods . At the very least, she said, it should be more forgiving than the standard method.

If I had used that option, my addition would likely have squeaked in under 198 amps, which would not have left enough margin to make me comfortable. The 220.87 route was clearly the smarter move. The 2026 version of the code expands the options by allowing both demand data and load discounting, although adoption may vary depending upon which version of the code a jurisdiction currently uses. The bigger challenge is making sure electricians and homeowners know about it.

For anyone who is short on capacity after using these approaches, load-management options like smart panels and switches are often the cheapest path to electrification. “There are,” said Low, “lots of ways to avoid a panel upgrade.”

As for me, contractors broke ground on the addition last week. If all goes to plan, I will spend a grand total of zero dollars on an electrification project that could have cost me well over $10,000.

scraped.title: Climate progressives won the midterms without saying ‘climate’
scraped.description: How the ideas behind the Green New Deal got an update for the Trump era.
scraped.author: Frida Garza
scraped.h1: Climate progressives won the midterms without saying ‘climate’
scraped.body_text:
We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

Δ

A nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to telling stories of climate solutions and a just future.

Δ

On October 20, the two candidates running to represent Michigan in the U.S. Senate, Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers, took questions for an hour at the Detroit Economic Club. El-Sayed, the Democrat who had previously run for governor, made a name for himself years ago by connecting public health to the climate crisis. He published a fierce defense of the Green New Deal at the time, touting its economic, health, and planetary benefits . But last month at the Detroit Economic Club, El-Sayed didn’t mention the Green New Deal at all.

Instead, the only mentions of such a plan came from his opponent, who used it as an attack on El-Sayed and the Democratic party as a whole. “We need to make sure we don’t have the largest tax increase in the history of the country,” Rogers said, “which is, that’s what the other team is talking about doing.”

A vote for El-Sayed would ring in an era of “big government, government control, more rules, more regulation, another Green New Deal,” Rogers continued. It’s become a common refrain since President Donald Trump’s effort to rebrand the climate movement’s push for widescale public investment in renewable energy as a “Green New Scam.”

Two weeks later, El-Sayed handily won the race.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Even though many of the newly elected Democrats did not talk about the Green New Deal by name, the think tank Climate and Community Institute describes El-Sayed as belonging to a new class of green economic populists who are running for public office (and winning) by connecting the need for climate action to soaring utility bills and the hoarding of wealth by a handful of individuals and companies.

El-Sayed “clearly gets it,” said Patrick Bigger, research director at Climate and Community Institute, or CCI. The senator-elect’s platform, which proposes stricter regulations on data centers and energy companies, is “really exciting,” he said. These are promising climate agenda items — even if Democrats don’t explicitly call them that. For example, voters may oppose data centers in their backyard for any number of reasons, but some number of them are required for our digitalized reality and progressives now have an opportunity to take the companies behind them to task and get them to commit to reducing their strain on the local environment . Likewise, where voters came out in support of lowering utility bills, electeds now can talk further about investing in cheaper renewable energy systems like solar and wind power.

Bigger led a recent analysis that scored candidates in this year’s primary and midterm elections based on three questions: Is the candidate pushing for renewable energy or other climate actions? Do they name the rising cost of living as a voter issue, and have a plan to lower those costs? Do they articulate a populist vision by blaming wealthy corporations and powerful individuals for both the climate and affordability crises? CCI argues that candidates like El-Sayed who check all three boxes are the climate champions of the moment.

Other progressives named in the report include Will Lawrence , a co-founder of the Sunrise Movement, the climate group that first sounded the alarm for a Green New Deal in 2018. Lawrence, who will represent Michigan’s 7th District in the next Congress, points to his history of climate organizing on his website: “I will be among the most knowledgeable and dedicated members of Congress on water, climate and energy policy,” he writes. “I will fight for investment to secure the climate we depend on, adapt to the changes we can’t prevent, and finally drive our electric bills down.”

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

These “new folks headed to the House and the Senate who are really on board with a robust transformative approach to climate,” said Bigger, represent “a major shift.”

But not all climate progressives heading to Washington next year are so allergic to calling it the Green New Deal: Representatives-elect Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York City name it specifically on their campaign websites and in the press . Still, this new wave of climate leaders may feel it’s time for the decarbonization agenda to get a refresh; Valdez and Avila Chevalier’s websites also include mentions of “a livable planet for all” and “a livable world for everyone,” respectively. In part, this diversity of messaging tactics reflects the fractured nature of the climate movement since Trump retook office with a checklist of Biden-era environmental regulations to roll back.

If progressive Democrats’ messaging on climate has shifted, said Aru Shiney-Ajay, executive director of the Sunrise Movement, it’s because the terrain they’re fighting in has changed, too. “I think, as the climate crisis gets worse and worse, it’s becoming increasingly clear that the strategy, policy-wise, needs to be incorporating climate change into every single aspect of what we’re doing,” she said. In other words, climate policy should not be framed as a separate issue from the economy, infrastructure improvements, or foreign policy. “It should be the defining framework within which we have to think about how we run our society,” said Shiney-Ajay.

In 2018, the Sunrise Movement burst onto the national stage by protesting outside House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi’s office — with the Green New Deal as their top priority. Just seven years later, members of the Sunrise Movement voted to reorganize around the priority of fighting authoritarianism and, in particular, the second Trump administration. Shiney-Ajay acknowledged that the climate movement has suffered in recent years.

But that doesn’t mean that the public has become disengaged from the climate crisis. In fact, voters across the political spectrum are more attuned to it than ever. “People are actually really hungry for something to do about climate change,” said Shiney-Ajay. “I think we will actually see a lot of momentum around stopping the climate crisis. And I certainly hope to build a movement that makes that possible.”

Wherever climate progressives or so-called “green economic populists,” are in office, the CCI report says, now is the time to govern. (It’s worth noting that a petition launched this week asking Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who famously joined Sunrise members in the protest outside of Pelosi’s office, to run in the 2028 presidential race.) It will, of course, take more than the next two years, or the next presidential term, to solve the climate crisis.

scraped.title: Climate change is coming for the cactus. Yes, the cactus.
scraped.description: One-quarter of nearly 1,000 cactus species could lose at least 80 percent of their habitat by 2100 due to relentless droughts.
scraped.author: Matt Simon
scraped.h1: Climate change is coming for the cactus. Yes, the cactus.
scraped.body_text:
We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

Δ

A nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to telling stories of climate solutions and a just future.

Δ

The humble cactus is an icon of resiliency. Stuck in a desert with little rain and abundant searing sun, these plants don’t just survive — they thrive and in turn provide habitat for owls and other birds, and flowers for bats and other pollinators.

Yet cacti are in serious trouble , due to habitat loss and the poaching of species for private collections. Now we can add worsening droughts to those woes, according to a new study in the journal Nature. Researchers modeled not just a future of relentlessly rising temperatures, but the attendant dry spells, finding that the majority of nearly 1,000 cactus species will lose habitat as the climate radically changes. More than a quarter of those species could lose at least 80 percent of that habitat by 2100.

“The public perception of cacti tends to be of these organisms that are extremely drought-adapted and are just resilient, can handle anything that you can throw at them,” said Michiel Pillet, a conservation ecologist at the University of South Florida and lead author of the paper. “In reality, cacti are absolutely amazing — and they’re my favorite plant group, clearly — but they’re not that different from other plants.”

That means cacti need water. In the deserts of the southwestern United States, for example, they rely on seasonal monsoon rains which tend to make July or August the wettest month in a given year . Because this is still a desert, cacti have evolved a range of adaptations to survive , like a waxy skin that helps them retain that bounty of rainwater. “Just like other plants, they evolved under conditions that they’re used to,” Pillet said. “When you take them outside of those conditions, they might not be able to handle that.”

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Think of these cacti like sick hospital patients. Someone might be admitted for heat-related illness, as their body struggles to cool itself. At the same time, though, they might be dehydrated. Cacti are dealing with the same stresses, as global temperatures rise and dry spells intensify. “When we consider drought conditions, then it turns out that they’re much, much sicker than we previously thought,” Pillet said. “These results really do change the outlook of cacti, and most likely plants more broadly under climate change.”

Instead of simply modeling these threats going forward, the researchers turned to the citizen science platform iNaturalist, where people upload photos of plants and animals. This provided 650,000 observations of cacti in the wild, helping paint a clearer picture of how species might be faring.

Really, this isn’t a simple matter of cacti withering and dying. Sure, if relentless droughts take hold, individuals can’t get water. But the stress could be temporally complex, too. “Now we can move towards questions of: What life stages are most affected?” Pillet said. “Is it the adults or is it the seedlings? But also, which processes? Is it reduced growth or is it increased mortality? Or are plants failing to flower?”

Put another way: Cactus species could be suffering from sublethal effects of drought — the lack of water may not kill them immediately, but still interfere with their reproduction. And without procreation, populations shrink. In the Sonoran Desert, for example, the iconic, towering saguaro is reproducing less frequently during prolonged droughts, because they’re not always flowering.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Part of the problem is that while desert ecosystems may look tough and hardened overall, they’re in fact quite fragile. “They don’t recover quickly once they are disturbed, or once they are degraded, just because there’s so little water and such higher temperatures,” said Marcos Robles, the Nature Conservancy’s lead scientist in Arizona, who wasn’t involved in the research. “It takes multiple decades to recover, and in some cases, they don’t recover.”

Now drought is compounding with other stressors, like habitat loss and poaching, to drive cactus species to the brink. On the opposite end of the spectrum, too much water from rising seas has led to the local extinction of the Key Largo tree cactus in Florida. Higher nighttime temperatures are a problem, too, since that’s when saguaro and other cacti respire to avoid water loss. “If the nighttime temperatures are very high, they can’t do it,” said Rod Haenni, president of the nonprofit Cactus and Succulent Society of America, who wasn’t involved in the paper. “Then if you water on top of that, the plants just rot.”

Still, some cactus species may persist by picking up and leaving. Well, not individual plants, but populations could creep into areas with climates that more closely match what the species adapted to all those millennia ago. A similar thing is happening in the Arctic, actually, where some plants are marching farther north in “search” of increasingly agreeable weather and more water.

In the end, the purpose of this sort of research is to better inform where conservation professionals might concentrate their efforts. They can’t stop droughts, of course, but they can evacuate enough cacti to establish populations in botanical gardens, where they can be cared for as the climate grows more unrecognizable to even the hardiest desert vegetation. Species can even be reintroduced to the wild in some cases, so long as drought and high temperatures don’t remain a threat to a population.

Governments, too, need to protect the lands where cacti are threatened, Haenni said. This new research, he added, could make that happen. “Hopefully, it’ll wake people up,” Haenni said. “But the problem is a lot of the governments involved are indifferent to this. There’s a lot of people in the countries that are not indifferent, but they’re not running the governments.”

By Jonathan Wosen

West Coast Biotech & Life Sciences Reporter

Jonathan Wosen

Jonathan Wosen is STAT’s West Coast biotech & life sciences reporter. You can reach Jonathan on Signal at jwosen.27.

A massive scientific collaboration meant to unravel the mysteries of the human brain has produced the most detailed map yet of the basal ganglia, a region closely associated with a wide array of psychiatric and neurologic disorders.

Researchers profiled more than 25 million cells, generating a deluge of data that allowed them to generate a “parts list” of what cells are present in the basal ganglia and how they’re arranged. In the process scientists discovered a new type of neuron that appears to play a role in schizophrenia. They also identified cell types linked to depression, bipolar disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Advertisement

Demonstrating the value of the work, the scientists produced preliminary evidence that they can use their more detailed understanding of brain cell types to deliver therapies with increased precision. Authors working in mouse models of Parkinson’s disease showed that a gene therapy designed to work in a subset of basal ganglia cells was as effective as a blanket approach; it was also safer.

scraped.title: The promise and peril of AI in government
scraped.description: In her book “Reboot: AI and the Race to Save Democracy,” Beth Simone Noveck warns that while AI can increase efficiency, predictive models pose significant ethical and societal risks.
scraped.h1: The promise and peril of AI in government
scraped.body_text:
Innovation

In her new book “Reboot: AI and the Race to Save Democracy,” writer Beth Simone Noveck warns that while AI can increase efficiency, predictive models pose significant ethical and societal risks.

In Taoyuan, Taiwan’s bustling industrial hub where 200 semiconductor manufacturing facilities are based, Mayor San-Cheng Chang is using AI to orchestrate an ambitious transformation. He brings a unique blend of technical expertise and government experience to the challenge of running the country’s fastest-growing city. Before becoming mayor, he served as Taiwan’s first nonpartisan premier and held leadership positions at both Google and Acer. As a former director of Taiwan’s National Center for High-Performance Computing, Chang embodies the intersection of technology and governance that helps explain Taoyuan’s embrace of AI.

As the home of Taiwan’s international airport as well as 2.2 million residents, Taoyuan must manage heavy truck traffic, air pollution, rapid population growth , and constant construction. Since March 2023, Taoyuan has run an AI-powered lung cancer screening initiative targeting citizens over 40 with risk factors that include occupational exposure and family history. Two years later, Taoyuan’s program had screened over 400,000 residents, detecting 233 lung cancer cases (90% in early stage), and achieving cost savings of NT$500 million ($17 million) through AI-aided diagnostics. To manage this volume without overwhelming local hospitals, the city deployed advanced AI software, which can predict cancer risk from a single low-dose CT scan without requiring additional clinical data, helping doctors to efficiently triage cases and focus resources on those most at risk.

Modern AI-powered predictive models are being dangerously relied on in more decision-making arenas, including the delivery of government services, without justification.

When residents complained about noise from illegally modified vehicle exhaust pipes, Taoyuan developed an AI system that analyzes exhaust pipe images and matches them against a database of legal configurations. Patrol cars equipped with cameras can now identify violations on sight, and complaints are down 20% over last year. Other AI-powered cameras monitor construction sites and factory chimneys for pollution, automatically triggering water sprays when dust levels rise too high, or alerting inspectors when chimney emissions change suspiciously. AI now optimizes traffic-light cycles at busy intersections, shaving about 10 seconds off each wait. More dramatically, when ambulances approach, electronic fences detect their presence and create green-light corridors, cutting the ambulances’ average travel times from four minutes to just over two — a difference that can save lives.

While Taoyuan exemplifies the opportunities to use AI to develop practical solutions to urban problems , Mayor Chang is circumspect in his choice of projects. He will not sanction the use of generative AI chatbots that could hallucinate, and he carefully distinguishes between using machine learning to detect existing conditions and employing it to predict future outcomes. His administration embraces AI tools that can spot patterns — like identifying an existing cancer or finding vehicles with illegal modifications. Taoyuan uses AI to pinpoint potholes for faster road maintenance or identify train station elevator passengers in wheelchairs so that assistance can await them when the doors open. In these cases, AI sees what is already there faster than human eyes can, but it does not automate away human decision making.

Unfortunately, governments and companies are increasingly turning to machine learning algorithms to anticipate future occurrences such as the risk of recidivism and relying on these predictive algorithms for life-changing decisions, from sentencing and parole to credit scoring and access to employment . In some cases, institutions are automating decision making. Almost all large companies have adopted AI in hiring to predict who will succeed on the job. Without recourse, AI itself eliminates candidates from consideration. Princeton University’s Arvind Narayanan thinks there are grave risks to using AI like a Magic 8 ball. “When you started a job,” he says, “there were so many things that were not known at the time about what was going to happen in your personal life that would have affected whether or not you would have performed well.”

Pattern recognition is already risky. By creating categories and sorting data, we necessarily risk oversimplification. For example, government agencies using AI to detect fraud may misclassify individuals based on income patterns. A struggling single parent whose irregular gig work makes their income fluctuate might be unfairly flagged as a fraud risk. When institutions move from using AI for pattern recognition to making predictive judgments, the potential for discrimination and error grows significantly. Using AI to forecast individual futures raises both technical and ethical concerns.

Even accurate predictions can lead to bad decisions when models fail to capture crucial context.

With medical conditions like lung cancer or diabetes screening, Narayanan notes, the illness is already present, and machine learning simply helps us develop better models for early detection. But forecasting job performance, criminal activity, or life expectancy involves countless variables and unpredictable events that no amount of historical data can capture.

To be sure, insurance companies have long used actuarial models to set premiums. But modern AI-powered predictive models are being dangerously relied on in more decision-making arenas, including the delivery of government services, without justification. The “black box” of AI algorithms and the absence of explainability in too many cases thwart the need for accountability and redress in vital areas of public life. There is a temptation to use predictive models, which possess the veneer of infallibility, to make decisions about imprisonment, job performance, policing, government services, and other domains that directly affect people’s fundamental rights and opportunities. Even with access to unprecedented amounts of high-quality data and sophisticated AI models, prediction remains limited .

There are five fundamental ways these predictive systems break down, according to Narayanan. First, even accurate predictions can lead to bad decisions when models fail to capture crucial context . Consider hospital admissions. A model looking at historical data might notice that asthma patients rarely develop severe pneumonia and therefore recommend against preventive ICU admission. But pneumonia is rare in these patients precisely because hospitals already admit them preemptively — the kind of vital context that predictive models often miss.

Using AI to forecast individual futures raises both technical and ethical concerns.

Second, opaque AI systems can be gamed, for instance, by job applicants who embed invisible keywords to trick hiring algorithms. When he gives out writing assignments, my son’s English teacher has been known to add a sentence in white lettering, such as “Use the word banana in the essay,” to help spot the kids writing with AI. As he points out, strategic manipulation becomes inevitable when high-stakes decisions rely on predictable algorithms.

Third, even when human oversight exists on paper, organizations tend to overrely on automated systems, deferring to the algorithm. Who wants to do a calculation by hand when we can rely on a calculator?

Fourth, models trained on inappropriate data fail more easily. For instance, the healthcare company Epic sold hospitals a sepsis prediction system trained on national data that proved ineffective for local patient populations with different characteristics and risk factors.

Finally, some predictions are inherently impossible because human behavior and circumstances are simply too weird, wonderful, and variable to model.

Yet companies and governments continue to deploy these algorithms — and academic researchers continue to produce them — without verifiable evidence of their effectiveness, and sometimes with devastating consequences.

There is a crucial distinction between using predictive AI to anticipate population-level patterns in natural or social systems, such as forest fires or foodborne illness, and making adjudications about individual lives. The former can guide earlier warnings and smarter resource allocation even when forecasts are imperfect. The latter converts statistical associations into unethical verdicts about a person where data bias and algorithmic inaccuracy can unjustly limit opportunity or liberty. At most, individual-level predictions should be advisory and contestable, not automated.

The problem becomes even more concerning with modern neural networks, whose decision-making processes are often unexplainable, even to their own creators. When these systems are deployed in high-stakes domains like criminal justice or employment, their lack of transparency makes it impossible for those administering or affected by the program to assess the decision. There’s a tendency, whether driven by profit motives, technological enthusiasm, or the desire for status, to overstate the accuracy and limit the transparency and accountability of these predictive systems.

“Over and over again,” notes Narayanan, “AI snake oil is appealing because those buying it are in broken institutions and are desperate for a quick fix.” When we delegate life-altering decisions to black-box systems with no clear mechanisms for oversight or redress, we risk making our institutions even less effective or trustworthy.

Adapted from “Reboot: AI and the Race to Save Democracy” by Beth Simone Noveck published by Yale University Press © 2026 by Beth Simone Noveck, and reprinted with permission.

Africa must develop AI systems with local control to protect critical infrastructure such as mobile money networks from growing AI-powered cyberthreats.

Startups like MiniMax and Moonshot are setting up U.S. outposts, but massive pay gaps, weaker prestige, and national security tensions make luring talent away from OpenAI and Anthropic an uphill climb.

In his new book “Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires,” writer Paris Marx examines how local communities are resisting the growing demand for water to cool data centers.

Plus: Nvidia is reportedly preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang.

This is today's edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.

Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists have gathered in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the annual UN climate talks. But this year’s negotiations are taking place against a particularly tense geopolitical backdrop, as the world falls further behind the Paris Agreement’s goals.

Energy prices are soaring, and there are big questions about how countries will tackle the climate crisis. Expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance, and whether negotiators can agree on meaningful action.

Here’s what you need to know about COP31 .

—Casey Crownhart

This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.

Far-thinking technologists are working on ways to keep your brain going beyond death. MIT Technology Review’s latest Roundtables event explores their ideas, from gradual brain replacement to uploading memories to the cloud.

Join science editor Mary Beth Griggs and senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado for this subscriber-only discussion.

Tune in live on Tuesday, November 17 at 5:00 p.m. GMT / 12:00 p.m. EST / 9:00 a.m. PST .

Want to join the conversation? Subscribe to MIT Technology Review for exclusive access to all our Roundtables.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Nvidia is reportedly preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang The board will meet as soon as today to determine his future. ( WSJ $) + Nvidia’s stock slid 8% after the report was published. ( BI ) + Huang allegedly also had an affair with an Nvidia colleague. ( NYT $) + His exit could send shockwaves across the AI industry. ( Axios ) + Stakes are high in AI's trillion-dollar gamble. ( MIT Technology Review )

2 The Nvidia spy scandal is set to tighten chip exports But Commerce Secretary Lutnick has stalled the curbs. ( CNBC ) + China has signaled it will retaliate if they pass. ( FT $) + Chinese firms have started stockpiling Nvidia chips. ( Reuters $) + Democrats appear to be preparing an investigation. ( Politico )

3 A startup has built an AI to detect AI-made bioweapons It runs offline on a laptop with a USB gene sequencer. ( Wired $) + Ukraine is opening up its battlefield data to train AI weapons. ( NYT $) + AI is making bioweapons easier to create. ( MIT Technology Review )

4 Anduril says its satellite can track spacecraft in orbital night It uses an infrared sensor to detect hidden satellites. ( Ars Technica ) + Anduril is also making smart glasses for warfare. ( MIT Technology Review )

5 Ukraine has reported new restrictions on SpaceX’s Starshield Zelenskyy says they’re hampering drone defenses. ( NBC News

6 Even remote Brazilian wildlife has microplastics in its blood Animals 100 km from waste sites carried them. ( Nature ) + AstroTurf is increasing microplastic levels. ( MIT Technology Review ) 7 A NASA space camera can spot invasive plants from orbit It detects how different species’ leaves reflect light. ( Economist $)

8 Astronomers have found an “invisible” object that defies stellar theory It’s likely an ultra-rare supermassive neutron star. ( 404 Media ) + New research has corroborated the first black hole image. ( New Scientist $) + The search for dark matter has been blown open. ( MIT Technology Review )

9 Life may have started with metabolism, not genes Self-sustaining chemical cycles could have come first. ( Quanta )

10 Brain surgery has left a man seeing cat eyes on people Researchers used AI to render what he sees. ( Gizmodo )

Quote of the day

—Alex Karp, Palantir's CEO, tells Politico that he's a devoted Democrat despite recently backing Trump.

One more thing

China’s short drama industry is fueled by bite-sized, melodramatic, and smutty shows built for smartphone scrolling. Now, many are being made entirely with AI: no actors, camera operators, cinematographers, or CGI specialists required.

An average of 470 AI-generated short dramas were released every day in January. Production timelines have shrunk from months to weeks, while costs have dropped by up to 90%. Storytelling is also increasingly driven by performance data.

The format is rapidly expanding overseas while reshaping the work of writers and production crews. Read the full story on AI’s dramatic impact on China’s short drama industry .

—Caiwei Chen

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .)

+ Watch Rome grow from 1000 BCE to the present day in a mesmerising 3D timelapse . + Hold your breath watching a skateboarder’s record-breaking 94.3mph run down a Québec hill. + A captivating photo essay has captured the heart-wrenching wail of flamenco at the Seville Biennial. + A majestic Chinese mural has sparked a rare US-China collaboration that unearthed new secrets from art history.

Plus: 22 nations have called for a new global body to oversee AI.

Plus: Hackers have disrupted the US Federal Election Commission’s website.

Plus: Hackers exposed 41,000 Homeland Security workers.

Plus: OpenAI has released 377 new math findings, further rattling the field.

scraped.title: What to know about this year’s UN climate talks
scraped.description: Climate finance and fossil fuels top the formal agenda at COP31.
scraped.h1: What to know about this year’s UN climate talks
scraped.body_text:
Climate finance and fossil fuels top the formal agenda at COP31.

It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey.

COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world. Turkey and Australia are cohosting this year’s talks, which are scheduled to wrap up on November 20.

This annual gathering can often serve as an indicator of where the world stands on addressing and adapting to the climate crisis. And this year’s talks are sure to be a doozy—expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular. Here’s what you should know about COP31.

In recent years, the tension always feels high when COP rolls around. (COP stands for “Conference of the Parties.”) But this year feels especially charged: The world is still grappling with the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and sent economic shock waves around the world as energy prices have spiked.

This year’s COP will be the second without a formal delegation from the US. President Trump formally withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement earlier this year and is in the process of withdrawing from the UN Framework Committee on Climate Change. That’s the treaty that allows formal participation in negotiations.

Meanwhile, things aren’t looking good for the Paris Agreement, which was established at UN climate talks 11 years ago, setting a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 °C over preindustrial levels. In a report published in September, the UN Environment Program acknowledged that global warming is set to exceed that 1.5 °C goal, “likely within the next few years.”

So as climate talks kick off, there’s an obvious, urgent question looming about how to quickly cut emissions to limit warming. There’s also the major issue of how to pay for efforts to address emissions and to help a warming world endure the inevitable damage.

Two years ago, talks ended in a goal of mobilizing $300 billion per year by 2035 to help pay to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. (Rich nations provided $136.7 billion in 2024, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. ) And last year, the COP30 agreement included a goal of tripling the money for adaptation over that period. (Such funding has been quite flat over the past few years.)

The world got a tragic reminder of just how high the stakes are earlier this year, when a glacier collapse caused devastating flooding in the Himalayas. The flood killed approximately 1,500 people, left over 5,000 missing, and caused nearly $5 billion in damage. The UN loss and damages fund committed $20 million to helping Nepal recover (less than 1% of the total estimated cost to the country).

Another key trend to watch is how the formal negotiations engage with the topic of fossil fuels. Three years ago, the final agreement text explicitly called for a transition away from them. But it felt as if things took a step back last year, when the final agreement didn’t even mention the phrase “fossil fuels” once. This will be an interesting conversation, especially because cohosts Turkey and Australia have both faced criticism over their relationships with these fuels—Australia is a major exporter of coal and natural gas, and Turkey’s grid relies heavily on fossil fuels, including coal.

Outside the formal negotiations, COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister, is spearheading a side agenda, including two informal initiatives that will be worth watching. These wouldn’t be part of the official agreement text, but countries could sign on to signal support.

One is a pledge to make AI more sustainable; this is almost comically squishy, even as voluntary COP pledges go. The text includes explicit wording that it creates no new obligations for countries, so don’t expect anything resembling enforcement there.

The COP leadership is also pushing to make electricity a larger part of member countries’ energy use. Today, only about 23% of global energy is used in the form of electricity. Fossil fuels, like gasoline in vehicles or natural gas for heating, make up the bulk of the rest. Shifting to more electricity use, and relying on cleaner sources for that electricity, could help drive down emissions. The new pledge’s target is for electricity to make up 35% of total energy consumption by 2035.

With leadership billing this as an “implementation COP,” it would be great to see some real, tangible progress on the global challenge of addressing climate change. I’m not expecting anything groundbreaking, but we’ll be tuned in to see what the final agreement shapes up to be.

This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here .
