scraped.h1: The Download: preserving minds and weighing open AI risks
scraped.body_text:
Plus: COP31’s flagship pledge to electrify 35% of energy use is sinking.

This is today's edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.

As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you.

To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are exploring ways to keep the brain going, even beyond death. Their ideas range from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones and uploading our memories to the cloud.

Here are six possible paths for keeping your mind going, and how feasible they might be .

—Antonio Regalado

This story is from the Impossible edition of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get every issue as soon as it lands.

Anthropic recently released a report arguing that a powerful new model released by the Chinese company Z.ai, poses a major cyberattack risk. Its core concern was that it is freely available for anyone to download and modify.

The warning was the latest flashpoint in the debate over open frontier AI models. Critics warn that bad actors can misuse them, while supporters argue they prevent a handful of companies from controlling the technology. The debate, however, is more complicated than it seems .

This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 COP31’s flagship pledge to electrify 35% of energy use is sinking Only around a dozen nations are reportedly ready to sign it. ( Politico ) + It requires quadrupling the pace of electrification. ( New Scientist $) + John Kerry says the US must follow China on clean energy. ( Guardian ) + But the US skipped the talks entirely for a second year. ( NYT $) + What’s the future of electricity? ( MIT Technology Review )

2 The Nvidia spy scandal reportedly involves $7.5 billion of chips Alice Huang allegedly obtained 240,000 restricted chips. ( Information $) + Trump was told of Huang’s spy link on Air Force One . ( NYT $) + Experts warn the scandal could erode America’s AI lead. ( Verge ) + Nvidia’s slide has let Microsoft overtake it in value. ( Reuters $)

3 Studies found AI agents go rogue because they’re “incorrigible” Their training rewards them for finishing tasks at any cost. ( NYT $) + This is why AI agents lie and cheat to reach their goals. ( MIT Technology Review )

4 Anthropic has scaled back its IPO valuation to $1.4 trillion It aimed for $2 trillion before the recent AI jitters. ( Guardian )

5 Drone strikes have wiped out 3% of Yandex’s cloud customer data Ukraine hit three of its data centers in October. ( Reuters $) + Ukraine’s drones are fighting data centers for fiber. ( Ars Technica )

6 Moderna says its new vaccine could prevent cancer in high-risk people The company’s CEO calls it the “holy grail” of cancer prevention. ( FT $) + Hong Kong is testing a next-gen ultrasound cancer treatment. ( SCMP )

7 Scientists have slowly reversed human cells’ ages by decades One age marker was set back as far as 60 years. ( Wired $) + “Reprogramming” is the buzziest de-aging idea. ( MIT Technology Review )

8 Robot vessels are hunting for mines in the Strait of Hormuz AI helps them spot mines camouflaged on the seabed. ( BBC )

9 Life may have started inside a tiny bubble That’s the idea behind the “lipid first” origin theory. ( Quanta )

10 As Voyager 1 reaches a light day from Earth, here's what it's taught us Its discoveries rewrote textbooks in real time. ( New Scientist $)

Quote of the day

—Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, accuses President Donald Trump of ignoring warnings about the alleged relationship between Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a Chinese spy.

One more thing

Bananas may not be chilled in the grocery store, but they’re the ultimate refrigerated fruit. It’s only thanks to a network of thermal control that they’ve become a global commodity. And that salad bag on the shelf? It’s not just a bag but a highly engineered respiratory apparatus.

According to Nicola Twilley—a contributor to The New Yorker and cohost of the podcast Gastropod—refrigeration has wrecked our food system. Thankfully, there are promising alternative preservation methods.

Read the full story on her research .

—Allison Arieff

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .)

+ A whisky made like wine is wowing the spirits world. + Britain lost in the fog makes for hauntingly beautiful photos . + Chronophoto is a fiendishly addictive game that challenges you to date old photos to the year. + Dozens of saxophonists met up in New York to play the gloriously cheesy riff from George Michael's “Careless Whisper.”

Plus: 22 nations have called for a new global body to oversee AI.

Plus: Hackers have disrupted the US Federal Election Commission’s website.

Plus: Hackers exposed 41,000 Homeland Security workers.

Plus: Binance has suffered the biggest crypto hack in history.

scraped.h1: You turn to us for voices you won't hear anywhere else.
scraped.body_text:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.

Alaska is the only Senate race yet to be called. Democratic challenger Mary Peltola is narrowly leading Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan with about 86% of votes counted. Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, a system where voters choose not only their top candidate, but can also indicate an order of preference for remaining candidates on the ballot. If no candidate wins a majority as the top choice, then second-choice votes are added to the totals and so on until there is a winner.

Rob Richie, president and founder of Expand Democracy and a senior adviser with FairVote, explains how ranked-choice voting has shaped the Alaska race and how it is “a system that promotes [candidates] reaching out, engaging, and, for voters, a lot of freedom.”

Richie adds that Peltola is “heavily favored to win at this point.”

AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! . I’m Amy Goodman, with Nermeen Shaikh.

NERMEEN SHAIKH : The Alaska Senate race is now the only Senate race yet to be called. Democratic challenger Mary Peltola is narrowly leading Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan with about 86% of the votes counted. The close race has drawn controversy because of a second candidate also named Dan Sullivan, retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., who’s also on the ballot.

Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, a system where voters choose not only their top candidate, but can also indicate an order of preference for remaining candidates on the ballot. If no candidate wins a majority as the top choice, then second-choice votes are added to the totals and so on until there is a winner.

AMY GOODMAN : Alaska and Maine use ranked-choice voting for statewide elections, and it’s also used in 36 cities and three counties nationwide. And it’s popular outside of politics. The Oscar for Best Picture is decided by ranked-choice voting. So, how might ranked-choice voting impact the results in Alaska?

Our next guest is an expert on voting reforms, including ranked-choice voting. Rob Richie is with us, president and founder of Expand Democracy, a senior adviser with FairVote.

Let’s start in this first few minutes explaining how Alaska votes. Explain ranked-choice voting. And does it have anything to do with the fact that we don’t know who’s won the Alaska Senate race?

ROB RICHIE : Thank you, Amy. Great to be here, and fun to talk about ranked-choice voting in such a prominent way. It is the last Senate race to be decided.

The delay is entirely due to the fact that it’s a very rural state. Mail takes a while to get to where it needs to go, and they create space for ballots to come late. And so, that’s what we’re waiting for. It’s just ballots to be processed. All the ballots that have been processed, those 86%, have actually been — the data has been provided, so we can see what ranked-choice voting does with those ballots. And so, it is just waiting to see what happens. So, here’s what — or, those ballots to be processed.

So, ranked-choice voting is one way to think about it. Anytime you’ve wanted to vote for a third party or an independent candidate, you’re in that position of saying, “Well, if I vote for that person and they can’t win, am I just throwing my vote away? Should I vote for my lesser of two evils?” In a ranked-choice system, you can say, “Well, here’s my first choice. That’s what I really want to say, and that’s why I want to support. Maybe that person wins. But if they lose, if they’re in last place, I want my ballot to go to this second choice.” And that’s the instant runoff.

One of the places they used it is New York City in the the primaries. And when Andrew Cuomo was the big front-runner and Mamdani was sort of rising, there were several people that he was aligned with, like Brad Lander, and they could run actually kind of as a team and say, “Well, vote for me first, and vote for you second.” And it’s a system that kind of promotes reaching out, engaging, and for voters, a lot of freedom.

Getting back to Alaska, there are different races that are still being decided. The governor’s race, where it looks like Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, the Democrat, is nearly at 50%, far ahead of three Republicans. And while ranked-choice voting will make that closer, because the Republican vote will consolidate, he will still very, very certainly win.

Then there’s a House race where the Republican incumbent is ahead by about eight points with the current ballots. There’s an independent who is second. And by the way, it looks like maybe 20% of the Alaska House will end up being independent. But anyway, the independent is second. And then there’s a Democrat, actually kind of a quirky candidacy because he doesn’t live in the state, is in third. His vote will make that closer for the independent, because those votes generally will go to the independent over the Republican, probably not turn the tide.

And then, in the Peltola race, yeah, the famous decoy Dan Sullivan, who was recruited in kind of an ignominious way to run and, you know, triggered Donald Trump and the DOJ , interestingly, when you look at his second choices, the people that vote for that candidate, they go more to Peltola than to Dan Sullivan, the incumbent Republican. And that’s because everyone sort of knew which was which, and it’s kind of protest voters. And it’s only like 1.5% of the electorate. There’s another Republican with maybe two-and-a-half percent. His votes will more go to Sullivan. So, overall, ranked-choice voting makes it a little closer in the Senate race. But the final part of this is the remaining ballots are expected to widen Peltola’s first-choice lead, maybe even put her over 50%, and she’s heavily favored to win at this point.

NERMEEN SHAIKH : So, Rob, can you also talk about how Democrats’ big wins at the state level in the midterms could potentially lead to the end of the Electoral College in future presidential elections? And explain to us what the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact is.

ROB RICHIE : It’s really exciting seeing these moving in tandem. Ranked-choice voting is spreading to more places, and the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact is on the cusp of winning. We could have a 2028 presidential election decided by a national popular vote, where my vote in Maryland and your votes in New York and all listeners’ votes, wherever they are, count the same, and the candidate with the most votes wins. Like, that’s the way we elect all our governors and most everything else, and that is within reach.

So, currently — so, the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact is a state agreement, grounded in the Constitution. The Constitution gives states certain powers, and one is that they can go into a binding agreement with other states. So, they have an interstate compact power. Things like the Port Authority and D.C. Metro system, that is a compact among the other jurisdictions. So, that’s a power that states can do.

And they have plenary control over their electoral votes. So, we know that the Electoral College is in the Constitution, but the mechanism of how states allocate electors is not in the Constitution. And the fact that currently almost every state gives all of their electoral votes to the popular vote winner in that state is really like almost game theory. Every state’s trying to maximize its support for its favored candidate. But they’re kind of all stuck in a situation where 40 states just don’t matter in every presidential election, and that includes almost — the great majority of Americans live in states that are outside of being competitive. And so —

AMY GOODMAN : We have 10 seconds, Rob.

ROB RICHIE : — it’s in our interests. It has strong popularity. OK. So, states can join together and allocate their electoral votes to the popular vote winner, and now five more states can join the existing states that have done it, and this can be implemented by 2028. That’s the gist of it. And people can check out NationalPopularVote.com to learn more about it.

AMY GOODMAN : I want to go back to the end of the Electoral College. Talk about how the Electoral College was established, Rob Richie, so unusual in the world, and now the movement to abolish it.

ROB RICHIE : It’s a really important question, because we can sometimes assume that the founders were dealing with the same realities that we are today, but they weren’t. They had just come together as in a young, very young nation. They had incredibly different suffrage rules in different states. Pennsylvania had more people voting than Massachusetts, you know, by exponentially different numbers. And so, there were people like James Wilson from Pennsylvania that were supporting a national popular vote for president, as part of “We the people” should act as Americans. But the realities made it difficult, particularly when you added in the slave states, Virginia and on South, that wanted to have their population matter even if a whole lot of it was slaves who were disenfranchised.

And so, their compromise was to have the number of members of Congress that each state has, which is grounded in population, be turned into electoral votes, so every state gets the number of electoral votes equal to their members of Congress regardless of their voter turnout, suffrage rules or, in the case of the 18th century, slavery. And that has been a system we kind of stuck with. So, every state has these electors. The states choose them, how to allocate them. They combine their votes. And if you win a majority of the Electoral College, then you become president. But the really is a different world from where we are today, which is why it’s time to really change it.

AMY GOODMAN : And so, how does it change? Talk about the first states that challenged this, and what it would take to ultimately end. And where are the polls of Americans on what they want?

ROB RICHIE : Well, first, on the polls, Americans overwhelmingly want a national popular vote. It’s generally, when it’s polled, at 65, 70%. In all the states that are about to be asking this question about whether they should act to have a popular vote for president, it has strong majority support. So that’s where the people are.

And the movement from this is — I guess one analogy is, when Dorothy is in Oz figuring out how to get home and she realizes she’s had her ruby slippers all along that allows her to do that, states have actually always had the power to make this change. And the recognition was in the early 2000s. A guy named John Koza sort of came up with the idea of a National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, which is states have these powers over what to do with their electors and to join with other states to act together, that allows them to make a change.

So, the first state that passed the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, back in 2007, was Maryland. And a new state senator who had just come into the body was Jamie Raskin, who had been on our board of directors at FairVote and a big democracy champion. And Jamie kind of made the argument very persuasively to his colleagues in Maryland to join the agreement. So, the agreement is to say, “We’re going to give all of our electoral votes not to the statewide winner, but to the national popular vote winner, once that action is decisive,” meaning that the number of states in the agreement have to collectively have a majority of the Electoral College. So, they’d want to be in a situation where they always know that by doing this, that the national popular vote winner will always become president.

So, that has been a slow process since Maryland in 2007, but just dogged, persistent work. More than 3,000 state legislators have sponsored or voted for the national popular vote plan as it’s moved around the country. There’s been bills in every single state. And 18 states and D.C. have actually passed the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact.

And now this election has opened up a path where, even though Republicans have had a history of backing this, Democratic votes have the power to now put this in play. So, we have new Democratic trifectas in Arizona, Michigan, Wisconsin, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and there could be other potential states.

AMY GOODMAN : Governor — trifectas meaning the governor and both houses of the legislature are Democrat.

ROB RICHIE : Correct, meaning that Democrats have the power. If they want to stand for a national popular vote, which has this strong majority support and would bring all the country into an equal way of electing the president, they have the power to do this. And once it goes over 270 electoral votes combined in the compacting states, then it governs the next election. Those states are now committed in this binding agreement to award their electoral votes to the candidate that wins the national popular vote.

There’s been a ton of conversations about this. It’s been something that every state legislator is an authority on elections, so you have to have just lots and lots of conversations. And again, thousands have been persuaded to support this, and now it’s moving in a very serious way in the final states to put it over the top.

AMY GOODMAN : What’s fascinating, I’m sure if you polled Americans and asked them, “Do you directly vote for president in the United States?” overwhelmingly, they would say yes. They would not say, “Oh no, there’s the Electoral College in between.”

ROB RICHIE : I know. It’s one of these, you know, weird artifacts — not the only one. You know, I’m a big critic of just only electing people people with single-member districts without proportional representation, and, as we talked about, having single-choice elections compared to a ranked-choice voting ballot. And there’s just a lot of things that we have done for a long, long time that we think just have to be that way, and it’s not the case.

And this is a really important time for stepping back and saying, “What is the best things that we can do for our democracy?” Voters did a lot of good things on the ballot this year, on ballot measures, on pro-democracy measures. And now our legislators can build on that and keep the momentum going.

AMY GOODMAN : Can you talk about what is called the Montana Plan and its significance?

ROB RICHIE : It’s a fascinating plan. A guy named Tom Moore from the Center for American Progress kind of came up with the idea. But corporations act in states based on having corporate charters that are defined in state law. And his insight, kind of one of these ruby slipper kind of moments of thinking about things differently, is that in those charters, you can regulate what corporations can do.

And in the Montana Plan, which just passed by some version of two to one, and, you know, is going to be litigated, as these things usually are, but the idea is that the corporate charters can say corporations do not have the power to give money to campaigns. And that affects their sort of general or, you know, political spending, but that it also means that if you’re trying to form, like, a super PAC or some entity, they always have to be incorporated, and that can be regulated, as well. So, essentially, it’s saying, yes, there can be a lot of money spent on campaigns, but it needs to be spent by individuals. And that sort of opens up an avenue to sort of take on Citizens United in the states.

AMY GOODMAN : Well, Rob Richie, I want to thank you for being with us, president and founder of Expand Democracy, senior adviser with FairVote. To see Part 1 of our discussion, go to democracynow.org. Thank you so much.

Special guests Angela Davis, Bruce Springsteen, Patti Smith, Michael Stipe and more came together to celebrate 30 years of Democracy Now! at a sold out Riverside Church event in NYC on March 23, 2026.

Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.

With Democrats set to take control of both chambers of Congress in January, Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders says he will not support Chuck Schumer for another term as the Democratic Senate leader, calling for the party to move in “a new and bold direction.” Michigan Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin has said she will not support Schumer unless he presents a plan to govern differently, and several senators-elect have called for new leadership or declined to endorse Schumer. Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen is considering challenging Schumer. Meanwhile, Hakeem Jeffries is facing questions about his leadership of House Democrats after 11 of the party’s members missed a key vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

After “a big win for the populist wing of the Democratic Party, … it would be a betrayal for that election to result immediately in the Democratic Party simply responding by reelecting the same leadership,” says David Sirota, editor-in-chief of The Lever .

AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report . I’m Amy Goodman, with Nermeen Shaikh.

NERMEEN SHAIKH : As Democrats prepare to take control of the House in January, their current leader, Hakeem Jeffries, is facing questions about his leadership after a vote this week that effectively derailed an effort to impeach Trump’s Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. On Tuesday, the Republican-led House voted 211 to 204 to send the articles to the House Judiciary Committee, effectively stalling the effort. Eleven Democrats were absent, including former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi. The vote prompted criticism of Jeffries, who is seeking to become House speaker, with some questioning why he had not ensured more Democrats were present.

AMY GOODMAN : The debate over Democratic leadership in the House and Senate is also intensifying in that upper house, in the Senate. Vermont independent Senator Bernie Sanders says he will not support Chuck Schumer for another term as the party’s leader, calling for Democrats to move in, quote, “a new and bold direction.”

SEN . BERNIE SANDERS : If this campaign was about anything, it was about change and the need for the Democratic Party, in my view, to move in a new and bold direction. I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody who works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view, the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader.

AMY GOODMAN : That’s Bernie Sanders. Michigan Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin has also said she will not support Schumer unless he presents a plan for a different vision. It’s not clear if she would throw her hat in the ring. Several senators-elect have called for new leadership or declined to endorse Schumer. Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen says he’s listening to colleagues and has not ruled out a leadership bid.

The debate over who should lead the Democratic Party comes as the party prepares to take control of Congress following its sweeping midterm victories. The question now is what Democrats will do with that power and whether they’ll deliver on the promises they campaigned on.

The Lever has launched a new video and podcast series hosted by David Sirota called Don’t F#*k It Up, Democrats — but they’re using the full word. Let’s go to a preview.

DAVID SIROTA : After election night, what comes next? I’m David Sirota, founder of The Lever and host of the award-winning investigative podcast Master Plan . Right now Americans are not politely asking for change. They’re mad. So, as the party looks towards the next Congress and the 2028 presidential election, we’re asking: What would it actually take for Democrats to get it right?

ROBERT REICH : How do Democrats not [bleep] this up again?

DAVID SIROTA : And so, our new series has a title that channels that anger and requires a bleep. It’s called Don’t [bleep] It Up, Democrats . I’m sitting down with politicians, economists, activists, former White House officials, power brokers and thinkers to talk about the big choices facing the party. How do you fight corruption when billionaires bankroll the political system? How do you make life affordable when corporations have so much power? How do you fix a healthcare system that’s bankrupting people? And how do Democrats win back working-class voters who’ve heard promises of change again and again? Winning elections is one thing, but actually delivering on your promises, that’s something else.

ROBERT REICH : Because Democrats do have an extraordinary capacity to grab defeat out of the jaws of victory again and again and again and again.

AMY GOODMAN : And that voice, that last voice, was former Labor Secretary Robert Reich.

Well, for more, we go to Lisbon, Portugal, where we’re joined by David Sirota, founder and editor-in-chief of The Lever , the author of the Master Plan: The Hidden Plot to Legalize Corruption in America .

David, that’s quite a provocative title for your podcast series, Don’t F#*k It Up . Can you talk about what’s just taken place? We’re speaking to you the day after the victory of Scott Colom, the first Black senator — he will be — from Mississippi since Reconstruction. And to say the least, in the last few days, he was very critical of the Democrats who refused to fund him, the leadership, until the very end. Talk about what you’re seeing in the House and the Senate now.

DAVID SIROTA : Look, I think what you’re seeing is, clearly, in the vote across the country, a massive vote for change. And let’s be really clear here: Many of the races that decided this election were won by candidates who were making a very crystal-clear critique of the status quo , of oligarchy, of the endemic corruption. Essentially, the way I see it, you see an election in which the politics, the anti-oligarch politics, that have been championed by people like Bernie Sanders, ended up winning the day, and winning the day in a huge way, particularly in places like red states.

And I think what you’re then seeing now reflected in the leadership races is whether that wave will result in some reflection of change. There would be an irony to have an election with a wave this clear, this anti-oligarch, this populist, a wave that was a big win for the populist wing of the Democratic Party, a wave that is about change — it would be more than ironic — some would argue it would be a betrayal — for that election to result immediately in the Democratic Party simply responding by reelecting the same leadership. So, I think you’ve got a lot of Democrats on Capitol Hill who are caught between knowing what the election was about, and also an existing current leadership, Democratic Party leadership, that doesn’t want the leadership of the party to have to change.

NERMEEN SHAIKH : So, David, if we could just, you know, go back and see: Why do so many progressives, progressive Democrats, and their supporters — why don’t they want to support Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer? If you could just give us a history of their — basically, their record?

DAVID SIROTA : Yeah, I mean, for sure. I mean, look, Hakeem Jeffries is somebody who, as an example, most recently, right before the election, said that he is not a supporter of Medicare for All. Hakeem Jeffries has promised to stack the House Foreign Affairs Committee with AIPAC — members who are very close to AIPAC , who are very supportive of the existing relationship, U.S.-Israel relationship. You have a steering committee in the House that’s supposed to be writing the Democrats’ AI policy, and it is comprised of lawmakers who are very close, not surprisingly, to the tech industry.

Chuck Schumer has been somebody who has danced around all sorts of issues. For instance, he ended up not supporting a major antitrust bill. He is not somebody who is perceived to have used the Senate, the power in the Senate, to really deliver on or really champion a populist agenda. And so, I think, look, I think with Schumer, there’s some generational change. I mean, Chuck Schumer has been leader for a very long time, through some very, very bad Democratic losses. So, Schumer’s got a generational question here, you know, a demand for new leadership. Jeffries hasn’t been speaker, but Jeffries is juxtaposing himself policy-wise in many ways against the base and against, in some cases, the majority of his own party.

NERMEEN SHAIKH : So, David, do you have any idea of who the candidates might be to replace Schumer or Jeffries?

DAVID SIROTA : Yeah, I mean, look, Chris Van Hollen, I think, is the most serious challenger, right now, to Chuck Schumer. Chris Van Hollen actually was on The Lever ’s podcast just before the election, making a clear line in the sand, saying Democrats should use the upcoming continuing resolution to try to block funding for the Iran war, something that Chuck Schumer has not been willing to do or say. Chris Van Hollen is somebody who has been a serious Iran war critic, a serious critic of war in general, and much closer to the progressive populist base of the Democratic Party than, I think, Chuck Schumer.

Hakeem Jeffries, an official challenger has not emerged yet. There’s been a huge petition, a set of — I think it’s a million signatures at this point — demanding a different leader than Hakeem Jeffries. A single candidate has not happened yet, has not emerged, although there is some talk — there is a push to have it be Ayanna Pressley from Massachusetts.

AMY GOODMAN : I wanted to go to Senator Van Hollen, who publicly criticized the Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee for refusing to support the campaigns of Democratic candidates who went on to win, like Dr. Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan and Troy Jackson of Maine.

SEN . CHRIS VAN HOLLEN : We have two members in that room, newly elected senators, who would not be there if Schumer and the DSCC had had their way. And, you know, Schumer and the DSCC sided with the crypto industry and AIPAC against these candidates.

AMY GOODMAN : I mean, this is very interesting. I wanted to get your response to this and to now Mississippi Senator-elect Scott Colom, who was speaking, sharply criticizing national Democrats for writing Mississippi off and failing to invest in his campaign early on. He said, quote, “Mississippi was never a lost cause. We were a betrayed cause.” He was speaking on NBC News before the election.

SCOTT COLOM : The reality is, our country does not do well when it ignores places like Mississippi. When America makes sure kids in Mississippi have good education, that teachers got the pay they need to actually teach the students, where we make sure that hospitals are open and that healthcare is accessible, and that we actually live up to our American values, the country does well. When the country ignores places like Mississippi, inevitably it catches up with the country, and we all suffer. So, we have to understand that the math and the morals in Mississippi have to matter. …

You can’t lead with doubt. You have to believe. You have to lead with belief. And that’s where the power is. When you believe things, you can actually achieve it. And there’s some people in the party that they are just treading water. Right? “What’s the path to least resistance to get to 51? Ooh my gosh, we did it.” That’s not the right way to think. In this particular moment, you have to think about how can we win everywhere, because we need to represent working people in a way where we actually deliver.

AMY GOODMAN : So, there you have Scott Colom speaking right before the election on NBC News. Respond to Van Hollen, what he has said, and Colom.

DAVID SIROTA : Yeah, I think — look, I think what they’re talking about is a Democratic Party that has a broader vision than the current Democratic Party. And I think all of this is pointing to not just how Democrats need to try to win, but also how they need to try to compete to deliver. And that is a — that is the biggest question of all right now. Will a Democratic Party, with margins that it has now, really think more transformatively than it has in the past when it has had such majorities?

And that fight is playing out right now in politics. You see factions of the Democratic Party competing to decide and define what is possible right now. You see one faction saying we should demand votes on Medicare for All, we should demand votes on a much — on a really expansive agenda. Then you see the corporate Democrats trying to say, “No, no, no, no. This was essentially a status quo election. So-called moderates won.”

I tend to agree, in one sense, that Bernie Sanders-style anti-oligarch, populist agenda has become and is now being recognized as a moderate centrist agenda, but you have a faction of corporate-friendly Democrats who are trying to already preemptively slow down a push for Democrats to try to deliver in a big way. There’s this big conference that’s coming up in Denver where a billionaire-funded group is convening Democrats right now. This is the same group that has said that Democrats, for instance, should not push for a Medicare for All vote, should not even try to put a Medicare for All or Medicare for All-style bill on Donald Trump’s desk.

NERMEEN SHAIKH : Well, The Lever has been closely reporting on the gathering. On Thursday, Democracy Now! reached The Lever ’s Luke Goldstein.

LUKE GOLDSTEIN : There are two things that are really distinct about the Majority Democrats/Bench political operation. For one, they sort of offer the candidates they work with access to a really illustrious and powerful donor network that they control. There’s a lot of dark money that funds these groups, as well as large donors, primarily from Wall Street and Silicon Valley, you know, tech and finance sectors, for the most part.

And then the other additional service that’s more unique is that these groups offer, essentially, a political-operative-for-rent service to candidates. So, they have a setup of real kind of insider political operatives, probably most prominently Lis Smith, who previously worked on the Pete Buttigieg campaign in 2020. And those candidates will work with different campaigns at the same time as they work with these outside PACs, and it allows these groups to really kind of control and have a centralized narrative and political messaging that you’ll see spread out across those candidates.

I think it’s fair to say that these groups have a more kind of moderate political orientation. They definitely don’t support policies, for example, like Medicare for All. I would say that they are uneasy about policies like a data center moratorium. And they’re fairly hostile to the more left-wing climate and immigration groups, certainly.

NERMEEN SHAIKH : So, that’s The Lever ’s Luke Goldstein. And the meeting is happening today. If you could say more, David, about this billionaire-backed group, the Majority Democrats?

DAVID SIROTA : I think it — let’s add some context here. Look, we have seen this is sort of the faction with a thousand faces. People who have watched this show know this faction as the old Democratic Leadership Council. It has become the so-called — the group Third Way. It is the so-called New Democrats. Now it is called Majority Democrats. This is the same faction over and over throughout the generations: corporate-friendly Democrats who believe that winning politics means coddling oligarchs, means incrementalist-at-best policies, means a sort of deal with the corporate class for very small changes. It is essentially the faction that broke the Democratic Party away from its New Deal coalition and its New Deal agenda.

And so, Majority Democrats is a billionaire-backed group that is convening Democrats to negotiate right now at its conference, try to negotiate and sculpt the party’s agenda. I think it’s obviously more than ironic that we had an anti-oligarch, populist election, and the first thing that many major Democrats are doing are rushing to a conference funded by a billionaire, a billionaire-funded group. There’s an irony there. There’s a tension there. And I think the question is: What comes out of it?

AMY GOODMAN : David, we just have 30 seconds, but I want to go back to one of the top headlines this week, and that is that the Democrats, just by not showing up, not by being outvoted by the Republicans, they basically scuttled the possible impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. This goes to Hakeem Jeffries, who would be the majority leader, is the minority leader in the House. What happened?

DAVID SIROTA : I think it raises serious questions about how serious the Democratic leadership is, and some rank-and-file members of Congress, really the party itself. How serious are you about understanding the assignment and understanding the most basic things that need to be done to challenge Donald Trump? And I do think it is a huge question, in particular, as you allude to, for Hakeem Jeffries. Getting members to show up is the most basic, basic job of being a House leader, and certainly a House speaker.

AMY GOODMAN : David Sirota, we want to thank you for being with us, founder and editor-in-chief of The Lever . It has a new series, Don’t F#*k It Up, Democrats .

Coming up, as votes are still being counted in Alaska Senate and governor’s race, we’ll speak with Rob Richie of Expand Democracy about how ranked-choice voting could shape the Alaska election, and the growing movement to elect presidents by national popular vote rather than through the Electoral College. Back in 20 seconds.

[break]

AMY GOODMAN : “Greed” by Sweet Honey in the Rock in our firehouse studio years ago.

Special guests Angela Davis, Bruce Springsteen, Patti Smith, Michael Stipe and more came together to celebrate 30 years of Democracy Now! at a sold out Riverside Church event in NYC on March 23, 2026.

scraped.body_text:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.

Democrat Scott Colom has defeated incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first African American senator since the post-Civil War Reconstruction era. The electoral breakthrough is particularly meaningful given Mississippi’s history in the civil rights movement. In 1964, three civil rights activists — James Chaney, Michael Schwerner and Andrew Goodman — were murdered by the Ku Klux Klan after traveling to the state to register Black voters. We speak with two of their relatives about Colom’s stunning upset.

“I believe that people were voting for help. And they evidently saw something in Mr. Colom that made them feel like that they could hope again and that he was the help that was needed,” says Angela Lewis, the daughter of James Chaney.

“The people of Mississippi have spoken,” adds David Goodman, the brother of Andrew Goodman. “And we have to cease and desist this divide-and-conquer business, because it’s not in our collective interest as the United States of America.”

AMY GOODMAN : We go now to Meridian, Mississippi, where we’re joined by Angela Lewis, the daughter of civil rights activist James Chaney. She was born just 10 days before he was killed by the Ku Klux Klan along with Mickey Schwerner and Andrew Goodman. The date, June 21st, 1964. They were killed by local white supremacists in Mississippi and buried in an earthen dam, not found until 44 days later. The three had traveled to Mississippi as part of the Freedom Summer campaign to register Black voters.

Angela Lewis, thanks so much for being with us. I’m wondering your thoughts today. And as you watched Scott Colom last night accept the vote as the next Democratic senator from Mississippi, the first time a Black senator will represent Mississippi since Reconstruction, your thoughts?

ANGELA LEWIS : Good morning, and thank you for having me today.

First, I would like to say congratulations to Mr. Scott Colom, his family, and to all of those newly elected officials. I’m very happy, and I just think that this is a day of celebration, not only for Mississippi and for those that won, but I believe that the ancestors are proud and that the work that has been done to get us to this point, it has paid off, and it’s paying off today.

NERMEEN SHAIKH : So, Angela Lewis, if you could talk about some of that work? Leon Russell, the chairman of the NAACP board, said, “This is purely the work of particularly the Black community. There was not a whole lot of money, but there was a whole lot of organizing.” Angela?

ANGELA LEWIS : Yes, the foot soldiers, the boots on the ground, and those that were making the phone calls and doing the work, those are the people, the unsung heroes, that deserve a lot of credit for the wins.

NERMEEN SHAIKH : And Mississippi, as we mentioned earlier, has voted for a Republican presidential candidate in every election since the 1980s, and just in 2024, two years ago, Trump won the state by 23 points. So, what do you think accounts for this shift?

ANGELA LEWIS : I think it’s the dedication of the people that stay hopeful and believe that change is possible. And I believe that that’s what we have seen in these recent elections and a lot of the flips and turnovers that we’re seeing. It’s just dedicated people, teachers and the people in the community that’s getting out and registering and getting information out.

AMY GOODMAN : I also wanted to get your response to the county that’s named after the first Ku Klux Klan grand wizard, Nathan Bedford Forrest, Forrest County. Colom won. He also won the county named after Jefferson Davis, the president of the Confederacy. Colom won with 70% of the vote. The significance of this?

ANGELA LEWIS : It’s very significant. But I just believe that people were not voting for a particular color, a particular party. I believe that people were voting for help. And they evidently saw something in Mr. Colom that made them feel like that they could hope again and that he was the help that was needed.

AMY GOODMAN : And I also wanted to ask you about the vote that you took. You’re a psychiatric nurse. You’re speaking to us from work. You voted in Meridian, Mississippi. What did you do when you got back in your car? What did you tell your kids?

ANGELA LEWIS : Well, actually, on voting day, I had gotten off from work, and I went to cast my vote. And I sat in my car for a minute and prayed, and I thanked my dad and all of those that worked to make it possible for me to even be able to cast my vote. And when I did cast my vote and I came back to my vehicle, I just had to take a moment again to realize the significance of what could happen in this state and to again just be grateful for those that worked that we would have the opportunity and the privilege to even be able to cast a vote.

AMY GOODMAN : And I also wanted to get your response — I mean, you were cited by Scott Colom, your father, James Chaney. The famous wanted FBI poster — or, it said not “wanted,” but “missing.” James Chaney, your dad, Andrew Goodman and Mickey Schwerner, Michael Schwerner, killed in 1964 when they’d gone to Mississippi as part of the Freedom Summer campaign to register Black voters. They were first arrested, held in a jail, looked like there was law enforcement involvement when they were followed and then killed and buried in an earthen dam. You had just been born. Your thoughts about your father fighting for African Americans to be able to vote, what he would be feeling this day, James Chaney?

ANGELA LEWIS : I think that he would be, just like the rest of us here in Mississippi, very proud. And I just believe that the day after the Tuesday, after we voted, I believe that next Wednesday, if not the same day, my dad would have gotten up and continued to work and to educate and to register people to vote.

AMY GOODMAN : Well, I want to bring in a person you know well, Angela Lewis, David Goodman. He is the brother of Andrew Goodman, who also, along with your dad and Michael Schwerner, were killed in June. It took 44 days for their bodies to be found, dug up in an earthen dam. The call to the White House — it was Lyndon Johnson, the president at the time — was taken by none other than the late, great journalist Bill Moyers, who was working for Johnson.

David Goodman, thanks so much for being with us. I spoke to you last night just as Scott Colom was about to speak. Your thoughts as you’re on this broadcast, as you’re on Democracy Now! with Angela Lewis today?

DAVID GOODMAN : Well, Amy, it’s — thank you for having us on the show. Hello, Angela. It’s always good to be with you in the spirit world that we live in.

My feelings are that we use words often that — like a “blue wave.” If the Republicans won, it would have been a “red wave.” We’re using the word “tsunami” now. This is not a tsunami. A tsunami is a destruction for all. This is a spiritual change of heart, and it wasn’t easy and a long time coming. And the people of Mississippi have spoken, but the people of the United States are benefiting, whether you’re a Republican or Democrat. And we have to cease and desist this divide-and-conquer business, because it’s not in our collective interest as the United States of America. And —

AMY GOODMAN : David —

DAVID GOODMAN : — [Senator]-elect Scott has taught us that.

AMY GOODMAN : David, you never stopped carrying on your brother’s work, Schwerner, Chaney and Goodman’s work, involved with supporting voter registration on colleges throughout the South. Is that right?

DAVID GOODMAN : Yes.

NERMEEN SHAIKH : And, David, you referred just now to a spiritual change of heart. How do you think this change of heart came about?

DAVID GOODMAN : You know, we’re a big country. We’re the third or fourth most populous country in the world, and one of the biggest. There’s 340 million of us, so making a generalization is tough. But there’s a lot of pain in our country. And I travel. I’ve been in every state. I’ve lived in many states. I’m in contact with people all over our exquisite and beautiful country. We’re complicated folks. We’re not a homogeneous race or identity group. We’re diverse. And we get fit into these little boxes: You’re Christian, you’re Jewish, you’re Muslim, this, that and the other. And it’s easy for power-hungry, authoritarian people to come in and drive wedges in between us. And this has caused massive problems. And we got hoodwinked by a con artist who’s in the White House using those wedges to make us fight with each other. And I think the American people are sick and tired of it. I am.

And the vote, look, these were just stunning messages. And the authoritarian force, which is heard all over the world, is doubling down. So, we’re not — we can’t stop. We can’t say, “Oh, we won an election. Let’s take a nap and go on vacation.” It’s going to go on indefinitely if we don’t continuously object to authoritarian small group of people running things. And that’s not what happened. I mean, I can’t make — you can’t make this story up. It’s just stunning. You have a person who’s the attorney general of one of our largest states, Texas, who was impeached by his own party and is running. The governor —

AMY GOODMAN : But, of course, he lost. James Talarico beat him, and there was —

DAVID GOODMAN : He did.

AMY GOODMAN : — to say the least, a blue wave in Texas. David and Angela, we do have to go, but I want to thank you both for being with us. David Goodman, the brother of Andrew Goodman. Angela Lewis, the daughter of James Chaney. Andrew Goodman, James Chaney and Mickey Schwerner were three civil rights activists who went to Mississippi to register Black people to vote. They were killed June 21st, 1964, cited by Scott Colom last night in his victory address at Tougaloo College, the historically Black college. Tomorrow, we’ll look at the legacy of Medgar Evers, also killed by the Klan, also cited by Scott Colom as the legacy on which he now will rebuild his state.

Coming up, David Sirota of The Lever . Stay with us.

[break]

AMY GOODMAN : “Nunca Más (Never Again)” by La Santa Cecilia in our Democracy Now! studio.

Special guests Angela Davis, Bruce Springsteen, Patti Smith, Michael Stipe and more came together to celebrate 30 years of Democracy Now! at a sold out Riverside Church event in NYC on March 23, 2026.

scraped.title: New Trump Rule Threatens Immigrant Families With Separation or Homelessness
scraped.description: A new HUD rule is on track to kick thousands of mixed-immigration-status families off of federal housing assistance.
scraped.author: Jessica Washington
scraped.h1: New Trump Rule Threatens Immigrant Families With Separation or Homelessness
scraped.body_text:
© THE INTERCEPT

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

A new HUD rule is on track to kick thousands of mixed-immigration-status families off of federal housing assistance.

The Trump administration is preparing to kick nearly 80,000 people, about half of them children, off federal housing assistance over their family’s immigration status, threatening to drive thousands into homelessness.

On Thursday, the Department of Housing and Urban Development published a final rule that’s on track to effectively bar families of mixed immigration status from receiving most federal housing assistance, which allow people to receive housing vouchers to reside in privately owned rental homes or in government-owned or -assisted public housing units.

As it stands, undocumented immigrants and temporary non-residents in the United States already are barred from personally receiving most forms of federal housing assistance. But if some members of the family are eligible, the eligible members can receive prorated assistance to help cover their housing, and the non-eligible family member can live with them.

Most Read Pentagon Officials Float Names of Hegseth’s Replacement Nick Turse Hegseth Survives Impeachment Attempt Matt Sledge, Nick Turse Is There a Left Candidate for President? Akela Lacy

The new rule, which goes into effect in mid-December, would disqualify an entire family if one member is ineligible after a temporary grace period, forcing them to choose between separation and eviction.

Families are “going to be faced with the impossible choice of deciding whether they want to split up so that some people can stay housed, or to stay together and risk homelessness and eviction,” said Marie Claire Tran-Leung, Evictions Initiative Project director at the National Housing Law Project.

Children will bear a disproportionate burden, Tran-Leung said. Of the nearly 80,000 people who could be affected, according to estimates from Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, nearly 37,000 are children.

Of the nearly 80,000 people who could be affected, nearly 37,000 are children.

Many families have one parent who doesn’t qualify, one parent who’s a citizen or otherwise eligible immigrant — i.e. a permanent resident — and kids who hold U.S. citizenship. According to Tran-Leung, the typical mixed-status family in HUD housing is a family of four that fits that profile.

This rule is “going to tear families apart and take adults away from their children,” said Deborah Thrope, chief program officer at the National Housing Law Project.

Beyond potentially leaving tens of thousands of families and children homeless or separated, the change could cost the already beleaguered federal housing agency hundreds of millions of dollars, housing experts told The Intercept. This would likely worsen conditions across the board for the roughly 9 million people in federal housing, who would now be subject to onerous documentation requirements.

“The impacts are not just limited to mixed-status families,” said Renee Williams, senior advisor for public policy at the National Low Income Housing Coalition.

This rule is “going to tear families apart and take adults away from their children.”

Currently, both U.S. citizens and non-citizens are required to submit a declaration under penalty of perjury attesting that their citizenship or immigration status makes them eligible for housing assistance. Non-citizens under age 62 must submit a document that proves their immigration status. And additional documentation can be requested by local housing agencies or landlords.

The rule change would upend the current system. U.S. citizens would have to go through the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements program, also known as SAVE, to verify their eligibility status.

“It’s a system that hasn’t been used to verify citizenship before but now is because of the work that DHS and DOGE did together on a very expedited timeline at the beginning of the Trump administration,” said Tran-Leung. “This causes a lot of concern for us about the very significant risks of residents who are citizens being caught up in verification issues and potentially losing their housing.”

If SAVE cannot verify someone’s eligibility , the new rule requires the person to provide documentation proving their status. The rule would give families 30 days to obtain evidence of immigration status, in addition to the initial 30-day grace period where families can receive pro-rated assistance before having to go through verification.

Tran-Leung and other experts worry that the new documentation requirements could make it harder for low-income tenants — particularly older immigrants over the age of 62 , who were previously exempted from verification requirements — to access the program.

Older people, low-income people, and people who’ve experienced homelessness are far more likely to lack access to proof of citizenship such as a passport, valid photo ID, or birth certificate. That means an untold number of the millions of eligible people in federal housing programs could lose assistance just for lack of documentation.

“For folks who may not have easy documentation accessible, who may not have access to a birth certificate, who may not have access to a passport, we’re really worried,” said Williams.

The changes would also burden housing agencies financially by requiring their staff to review documents that were previously not required by federal law.

It is unclear just how expensive these additional administrative costs will be for HUD. But an analysis from HUD itself found that because mixed-status families receive assistance prorated, it would cost the federal government $300 million in additional funds to serve the same number of families as it does now.

For example, a family of four with one ineligible member currently receives 75% of a full household subsidy. A family of four that is not mixed status receives 100% of the subsidy, making it more expensive for the agency to house the non-mixed-status family even though the two families have the same number of people.

“At the same time, HUD is requesting fewer funds from Congress to end homelessness,” said Kayla Blackwell, senior housing policy analyst at the National Low Income Housing Coalition. President Donald Trump recently proposed cutting $3.8 billion from the agency’s affordable housing, homelessness, and community development programs.

HUD Secretary Scott Turner has justified the rule by claiming that mixed-status families are “pushing aside hardworking U.S. citizens” for housing. But experts said the changes will make the system worse for everyone.

“This is scapegoating immigrant families, and HUD is doing less,” said Blackwell.

For the families who either are forced out of the program or leave willingly due to fears around their status, the road ahead is difficult. The majority of mixed-status families live in California, Texas, and New York, where the cost of living can be incredibly high.

“It’s going to be really difficult, I think, for families to be able to stay in their communities and not be displaced if they lose their access to HUD assistance,” said Blackwell.

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.

This is not hyperbole.

Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.

Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”

The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.

Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.

In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

scraped.title: Humanitarian Orgs Demand Answers on Yemen War After Hegseth Impeachment Fails
scraped.description: A dozen groups are urging congressional oversight of civilian harm in Trump and Hegseth’s “forgotten war” on Yemen.
scraped.author: Nick Turse
scraped.h1: Humanitarian Orgs Demand Answers on Yemen War After Hegseth Impeachment Fails
scraped.body_text:
© THE INTERCEPT

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

A dozen groups are urging congressional oversight of civilian harm in Trump’s “forgotten war.”

With Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth temporarily safe from impeachment, a dozen humanitarian groups are calling on Congress to investigate one of the eight shelved charges lodged against him: his role in the deaths of hundreds of people during the “unauthorized war in Yemen.”

“We urge members of Congress to conduct robust oversight into Operation Rough Rider and the resulting human toll,” reads a new letter shared exclusively with The Intercept, using the Pentagon’s term for its war against Yemen’s Houthi government . The 12 groups — including Airwars, Amnesty International USA, the Center for Civilians in Conflict, and Mwatana for Human Rights — seize on civilian harm prevention efforts that Hegseth’s War Department slashed, demanding “more information about how and why civilian harm incidents occurred, what lessons the Department learned from these operations, and the status of ongoing civilian harm assessments and investigations.”

The push for accountability follows last week’s electoral rout of the GOP and immediate calls by top Democrats for scrutiny of war powers abuses by the Trump administration. But with Democrats taking the gavel in both chambers next year, a defense official told The Intercept that the Trump administration’s failed 2025 conflict in Yemen risks becoming a “forgotten war” amid a push for accountability focused on higher profile conflicts.

Most Read Pentagon Officials Float Names of Hegseth’s Replacement Nick Turse Hegseth Survives Impeachment Attempt Matt Sledge, Nick Turse Is There a Left Candidate for President? Akela Lacy

Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the House Armed Services Committee’s incoming chair, announced last week that the committee’s “top priority will be to conduct vigorous oversight of the Department of Defense and the Trump Administration,” specifically singling out “the illegal war against Iran” and “unauthorized military strikes in the Caribbean and Latin America.” Smith did not mention Yemen, and his office did not respond to repeated queries about whether Yemen would also be a priority. The office of Sen. Jack Reed, D-R.I., who is slated to head the Senate Armed Services Committee, also did not immediately respond to questions about whether oversight of Rough Rider would be a focus.

Over just 52 days, from March to May 2025, Rough Rider caused “extraordinarily high numbers of civilian casualties,” the groups noted. As The Intercept first reported in August, the Pentagon’s annual report to Congress on civilian harm acknowledged almost 400 civilian casualties — 153 deaths and 243 injuries — from just three attacks in Yemen: a strike in Sanaa on April 6, a strike on the Ras Isa Port on April 17, and a strike on a migrant detention center in Saada on April 28.

Amnesty, one of the signatories, spoke with five survivors of the strike in Saada who cannot work because of their injuries. “If I don’t take a painkiller, I feel hopeless and wish to die,” said a 22-year-old Ethiopian man who sustained a serious arm injury in the U.S. attack. “I think about how at such a young age I can’t even support myself and still rely on help from others. The metal rod inside me is very painful and uncomfortable. It drives you insane.”

A U.S. official called the Pentagon’s civilian casualty count “lowball numbers.” According to the Yemen Data Project , the estimated toll was higher: at least 238 civilians killed and 467 injured.

“It’s striking that the Department acknowledged nearly 400 civilian casualties from just three incidents — a staggeringly high rate — without any explanation whatsoever about what happened and why, how they’ll respond to victims and their families, and how they’ll prevent it from happening again,” Annie Shiel, the U.S. director of Center for Civilians in Conflict, told The Intercept.

“How will they get through hundreds of cases for Iran if their one civilian harm person still hasn’t finished Yemen?”

More than a year after Operation Rough Rider ended, 15 additional attacks were still under assessment, according to the civilian harm report. One official told The Intercept in August that the backlog would likely carry over several years. Under Hegseth, the 10-person civilian harm mitigation team at Central Command, or CENTCOM, has been reduced to just one individual .

This lack of attention doesn’t bode well for understanding civilian harm in Hegseth’s longer-running and even more destructive war efforts, officials said.

“How will they get through hundreds of cases for Iran if their one civilian harm person still hasn’t finished Yemen?” a U.S. official asked in August.

At present, CENTCOM claims that the U.S. attack on the Shajarah Tayyebeh elementary school in Minab, Iran – that killed more than 150 people, most of them children — is the lone civilian harm incident of that burgeoning forever war. For months, CENTCOM has failed to answer questions about that attack and additional Iranian civilian casualties, including eight members of a family — the youngest, a 20-day-old infant — killed in a strike documented in an investigation by The Intercept.

Shiel highlighted the connections between the civilian casualties during Rough Rider and those in Iran.

“There is a through-line here from Yemen. We’ll never know if the devastation of Minab would have been prevented through a fully staffed civilian protection program and a more robust inquiry into what happened in Yemen, but it’s clear that important reckoning didn’t happen,” she said. “This is part of a broader trend of focusing on ‘lethality’ over civilian lives, ignoring hard-learned lessons in the process.”

A group of Democratic lawmakers told Hegseth in a July letter that his “gutting” of Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response efforts has left the Pentagon unable to “comply with the law and its congressionally-mandated CHMR responsibilities.” Sent by Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and nine other lawmakers, the letter echoed concerns raised by a War Department inspector general report that described civilian protection efforts as largely “inactive.” The May missive by the Pentagon’s top watchdog says cuts to civilian harm mitigation and response efforts have been so severe under Hegseth that the United States cannot adequately protect civilians in conflict zones or track harm when it occurs.

These criticisms were echoed in an another report , first revealed by The Intercept in July, that found Hegseth’s Pentagon gutted its premier center devoted to preventing civilian casualties in war zones. The War Department’s Civilian Protection Center of Excellence slashed its staff from 40 personnel in January 2025 to just nine by the end of the year, according to the report.

Last week, The Intercept published an exposé quoting six current and former defense officials under Hegseth who called for his ouster, including a former senior adviser at that center. “He is conducting state terrorism. He is 100 percent a war criminal. He needs to be prosecuted,” said Wes J. Bryant, who was pushed out of his job for blowing the whistle on Hegseth’s efforts to undermine protections for civilians .

The 12 humanitarian groups called on Congress to “fully restore” the Pentagon’s civilian harm mitigation program, “including by mandating minimum staffing levels and earmarking funding in annual appropriations and maintaining robust oversight over DoD implementation of congressionally-mandated policies.” The groups also specifically requested the release of the Civilian Protection Center’s lessons-learned study on Operation Rough Rider, which has been bottled up for months.

During a rare Pentagon press conference on Tuesday, ahead of the impeachment vote , Hegseth celebrated Rough Rider, claiming the Houthis “cried uncle.” But a post-mortem of the operation in the CTC Sentinel — published by the Combating Terrorism Center at the U.S. Military Academy at West Point — said that because of Rough Rider, the Houthi leadership “will have the confidence that, like the Taliban in Afghanistan, it can simply outlast the United States.”

The U.S. has, to date, failed to come to the aid of its staunch ally Saudi Arabia as the Houthis have battered that country’s airports and energy infrastructure for weeks. On Monday, an attack on the financial district in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, damaged an office of Aramco, the state oil giant.

The White House failed to respond to questions about the Yemen war from The Intercept. CENTCOM did not reply to a request for information on the status of civilian harm assessments or formal investigations stemming from Rough Rider.

Shiel was emphatic about the necessity of accountability, telling The Intercept, “Congress needs to step in and force that reckoning through oversight over civilian harm incidents and by mandating and funding the restoration of the civilian harm mitigation program.”

In their letter, the 12 humanitarian organizations urged the U.S. to make amends to survivors and the families of victims.

“The Department’s 2025 report also stated that ex gratia or condolence payments to victims and survivors were ‘determined to not be appropriate’ in the three Yemen incidents. This decision is premature and seemingly arbitrary,” they wrote. “Rather than dismissing amends out of hand, the Department should undertake a good-faith effort to understand families’ needs and preferences for responses.”

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.

This is not hyperbole.

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.

In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

© THE INTERCEPT

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

Trump loyalist Gary Lawkowski has no national security experience to speak of. He could become the top lawyer for the nation’s spy chief.

As a lawyer on President Donald Trump’s 2024 reelection bid, Gary Lawkowski filed a complaint against the Washington Post for supposedly making an in-kind contribution to the Kamala Harris campaign by buying social media advertising for its articles.

In the White House, he played a pivotal role in the pardons process that rewarded Trump cronies and donors.

Now, Lawkowski could serve in an obscure but crucial role within the nation’s top intelligence agency, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. On Monday, Trump nominated Lawkowski to serve as general counsel of ODNI.

It is unclear when Lawkowski will appear before a confirmation hearing or whether Democrats will look favorably upon him when they take control of the Senate in January. His nomination is already drawing pushback, however, from a progressive group that says it represents another attempt to politicize the ODNI after Trump’s bid to install loyalist Bill Pulte as its director fizzled .

“Lawkowski has been a key player in Trump’s corrupt pardon scheme and his nomination tells us that the administration is trying to stack the intelligence community with cronies so they can further weaponize it against their perceived political opponents and innocent Americans,” Hajar Hammado, senior policy adviser at Demand Progress, said in a statement. “Senators must oppose his nomination.”

Most Read Pentagon Officials Float Names of Hegseth’s Replacement Nick Turse Hegseth Survives Impeachment Attempt Matt Sledge, Nick Turse Is There a Left Candidate for President? Akela Lacy

The ODNI is a relatively small agency, and it doesn’t hoover up its own raw data. As the only intelligence body operating at the Cabinet level, however, it is tasked with coordinating and overseeing intelligence collection and analysis at other spy agencies like the CIA and National Security Agency.

Under former Director Tulsi Gabbard, the ODNI took an unusually prominent role in declassifying information that cast a negative light on Trump’s enemies or fed into right-wing obsessions, such as the Covid lab-leak controversy .

The general counsel plays an important role in interpreting spying law — meaning that Lawkowski could either facilitate or block intelligence community abuses.

In recent months, Trump has displayed an unusual interest in the ODNI, installing housing czar Pulte to replace Gabbard before bipartisan pushback forced him to tap former prosecutor Jay Clayton as a permanent replacement.

In his current role at the White House, Lawkowski serves as deputy assistant and deputy counsel to the president, according to his most recent ethics disclosure , and it is unclear whether he has relevant national security experience.

There is ample evidence that he is a loyalist to Trump. As a lawyer on the Trump campaign, he blasted off a complaint to the Federal Election Commission claiming that the Washington Post’s online advertisements about stories on Trump represented an in-kind contribution to Harris’s campaign. Campaign finance law experts said the claim was baseless. Lawkowski also represented Trump in litigation over the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol.

In the White House, he has helped decide who does and does not receive pardons, according to reporting last year in the New York Times. Under Trump, the White House has asserted authority over a pardons process that traditionally flowed through the Department of Justice.

Trump’s blanket clemency for January 6, 2021, insurrectionists preceded a parade of pardons for people who donated to his campaign or causes , or Republican officials who had been convicted of corruption , drawing widespread criticism.

One of the many who received a Trump pardon was former Tennessee state senator Brian Kelsey , who had been represented by Lawkowski before the lawyer went to the White House. Lawkowski did not respond to a request for comment on whether he recused himself from that pardon.

The likely incoming intelligence chair, Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., was harshly critical of Trump’s temporary appointment of Pulte at the ODNI. He ultimately voted against Clayton’s nomination after touting him as a more acceptable alternative to Pulte. (Warner’s office did not respond to a request for comment.)

Lawkowski was tapped to replace John “Jack” Dever, who was confirmed by the Senate to serve as general counsel a little over a year ago. Members of the Southern Negro Youth Congress meet with Idaho Senator Glen Taylor.
