“B ehold the land, the rich and resourceful land, from which for a hundred years its best elements have been running away, its youth and hope, black and white, scurrying North because they are of each other, and dare not face a future of equal, independent, upstanding human beings, in a real and not a sham democracy.” This line was spoken by W. E. B. Du Bois near the end of arguably his greatest speech, titled “Behold the Land.” It was delivered on October 20, 1946, at a convention hosted by the Southern Negro Youth Congress (SNYC), where Du Bois thundered from the dais at Antisdel Chapel at Benedict College in Columbia, South Carolina. He and the SNYC had, for a brief moment, made the Palmetto State the center of the struggle for global human rights in the post–World War II years.

Founded in 1937, the SNYC represented the radical wing of the early phase of the civil rights movement. Its radical politics lay in the organization’s recognition of the links between racial and class problems in the US South and throughout the nation. At times, it made alliances on the ground with various Communist Party USA organizations in the South. While many historians have come to see the civil rights era as extending longer than the “classic” phase of 1954 until the mid-1960s, what makes the SNYC unique is how many of the issues they attacked would come up again during both the 1960s and the early decades of the twenty-first century.

As part of the youth wing of the National Negro Congress (NNC), the SNYC went well beyond organizing the black youth of the Jim Crow–era South. It offered them an opportunity to voice and do something about the growing frustration many of them felt living in the grip of Jim Crow segregation.

Through the course of the Great Depression and World War II, the SNYC pressured political and social leaders throughout the South. As they pressed for greater freedom for all people in the former Confederacy, the SNYC became a beacon of hope during the fight against fascism at home and abroad. The SNYC always linked the struggles against Jim Crow segregation at home to the rising tide of fascism, Nazism, and militarism abroad, even before the advent of the better-known “Double V” campaign among black Americans during World War II, pushing for victory over fascism abroad and Jim Crow at home.

The bread and butter of the organization was the organizing of previously disenfranchised workers in the South. Their earliest campaigns included the organizing of black tobacco farmers outside their first headquarters of Richmond, Virginia. At other points, the SNYC would participate in voter registration drives and work with unions to increase labor organizing across a region that, by the Great Depression, had earned a staunchly anti-labor reputation. Other efforts included the investigation of cases of murder in the South via private investigators, such as the case of William Daniel’s 1946 murder by Birmingham police. In short, like the NNC and other radical organizations of the Great Depression and World War II eras, the SNYC used virtually every method at their disposal to fight against Jim Crow segregation.

But the challenges facing the SNYC were more dangerous after America’s triumph in World War II. A rift formed between liberals and leftists after the war; the wartime exigency of the American-Soviet alliance gave way to fears of another world war, this time between the United States and its allies against the Soviet Union and a growing postwar Communist bloc. At the same time, anti-colonial campaigns were spreading like wildfire across Asia and Africa. This, coupled with black frustration at home due to renewed white backlash to civil rights, gave the SNYC ample reason to step up their efforts in a place like South Carolina.

B y 1946, South Carolina already had a growing movement for radical human rights. The Progressive Democratic Party (PDP), led by black South Carolinians Modjeska Simkins, John Henry McCray, and Osceola McKaine, built a progressive black alternative to South Carolina’s white-supremacist Democratic Party of South Carolina. Registering black South Carolinians to vote, putting up their own slate of candidates for state and national office, and even traveling to the 1944 Democratic National Convention to challenge the legitimacy of the South Carolina Democratic Party, the Progressive Democratic Party presaged the better-known Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party ( MFDP ) by twenty years in using grassroots democratic traditions to attempt to upend the old system.

Their efforts to overturn the ironclad rule of the white-supremacist Democratic Party did not result in electoral victory. Osceola McKaine, the black nominee of the PDP who campaigned against incumbent Olin Johnston in 1944, fell short in his campaign. But McKaine’s own personal story is a reminder of why black South Carolina, in 1944, was so thoroughly galvanized to fight back against Jim Crow.

McKaine, a native of Sumter, South Carolina, served in the United States military during World War I. After his term of service ended, McKaine, tired of the hypocrisy of American calls to “make the world safe for democracy” abroad while not doing so at home, settled in Ghent, Belgium, and opened a successful nightclub. Forced to flee Belgium due to World War II, McKaine returned to Sumter determined to fight for democracy in his home state. He was defeated in 1944 by Johnston, who was governor of South Carolina when the state condemned to death fourteen-year-old George Stinney, who some believe is the youngest person condemned to death in US history.

The PDP, like the MFDP twenty years later, was important not due to victory at the polls but due to the organization’s ability to give voters hope who had had none for generations. Thousands of new black voters became part of South Carolina’s voting process for the first time since the immediate aftermath of the collapse of Reconstruction. Meanwhile, growing pressure to restore the right to vote for black citizens in the South was also enhanced by the 1944 Smith v. Allwright Supreme Court decision, which declared the all-white primaries of Southern Democratic parties unconstitutional.

Again, South Carolina played a crucial role in resisting this, with Governor Johnston himself calling a special session of the state legislature in 1944 to pass new laws to continue the white primary. It was not until another federal court case, Elmore v. Rice , originating with the challenge of black South Carolinian George Elmore and decided in 1947, that the white primary was broken.

S outh Carolina, therefore, had already made itself the nexus of domestic political battles over racism and citizenship. But the state was also important as a site of international debate over the future of peace in the post–World War II landscape. One of the chief architects of the post–World War II foreign policy, which quickly became antagonistic toward the Soviets, was South Carolinian James Byrnes.

Often overlooked in twentieth-century American foreign and domestic policy history, Byrnes holds the unique distinction of being one of the few politicians in American history to hold virtually every possible office in the federal government. He served as congressman, and later senator, from South Carolina in the 1920s and 1930s. As a close friend to President Franklin D. Roosevelt, Byrnes briefly served on the Supreme Court before being named director of the Office of Economic Stabilization, and later director of the Office of War Mobilization during World War II. In that role, Byrnes became one of the most important people in America’s war effort. Afterward, under President Harry Truman, Byrnes was named secretary of state in 1945.

But Byrnes coveted the presidency. As was the case with another South Carolinian, John C. Calhoun, in the nineteenth century, Byrnes’s ties to South Carolina and white-supremacist ideology became the chief impediments to higher office. Most notably, liberals and progressives within the New Deal–era Democratic Party stymied efforts to make Byrnes the vice president under Franklin Roosevelt during his 1944 campaign. Still, Byrnes remained a powerful force within Southern and national politics. And as the Cold War intensified, a massive campaign for social change in his home state made perfect sense.

The SNYC, committed as it was to racial justice at home and peace abroad, knew that targeting Byrnes’ home state was a major rallying point for the radical wing of American politics in the post–World War II years. Also, the fact that South Carolina was home to a growing radical movement for human rights helped make it a logical choice for the SNYC’s annual convention.

Bringing both foreign and domestic crises together, finally, was the saga of Isaac Woodard, which galvanized activists and brought global attention to South Carolina. A black World War II veteran blinded by police on February 12, 1946, in Batesburg-Leesville, South Carolina, Woodard’s case became a symbol of the brutal attacks on black veterans and their allies that occurred throughout the South after World War II. A backlash similar to the Red Summer of 1919 , the post-1945 political and social environment was incredibly difficult and reactionary, but also presented incredible opportunities to SNYC leaders.

The SNYC needed a place to not only bring together their members but a location where a new, militant human rights movement was evolving on the ground. Columbia became that place, due in large part to the work of Modjeska Simkins in welcoming the organization to her hometown.

The 1946 convention in Columbia, South Carolina owed a great deal to Modjeska Simkins. A human rights activist born and raised in Columbia, Simkins had become, by 1946, one of the leaders of a radical human and civil rights movement in the Palmetto State. She became secretary of the South Carolina State Conference of the NAACP in 1941 after working tirelessly in black communities across the state as director of negro work for the South Carolina Tuberculosis Association, and after playing a pivotal role in the formation of the state conference in 1939.

Many years later, in an oral history interview with Jacquelyn Dowd Hall, Simkins argued that the SNYC represented something unique and powerful in the broader human and civil rights movements of the twentieth century. “The power structure,” Simkins stated, “has always feared the combining of the forces of black and white masses.”

This was what the SNYC represented. On the first insert page of the 1946 conference program , the Southern Youth Legislature, which was the organizing body within the SNYC that spoke for the organization, made their demands clear. “We meet in solemn session,” they began, as “militant, courageous Negro youth of the South. Youth. . . . which must and will be served. Youth. . . . dedicated to the struggle for freedom. Youth determined to achieve that freedom in its lifetime.” For members of the SNYC, the opportunity arose to finally make a serious blow against segregation. Or, as the title of Erik Gellman ’s groundbreaking 2012 work on the National Negro Congress goes, a “death blow to Jim Crow.”

Some of the leaders of the 1946 conference, like Modjeska Simkins or Dorothy Burnham, would become better known throughout the twentieth century for their work in various strands of the civil and human rights movements. Others, such as Columbia SNYC leader Harold H. Poole or Benedict College student Ethel Bigby, are not as well known nationally or even regionally. But they all were pivotal leaders in a movement that, in 1946, seemed poised to tackle the crises that Dr Martin Luther King Jr so eloquently described a generation later: militarism, racism, and capitalism.

Alas, the Second Red Scare at home and the Cold War abroad destroyed the SNYC. The organization was constantly harassed by the FBI and local police forces in the South. Ultimately, the organization was also brought down, like others, due to its alliance with the 1948 Progressive Party campaign of Henry Wallace. Eugene “Bull” Connor — better remembered for his vicious treatment of activists in Birmingham in 1963 — created havoc for left-wing activists in Birmingham.

Its 1946 convention remains the high point of the organization’s history, leaving behind a legacy of activism in South Carolina and throughout the nation. Many of the members of the SNYC, or those affiliated with the organization, continued to be involved in activism deep into the twentieth century. For example, several of the founders of the legendary Freedomways magazine, which between 1961 and 1985 served as a key periodical for the black left, were veterans of the SNYC. Editors and writers such as Esther Cooper Jackson, Louis Burnham, and even Du Bois himself all had significant ties with the organization.

In that sense, the SNYC is part of the larger connective tissue of twentieth century radical social movements — and the 1946 convention in South Carolina was its moment of triumph.

Robert Greene II is an assistant professor of history at Claflin University and publications chair for the Society of US Intellectual Historians and lead associate editor for Black Perspectives .

scraped.title: How Cultural Marxism Became a Right-Wing Obsession
scraped.description: The term “cultural Marxism” has become one of the main rallying cries for the international right. This lurid conspiracy theory about the influence of the Frankfurt School has little connection to reality, but that doesn’t make it any less dangerous.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

The term “cultural Marxism” has become one of the main rallying cries for the international right. This lurid conspiracy theory about the influence of the Frankfurt School has little connection to reality, but that doesn’t make it any less dangerous.

The cultural Marxism conspiracy theory is the political right’s attempt to explain why the culture of Western societies has changed since the 1960s. It blames the Frankfurt School for the rise of multiculturalism, feminism, and environmentalism. (The Marcuse family, represented by Harold Marcuse / CC BY-SA 3.0 [lightly cropped])

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

I n December 2021, the term “cultural Marxism” was added to the Oxford English Dictionary . It was, according to the OED , a phrase with a sinister and controversial past. Its etymology could allegedly be traced to 1930s Nazi propaganda; its first recorded English-language use was in a 1938 issue of a British Union of Fascists magazine.

Despite its dark history, this expression has recently surged in popularity. College campuses and city streets have been plastered with stickers that urge passersby to “smash” cultural Marxism. Prominent US Republicans, such as Texas Senator Ted Cruz and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, have written book-length polemics to blame America’s decline on cultural Marxist ideologies.

Leaders in Latin America, like Brazil’s former President Jair Bolsonaro and Argentina’s President Javier Milei, have vowed to rid their governments of this left-wing scourge. In the United Kingdom, Conservative Party MPs have said that cultural Marxists are “destroying” children’s souls and “snuffing out” the right to free speech.

Even the world’s richest man, tech-mogul-turned-Trumpian Elon Musk, has voiced concerns about a Wikipedia article that dismisses cultural Marxism as a “conspiracy theory.” This buzzword has now become a fixture in the lexicon of the contemporary Right — but what does it mean?

“C ultural Marxism,” or the “cultural Marxism conspiracy theory,” is the political right’s attempt to explain why the culture of Western societies has changed over the past sixty years. According to this theory, a group of German thinkers known as the Frankfurt School (or the Institute for Social Research) invented the “ideologies” of multiculturalism, fem­inism, and environmentalism to trigger the demise of Western civilization.

When Theodor Adorno, Herbert Marcuse, and other Frankfurt School theorists fled Nazi Germany, they trav­eled to the United States and successfully injected their ideas into the 1960s student movement — or so the story goes. In the late twentieth century, their indoctrinated disciples performed a “long march through the institutions” (a phrase coined by German New Left activist Rudi Dutschke) to promote cultural Marxism in education, the media, the government, and the church.

More recently, right-wing activists and conservative pundits have used this theory to understand the rise of the Black Lives Matter movement, the increased visibility of LGBTQ+ communities, and the efforts to tackle the climate emergency. Even in countries outside the United States, conservatives have engaged in a “culture war” to defend their societies from this supposed menace.

What is cultural about this cultural Marxism? What is Marxist about cultural change? Conservative critics speculate that the Frankfurt School developed a fresh strategy of commu­nist subversion in the 1930s. Instead of building a vanguardist party or seizing the factories, the Frankfurt School decided to infiltrate the cultural apparatus of bourgeois society to under­mine Western capitalism.

Once ensconced in these positions of power, the critics maintain, cultural Marxists catered to the petulant demands of various minority groups — Black people, LGBTQ+ people, feminists — and dismantled the civilizational inheritance of the (white) majority. The Frankfurt School apparently believed that this strategy would cause a Marxist egalitarian utopia to emerge from the ruins of Western culture.

As the art historian Sven Lütticken observes, this alternative intellectual history relies on a theory of culture that mixes “conservative essential­ism” with “schematic superstructuralism.” Culture, according to this right-wing conception, naturally reflects the values of a native populace. These values fuse a nation’s citizens into a harmonious unity that annuls antagonism and difference.

Yet this essentialist notion of culture cannot account for the drastic social changes that have taken place since the 1960s, because it treats the subordination of minorities as “natural” (or even as virtuous). Consequently, conservatives must conclude that an outside agent has seized the organs of cultural production to destroy the West.

In an act of self-defense, the opponents of cultural Marxism propose to eliminate every instance of “political correctness” or “wokeness” in public life through legislative reform, lifestyle changes, or violence. In this version of global events, the Frankfurt School and their devotees are blessed with a magical level of agency that can overcome all contradictions and countervailing forces.

O f course, no one can deny the historical existence and importance of the Frankfurt School. But why does this narrative of cultural degeneration focus so much on a collective of German Marxists? How does it continue to convince and excite the forces of political reaction? What is the genealogy of this idea we call the “cultural Marxism conspiracy theory”?

Some scholars suggest that “cultural Marxism” is simply an updated version of older antisemitic conspiracy theories like “Judeo-Bolshevism” or “cultural Bolshevism.” Of course, there are some eerie parallels between these earlier ideas and “cultural Marxism.” The British Union of Fascists translated Kulturbolschewismus as “cultural Marxism” in 1938, even if their use of the term was long forgotten by the time it was “recoined” in the early 1990s.

Contemporary far-right activists and authors tend to emphasize that several members of the Frankfurt School were Jewish, as if to suggest that these thinkers were genetically predisposed to operate as agents of cultural degeneracy. Even more damningly, the fascist online encyclopedia Metapedia once maintained an entry on cultural Marxism that presented the term as interchangeable with “cultural Bolshevism.”

It is ahistorical, however, to claim that “cultural Marxism” is nothing more than a rebranding of these previous tropes. This argument presupposes that Judeo-Bolshevism, cultural Bolshevism, and cultural Marxism are substantially identical, as though they share a transcendental essence that precedes their historical manifestations. It ignores the distinct trajec­tories of these ideas and implies that all right-wing politics are fundamentally the same.

The phrase “cultural Marxism,” as well as the conspiratorial narratives about the Frankfurt School that it often denotes, had its own bizarre history long before it ended up in the neo-Nazi thesaurus as a synonym for cultural Bolshevism. Where do we start? While I recognize the parallels between cultural Bolshevism and cultural Marxism, I do not think that the story begins in the 1920s or 1930s. For me, the 1960s is a better starting point for our analysis.

The history of cul­tural Marxism cannot be understood unless we reflect on the many overlapping shifts and realignments that stemmed from the ’60s. We must remember not to limit our notion of that decade to the spectacular images of May 1968 or Woodstock. As many scholars now agree, the 1960s were long — some claim that the 1960s lasted from 1955 to 1974 — and global .

It was a conjuncture that opened possibilities for revolution, dissent, and counterculture. However, it also involved the exercise of vast political power to defend social and racial hierarchies, control subversive energies, and protect modes of domination and exploitation.

I n his groundbreaking essay “Periodizing the 60s,” the cul­tural critic Fredric Jameson argues that the beginning of what would become known as the 1960s can be traced back to the struggles for national liberation and decolonization that broke out in 1950s Africa. Events in the Global South, such as the independence of Ghana and the Algerian War, ignited nearly two decades of struggle that shook the postwar global order.

Radicals in America and Western Europe drew inspiration from the successes of revolutionary and anti-imperialist movements around the world. They read Frantz Fanon’s The Wretched of the Earth , Mao Zedong’s The Little Red Book , and Che Guevara’s Guerrilla Warfare . Students in the American New Left marched in the streets, held teach-ins, and occupied university buildings to protest their government’s military interventions in Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos.

The truly global nature of this 1960s revolt, with all its fissures and contradictions, gave rise to the hope that the “marginalized” and “minoritized” of the earth would be at the forefront of an unstoppable worldwide revolution. The days of an all-supreme Western civilization looked like they were coming to an end.

The 1960s saw the flourishing of new social and political categories of race, gender, and sexuality. Traditional modes of class-based struggle had lost their radical edge. The Taft-Hartley Act of 1947, as well as the merger between American Federation of Labor and the Congress of Industrial Organizations, tamed the labor movement in the United States and integrated unions into the anti-communist Cold War consen­sus. Uprisings against bureaucratic communism in the Soviet Bloc — Hungary, Poland, Czechoslovakia — demonstrated the need for a non-Stalinist and antiauthoritarian left.

New ways of doing politics were tested and elaborated. The slogan “The personal is political,” popularized by second-wave femi­nism, emphasized the importance of finding the links between individual experiences and wider structures of repression. Movements for Black power, women’s liberation, and gay liber­ation introduced a vibrant politics of identity that fused potent critiques of the existing order with daring visions of a liberated future.

They exposed the social exclusions, subordinations, and restrictions that underpinned the status quo of postwar capital­ist societies. In the United States, these movements fought for the establishment of women’s studies, Black studies, and ethnic studies departments in American universities. Racial, sexual, and gender identities were embraced as epistemological bases for developing new forms of knowledge that could identify the multiple dimensions of power and oppression.

In the decades following the 1960s, many countries experienced something of a social and cultural revolution as women, racial minorities, and LGBTQ+ people acquired civil rights and started to play a more active and visible role in the public sphere. While these forms of equality and inclusion were usually partial and con­tradictory, they represented a significant liberalization of social life and an unsettling of old hierarchies.

O ne of the most significant developments of the 1960s was the drastic expansion of “culture.” In the middle of the twentieth century, many “developed” countries transitioned from a predominantly industrial model of production to a largely service-and information-based one. During the rise of the postindustrial economy, culture burst into the foreground of day-to-day life.

The mass media — film, television, music, fashion, advertising, newspapers, and magazines — started to exert tremendous power and influence over the rhythms of everyday existence. The growing demographic of teenagers and young adults became an eager audience for the offerings of a new and exciting “youth culture.” The rise of this youth-oriented popular culture even altered conventional habits of speech, dress, and behavior.

These rapid changes spurred a “cultural turn” in humanities and social sciences scholarship. The thinkers of British cultural studies drew on the resources of Gramscian theory to rethink the nature of cultural produc­tion and consumption in postwar capitalist societies. Instead of assuming that mass culture turned people into passive con­sumers, these cultural theorists suggested that popular culture, especially youth subculture, constituted a site of potentially subversive political struggle.

As the forces of Western Marxism cut ties with Moscow, these intellectuals engaged with other radical causes and movements to promote a broad and populist form of cultural politics. Since the 1960s, cultural questions have become increasingly central to political debate.

It would be a mistake to believe that the 1960s were nothing but an outburst of liberal acceptance and youthful rebellion. From right-wing coups and neocolonial economic policies to police repression and state surveillance, the 1960s featured the use of extraordinary force to preserve arrangements of power and privilege.

Various right-wing and reactionary political movements ventured into this conjunctural terrain to defend the existing hierarchies of a supposedly pristine Western civilization. These forces required intellectuals who could explain away the causes of perceived cultural decline, organize their supporters into a coherent political identity, and offer compelling visions of con­servative revival.

All cultural Marxism narratives derive from these efforts to resist and reverse the social changes that started to unfold in the long and global 1960s. It is important to understand how these intellectuals operated within their own political movements. How might we investigate the function and activity of these intellectuals? What kind of theory would illuminate the specific ideological practices that shaped their approaches to this cultural tumult? What this task requires, I suggest, is a return to Antonio Gramsci’s theory of intellectuals.

A central theme of Gramsci’s Prison Notebooks is a sustained and innovative rethinking of the concept of the intellectual. In a letter to his sister-in-law Tatiana Schucht, Gramsci remarked that he wanted to extend this concept beyond the limits of “the current notion that refers only to the preeminent intel­lectuals.” Instead of sticking to this abstract notion, Gramsci examined how specific types of intellectual were formed his­torically and how they functioned politically.

The sociologist Jerome Karabel describes this reorientation as a shift from a normative framework, which “treats intellectuals not as they actually are, but as they should be,” to an analytical one that identifies “the conditions and processes that shape the actual political consciousness and actions of different groups of intellectuals.” In the Prison Notebooks , Gramsci started from the “immediate, direct, and vivid impression” — the details of social practice and material circumstance — to reveal larger historical patterns.

His entries on intellectuals included several reminders about the importance of grounding one’s research in material reality. He specified that the formation and elabora­tion of intellectual strata did not “take place on the terrain of abstract democracy, but in accordance with very concrete tra­ditional historical processes.”

The elements of cultural Marxism have been deconstructed and reconfigured time and time again as reac­tionary political forces across the world search for new ways to justify their opposition to equality, democracy, and justice. We will never understand these stories if we cling to the language of individual pathology.

Our approach to cultural Marxism must be rooted in the institutional, the conjunctural, and the structural. As Gramsci once put it:

Ideas and opinions are not spontaneously born in each individual brain: They have had a center of formation, of irradiation, of dissemination, of persuasion [that] has developed them and presented them in the political form of current reality.

It would be impossible — and uninteresting — to refute all the claims that every critic of cultural Marxism has made. After all, most cultural Marxism narratives include several factual obser­vations, such as Herbert Marcuse’s endorsement of the “long march through the institutions” as a potential strategy for the post-1960s New Left. Yet these little facts are rarely used to provide us with an accurate account of either the Frankfurt School’s influence or contemporary social realities. Instead, they are mobilized to fuel political campaigns that seek to denigrate and disempower certain groups.

The Right has declared war on cultural Marxism. Only when we understand the practices — and weaknesses — of those reactionaries who have signed up for this war can we hope to resist their attacks and fight for a better future.

This is an extract from The Cultural Marxism Conspiracy: Why the Right Blames the Frankfurt School for the Decline of the West , now available from Verso Books.

A. J. A. Woods is an intellectual historian who lives in Brighton, England, and is the author of The Cultural Marxism Conspiracy: Why the Right Blames the Frankfurt School for the Decline of the West .

Abdul El-Sayed’s ease in talking sports built rapport with skeptical voters and defies the stereotype of progressives hating what average people find fun. His knack for finding common ground is central to his broad political appeal.

Abdul El-Sayed’s athletic bona fides and fluency in Michigan fandom allow him to reach skeptical audiences and challenge the idea that sports belong to the Right. (Finn Gomez / Getty Images)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

O ne of Abdul El-Sayed’s greatest skills is his ability to deploy the language of sports to make his case. His fluency in sports allows him to find common ground with interlocutors and audiences, complicating the stereotype that progressives are anti-sports.

What makes him convincing and harder for his opponents to dismiss is that he played competitive team sports: El-Sayed was a hockey goalie in middle school. At Bloomfield Hills High School in the suburbs of Detroit, he played football and lacrosse and wrestled, becoming football team captain. These are sports conservatives embrace or consider quintessentially American. At the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, he continued playing sports at the club level, which is more competitive than intramural sports but separate from varsity athletics. As a Rhodes Scholar, he also played on and captained the University of Oxford men’s lacrosse team.

In a now-viral interview with Fox News’s Jesse Watters, El-Sayed did what so few progressive politicians manage: he disarmed a skeptical, even hostile, interlocutor not with talking points but with sports camaraderie. “We both played football and lacrosse. We both love America. We both love freedom,” he responded to the first question, before bantering about football ticket prices and ribbing his critics. The next night, Watters admitted to viewers, “I actually like Abdul. I probably shouldn’t like him, but I do.”

B y leaning into the language of sports, El-Sayed flips the script on the “bro culture,” especially among young men, that has long fueled right-wing politics and Trump-era masculinity. Rather than ceding that terrain, he claims it on his own terms. He repeatedly cast his opponent Mike Rogers as a subordinate “beta” in Donald Trump’s “alpha” orbit, turning the hierarchy of masculine posturing against them. Some skeptics, drawn in by his athletic bona fides, may find themselves unexpectedly receptive. It’s as if El-Sayed is saying: sports don’t belong exclusively to conservatives.

One of his most effective rhetorical strategies was to draw on the local loyalties and rivalries that shape Michigan’s fandom.

El-Sayed repeatedly invoked the long-standing rivalry between the University of Michigan Wolverines and the Ohio State Buckeyes, particularly their annual college football matchup, in which Michigan has the upper hand, sixty-two total wins to Ohio State’s fifty-three wins. His jabs at neighboring Ohio — and at J. D. Vance in particular — may seem strange and personal to outsiders, but they make perfect sense within Michigan’s political and cultural landscape. He was directing the taunt at Vance, an Ohio State alumnus who had repeatedly attacked El-Sayed with inflammatory racist and Islamophobic rhetoric. By turning the rivalry into a political jab, El-Sayed displayed local cultural fluency.

Some athletes agree. One high-profile supporter of El-Sayed is San Diego Padres pitcher Lucas Giolito. Front Office Sports previously reported that Giolito donated $1,250 to El-Sayed’s campaign. On election night, journalist Eli Kronenberg wrote on X that Giolito told him, “Although I don’t live in Michigan, I believe he’ll be a great progressive voice in the US Senate.”

On his book tour, Colin Kaepernick was asked which politicians he was most excited about. He answered quickly: “The ones that are interesting to me are obviously Mamdani in New York . . . [and] Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. I really like the approaches they’re taking. They’re staying very focused on the needs of the people. They don’t seem to be bought or swayed,” he said, adding that they represent a growing rejection of the establishment.

A few days before the election, former Michigan State long snapper Taybor Pepper, who played in the NFL for seven seasons, interviewed El-Sayed. After speaking with El-Sayed, Pepper wrote on X:

I understand why people want sports to be an escape from politics, but the reality is that throughout history, sports and politics have been deeply intertwined. From breaking racial barriers to fighting for equality and civil rights, athletes have played a pivotal role in pushing society toward meaningful social change.

Like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, El-Sayed supports English football club Arsenal FC, whose large, diverse global fan base has much in common with the New York Knicks, another of Mamdani’s passions.

This is not the first time El-Sayed has weighed in on sports’ cultural and political significance. In an April 2021 post on his now private Substack, The Incision , he analyzed the influence of big money on European football and fans’ successful resistance to major clubs’ attempts to commercialize the game further through the European Super League. He drew a parallel to the exploitation of the health care system back home: “If English soccer fans can stand up to fight for their soccer clubs, perhaps we too can fight for our healthcare, our prescription drugs, our schools, and our lives.”

In another post in October 2021, following the firing of former Raiders coach Jon Gruden over racist, homophobic, and misogynistic comments, El-Sayed argued that the problem was more systemic: “The toxic masculinity at the heart of America’s most popular sport — and men’s sports culture more generally — is way deeper than a few emails or a Jay-Z turnaround.”

Finally, about a month ago, El-Sayed’s campaign posted a short video on his social media in which one of his former high school football teammates, Nikita Sanches, speaks about El-Sayed as a teammate. Sanches, who was born in the Soviet Union and was a shy teenager when they first met, recalls how El-Sayed befriended him and took him under his wing. He also described how El-Sayed negotiated Islamophobia in the wake of 9/11. Sanches, now a chef, explains how, a year later, “we elected him our leader and our captain. Not just because he was our friend and our classmate, but because of the way he carried himself.” The same qualities that made El-Sayed a trusted teammate now help him use sports to connect with audiences beyond his political base.

Sean Jacobs is a writer and researcher based in Brooklyn, New York. Until recently, he was a tenured professor at the New School.

Ivan Pech is a writer from Mexico. He studied at the New School for Social Research.

scraped.title: A Maryland county unconstitutionally disarmed Jews facing antisemitic threats, a synagogue says
scraped.description: The synagogue says the 100-yard buffer zone keeps congregants from carrying firearms to worship on the Sabbath amid antisemitic threats.
scraped.author: Jacob Sullum
scraped.h1: A Maryland County Unconstitutionally Disarmed Jews Facing Antisemitic Threats, a Synagogue Says
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Second Amendment

Jacob Sullum | 11.12.2026 3:20 PM

Last July, Montgomery County, Maryland, enacted a ban on firearms in any "place of public assembly," which it defined to include parks, schools, and houses of worship, or within 300 feet of those locations. Three days after that law took effect, the Silver Spring Jewish Center (SSJC), an Orthodox synagogue, sued the county, arguing that it had unconstitutionally disarmed congregants at a time of rising antisemitic threats. A federal judge agreed in September, when she issued preliminary injunction that allowed carry-permit holders to possess guns inside the synagogue but left in place the 300-foot rule, which applies to pedestrians but not motorists.

That order, the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty notes , created "a bizarre constitutional catch-22 where Jews can carry firearms inside the synagogue, but they cannot cross the street to bring them there." This week the SSJC and Menashe Shapiro, a congregant who is also an ordained rabbi, asked the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit to remedy that puzzling situation, arguing that it violates the plaintiffs' Second Amendment right to armed self-defense and their First Amendment right to the free exercise of religion.

" Protecting synagogue members' right to carry within their synagogue but prohibiting them from carrying to the entrance is no protection at all," says Becket Fund Senior Counsel Eric Baxter, who represents the SSJC along with lawyers at the New Civil Liberties Alliance (NCLA). "We're asking the Fourth Circuit to end this assault on Marylanders' bedrock constitutional rights."

Especially since the October 2023 Hamas attack on Israel and the ensuing war in Gaza, "antisemitic incidents have threatened" the SSJC, the plaintiffs say . "For example, in October 2024, a visibly Jewish member was attacked just outside the building, and in June 2026, an unknown individual attempted to gain entry." In response, the SSJC created "an armed volunteer security team" consisting of carry-permit holders like Shapiro.

In addition to barring those volunteers from bringing their guns into the synagogue after parking nearby, Montgomery County's law, even as modified by U.S. District Judge Deborah Chasanow's injunction, presents a special problem for Orthodox Jews, who do not use automobiles on the Sabbath or on holidays that entail similar restrictions. That means SSJC members cannot even legally transport their guns to the vicinity of the synagogue on those occasions, since they would pass within 300 feet of parks, schools, and other houses of worship while walking there.

"The Second Amendment protects everyone's right to carry a firearm as they go about daily life," NCLA senior litigation counsel Jacob Huebert notes . "The First Amendment protects the right to freely exercise one's religion. The 100-yard rule deprives Silver Spring Jewish Center members of both."

Although Montgomery County's buffer zones are ostensibly aimed at protecting public safety, they have the opposite effect as applied to the SSJC. "Our synagogue has long been a sanctuary for Jews to worship, pray, and gather in peace," says SSJC Rabbi Yaakov Greiniman. "As the scourge of antisemitic violence grows more widespread and brazen, we have a sacred duty to defend our congregation. Montgomery County has made that impossible."

The plaintiffs' Second Amendment argument relies on New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen , the 2022 decision in which the Supreme Court recognized that the constitutional right to bear arms includes the right to carry guns in public for self-defense. Under Bruen , restrictions on that right must be "consistent with this Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation." To meet that test, Montgomery County has the burden of citing historical analogs that are "relevantly similar" to its law in motivation and scope.

The county has identified "no historical support for a 100-yard buffer around places of worship," the plaintiffs say. As for parks, they argue, the local ordinances cited in prior litigation are not sufficient to establish a historical tradition. They note that "three of the five ordinances come from Pennsylvania, so only three States are represented" and that all but one were enacted in the late 19th or early 20th century.

Chasanow perceived a historical tradition supporting Montgomery County's buffer zone around schools. But she relied on a case from the Eastern District of California that involved the federal Gun-Free School Zones Act, which makes an exception for people with state-issued carry permits. "The federal statute is therefore not relevantly similar to Montgomery County's law," the plaintiffs say.

Montgomery County offered several more purported historical analogs, including polling-place laws that "do not concern places of worship, parks, or schools" and "applied only on election or registration days." Its other examples were similarly inapposite. The county, in short, "has identified no historical tradition of banning firearms within 100 yards of places of worship, parks, or schools."

The plaintiffs also argue that Montgomery County's law impinges on religious liberty. "Talmudic and later religious sources command Jews to proactively provide their own security and the security of other Jews," they say. "In light of the threat environment, SSJC considers it a religious obligation to ensure that at least some members carry firearms." They add that Shapiro "holds the sincere religious belief that Jewish law requires him to carry a firearm for personal, family, and communal protection, a duty he must perform personally."

Chasanow agreed that "SSJC and Rabbi Shapiro have demonstrated a burden on their sincere religious practice." She also concluded that Montgomery County's ban on guns in houses of worship implicates the Free Exercise Clause because it is not "neutral and generally applicable," noting that it does not cover fraternal lodges and "numerous other privately owned businesses and properties" where people gather. Chasanow said the law was therefore subject to "strict scrutiny," a demanding test that the county did not even try to pass: "Defendants have not made any showing as to whether the law's application to places of worship is the 'least restrictive means of achieving some compelling state interest.'"

The plaintiffs argue that Chasanow nevertheless erred by treating their argument against the buffer zones as a facial challenge, meaning they had to show the rules were unconstitutional in every application. Given the specific relief they sought, they say, it should have been clear that they were challenging the restrictions as applied to them.

"It takes a lot of chutzpah to trample on the First and Second Amendments at the same time," Shapiro says . "Yet that's precisely what Montgomery County has done here, forcing Jews to choose between different tenets of their faith and simultaneously compromising their safety. Our Constitution forbids such impossible choices. I pray the court ends this senseless ban for good and allows my community to defend itself from threats."

scraped.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Resigns Amid Spy Affair Scandal
scraped.description: State of the Union: The chipmaker’s shares plummeted amid concerns about the company’s future.
scraped.author: Juan Rojas
scraped.body_text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday following revelations that he had extramarital affairs with an alleged Chinese spy as well as an executive who reported to him. Huang admitted Sunday to having a romantic relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at the Singaporean data center firm Megaspeed, whom U.S. intelligence agencies determined was gathering information for Beijing. He was also found to have engaged in an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, according to five firm employees who choose to remain anonymous.

Huang was widely regarded as irreplaceable after having served as Nvidia’s CEO since 1993 with no clear succession plan. The firm’s board named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.

Huang had previously persuaded President Donald Trump to roll back a ban on chip sales to China. Analysts regard his ouster as a setback for both the U.S. and China in the AI race.

Nvidia is the world’s second-most valuable company, accounting for 8.5 percent of the S&P 500. Shares of the firm dived roughly 10 percent following Huang’s resignation.

Juan David Rojas is a columnist at UnHerd covering Latin America and the Iberian Peninsula.

scraped.title: Iran War Day 258: Trump Says No Deal Necessary With Iran
scraped.description: State of the Union: In a social media post, the president said he was redirecting Vice President J.D. Vance to focus on domestic corruption.
scraped.author: Jude Russo
scraped.body_text:
President Donald Trump posted Thursday on Truth Social that he is redirecting Vice President J.D. Vance to domestic issues because “we don’t need a deal with Iran.”

“I have asked Vice President Vance to focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.,” the president wrote , alleging widespread fiscal misconduct in blue states like Minnesota and Illinois. “CORRUPTION is in the Democrat Leadership’s blood! We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

The statement followed reports about Vance’s intensifying role in diplomacy with Iran, including a potential meeting with the Iranian Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei in Doha. Trump appeared to confirm reports from Axios and others that his inclination is to follow Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent’s preferred course by maintaining the economic war against Iran without returning to high-intensity combat operations.

The Iranians are still harassing traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, claiming to have stopped two tankers Wednesday night. Fighting of varying intensity also continues on other fronts in the regional crisis. Israel struck a hospital in Gaza Wednesday, killing six, according to Gaza’s health ministry. Yemen’s Houthis continued their siege of Taiz, prompting warnings Wednesday from the Arab League about impending humanitarian disaster.

Brent crude opened Thursday at $92.22 a barrel and began rising after Trump’s statement. AAA reported national average prices per gallon of $3.91 for gazoline and $6.10 for diesel.

Jude Russo is the managing editor of The American Conservative and a contributing editor of The New York Sun . He is a 2024–25 James Madison Fellow at Hillsdale College and was named one of the ISI Top 20 Under 30 for 2024.

Dear reader,

The subject line says it all. From the February 28 outbreak of the Iran War, The American Conservative has argued that the United States’ latest adventure in the Middle East would prove futile, destructive, and politically catastrophic for an administration that came to power with a promise of economic normality and no new wars.

We were right.

Last Tuesday’s midterm elections saw Democrats take previously unimaginable majorities in Congress and at statehouses throughout the country—including in Republican strongholds like Kansas, which has not elected a Democratic senator since 1939. Exit polls found that voters consistently rated the war and its economic consequences as their top issues. At the same time, the Islamic Republic remains in power, and the eight-month war has no end in sight.

The American people have again rejected empire and its costs at the ballot box. Will you help us in our mission to show there is another way?

A tax-deductible donation will help The American Conservative to do high-quality reporting and analysis in support of foreign policy restraint, immigration sanity, and economic strength. Would you consider helping us?

We are deeply grateful for our readers and supporters, whose loyalty has been unmatched for nearly a quarter century. Thank you. We cannot do this without your help.

Sincerely, Curt Mills Executive Director

scraped.h1: How CIA used Ukraine as a platform for covert war against Russia
scraped.body_text:
Project Aerodynamic became the Cold War template for Washington to exploit postwar poverty and anti-Soviet sentiment to Great Power benefit. How did that all work out?

The following is an excerpt from Stephen Kinzer's new book: Boiling Point: How America Brought War to Ukraine (Henry Holt and Company, November 2026)

Huddled beside an airstrip in southern Germany, a handful of anti-Communist warriors prepared to fire the first shots of the Cold War. A CIA officer from the Munich Operations Base was in charge. The Hungarian crewmen he had recruited stood nearby in flight suits. With them were two Ukrainian exiles who had volunteered to parachute into their homeland. They were code-named Apostle 1 and Apostle 2. Each carried forged identity papers, a miniature radio transmitter, a pistol, a machine gun, hand grenades, a purse full of gold coins, and a poison pill to be taken in case of capture. An unmarked C-47 transport plane was waiting.

The CIA officer overseeing this operation, a twenty-six-year-old Yale graduate named Stephen Tanner, watched the plane take off and disappear into the night. It flew over East Germany and Poland, then crossed into Soviet airspace. As it approached the Ukrainian city of Lviv, a cargo bay swung open. The two Ukrainians jumped into the darkness. Their mission was to link up with partisan fighters, seize territory, and establish a clandestine base through which the CIA could send them weapons.

That flight, on September 5, 1949, was the first American act of covert war in Ukraine. The two would-be commandos who jumped that night were an advance guard for what became Project Aerodynamic, the most ambitious and furthest-reaching project the CIA ever launched inside the Soviet Union. Its aim was to foment subversion in the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic. Behind it lay a simple calculation: The Soviet Union is America’s mortal enemy; its greatest internal threat comes from Ukraine; the CIA should do everything possible to intensify that threat.

From their base in Munich, Tanner and other CIA officers anxiously awaited messages from the two Apostles. None came. An after-action report concluded tersely that “the Soviets quickly eliminated the agents.” It added, though, that this mission “sparked considerable interest at headquarters.” Losing two agents was hardly enough to derail such a promising project.

On May 19, 1950, another C-47 took off from the same base in Germany. This time it carried four Ukrainian volunteers. They parachuted into western Ukraine with a cargo their CIA overseers had packed. It was enough to arm a potent guerrilla band, including fifty submachine guns, thirty rifles, twenty-five pistols, and a hundred phosphorus grenades. The four volunteers hit the ground. They radioed news of their safe landing with cargo. Then they disappeared.

Later that summer, two more Ukrainian volunteers bade their comrades an emotional farewell. According to a CIA cable, “a round of drinks was served, toasts were made…hands were shaken, tears were shed.” Their plane departed at 6:55 p.m. on August 12. The pilot missed their drop zone in Ukraine, and they jumped twenty miles away. Neither was ever heard from again.

These flights were the centerpiece of a far-reaching operation in which the CIA sought to foment armed uprisings in Soviet-controlled territory. Between 1949 and 1952, the CIA dropped about eighty-five men, all equipped for guerrilla warfare, behind what was then called the Iron Curtain. Three-quarters were quickly captured or shot.

“You’ve got to have a few martyrs,” reasoned Allen Dulles, chief of covert operations for the CIA. “Some people have to get killed.”

Project Aerodynamic was a match made in covert-action heaven. Thousands of Ukrainian partisans had refused to lay down their arms after their Nazi allies surrendered on May 8, 1945. They wanted to keep fighting the Red Army— if they could find a new sponsor. At that same moment, the CIA was looking for a force that it could use to strike against the Soviet Union from within its own territory. Aerodynamic was the progeny of this union. It set off three-quarters of a century of American intervention in Ukraine.

Fear and uncertainty marked the first encounter between Americans and anti- Soviet Ukrainians. In the autumn of 1947, two years before the first CIA airdrop into Ukraine, officers from the Army Counter Intelligence Corps in occupied Germany learned that a band of armed Russians had appeared in the countryside near Munich. At first they thought this might be an advance guard preparing the ground for a Red Army invasion. A patrol was sent to investigate. Soldiers scoured the hills and meadows around the Bavarian village of Waldkirchen. Early on the morning of September 10, they heard voices. They closed in on a campfire around which men wearing military uniforms were singing in what sounded like Russian. After a moment of tension, the soldiers willingly surrendered their machine guns and hand grenades.

These thirty-five men, along with four other members of their band who were picked up nearby, were brought to an American base and debriefed for three weeks. It turned out that they were not Red Army soldiers, but Ukrainians who had consecrated their lives to fighting the Red Army. They belonged to a partisan force that was unknown to most outsiders: the Ukrainian Insurgent Army. Their commanders had ordered them to walk westward, find Americans, and seek help for the partisan rebellion.

One of the partisans told an interrogator that the Ukrainian Insurgent Army was “engaged in armed combat with Soviet troops in the Ukraine at present” and that more Ukrainians were “ready to revolt” if given support. An officer who helped supervise the interrogations cabled to Washington that the Ukrainians were offering services “which may be of interest to you and may tie into an idea which, I believe, is being worked on at home at the present time.”

“If, as I understand, there is some planning going on with regard to how such groups as referred to above might be best used in our interests,” he suggested, “it might be useful to follow up this matter.”

Americans had just begun fighting the Cold War. Their great handicap was that they knew almost nothing about what was happening inside the Soviet Union. Now they learned that Ukrainians were waging war against the Red Army. This was an intelligence bonanza that opened new landscapes of possibility.

Some of the CIA’s most impassioned Ukrainian agents had fought alongside the Nazis just a few years earlier. Among them were veterans of SS Einsatzgruppen — mobile death squads assigned to massacre Jews and other civilians. This history troubled some of their American handlers, but not enough to disrupt their partnership.

Across Europe , American intelligence officers scoured teeming displaced persons camps looking for Ukrainians who were willing to join a covert anti-Soviet war. Recruitment was easy. Hundreds of thousands of young men — not just Ukrainians but refugees from all over the continent — were huddled in the bleak purgatory of these camps. The best they might hope for was work clearing rubble or picking crops. When men introducing themselves as part of the “American Intelligence Service” offered them paying jobs with good living conditions, plus the prospect of returning to war against Bolshevism, many jumped to accept. Vetting was minimal, so recruits included more than a few who had worked with the Nazis as militia members, police officers, and executioners. One recruiting officer said his job was easy: “You’d go to a refugee camp and say, ‘Here, Joe, you want to join a special project?’ Most of these people were, like, the homeless.”

This recruitment laid the foundation for Project Aerodynamic. Over the following years, it would overlap with other CIA projects using various cryptonyms, among them Acrobat, Androgen, Antler, Cartel, Carthage, Crust, Outbound, PDDynamic (PD was code for the Soviet Union), Plumb, and Red Sox. The goal — using Ukraine as a platform for covert war against Moscow — never changed.

scraped.title: Kushner & Witkoff do the Abu Dhabi shuffle: Ukraine peace ahead?
scraped.description: Hopeful signs in this week's talks, but the stickiest of sticking points remain, and the Europeans continue to loom as spoilers
scraped.h1: Kushner & Witkoff do the Abu Dhabi shuffle: Ukraine peace ahead?
scraped.body_text:
Hopeful signs in this week's talks, but the stickiest of sticking points remain, and the Europeans continue to loom as spoilers

The talks in Abu Dhabi demonstrate that the Ukraine peace process is finally moving in the right direction. Whether it will reach its goal is of course another matter.

Firstly, the U.S. negotiating team has introduced to the talks the critical issue of a future European security architecture. President Trump has written of the need for a "very big, beautiful agreement that might involve all of Europe ."

As Jared Kushner wrote before the talks:

“For more than 30 years, Europe and Russia have struggled to establish a sustainable security framework. Decades of mistrust, competing security concerns, and the devastating consequences of this war make this an extraordinarily difficult challenge, but one that is essential to lasting peace.

Our objective is to develop practical arrangements that address the security concerns of all sides, reduce the risk of future conflict, and create a more stable and predictable security environment.

We are exploring five principal goals: permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.”

These words produced a neuralgic reaction among many Europeans, but in fact Kushner followed them up with a qualification which, if insisted upon, will also be categorically rejected by Moscow:

“Any arrangements must fully respect the sovereignty, territorial integrity, and independent decision-making of every nation. Each country will retain authority over its own security and alliances, and no country would have a veto over another’s sovereign choices. NATO will remain central to European collective defense, and this initiative would build upon existing institutions and commitments.”

The need for a new European security architecture is an issue that the Russians have been raising since 2008; and as the Quincy Institute has long argued, it is only by addressing Russian concerns about European security that the West has any chance of getting Moscow to abandon its more radical demands vis-a-vis Ukraine. As a Russian official told Reuters:

"The Ukrainian settlement, while it is a matter of ⁠critical importance, is just one aspect of this wide-ranging discussion and is subordinate to the main objective — the creation of a comprehensive and indivisible security architecture for the entire continent."

However, it is very unlikely that the Russians will agree to a new security architecture if this simply involves Kushner’s idea of a revival of the NATO-Russia Council (suspended since 2014), which as far as the Russians are concerned was simply a vehicle for NATO countries to agree a common position and then present it to Russia as a fait accompli, and which wholly failed to prevent the crises of 2008 with Georgia and Ukraine in 2014.

Moreover, as Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have recognized , talks on an agreement concerning wider European security have by definition to include the Europeans. European representatives were present in Abu Dhabi, but the Russians refused to allow them to take part in the meeting itself.

This may seem both illegitimate and absurd if they wish to discuss European security architecture, but the Russians have a point. There are two huge problems with a common European approach to a peace settlement. They don’t have one, and if they did have one, it might very well make peace impossible.

As Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni complained earlier this month:

“I’m convinced that we all realize how, by projecting the image of a Europe that’s all over the place, we’re doing nothing but serving the interests of those who want this war to continue, and I think this is unacceptable, given that human lives and the future of our security are at stake…Proceeding in a disorganized manner, with initiatives that chase one another and overlap, will not help us — neither with our partners nor with those we must convince to stop this senseless aggression.”

But is a common European position even possible, given the deep hostility of certain European governments to any compromise whatsoever with Russia? Certainly a European strategy presided over by EU foreign policy chief (and former Estonian prime minister) Kaja Kallas looks like a non-starter, given her pathological hostility toward Russia . More hopeful might be a process conducted by the “E3” of Germany, France and Britain; but would an agreement negotiated with them be considered binding by all the other EU and NATO member states, every one of which has a veto over any formal agreement with Russia?

Moreover, insofar as there is a common European position, it appears to be to reject any serious talks on European security, by insisting that these can only take place after Russia agrees to a ceasefire. This position is either utterly stupid or utterly insincere. Of course Russia is not going to stop the war and abandon its only source of leverage for a quasi-promise to maybe talk about European security later, with no guarantee at all that in the end the Europeans would agree to anything.

Why on earth should Moscow trust the Europeans to negotiate seriously about this in future, given that German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said this week that "Europe does not need a new security architecture, as Russia wants us to believe, but rather the simple restoration of the existing security architecture." If Moscow is to be incentivised to end the war, then talks on European security have to be part of the peace negotiations, and agreement on this has to be part of the final peace settlement.

As Kushner has acknowledged, the other chief barrier to progress at present is the question of Russia’s demand for control over the whole Donbas region, meaning Ukrainian withdrawal from the approximately 2,000 square miles of that region that they still control. Most Ukrainians regard such withdrawal as militarily and morally impossible.

On this, the U.S. team proposed a commonsensical solution that is in fact the only way that this issue can be resolved peacefully: namely, that Ukraine and Russia agree to redraw the borders of the two Donbas provinces so that the territory still held by Ukraine is transferred to adjacent Ukrainian provinces that Russia does not claim.

The Russian response to this is not yet clear. It should be noted however, that Russia may have already in effect accepted this solution for the other two provinces of Ukraine (Kherson and Zaporizhia) that it claims as Russian territory but has only partially occupied; since Moscow is no longer demanding Ukrainian withdrawal from these provinces as a condition of peace.

On the other side, a “Ukrainian source” told the British Daily Telegraph newspaper that the Ukrainian side had promptly rejected the U.S. proposal: “Ukraine’s delegation never discussed any concessions on any territories which Russia occupies…Ukraine will never recognise it, neither de facto nor de jure. And this has always been our position at the table.”

If rejection of even de facto Russian control of these territories is in fact the official Ukrainian position, then it would render any agreement with Moscow completely impossible, and commit Ukraine — and its Western supporters — to an unending war for the impossible goal of reconquering all the land held by Russia.

So we are still far from getting answers to the issues frustrating progress towards an end to the Ukraine War . At least however, as the talks in Abu Dhabi demonstrate, the U.S. side has begun to ask the right questions.

scraped.title: Disgraced neocons Feith & Libby: stop whining about 'endless war'
scraped.description: For some reason the Washington Post thinks we care about what these Iraq War architects have to say about anything
scraped.h1: Disgraced neocons Feith & Libby: stop whining about 'endless war'
scraped.body_text:
For some reason the Washington Post thinks we care about what these Iraq War architects have to say about anything

Apparently, it takes the prospect of ending the war on Iran to get the blood running hot in aging and otherwise reclusive neoconservatives — particularly those whose tenures as key architects of the 2003 Iraq invasion and subsequent occupation were both short-lived and disastrous.

Douglas Feith , who served as undersecretary of defense for policy (2001-2005), and Lewis “Scooter” Libby , Vice President Dick Cheney’s powerful national security adviser and chief of staff (2001-2005), co-authored an op-ed published Monday by the Washington Post entitled “’Endless wars’ is a catchy phrase, not a reason to shift policy.”

Evoking the wartime steadfastness demonstrated by Abraham Lincoln in the Civil War; Winston Churchill – naturally, these are neoconservatives, after all — against the Nazis, Dwight Eisenhower in Korea; and Ronald Reagan in concluding the Cold War, the duo urged America to steel itself for more war.

“None of these leaders wanted endless sacrifice and risks, but none buckled for fear of them,” they wrote, suggesting a parallel with the current war on Iran. “Each understood that an enemy’s willingness to endure a long struggle does not make one’s own ‘endless’ resistance foolish.”

In assessing the wisdom behind their words, some context may be in order.

First, the authors, both proteges of the “Prince of Darkness,” Richard Perle , who served as chairman of the Defense Policy Board in the run-up to the 2003 Iraq invasion, are dyed-in-the-wool, hard-core neoconservatives in that they believe as much, or perhaps more, in Israel’s exceptionalism as they do in America’s. Their Middle East policy preferences have long paralleled those of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his right-wing Likud Party.

Their institutional associations since their departures from government in 2005 tend to confirm their Israel-centrism. Feith has been a senior fellow at the neoconservative Hudson Institute , while Libby, who was also based at Hudson for many years, is currently serving as a distinguished fellow at the Foundation of Defense of Democracies (FDD).

A survey by RS of four commonly used AI programs in April found that both organizations were among the five think tanks that were “the most prominent in promoting military action” against Iran across mainstream and social media in the six months leading up to the current war that was launched by massive air strikes against key targets across Iran on February 28. FDD, whose original submission to the IRS when it was founded in 2001 described its mission as “enhance(ing) Israel’s image in North America…,” ranked number one in promoting military action in all four programs.

Second, both Feith and Libby may be best known for their roles in shaping, manipulating, distorting, leaking, and promoting fabricated intelligence – often in close cooperation with Iraqi expatriate Ahmad Chalabi and his Iraqi National Congress — that would justify the invasion and occupation of Iraq and rally public opinion behind that enterprise. Feith created offices in the Pentagon whose missions were to collect and disseminate any information that suggested a cooperative relationship between Saddam Hussein’s regime and al-Qaida and major advances in Iraq’s alleged (but non-existent) nuclear-weapons program.

As Cheney’s chief adviser and enforcer – “Dick Cheney’s Dick Cheney” – Libby provided a direct channel to the White House for the “intelligence” produced by Feith’s office and Chalabi’s purported “defectors,” much of which then appeared in speeches by the vice president and other top administration officials, without being vetted through the normal intelligence processes. Libby became notorious in the intelligence community for his frequent visits to CIA headquarters to question – some say harass – analysts about their work, culminating in a frantic, last-minute efforts to include a particularly dubious piece of intelligence linking Saddam to al-Qaida in Secretary of State Colin Powell’s infamous address to the U.N. General Assembly on the eve of the invasion.

Third, both authors left their government service under a cloud, if not in disgrace. Libby’s was the most spectacular fall. In October 2005, he was indicted by a federal grand jury resulting from an investigation into the leak of the covert identity of a CIA operative, Valerie Plame, as part of an apparent effort by Libby and his boss to discredit her husband, a former U.S. ambassador who had publicly exposed the falsity of a key administration claim regarding Saddam’s alleged nuclear-weapons program. Libby resigned his positions immediately following his indictment, was subsequently convicted by a jury of making false statements and sentenced to 30 months in prison, which President George W. Bush later commuted. He received a full pardon from President Donald Trump in 2018.

Feith — who, besides his collaboration with Chalabi, had overseen a number of other fiascoes during his tenure, including the disastrous de-Baathification program in Iraq — resigned in August 2005, by which time it had become clear that the occupation faced a serious insurgency. He may be best known, however, for the characterization applied to him by then-U.S. Central Command chief Gen. Tommy Franks, who led the invasions of both Afghanistan and Iraq, as “the f*cking stupidest guy on the planet.”

Given that context, it’s no wonder that both men appear to have preferred the relative tranquility and obscurity of those Washington “think tanks” where their colleagues share the same or very similar world views, and “groupthink” rules the roost, much as it did during the heyday of neoconservative power during Bush’s first term. Perhaps somewhat chastened by their failures, they have seemingly been reluctant to engage in the public square in recent years.

Indeed, over the past decade, Libby had published only one op-ed in any of the country’s three most influential national newspapers, and that was back in 2021 on the evils of China’s “Covid wrongdoing,” as the Wall Street Journal’s editorial page editors called it. As for Feith, he hadn’t published a single op-ed in the Journal, the Washington Post, or the New York Times since 2015.

Until Trump launched the war against Iran on February 28, that is. That apparently got the old juices going, with Jeff Bezos’ recalibrated editorial pages of the Washington Post serving as willing host. On March 9, Feith broke his silence with the giddy title, “Trump is trying something new in Iran. Hold on tight.” Then, after Trump signed a dreaded ceasefire agreement, he evidently felt compelled to warn that “The Iran deal comes with a familiar false promise.” On September 10, he extolled his glory days in “The 9/11 response got the most important thing right.”

Libby was not as prolific. But on September 18, he co-authored an op-ed in the Post calling, among other things, for the destruction of “Iran’s major oil production and export facilities, as the Allies did to Germany and Japan in World War II” and for “ground troops” to seize Iran’s “coastline or the regime’s enriched uranium stockpiles…”

And now, on the very eve of Veterans/Armistice Day, these two strategic geniuses have taken once again to the Post’s op-ed page to earnestly warn us against listening to those who have grown weary of “endless wars.”

It’s time to thank them for their service.

items.title: Democrats Preached ‘Affordability’ To Win Midterms, But Their Base Always Knew It Was About Lawfare
items.summary: If it wasn't clear before the elections, it should be clear now that Democrats and their base knew what this election was about -- and it certainly wasn't affordability.

scraped.title: Dems Duped Americans By Switching Affordability For Lawfare
scraped.description: Democrats and their base knew what this election was about -- and it certainly wasn't affordability.
scraped.author: Brianna Lyman
scraped.h1: Democrats Preached ‘Affordability’ To Win Midterms, But Their Base Always Knew It Was About Lawfare
scraped.body_text:
If it wasn’t clear before the elections, it should be clear now that Democrats and their base knew what this election was about — and it certainly wasn’t affordability.

Democrats spent months telling Americans if they wanted someone in office who cared about what it costs to fill up the car or feed a family, then vote Democrat. It was a smart pitch. A preelection Pew Research poll found the economy ranked as a top issue for 84% of registered voters. Politico released a report on Election Day finding that “Republicans don’t think their party is focused enough on … the economy.” Bloomberg reported that 2024-Trump voters are “disappointed” about how the economy has been over the past two years.

That pitch resonated with voters and helped Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress. For example, Latino voters who swung for Trump in 2024 swung for Democrats this year, with the Los Angeles Times reporting that economy and cost of living were Latino voters’ top priority.

So when I went out on the streets of New York City for an exclusive segment with Hannity and asked people what they wanted the incoming Democrat Congress to do in January, I figured somebody would say something about how expensive it is to live — after all, it was New York. You could spend an entire hour talking about what people pay in rent alone.

Yet not a single person I spoke with mentioned affordability as a top priority. I heard about the environment, “women’s rights,” abortion, and “humanity.” One common answer I got from multiple people was that Congress should focus on impeaching Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, though nobody calling for his impeachment could tell me what high crime or misdemeanor Hegseth would be charged with.

Then I realized that the people I spoke to sounded a lot like Democrat candidates who — after having spent months campaigning on affordability — championed lawfare in the hours after their victories.

“Thank you, Mr. President. Our thank you will come in January — with subpoenas,” Rep. Yassamin Ansari , D-Ariz., posted on X.

Rep. Delia C. Ramirez , D-Ill., (the child of illegal aliens) had a similar message: “Noem, Markwayne, Miller, Homan, Bovino, what’s up? Clear your schedule.”

Rep. Robert Garcia , D-Calif., warned Republicans to “LAWYER UP.” An identical post was made by host of The Bulwark Podcast Tim Miller .

Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., simply posted “Subpoenas,” while Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., posted “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing.”

Communist streamer Hasan Piker was a bit more explicit in leftists’ goals: “WE’RE GONNA PUT YOUR ASS IN JAIL EVERYONE GET MORE WOKE RIGHT NOW!!!!!!!!!!!!!”

Democrats’ knee-jerk reaction to winning the midterms was to talk about the upcoming lawfare rather than affordability, the very thing they campaigned on. After months of hearing how urgently we needed relief from high prices (and we do), I figured at least one person I spoke to in deep blue Manhattan would want the new Congress to do something about it. Yet nobody did.

They brought up abortion, the environment, and impeaching Hegseth. Nobody brought up affordability. Then I remembered Democrats in Congress who started posting about “lawyer[ing] up” immediately after their victories, and the answers I’d gotten in Manhattan made a lot more sense.

The people who wanted lawfare and Hegseth impeached had every reason to vote for Democrats because they understood what so many voters apparently didn’t: the affordability pitch was just meant to deceive voters and was not a promise Democrats intended to keep.

Democrats used the affordability pitch to win over voters who wouldn’t have crossed over for an agenda of lawfare or the “environment.” An independent worried about gas prices or groceries had a reason to give Democrats a shot when all they talked about was affordability and how bringing costs down would be a priority. If it wasn’t clear before the elections, it should be clear now that Democrats and their base knew what this election was about — and it certainly wasn’t affordability.
