items.title: Like Screech And Urkel, Mark Levin Has Become A Pathetic But Lovable Sitcom Character
items.summary: Trump might still take Mark Levin seriously. Hopefully he'll soon see his real purpose is to be a widely recognized, fondly welcomed joke.

scraped.title: Mark Levin Has Become A Pathetic But Lovable Sitcom Character
scraped.description: Trump might still take Mark Levin seriously. Hopefully he'll soon see his real purpose is to be a widely recognized, fondly welcomed joke.
scraped.author: Eddie Scarry
scraped.h1: Like Screech And Urkel, Mark Levin Has Become A Pathetic But Lovable Sitcom Character
scraped.body_text:
Trump might still take Mark Levin seriously. Hopefully he’ll soon see his real purpose is to be a widely recognized, fondly welcomed joke.

Sometimes a person in the political realm can become so relentlessly irksome and absurd, almost willfully self-humiliating to an impressive degree, that they end up becoming kind of cute, in a pathetic, endearing way. Mark Levin has reached that point.

In recent days, Levin, a Fox News content creator and informal White House adviser, has exhibited a series of wild public crash-outs related to Israel, the Iran war, and Vice President J.D. Vance. There was even one about his AOL email account. (Yes! Just how lovable loser Steve Urkel of Family Matters drove a comically tiny buggy car for transportation, Levin uses AOL to correspond with his friends in Israel. Aww! Haha! )

In one such outburst, Levin attempted to pre-but a coming Politico story on how attacks from himself and others on the vice president might actually benefit Vance in the 2028 election. “Now, folks, I’ve been around a few years,” wrote Levin , using the word “folks,” which he invariably uses before saying something cartoonishly corny. “I’ve seen presidents and vice presidents come and go. I’ve seen politicians come and go. I’ve also seen campaign operatives and surrogates manipulate a willing media in hopes of creating a pseudo-news story to advance an agenda.” Levin then struck a defiant pose, possibly with his chest out and his hands on his love handles. “We are not going to be played,” he declared.

You can practically hear the canned laughter and encouraging “Woo!” track played over Levin’s lines. He’s the breakout character who gets lunchbox stickers made out of his zany facial expressions and catchphrases.

The day before, Levin earnestly shared his AOL woes. “Folks,” he said (naturally), “I have spent literally the entire day trying to get someone at AOL to unlock my email. For the last eight hours, I have been told that the issue has been escalated to supervisors who would contact me. I haven’t heard a thing.”

This is the man who the president of the United States this year has urged the public and even Supreme Court justices to watch on TV. I hadn’t considered it was because he thought we’d all get a laugh out of Levin’s latest meltdown. I wish I had been watching sooner.

If it weren’t enough that Levin publicly shared his frustrations with a long-forgotten internet provider, he followed up by suggesting it must have been a plot against him by the Iranian government. “My wife and I were warned yesterday by the appropriate federal agency that we might be targeted by the Iranian regime,” he wrote on X. “Specifically, by a possible cyber attack. Well, that appears to have occurred.”

Iran can never be allowed to have a nuclear weapon. Just the same, it can never, ever again have the capability to lock a neocon out of his AOL Buddy List. Hey, Hezbollah! You’ve Got Jail! (Cue more canned laughter.)

It’s like the episode of Saved By the Bell where the beloved Screech dreams that he has transformed into “Robo Screech,” a robotic high school hall monitor, who impresses the hot girls by disrupting bullies. By the episode’s end he wakes up to find out he’s still a hapless nerd used for comic relief, just like Levin.

Trump might still take him seriously as the prolonged Iran war continues to make the president and Republicans more and more unpopular. But hopefully he’ll soon see Levin’s real purpose is to be a widely recognized, fondly welcomed joke.

items.title: Nvidia Scandal Shows Why SCOTUS Must Allow Catherine Herridge To Protect Her Sources
items.summary: The entire Nvidia scandal illustrates the importance of confidential sources, not merely to journalism, but also to our national security.

scraped.title: SCOTUS Must Allow Catherine Herridge To Protect Her Sources
scraped.description: The entire Nvidia scandal illustrates the importance of confidential sources, not merely to journalism, but also to our national security.
scraped.author: Margot Cleveland
scraped.h1: Nvidia Scandal Shows Why SCOTUS Must Allow Catherine Herridge To Protect Her Sources
scraped.body_text:
The entire Nvidia scandal illustrates the importance of confidential sources, not merely to journalism, but also to our national security.

“Nvidia Chief Seen as Target of Chinese Spy Plot,” headlined the New York Times article from two weeks ago that broke news of a relationship between the chip maker’s founder and a Chinese businesswoman, who, according to the article, “was found to be passing intelligence to Beijing.”

Since then, Jensen Huang, the founder and CEO of Nvidia, has admitted to an extramarital affair and apologized for his conduct. Nvidia’s Board of Directors has also announced an independent investigation.

The Times’ reporting further prompted the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence to request Huang “appear before their committees for a joint, closed-door briefing on Huang’s interactions with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, a publicly reported People’s Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset, and NVIDIA’s security protocols against foreign adversary espionage.”

It will be some time before the public learns of the depth and seriousness of this scandal, but this recent reporting should serve as a wake-up call to another stealth threat to our national security — the weaponization of the Privacy Act.

For some four years, Yanping Chen has aimed the tip of the Privacy Act spear at Catherine Herridge, the renowned national security journalist. Herridge, then Fox News’ Chief Intelligence Correspondent, reported on an FBI counterintelligence investigation into Chen, who at the time ran the University of Management and Technology (“UMT”) in Northern Virginia, where, among others, many members of the U.S. military completed coursework.

In her Privacy Act lawsuit, Chen alleged federal government employees leaked FBI records pertaining to an investigation of Chen to “one or more employees or agents of Fox News.” Chen alleged that as a result of the allegedly “illegal leak or leaks of Dr. Chen’s private information to Fox News, three Fox News reports were published and broadcast, leading to the destruction of Dr. Chen’s livelihood and the termination of the University of Management and Technology’s participation in DOD’s Tuition Assistance program.”

Herridge served as the senior journalist for the three Fox News reports that formed the basis of Chen’s lawsuit. Among other things, one Fox News segment reported “Chen had lied on her immigration forms about whether she had previously worked for the Chinese military.” According to the complaint, one Fox News report “also displayed images of personal photographs seized from Dr. Chen’s home during the FBI search” — left unsaid by Chen was that the picture showed her wearing a Chinese People’s Liberation Army (“PLA”) military uniform. Chen also complained that the reports included “data taken from, and images of, Dr. Chen’s immigration and naturalization forms . . .”

However, much of the information included in Herridge’s reports came from an informant who spoke with the national security journalist or from details contained in a search warrant affidavit filed on the public docket. According to Herridge’s pending Supreme Court petition — more on that shortly — that search warrant affidavit included nearly all the details included in the Fox News reports, with the exception of the images displayed by the network of Chen’s immigration forms, wherein she denied ever belonging to the Communist Party, and the photographs depicting Chen in her PLA uniform.

The Fox News exposé of Chen also included Herridge’s on-camera interview of Stephen Rhoads, a former UMT employee turned FBI informant. Rhoads told Herridge that Chen said she had been a PLA colonel and had told him to lie about it to a grand jury. Rhoads also told Herridge that UMT collected information about U.S. servicemembers’ military histories that could be accessed remotely, while the Department of Defense paid the school Chen founded between $250,000 and $300,000 a month through its tuition assistance program. Herridge also interviewed Peter Mattis, an expert on the Chinese military, who explained why the PLA might value those personnel records UMT collected.

Following Herridge’s reporting, in 2018, the Department of Defense suspended tuition payments to UMT on “national security” grounds. Chen responded by filing a Privacy Act claim against the FBI, DOJ, DoD and DHS on December 21, 2018.

Unlike a case alleging defamation, to prevail on her Privacy Act claims, Chen need not prove that the information Herridge published was false. Instead, Chen must only establish that a federal agency “intentionally or willfully” disclosed a “protected record,” and that the disclosure caused a financial harm.

Among other things, Chen argued that Herridge’s reporting prompted the Department of Defense to drop the university Chen founded from its tuition-assistance program, financially paralyzing the school. While Chen did not sue Herridge, Chen subpoenaed Herridge as part of her Privacy Act case against the government, arguing she needed Herridge’s testimony to prove that a member of one of the federal agencies sued had intentionally (or willfully) disclosed her immigration paperwork and the photograph of Chen in her PLA uniform.

In August of 2023, the district court ordered Herridge to sit for a deposition, which she did, but Herridge nonetheless refused to reveal her source (or sources) to Chen. The presiding judge, Christopher Cooper, later held Herridge in civil contempt of court, ordering her to pay $800 per day for refusing to disclose to Chen how she had obtained the immigration papers and photographs, although Judge Cooper stayed the fine pending an appeal.

On appeal, the D.C. Circuit, in September 2025, upheld the lower court’s decision that Herridge must identify her source (or sources) to Chen. The Supreme Court would later refuse to stay the fine and Herridge paid over $14,000 in sanctions before the district court put the fines on hold pending the completion of any Supreme Court proceedings.

Herridge then turned to the U.S. Supreme Court, filing a petition for review in the high court on August 20, 2026. The petition details the many important reasons why the Supreme Court should grant the petition, including the fact that it has been over fifty years since the justices weighed in on a reporter’s privilege — and even then, only in the context of a criminal case. Since then, Herridge’s petition stressed that the lower courts have crafted a variety of standards for assessing whether a journalist may be forced to reveal a confidential source.

On Friday, a handful of amicus curiae, or friend-of-the-court, briefs hit the docket supporting Herridge’s petition for review. While several media organizations filed briefs stressing the importance of confidentiality to their professions, it was the brief submitted by Sens. Ted Cruz, Mike Lee, and Cynthia Lummis that proves particularly significant in light of the New York Times coverage of the affair between Huang and Alice Huang, the latter of whom the Times claimed passed “intelligence to Beijing.”

In their amicus brief, the trio of senators argued that the Supreme Court should take Herridge’s appeal because the lower court’s decision failed to give any weight to the fact that it was ordering the release of the identity of government sources to Chen — an individual who had self-identified as a PLA colonel and whose school the Department of Defense axed from its tuition-benefit program on national security grounds.

Led by Cruz, the legislators further argued in their amicus brief that allowing Chen to use the Privacy Act to obtain this information represents a further threat to national security because it will leave whistleblowers hesitant to speak with the press for fear of being outed. “Congress’s oversight of the Executive Branch,” the brief stressed, “depends in part on the press.” “Members, including amici, learn of waste, abuse, and security lapses from reporters like Herridge,” the senators continued, adding: “A rule that lets any investigation’s subject unmask those sources through civil discovery will dry up that reporting, and with it impede Congress’s critical oversight of executive agencies.”

And this brings us back full circle to the Nvidia scandal. According to the New York Times’ reporting, “American spy agencies” had surveilled Alice Huang, with U.S. officials reportedly concluding “she was a Chinese intelligence asset, funneling information to Beijing.” This reporting prompted both Nvidia and two House committees to launch investigations into the situation.

Admittedly, after the Times’ role in the Russia-collusion hoax, it is difficult to trust the legacy outlet’s reporting. That is particularly true here given the story had a get-Trump taste to it, with the authors writing “[r]oughly a year ago, Mr. Trump was briefed about the intelligence findings, which have not been previously reported, and chose not to do anything with the information.”

But assume for the moment that the New York Times’ reporting is accurate: Under the currently standing Herridge precedent, a plethora of federal agencies could still face a lawsuit for violating the Privacy Act, and a judge could force the New York Times to reveal its sources. Now, that is unlikely, because unlike Chen, Alice Huang is not a U.S. citizen and the Privacy Act — with limited exceptions — only protects citizens and lawful permanent residents. And given the scandal, it is unlikely the embattled Nvidia CEO would want to file suit.

Nonetheless, the entire Nvidia scandal illustrates the importance of confidential sources, not merely to journalism, but also to our national security, for without an assurance of confidentiality, it is unlikely sources will speak to the press.

Cruz, Lee, and Lummis understand that reality and so does Catherine Herridge. Hopefully, the Supreme Court will too.

scraped.title: Jensen Huang’s Downfall Isn’t Just About Sex
scraped.description: Huang’s two affairs got him ousted as the CEO of Nvidia. But if his Chinese mistress was smuggling Nvidia chips into China—and he knew about it—his problems are a lot bigger than most people thought.
scraped.author: Patrick McGee
scraped.body_text:
On Monday, a day after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang acknowledged he’d had an affair with a woman that U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy, the biggest question was whether he could remain CEO. Three days later, we know the answer to that: This morning, after The New York Times disclosed that he had also had an affair with an Nvidia subordinate, he tendered his resignation. The biggest question now is whether he has committed a federal crime.

The tabloids might be right that the heart of the issue is Jensen Huang’s mistress, Alice Huang, but ironically the bigger scandal might have less to do with whether she’s a Chinese asset and more to do with her alleged “legend,” or cover—being the top executive of a Singaporean front company running a sophisticated operation to evade U.S. export controls and get Nvidia’s most advanced chips into China.

scraped.title: Tough Love: My Kid Has Gone ‘No Contact’
scraped.description: ‘Yesterday she wrote to ask if I would bring her one of her belongings that she left behind,’ writes a 51-year-old dad. ‘I just don’t know what to do.’ Our advice columnist weighs in.
scraped.author: Abigail Shrier
scraped.body_text:
Abigail,

My 21-year-old daughter pretty much hasn’t spoken to me or my wife in one year. I say “pretty much” because she has exchanged short texts on practical matters, and she did agree to see us when we offered to let her say goodbye to the family dog, who was dying. But otherwise she won’t tell us anything about what she’s doing or where she’s living. She has blocked us on social media, but we know from other family members that she has a job, has declared personal bankruptcy, and is living an hour and a half away.

Yesterday she wrote to ask if I would bring her one of her belongings that she left behind in our house. She’s doing an internship in a few days and wants the item for the new job. She called the request “a shot in the dark,” and described her behavior over the past year as “an active effort to distance myself from our family.”

Doing her this favor feels like giving in. But not doing it feels petty, as does trying to use it as leverage to get her to open up about her reasons for walking away. I’ll spare you the full details, but she had an argument with her mother that ended with her calling the police and leaving in an ambulance (nothing physical had occurred between them—she essentially used the ambulance to get a ride off our property). When we subsequently refused a “safety plan” to allow her to return home, she basically went “no contact,” as the kids say.

Now she’s asking us for this favor, and I just don’t know what to do.

—Kidless in New England, 51

Dear Kidless,

Enter the Foreign Service or the Merchant Marine. Run away to the circus. Go West. Join the Peace Corps. Each was an attempt to put down stakes on a tract of adulthood.

The calling was always the same: to go where your parents can’t follow.

Today, young adults don’t leave their parents’ home—not really. From the time they were little, we conditioned them to life inside the cage: tracked, monitored, and, by the standards of past generations, unimaginably tied to their mothers’ apron strings. Even in college, they check in constantly via text. This is the first generation to hand their phones to a professor or boss, with Mom waiting on the line to argue on the ostensible adult’s behalf.

The anxious over-involvement of today’s parents turns out to be intimately connected to the rise in estrangement—young adults going “no contact” and cutting off their parents.

scraped.title: ‘I’m Using AI to Try to Cure Cancer—and Save My Own Life.’ Plus. . .
scraped.description: In today’s Front Page: Meet the doctor using AI to cure his own lung cancer. Rod Dreher reviews Ben Shapiro’s new anti-communist film. Ross Douthat on Trump’s lame-duck presidency. And more.
scraped.author: The Free Press
scraped.body_text:
It’s Thursday, November 12. This is The Front Page , your daily window into the world of The Free Press —and our take on the world at large. Today: Rod Dreher reviews Ben Shapiro’s new movie. Ross Douthat on the legacy-defining decisions Donald Trump now faces. Yuval Levin on the tech that may stunt our next generation of leaders. And more.

But first: The man trying to save his own life with AI.

This week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei predicted that, thanks to the help of artificial intelligence, cancer will become a “relic of the past within a decade.”

Dr. Bryant Lin might not have that long. In the spring of 2024, he was diagnosed with stage 4 lung cancer. A physician himself, he’s tried all kinds of treatments to beat the disease. “There is one class of therapies approved by the Food and Drug Administration that I haven’t tried yet, but after that, I join the millions of patients left with nothing but clinical trials and hope,” writes Bryant in our pages today in a piece inspired by his new book, Sunshine: An Exploration of Living While You Are Dying . “And thus, with very little to lose, I have turned to AI.”

There is a burgeoning field of researchers using AI to help cure cancer. But can it actually save a patient’s life? Bryant is putting that question to the ultimate test. Read how in his essay for us today.

This week, conservative media mogul Ben Shapiro released his first film as a screenwriter. It’s called Confession, and it’s set in Moscow’s infamous Lubyanka prison in 1938. Its star-studded cast includes Rob Lowe as a literature professor faced with a Dostoyevskian dilemma and James Franco as his interrogator. We asked Rod Dreher, whose book Live Not by Lies is all about Christian dissidents in the Soviet Union, to watch it for us. His verdict? A masterpiece, and “one of the most profoundly Christian films I’ve ever seen.”

As you may know, our columnist Ross Douthat has a day job as a correspondent for “60 Minutes.” It was in that role that, in the wake of the Republicans’ midterm defeat, he sat down with President Donald Trump last week. The gripping interview covered everything from the Iran war and the future of his party to whether he thinks he’s going to heaven. Now, in our pages, Ross reflects on his conversation with Trump, and the choices the commander in chief faces as he enters his last two years in office.

What role should AI play in American life? Voters gave something of an answer in the midterms last week, passing a series of ballot measures to impose new guardrails on the technology, but the debate is far from settled. On the latest episode of School of War, political analyst Yuval Levin joins Aaron MacLean to discuss how AI transcends traditional left-right political divisions, what he learned on a recent visit to Anthropic, and how the technology threatens to stunt the development of America’s next generation of leaders—including in the military.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair with an executive who reports to him, according to several sources within the company. The latest revelation comes just days after he admitted to another extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy, which triggered calls for his resignation.

The White House sent a letter cautioning Rep. Robert Garcia, the Democrat set to become House Oversight Committee chair, against pursuing illegal investigations into the Trump administration. The document states that some lines of inquiry “may cross the line into blatant criminality,” and threatened to counter those actions with investigations of their own.

Hundreds of schools in Italy were evacuated on Wednesday, due to a massive wave of bomb threats. The country’s education ministry says that about 6,300 schools have received threats, placing the region on high alert as they continue to investigate the source.

Judge Richard A. Posner has died at 87. The most-cited legal scholar of the second half of the 20th century leaves behind a towering legacy after 36 years on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 7th Circuit in Chicago, more than 3,300 judicial opinions, and more than 40 books.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has moved from his home in Washington, D.C., to a military base. The relocation comes as Iran issues a series of threats to Bessent, who has pursued an “economic onslaught” against Tehran.

The head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council said Wednesday that the country will not give up “a single particle of enriched nuclear material” in peace negotiations. One of President Trump’s major goals in the war is now further out of reach, as Americans continue to endure the conflict’s economic consequences.

Russia and Ukraine agreed to a major prisoner swap on Wednesday. The decision marks one of the first significant signs of progress in the region since they paused peace talks nine months ago.

United Airlines announced a new policy preventing AI bots from booking flights. The company attributed the decision to major privacy concerns, as the new technology continues to pose hacking risks .

Interesting with all the billions spent on mid-term politics I don’t recall one sentence about the $40.5 Trillion in US debt. 🤔. And I noticed how all the talk about “affordability” was misquoted and has been replaced by “accountability”. And lastly today before my tee time, AI is a useful new tool as was Google, but i am dumbfounded by folks who now govern their entire lives from finance to healthcare to dinner with AI. Just like a generation that can’t read a Rand McNally map they will become victims of decision making illiteracy.

The Iranians declare the will not give up "a single particle" of nuclear material for a bomb, meaning "one of President Trump’s major goals in the war is now further out of reach, as Americans continue to endure the conflict’s economic consequences." That goal is no more out of reach than it was before. The Islamic Republic never intends to peacefully quit pursuing nukes and won't until the regime has been completely defeated.

scraped.title: Why the future is Henry the hoover
scraped.author: Aris Roussinos
scraped.h1: Why the future is Henry the hoover We need more simplicity, not complexity
scraped.body_text:
Are you a Dyson or a Henry? (Leon Neal/Getty)

Are you a Dyson or a Henry? (Leon Neal/Getty)

Rather than progressives or conservatives, or Roundheads or Cavaliers, a more compelling barometer of intrinsically opposing worldviews might be whether you identify more with a Dyson vacuum cleaner or with Henry the Hoover. The Dyson represents technological advance for its own sake: expensive products of highly sophisticated engineering, produced at the end of long supply chains in the Far East. The brand increasingly incorporates robotics and AI at every stage from manufacture to consumer use, with online apps for software updates and user personalization. You would not, however, risk kicking it down the stairs.

On the other hand, the cheap and needlessly cheerful Henry, as any builder or renovator knows, will accept any amount of punishment with its trademark idiot smirk. Originally designed to clean out commercial boilers, the Henry is a second-order product of Britain’s lost age of heavy industry, still assembled by hand in a Somerset factory. It does one job, sucking up dirt and dust, and does it as well as it needs to do, without communicating its performance, or user data, or its first flickering doubts and anxieties of consciousness, to distant data centers. When it comes to it, I don’t need my hoover to decide what to clean, or how to do so most efficiently, or act as a high-performance showcase for innovation, but just to perform a simple task, well and reliably. It is more reliable, more robust, simply, because it is less complex. If only the British state were a Henry, we would all be in a much better place.

For there is, we are reminded by the barrage of warnings on domestic preparedness for some dread coming event issued by the state with increasing regularity, really only so much we can do, as individuals or households, when presented with the sudden breakdown of complex systems. It is often, rightly, said of much of modern environmentalism that it places the burden of responsibility on the individual consumer, and not on the giant corporations and national governments most culpable for ecological harms, and most capable of resolving them. What is the point, I ask myself weekly, of carefully sorting and separating my household rubbish and trundling it to the street for collection when I know that the likelihood is that it will end up on the far end of the world to be flung haphazardly in a river? If my carefully washed bottle cap ends up wedged in some Pacific turtle’s gullet, it is not my fault, I tell myself as I consign it to its final journey: all the right boxes were ticked at every stage, and compliance was carefully assured. It is similarly intolerable cheek of BP to popularize the environmental guilt complex of the carbon footprint, when its own sins are far greater than my modest peccadilloes. If we accept this principle, then the same criticism must be leveled at the government’s increasingly panicked warnings to prepare for — well, what exactly we should prepare for is not made clear, nor the reasons why, but we should expect it to be bad, and get in a stock of drinking water and torches and tinned food just in case. Fine, we say, as we browse jerry cans on Amazon and contemplate the threatened 72 hours of heating sardines over a candle, but what have you done to prepare?

Being a simple man, I do not expect Britain’s National Grid to be the envy of the world, nor a showpiece of global climate leadership, but merely to ensure that whenever I choose to flick a switch in the dark, the light will turn on. If it cannot reliably be predicted to do so — and it increasingly appears it cannot — then this is nothing less than a failure of governance. I expect water companies to ensure that when I turn on the tap, water pours out in consequence. If necessary, this may entail them digging large holes in the ground to collect water falling from the sky, and then to keep it there in case of subsequent need. Neither aspiration would require any great technological leap: they are both the very basic functions of their role. If they are unable to do this, or if they are prevented from doing so by political demands, or simply political fancies, then this too is a failure of governance. Like the power companies, or water companies, the state itself, though richly compensated by the taxpayer for its task, seems to have neglected its ability to manage its core function, of reliably delivering the basic utilities of daily life.

Burnham’s recent, limited pivot on North Sea gas drilling was correctly framed as “boosting our energy security”, noting that “at a time of global instability, homegrown energy can be a source of national strength”. But this rare outburst of Westminster common sense, swiftly undercut by a new ban on any further North Sea exploration, would be better applied to Net Zero as a whole. Even in a far more clement geopolitical climate, the idea that Russia or China or the United States would look on any aspect of modern British governance, let alone its economy-hobbling energy policies , with a jealous aspiration to follow our lead would be a delusion. But the idea that Britain can single-handedly lead a historic energy transition at the same time as the great and middle powers of the world are hoarding and fighting over their actual, in-use energy sources, building up and hardening their vital industries at a time of global re-ordering that already bears many of the hallmarks of a world war, is nothing less than madness. We could renounce any interest in world affairs, distance ourselves from the great geopolitical dramas of the day, and quietly count our windmills: but as long as Britain faces the threats it does, from the international situation that already exists, actively weakening Britain’s energy security in pursuit of second- or third-order moral aspirations is an act of reckless irresponsibility.

Behind the recent flurry of warnings over preparedness, it is increasingly clear that the Government’s overriding fear is of looming cyberattacks, in which the interconnectedness of modern life has itself become the primary risk. Last week’s continent-wide attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems , and seemingly now bloodbanks , like that on commissary stores in US military bases in August , shows this is not an abstract threat. The ability to monitor and amend fridge temperatures remotely is, no doubt, useful in assuring quality control and optimizing energy usage. But by linking these widely distributed systems to a public-facing internet, innovators have introduced a single, catastrophic point of failure harmful to the core function of refrigeration — the simple business of keeping items cold, a problem our civilization solved a century ago. The American military is now planning to ensure its bases can generate their own power, water and electricity for a 90-day period, essentially functioning as self-contained fortresses, disconnected from the wider world. Security is to be found in reducing complexity: what is simplest is safest of all.

In just such a way, the apparent “Black October” paradigm shift in hacking abilities enabled by generative AI has produced a welter of cybersecurity advice for panicked users. Some are predicting a massive consumer growth in defensive AI agents battling AI hackers across the internet, much as a medieval peasant imagined giant armies of angels and demons warring invisibly for his soul. But the opposite advice, of “ reducing attack surfaces ”, possesses the more instinctive security of simplicity. If you will shortly require a physical hardware key, and a complex and easily-forgotten algorithmically generated password to mindlessly scroll Instagram, then isn’t it easier to just not have Instagram at all, and no longer have to worry about it? The explosion of personal portals into the internet, manifest in past decades, looks less attractive when every electronic device, from your television to your fridge, must now be assumed to contain a malicious gremlin wishing to do you harm. The future tendency then, is surely a series of tactical withdrawals from the web, on the level of individuals, reducing their exposure, and of governments, tightening their control of ever-smaller and more easily managed internet realms. Like the growth of dumb phones , expensively allowing consumers to return to the level of disconnectedness from the world they enjoyed for free a generation ago, we should expect a revival of dumb fridges , dumb cars and dumb central heating systems which perform their core function reliably in a closed loop isolated from the outside world. It is no less than the fortification of our daily lives, like the transmutation of Roman villas, built for a world of frictionless, peaceful commerce, into the stockaded compounds of the Dark Ages — ruder and simpler but clearly preferable in their security.

Yet a sudden reduction in complexity is the very definition of collapse. Indeed, in his great work The Collapse of Complex Societies , the American anthropologist and historian Joseph Tainter observes the fact that societal complexity by itself increases the risk of collapse. “As systems develop more parts,” he argues, “and more complex interactions among these parts, the potential for problems, conflicts, and incongruities develops disproportionately.” Writing in 1988, Tainter did not have the example of 2020s Britain to hand when he warned, “Consider, for example, the plight of a society that must simultaneously face declining marginal productivity in any combination of the following: agriculture, minerals and energy extraction, science, education and information processing, size and costs of civil and military organizations, upkeep of capital stock etc. As each of these spheres requires an increased proportion of the society’s budget, the portion available for investment in future growth must decline.”

These are all the problems Britain’s recent carousel of prime ministers has tried, and failed to resolve; these are the problems Britain’s voters now live with. It is often the logical solution, Tainter observes, to accept a reduction in complexity as the safer, cheaper option. Many of the ordinary subjects of Rome, he notes, welcomed the barbarians as a relief from the onerous burdens of an empire that could no longer handle its own complexity: Rome’s collapse, devastating on a civilizational level, may have often been personally experienced as a form of liberation. Indeed, the archaeologist Bryan Ward-Perkins suggests that, had the Roman Empire been less complex, the collapse would have been less catastrophic. Instead, by transferring the functions of trade and production to ever-higher levels of sophistication, beyond the grasp or control of ordinary consumers, when the legions left, the inhabitants of Britain found themselves left with a lower level of material culture than they possessed when they arrived.

By Aris Roussinos

The argument presents itself, then, that carefully and consciously reducing complexity now is preferable to having it reduced for you by a malicious line of code. In its inability to be hacked, the dumb National Grid of the Fifties must be considered more secure than the smart one of this decade: it performed one simple function, generating power, using domestic resources, and did so in a way difficult to interrupt. Yet there is entirely another way of looking at the problem: if the risks are of catastrophic failure at a single, centralized point, then security would also be found in dispersal of assets, like the advice, of cybersecurity pessimists, to distribute your wealth across multiple bank accounts in case any single one is hacked, or the practice of Air Force planners, in time of war, of dispersing their aircraft across multiple bases. If the risk is of grid failure at a single vulnerable point, then both energy security and environmental aspirations would be better met by subsidizing solar panels and batteries to individual households, than transforming the entire grid at the cusp of war.

The Government’s vague but increasingly shrill warnings about the forthcoming Event are not wrong in themselves. The assumption being made is of a three-day disruption to the national grid or the internet, after which the state will reboot and resume normal service. A more realistic possibility than total collapse is one of regular low-level disruptions, of brief power cuts and outages rather than civilizational meltdowns. It is entirely sensible, if this is the Government’s fear, to ensure that you are able to heat your home, and cook, in the event of power loss, or to be able to collect rainwater in a butt so that you can at least flush your toilet. But if we are to accept this reduction in societal complexity, then it is only right to ask our rulers to accept their own reduced circumstances. If the state cannot reliably deliver its basic functions, it cannot demand adherence to its ever more refined whims.

If we should all acquire woodburning stoves, then it would be helpful if government bodies did not simultaneously mutter about banning them to fulfill environmental aspirations. If we should secure our own personal food supply in the event of supermarket distribution failure, then the Government should be expanding access to allotments and not selling already existing allotments off, as Jeremy Corbyn rightly warned last year . In the Second World War, when the government urged households to keep chickens and rabbits in their back gardens for protein, it encouraged their keepers to feed their domestic livestock on kitchen scraps, where today it would prosecute them . Even as the state’s ability to deliver basic services has waned, its desire to regulate, and enforce, and ensure compliance with ever-more refined best standards still grows exponentially. This is unsustainable: if we are being asked to do more ourselves to fill in for what the state is increasingly incapable of doing, then the state must accept it must ask less of us, and stand out of the way.

As with the internet, as with Net Zero, the obvious solution, in times of threat, is to harden security by reducing the attack surfaces. That which is necessary to the core function of any system should be hardened, and made secure: that which is not a core function, and offers new vectors of risk, should be examined carefully for its utility, with an eye to being cut. The managers of the British state have grown too comfortable imagining themselves at the helm of a sophisticated piece of machinery, inspiring the envy of the world through its acquisition of new and fundamentally unnecessary functions.

We would all be much safer if they saw themselves as a Henry, reliably and capably performing the basic functions we demand of it, and left the rest to us. But as it stands, and the Government tells us what to stockpile, and warns us in panicked voices not to panic, a level of unnecessary complexity has been added to something that is, at core, extremely simple: keep the lights on, keep the water running, keep the country safe. If the British state is not confident it can do so, then what is it for?

Aris Roussinos is an UnHerd columnist and a former war reporter.

scraped.title: The war against Michel Houellebecq
scraped.author: Simon Heffer
scraped.h1: The war against Michel Houellebecq The French take their freedom for granted
scraped.body_text:
(Benjamin de Diesbach/Getty)

(Benjamin de Diesbach/Getty)

Michel Houellebecq is in trouble again. Prosecuted in 2002 for insulting Islam, he was acquitted. After Soumission , the novel many of his devotees — of whom I am one — felt was his masterpiece, he had to go into hiding for a time for once more being less than complimentary about Islam. Now, after four years of procedural table-tennis, he is accused of complicity in incitement to discrimination, hatred or violence against a specific group of people, in an interview with the magazine Front Populaire , given in 2022. Houellebecq’s original alleged offense in 2002 was to call Islam “the stupidest religion”: he doesn’t do understatement or subtlety. This time the remark that threatens to get him into trouble is that “when entire territories come under Islamist control, I think acts of resistance will take place. There will be attacks and shootings in mosques, in cafés frequented by Muslims, in short, Bataclans in reverse,” he said, referring to the murderous Islamist attack in Paris in November 2015.

The decision to charge Houellebecq has been criticized as a freedom of speech issue; and so, to an extent, it is. French law in that respect differs somewhat from English, but doubtless his lawyers will have hours of lucrative fun arguing over the difference between inciting people to do something unspeakable and simply warning that society is moving in a direction where something unspeakable is likely to happen. Nearly 60 years ago Enoch Powell was in the same position over dire prophecies he made in his so-called “Rivers of Blood” speech.

By Michel Houellebecq

But this prosecution of Houellebecq provokes concerns that go far beyond freedom of expression. In just over 30 years as a novelist writing mainly about the misery of bourgeois French life, he has lifted up a number of stones and allowed some pretty unsavory things to crawl out from under them. In no particular order these include sex tourism, paedophilia, mental illness, rampant narcissism, family breakdown, betrayal, social alienation, self-hatred, nihilism, prostitution and, inevitably, racism. But then anyone who understands what French society is really like will find none of this surprising. It is not the mark of a happy country when the two people most likely to end up competing in the final round of next year’s presidential elections are Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Years of decadence and failure under the Fifth Republic — conditions about which Houellebecq has written extensively in all his novels — have led to an embrace of one form of extremism or another as a means to counter or, at least, manage them. That, if you like, is the end product of the society about which Houellebecq has spent all these decades writing.

By Darran Anderson

If he is not allowed to be himself, to express what he feels, his natural powers of observation will be suppressed. No-one sensible can defend incitement, but was the novelist really inciting anyone in that 2022 interview? Was he not merely simply presenting another aspect of a deteriorating society, in which the people have failed themselves through their willful decadence and whose traditional political class has not even dared to try to treat the underlying problems? Houellebecq’s lawyers have on his behalf issued a statement in which it is claimed he feels manipulated and exploited by those to whom he gave the interview. Maybe he does, but he should have seen it coming. Again, this is not simply about free speech: it is about a creative artist having the permission to express the depths of his creativity in order accurately to reflect his society or, in this case, his fears for his society. If others have chosen to exploit that then it may be, as the statement also said, out of greed — Houellebecq is probably France’s greatest and most famous living novelist and therefore big box office — but it might just as plausibly be that they shared his fears, and saw no reason not to share them with a wider public. In the present unhappy state of France this is inevitable.

By Simon Heffer

But then French writers have often courted trouble for displaying radicalism or for perceived insult. Molière scandalized polite society with Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme ; Flaubert was rude about Norman peasants (and the middle class) in Bouvard et Pécuchet and quite shocking in Madame Bovary ; Zola was prosecuted for criminal libel over J’Accuse ; Céline was fascist but still one of the most glittering writers in the French canon. Houellebecq has long been in a distinguished Gallic tradition of saying the unsayable, but saying it beautifully; all that is shocking is that a feeble and gutless French state is once more trying to punish him for it.

I recall being in my office on a January morning in 2015, reading an article about Houellebecq in Le Figaro about his new novel, Soumission , published that day. The novel’s action was set seven years later at the 2022 presidential election. As usual, the two highest-scoring candidates in the first round contest the prize in the second: and Houellebecq imagines these to be Marine Le Pen and a fictional creation, Mohammed Ben Abbes, leader of the Muslim Fraternity. The leaders of the main parties, frozen out of the contest by their poor performances in the first round, meet to decide where to advise their voters to go. They agree that Mme Le Pen cannot possibly be allowed to win, and tell their followers to vote for Ben Abbes. He wins; France is Islamified. The anti-hero of the novel, a lecturer at the Sorbonne who, in true Houellebecqois style seems most attracted to his vocation because of the opportunity it gives him to sleep with his young female students, flees Paris for a time and wanders aimlessly around a country in ferment. Returning to his faculty — now part of the renamed Islamic University of Paris — he is welcomed back to his job by his (ethnically French, formerly Catholic) superior, who has himself converted to Islam and is very much going with the flow. He tells him Islam isn’t too bad, not least because he now had four wives, and the youngest is only fifteen.

Reading the Figaro interview, I looked up from my newspaper and saw something shocking happening on the television in the corner of my office. A news channel was relaying, live from Paris, the immediate aftermath of the Charlie Hebdo massacre. The coincidence of this horrific event and the publication of Soumission was not lost on the French media in the succeeding days. Once more, Houellebecq had shown he was not only a great novelist but a great prophet. However, the controversy over that magnificent book continues to this day.

It is a book that takes us to the heart of Houellebecq, and reminds us why for the sake of France and for those who, like General de Gaulle, have a certain idea of France, he must be preserved and allowed free rein. He said at the time that he was not attacking Islam: he was attacking the so-called custodians of France’s glorious culture for being willing to abandon it, which he was convinced they were. He was attacking, in that regard, not merely the cynics and self-servers of the political class, but many French people themselves, who took their way of life and their freedoms for granted. It appears that, still, no lessons have been learned. With luck Houellebecq’s lawyers will see him safe: but what this climate of suppression will mean for the mood of France in the imminent presidential election one dreads to imagine.

Simon Heffer sits as a Conservative in the House of Lords as Lord Blackwater.

scraped.title: Don’t torch Gangsta Granny
scraped.author: Tracy King
scraped.h1: Don’t torch Gangsta Granny Children love reading David Walliams books
scraped.body_text:
"The Boy in the Dress". (Leon Neal/Getty)

"The Boy in the Dress". (Leon Neal/Getty)

David Walliams should have one of the most expansive and lucrative legacies in kids fiction. His fart jokes and stereotypes have sold 60 million books across the world, translated into 55 different languages. His characters even made it to Alton Towers, where a themed Walliams area featured “Gangsta Granny: The Ride”, as well as “Raj’s Bouncy Bottom Burp”. Until, that is, it was shuttered last week, just before the Walliamsverse imploded with allegations of grooming and abuse. Now no plucky tween hero with a sidekick dog can save it. His publisher has not only dropped him, but is no longer printing or distributing his back-catalog of 22 novels and seven collections of short stories. No more new Walliams, no more old Walliams. That’s incredibly rare for a canon of that size and value.

And so, David Walliams ascends into that ever-growing anti-pantheon of writers who have been canceled either posthumously or in vivo. While some parents proscribe Roald Dahl because the humor is crass, others object to his anti-semitism. Neil Gaiman lost his comic book publishing deal, and JK Rowling’s Harry Potter — give or take an evangelical book-burning session or two — is now protested more for the political beliefs of the author than the content of the books. But fan loyalty persists, even for the most egregious offenders. It’s easier to justify buying a problematic favorite when the author is long-dead and no longer in receipt of royalties, but walking home with a bagful of Harry Potter novels is likely to result in accusations of directly funding hate. The same is true of the upcoming Potter TV reboot, which will turn into a game of social-media chicken as viewers decide whether or not to risk admitting they watched it. At least they’ll have the choice. In the wake of the Walliams news, the BBC promptly removed an episode of Doctor Who he was in.

By Tracy King

The trouble is, Walliams is one of a very small number of writers whom today’s children will insist on reading. Broadly aimed at ages eight to 12, the books have a natural constituency of readers who are old enough to have their own taste in stories, and young enough for that taste to center on Walliams-style crassness. Theirs is the demographic for which fiction carries its strongest and most basic moral instruction, typically via colorful stories in which good behavior is rewarded and bad is punished. The protagonist is invariably a child of similar age to the reader; all children are different, but not so different that they can’t relate to 11-year-old Harry, Ron or Hermione. Naturally, parents want the books to deliver appropriate messaging but, increasingly, they are expected to police their children’s interests based on very adult considerations. It’s no longer enough to decide whether the contents of a book are appropriate; the author must also pass a purity test. It’s not so long ago that Walliams’ first children’s book, The Boy in the Dress , was hailed as a progressive anthem, embraced by liberal parents for its message of acceptance and tolerance. Today, he’s not getting the grades. And parents are left wondering whether to explain that the funny man really was a baddie in disguise. It’s frustrating, because in the current childhood literacy crisis, kids need all the enjoyable books they can get. It is boys who are least likely to read for pleasure, and Walliams was one of the rare authors primarily read by them. Is it fair to demand they read something they enjoy less?

By Julie Burchill

Some parents and teachers will greet Walliams’ demise with relief. The books might be popular with tweens, but have long been criticized for lazy writing, racial and class stereotypes and the general suspicion that four books a year smells a bit like a pocket-money grab. I have read several of them, and if they are turds, they’re the highly-polished variety. They are readable (damned with faint praise), sometimes linguistically witty (alliteration does a lot of lifting), and less reliant on snot, poo and farts than you might think. In a few years the whole thing will be moot, a cautionary tale fit for the fireside. In the meantime, what to tell the kids?

Becky, a mother of two, isn’t going to take the books off her shelves. “Partly because I feel squeamish about censorship, and partly because I don’t want to have to explain why to a nine- and eight-year-old. I try to keep the reality of sex crimes from them just now. They’re too young.”

Richard, now 24, was a Walliams superfan when he was eight. Little Britain was extremely popular on the playground, and the books were marketed as a natural successor to Roald Dahl. “I saw Walliams as a role model. I was a huge comedy fan in general, and wanted to be a comedian or performer of some sort. Little Britain and the Walliams books gave me permission to be silly, to create characters and not conform to male stereotypes, which of course is bleakly ironic in hindsight.” He tells me his older brother was reading the books, as were his peers. “Walliams was very popular even with boys who didn’t normally read, and it wouldn’t have crossed our minds to question why we were enjoying them. They were just instantly rewarding.”

By the age of 11 he had moved on to more mature prose, but this didn’t stop him from wanting Walliams to sign Mr Stink , his favorite novel by the author, at an event in a local bookshop. “I remember thinking he wasn’t particularly warm,” Richard says. “But afterwards, the book felt different. It was exciting that he had interacted with something that was in my hands and my house.” Richard’s edition became a venerated object; playground boasting rights, a core memory to be thumbed through at any time. He has no plans to get rid of it. He says that “by keeping the book, I’m not complicit in anything. It doesn’t mean I’m okay with what he’s alleged to have done.”

But while individuals can use their own discretion when it comes to Walliams and beloved tomes, schools have little choice in the matter. Many have already sent out emails reassuring parents they are on the case. One primary school teaching assistant told me this week that the kids had not mentioned the news, it perhaps being “above their heads”. But she still felt she had little option but to remove the books — because of the parents. “The only reason we are removing them is potential reaction from parents if their kid brings one of the books home,” she says. It’s hard to say whether those parents would be justified in complaining should their child be caught innocently reading The Boy in the Dress under the covers. But it’s easier for schools to avoid the issue entirely, undoubtedly damned either way.

We’re only briefly children, and those of us lucky enough to have been keen readers will be reluctant to let go of a foundational joy. I ask the school assistant to ask what will be done with the removed titles. She tells me the kids make Christmas tree collages from old books, so they might be used for that. “If not,” she says, “they’ll go in the bin”.

Tracy King is a writer and producer based in London and Birmingham, UK. Her memoir is Learning To Think .

scraped.title: "Counted Every Single Bar": Tether Gold Gets Clean KPMG Audit Confirming $2.2B In Physical Gold
scraped.description: ZeroHedge - On a long enough timeline, the survival rate for everyone drops to zero
scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: "Counted Every Single Bar": Tether Gold Gets Clean KPMG Audit Confirming $2.2B In Physical Gold
scraped.body_text:
Via Decrypt ,

Tether's gold-backed stablecoin, Tether Gold (XAUT), has completed its first full audit by KPMG, which found the token fully backed by physical gold , the company announced on Thursday.

KPMG issued an unqualified opinion on the financial statements of TG Commodities, which issues XAUT, for the year ended December 31, 2025. An unqualified, or "clean," opinion means the auditor found that the statements fairly present the company's financial position, without reservations.

Tether Gold (XAU₮) Becomes Tether's Second Stablecoin to Complete a Big Four Audit Learn more: https://t.co/eO0asUwvlI

— Tether (@tether) November 12, 2026

As of the end of 2025, TG Commodities held 520,089.350 troy ounces of allocated gold, valued at $2.246 billion, against 520,089.300 XAUT tokens in issue , according to Tether. The gold is held in vaults in Switzerland, and each token represents an ownership interest in gold on specific bars.

As part of the audit, KPMG physically counted and inspected every gold bar backing the token, rather than relying only on confirmations from custodians, Tether said.

"KPMG counted every single bar as part of its Tether Gold audit," Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said, adding that he believes XAUT "is on track to become the first true competitor to the gold ETF market."

The XAUT audit is Tether's second by a Big Four firm. In August, KPMG issued a clean opinion on Tether International, the issuer of its flagship USDT stablecoin , in what the company called the largest inaugural audit in history, Decrypt reported at the time.

For years, Tether faced criticism for relying on quarterly attestations, which offer a snapshot of reserves at a single point in time, rather than a full audit of its finances . The company first said earlier this year that it was being audited by a Big Four firm without naming it, before confirming KPMG.

Tether still publishes quarterly attestations for USDT. Its latest, prepared by accounting firm BDO and covering the period to September 30, showed total reserve assets of $191.5 billion against $183.5 billion in liabilities, giving it an excess reserve buffer of almost $8 billion , according to the report . Tether said it made $1.5 billion in net operating profit in the third quarter.

"These milestones advance the progress towards audits across the whole of Tether," said chief financial officer Simon McWilliams.

Separately from the gold backing XAUT, Tether has also built up its own large gold reserves, and Ardoino has said it will keep adding to its stash, which it stores in a former nuclear bunker in Switzerland .

scraped.title: Massie's Last Stand: Epstein Files Petition Hits 218 - And Doesn't Need Speaker Signoff
scraped.description: ZeroHedge - On a long enough timeline, the survival rate for everyone drops to zero
scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: Massie's Last Stand: Epstein Files Petition Hits 218 - And Doesn't Need Speaker Signoff
scraped.body_text:
Rep. Thomas Massie's (R-KY) discharge petition for a second Epstein files bill reached 218 signatures on Wednesday morning, less than two months before he leaves Congress - enough to force a House vote on legislation that would let Epstein's victims, state prosecutors and members of Congress sue the Justice Department over records it is still holding back.

🚨This morning we reached the required 218 signatures on my discharge petition for Epstein Files Transparency Act II ! I'm working closely with @RepJayapal , @RepTeresaLF and @RepRoKhanna to get this to the floor for a vote soon.

— Thomas Massie (@RepThomasMassie) November 11, 2026

Rep. John Garamendi (D-CA) supplied the 218th signature, a day after Rep. Adam Smith (D-WA) signed. The petition carries all 214 House Democrats and four Republicans: Massie, Nancy Mace and Ralph Norman of South Carolina, and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, none of whom returns in the next Congress . Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-CO), who backed last year's petition, did not sign this one.

The bill, the Epstein Files Transparency Act II (H.R. 9694), goes after the gaps in last year's law. It lets a state attorney general or district attorney, a victim, or a member of Congress sue the attorney general over the "unlawful withholding, redaction, delay, removal, concealment" of Epstein records, and it bars the Justice Department from invoking deliberative process, attorney-client, work product or law enforcement privilege to keep material back.

Victims could demand the full, unredacted records that relate to them, FBI interview reports (FD-302s) included. Members of Congress would get unredacted access within seven calendar days of a written request, and classified records would have to be made available in a secure facility, with no refusal allowed on the grounds that they are classified. DOJ, FBI and US attorney's office personnel who conceal, destroy, falsify or withhold the records would face the existing federal penalties for false statements, obstruction and destroying records.

The bill also switches off the Justice Department's Touhy regulations , the rules it uses to decide whether to hand records to outsiders, for any request under the Act. New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez sued the department over exactly those rules in August, alleging that it ran the state through Touhy requests for unredacted files on Epstein's Zorro Ranch, where New Mexico has reopened its investigation.

When he introduced the bill on July 15, Massie said the department "has flagrantly and consistently ignored EFTA's disclosure requirements" and "continues to unlawfully withhold over 3 million Epstein files." Khanna, his Democratic co-author on both bills, and Sens. Jeff Merkley (D-OR) and Ben Ray Luján (D-NM) introduced it with him in both chambers.

On Jan. 30 the Justice Department published over 3 million more pages, with more than 2,000 videos and 180,000 images, bringing its total to "nearly 3.5 million pages released in compliance with the Act," more than a month after the law's December deadline. Pam Bondi told the House Oversight Committee in May that "to the best of my knowledge, the Department produced everything required" ( while admitting redaction errors), and Attorney General Todd Blanche said last month there is "not some tranche of super-secret documents about Jeffrey Epstein that we're withholding" - even as an FBI inventory lists CDs of classified material , as we reported this month.

Massie and Khanna used the same maneuver last year. Their first discharge petition forced the original Epstein Files Transparency Act to the floor, Trump dropped his opposition, and the bill passed the House 427-1 before the Senate cleared it by unanimous consent and Trump signed it on Nov. 19, 2025.

Massie is pushing this one as a lame duck: Trump-backed Ed Gallrein beat him in Kentucky's May 19 primary, and this week he was the only Republican to side with Democrats as the House shelved his articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, 211-204. Asked about the Epstein files, the White House pointed Newsweek to Trump's Truth Social post on that vote instead: "Every single Republican, except Thomas Massie, a major LOSER, voted in favor of Pete."

Under House rules the petition now sits for seven legislative days before a signer can call it up, and the Speaker then has two legislative days to act on it. ABC News puts the earliest floor action after the Thanksgiving recess, as soon as Dec. 2 or 3 , before the new Congress is sworn in in January. Last year Speaker Mike Johnson scheduled the vote on the first bill before that clock ran out.

A House win would send the bill to the Senate, where Merkley and Luján carry the companion. From there it would go to Trump, who signed the first Epstein bill only after dropping his opposition to it.

scraped.h1: Watch: Joy Behar Has No Idea the ‘Abe’ Mentioned in Civil War Discussion Is Abraham Lincoln
scraped.body_text:
Veterans Day on “The View” did not disappoint for anyone hoping to find yet another reason to wonder how this program is still running on daytime television.

The conversation — this is not in the least bit surprising — devolved to the topic of race during a discussion of American service members and the wars our country has fought.

“The View” co-host Sunny Hostin made an odd remark about former President Abraham Lincoln not emancipating the slaves, but the slaves doing it themselves.

But putting the absurdity of that remark aside, how many viewers noticed co-host Joy Behar’s reaction when Whoopi Goldberg referred to him as “Abe” when crediting the 16th president?

“You have to give it to Abe. You have to give it to Abe,” Goldberg told the room.

“Abe?” Behar asked.

“Abe Lincoln,” Goldberg determined.

Sunny Hostin celebrates Veteran’s Day with racism and some serious revisionist history. She claims Abraham Lincoln didn’t emancipate anyone and the North didn’t free the slaves. She claims the slaves did all “themselves”:

“People often say that Abraham Lincoln emancipated the slaves. The slaves basically emancipated themselves because they wanted freedom and they fought for their freedom.”

— Nicholas Fondacaro (@NickFondacaro) November 11, 2026

Does Behar not know that Lincoln was president?

Was she just confirming that “Abe” was the very same?

It is hard to say after countless missteps, nonsensical takes, and a history of litigious comments made on this program.

Maybe Behar, a diehard Democrat , was apprehensive to credit Lincoln, a Republican, with such a feat.

Hostin seemed uninterested in doing so.

Liberal women continue down a path of derangement they mistake for thought-provoking, insightful commentary.

It may seem harsh to chastise “The View” to such a degree, but the criticism does not lie in their position on a nuanced take about an incredibly niche topic.

They are having trouble comprehending the fundamental history of the Civil War, something a middle school or high school student could easily do.

Although conservative detractors only watch “The View” to see what piffle the hosts will spout next, we need to ask if their key demographic actually watches for similar reasons.

Is it possible that middle-aged and older women just hate-watch this program? Are they just sitting in their living rooms, judging the co-hosts on anything from their outfits or hairstyle to these outlandish takes?

If there are genuine fans and defenders of this program, do speak up.

This article appeared originally on The Western Journal .

scraped.body_text:
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth did not dodge accountability or pull rank when a young Army sentinel did his job at one of the most sacred sites in America.

On Thursday, Hegseth hosted members of the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment (The Old Guard) at the Pentagon and personally awarded Specialist Thomas Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Veterans Day.

On Wednesday, November 11, after the official Veterans Day wreath-laying ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery that included President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, Hegseth, his wife Jennifer, Chief of Staff Ricky Buria, Deputy Chief of Staff Patrick Weaver, and Senior Adviser and Deputy Assistant Tami Radabaugh posed for photographs on the steps near the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

Video captured by news outlets showed members of the group laughing and chatting as they moved away from the photos.

Spc. Iglesias, serving as the sentinel on duty from The Old Guard, stopped his patrol, turned toward the group, and called out the standard reminder: “All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times!”

WATCH: Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and his group were scolded by an Army sentinel at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier during a Veterans Day ceremony after a disruption of the solemn atmosphere.

“All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times.”

The chief Pentagon spokesman defended Hegseth’s commitment to honoring the sacrifices of service members while acknowledging the lapse:

“While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum.”

Get the full story behind the tense exchange: https://t.co/OtUltYn5xZ

— Fox News (@FoxNews) November 12, 2026

Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell later stated that the soldier “correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum.”

The Tomb has been under continuous 24-hour watch by Old Guard sentinels since 1948. Enforcing silence and respect is routine duty at the site, which holds the remains of unidentified service members from World War I, World War II, and the Korean War.

Rather than ignore or minimize the moment, Hegseth brought the Old Guard to the Pentagon the next day and awarded Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal specifically “for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026,” according to a Pentagon official.

Hegseth posted photos of the ceremony on X, including one of him pinning the medal on Iglesias, with the message: “We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist. Carry on Patriots.”

We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist.

Carry on Patriots. https://t.co/Uk6ek6oOso

— Secretary of War Pete Hegseth (@SecWar) November 12, 2026

scraped.h1: Trump Directs Vance Give His ‘Complete and Total Attention’ to Blue State Fraud, Says Iran Deal No Longer Needed
scraped.body_text:
President Donald Trump has directed Vice President JD Vance to focus on investigating “Massive Corruption and Crime” in Democrat-led states, saying his peace negotiations with Iran are no longer needed.

In a post on Truth Social Thursday morning, Trump characterized blue states such as Minnesota, California, Illinois, Maine, and New York as “poorly run, corrupt disasters” that steal billions in taxpayer dollars each month.

“Our Budget could be quickly BALANCED with the correction of this large scale criminal activity,” the president asserted. “CORRUPTION is in the Democrat Leadership’s blood!”

Earlier this year, Trump officially designated Vance as both the “Fraud Czar” and as a lead U.S. negotiator with Iran.

During his State of the Union address in February, Trump directed Vance to lead the nationwide crackdown on fraud in federal benefit programs. This role was formalized through an executive order establishing the Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, which Vance chairs.

The anti-fraud task force claims to have identified over $260 billion in fraud and has already suspended hundreds of healthcare providers in California alone.

Vance was also tasked in April with spearheading negotiations with Iranian officials, alongside Trump’s chief diplomatic envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.

On Thursday Trump said he wanted Vance to give his “complete and total attention” to combatting fraud and no longer focus on Iran.

“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” Trump explained. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” Trump declared.

Trump also had a message Thursday for Senator Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), who has repeatedly stated that Senate Democrats will prioritize fighting against corruption in the United States when they take over in January.

The Honduran man had been deported twice, but a third time was the charm.

An illegal alien who was arrested after allegedly claiming to have a bomb on a flight had been granted asylum to stay in the U.S. after claiming to identify as transgender, Immigration and Customs Enforcement has confirmed.

Rony Alexander Gomez-Alberto allegedly tried to force his way into the cockpit of a United Airlines flight going from Newark, New Jersey, to New Orleans, Louisiana, on Monday.

'This twice-deported criminal illegal alien was allowed into our country because of a weak asylum system that allowed him to game the system.'

Pilots on the flight triggered a hijacking alarm, according to the Daily Mail, and Gomez-Alberto was taken into custody when the plane landed.

The Department of Homeland Security confirmed that Gomez-Alberto had been deported twice after entering the U.S. illegally. But after he was caught a third time, he was allowed to stay in the U.S.

On Thursday, ICE confirmed that Gomez-Alberto identified as transgender to request asylum, as first reported by the Daily Wire.

"I am also afraid that I will be killed — either by private citizens or the police — in both of these countries because I am transgender," he wrote on his asylum application, according to ICE.

The Daily Wire reported that Gomez-Alberto claimed he feared for his life in his homeland of Honduras and also told authorities that he was HIV-positive and an avid marijuana user.

"This twice-deported criminal illegal alien was allowed into our country because of a weak asylum system that allowed him to game the system,” said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin in a statement Thursday.

"Thanks to law enforcement, he is now behind bars," he added.

United Airlines identified the plane as a Boeing 737 Max 9 with 46 passengers and six crew members.

RELATED: 7 illegal aliens and 7 others charged after horrific deaths of 7 migrants, including a child

ICE added that it had issued a detainer request to ensure that Gomez-Alberto was not released by local authorities without notifying ICE.

"With 2,312 known or suspected terrorists arrested, ICE is putting American safety FIRST and cracking down on those who exploit our asylum system," read the statement from ICE. "There is NO place in our country for illegal aliens who terrorize American citizens."

scraped.body_text:
El-Sayed laughed at the 'delicious irony' that Vice President JD Vance will swear him in.

Democratic U.S. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan says he is going to be sworn into office with a Qur’an.

El-Sayed will become the first Muslim to serve in the U.S. Senate after beating Mike Rogers in the midterm elections.

'It really doesn't matter what your name is, doesn't matter how you pray. Like, America is big enough.'

El-Sayed also mocked Vice President JD Vance while pointing out the "delicious irony" that Vance is "constitutionally obligated" to swear him in as senator.

"I will likely swear in on the Qur’an," said El-Sayed in an interview with NPR host Leila Fadel that published Thursday.

"Which Qur’an, we're not sure. I mean, Thomas Jefferson had a copy of the Qur’an. So when Keith Ellison was sworn in to Congress, he swore in on that copy. There's also the University of Michigan holds the first Qur’an in the state of Michigan. It's very, very old," he added.

"And that might be the choice. So I don't know," El-Sayed said. "But I will swear on the Qur’an."

He went on to say that it was more important to America than it was to him personally that a Muslim be sworn in to the U.S. Senate for the first time in history.

"It 's less about what it means to me and more about what it means for America. I mean, everybody has the experience of being told they're less-than or excluded or that they don't belong," said El-Sayed.

"I hope that when people see that, there is this sense that America really is big enough for you, right?" he added. "It really doesn't matter what your name is, doesn't matter how you pray. Like, America is big enough."

RELATED: 'Fire will rise': Muslim pundit promises 'reckoning' if El-Sayed loses — and also if he wins

El-Sayed easily defeated Rogers and was one of the beneficiaries of the blue wave of Democratic victories in the midterms.

Rogers garnered only 45.5% of the vote, while El-Sayed got 52.5%, according to the latest count in the Michigan election.

The University of Michigan does have many old Qur’anic manuscripts, but it is unclear whether it has the "oldest" in Michigan.

scraped.body_text:
The brawl left the fighter bloodied and in disbelief.

A gang attack on a popular UFC fighter has led to the arrest of 10 people, and it was all caught on video.

Ahead of a star-studded wrestling event set for this weekend, the mixed martial arts world was rocked by a brutal group assault led by a fighter from Dagestan, a Russian republic with a high Muslim population.

'You guys came from behind, bro.'

It all started in a Hilton hotel on Yas Island, Abu Dhabi, which has become a hub for martial arts since it opened its doors to UFC events during the COVID-19 lockdowns.

Merab Dvalishvili — a devout Christian, Georgian national, and UFC star — said he was doing an interview with wrestling company RAF ahead of the event when he was approached by Usman Nurmagomedov, a member of one of the most prominent martial arts families in the world and a Muslim.

In a video allegedly taken by a member of Nurmagomedov's entourage, the 22-0 fighter walks up to the much smaller Dvalishvili and seemingly says something to him before slapping him across the face.

Dvalishvili backs off and covers his head before he is attacked twice more by two members of Nurmagomedov's crew, at which point the altercation turns into an all-out brawl, according to the video.

The violent incident reportedly led to 10 arrests, including the men from Nurmagomedov's side who reportedly filmed the attack.

RELATED: Dana White to meet with Trump after 'joke' job offer

"The incident was a fighting over previous disputes between a number of individuals. It took place at the entrance of a hotel," Abu Dhabi police said in a statement, according to The National News .

Police said they would "deal firmly with behaviour that threatens public safety or disrupts public order."

Dvalishvili, who is 5 foot 6 inches and fights at 135 pounds, shot a video showcasing his injuries following the attack; Nurmagomedov is 5 foot 11 inches and fights at 155 pounds.

"Usman Nurmagomedov and his friends came like a snakes from behind," the Georgian said as his wounds were tended to.

"What kind of fighters you guys are? What kind of man does this, bro?!" he went on.

"You guys came from behind, bro. Then I don't know how many guys. ... All your friends waiting for us in the sneaky way?! Wow."

Dvalishvili is scheduled to wrestle at the RAF event on Saturday, as is Nurmagomedov's older brother, Umar.

RELATED: Be like Mike: Michael Jordan NBA Finals jersey sells for world-record price at auction

Reactions from the MMA world overwhelmingly condemned the attack, including recent UFC champion Ilia Topuria, also a Georgian, who said on X that Nurmagomedov had reportedly been "detained." Topuria called Nurmagomedov's group "a bunch of absolute cowards."

"I always thought you were a bunch of mediocre individuals. Now you've removed every last doubt. Honor, respect, and humility aren't words you preach. They’re values you live by. And you've shown none of them."

On the other side, fellow Dagestani and UFC champion Islam Makhachev wrote , "To those who are now condemning Usman and the guys and insulting them. Why were you silent when Merab hit a Dagestani wrestler for no reason and insulted his honor? The man approached him to talk with no ill intent," according to MMA Mania.

"What happened today was started by Merab in his own homeland when he took it upon himself to hit a guest and insult his mother," Makhachev added.

Makhachev is referring to a July incident in Georgia where Dvalishvili slapped a training partner of Nurmagomedov during another large group scuffle, footage showed.
