items.title: Final Ohio results disprove ‘spoiler’ nonsense about socialist Greg Levy
items.summary: Levy’s support came from working-class communities of all types – all the places this political system has left out.

scraped.title: Final Ohio results disprove ‘spoiler’ nonsense about socialist...
scraped.description: In the months leading up to the election, the Democratic establishment and national media repeatedly attacked Greg Levy’s socialist Senate campaign in
scraped.author: Deja Gaston
scraped.h1: Final Ohio results disprove ‘spoiler’ nonsense about socialist Greg Levy
scraped.body_text:
In the months leading up to the election, the Democratic establishment and national media repeatedly attacked Greg Levy’s socialist Senate campaign in Ohio as a “spoiler” that would lead to the defeat of the Democrat, Sherrod Brown.

Both billionaire parties bet real money on the “spoiler” idea. In October, a shady MAGA-linked super PAC spent more than $2 million on mailers promoting Levy, hoping to peel votes away from the Democrat Sherrod Brown. The Democratic machine spent its own millions on mailers and ads, saying “a vote for Greg is a vote for MAGA.” Shameful as these moves were, both rested on a shared assumption that a socialist’s base of support comes from votes that would otherwise be reliable Democratic Party voters.

A week after the election, all the wild speculation about the impact of the Greg Levy campaign can be put to rest. The results paint a clear picture. Sherrod Brown won by nearly five points, part of the country-wide referendum on Trump and the reactionary MAGA agenda. Meanwhile, nearly 95,000 Ohioans refused the two-party trap and voted for an independent socialist candidate.

The spoiler story never came to pass, but not just because the Democrat won by a significant margin. The data shows the impact of the socialist campaign was very different than what was assumed by both the Democrats and Republicans who wasted millions on ads to confuse voters. The socialist campaign clearly reached the state’s growing base of political independents and voters disillusioned by both billionaire parties, who, regardless of how they’re registered, would likely not have otherwise voted. If Levy “pulled” votes from anyone — as if votes belonged to a party to begin with — he actually pulled from Husted, the Republican. After months of shaming voters for following their conscience, all those parroting “a vote for Greg is a vote for Husted” had it backwards.

Across the state (and the country), the Republicans did worse in 2026 than in 2024. The “spoiler” claim hinges on the central idea that any vote for Levy would have otherwise gone to Brown, the Democrat. If that were true, Brown should have gained less, relative to the Republican candidate, wherever Levy did well. Wherever the socialist surged, that should have been good for the Republicans. The county results from 2024 and 2026, and the precinct-level data from the state’s four largest counties, show this wasn’t the case.

In fact, the Republican share fell furthest in the counties where Levy ran strongest. For every point Levy picked up in a county, Husted ran about 1.6 points further behind the Republican’s 2024 result. On the other side, the Democrat Brown’s gains remained consistent regardless of how Levy did. Nowhere is this clearer than in Wyandot County, where the Republican won 69% of the vote in 2024. Levy won 11.5% there in 2026, his best result in the state. The Republican share fell 13 points from 2024, while the Democrats’ share barely moved.

The same pattern held across the state’s four largest counties – home to Cleveland, Columbus, Cincinnati and Akron. In the fifth of precincts where Levy was strongest, the Republican share fell 5.9 points, more than double the 2.6 point drop where Levy’s results were lowest. Across the 2,270 precincts compared, Brown’s gain relative to 2024 held steady regardless.

Levy’s support came from working-class communities of all types – all the places this political system has left out. In the state’s four largest counties, his support in the lowest turnout precincts was more than triple his share in the highest-turnout precincts. Turnout in these counties directly corresponds to the dynamics of income and race. Statewide too, Greg ran strongest in Ohio’s lower income counties and lowest in its wealthiest. This indicates the campaign more likely brought working-class people into the political process, who would otherwise have stayed home, more than it “stole” any candidate’s votes. The campaign had a class appeal that defied the “red-blue” divide.

Both capitalist parties have betrayed and overlooked the very communities and constituencies they take for granted, and this is where a proudly socialist message found its strongest support. It resonated with working-class and poor people fed up with both ruling class parties, and the growing base of voters who no longer see a future tied to capitalism or its parties. That is the base this campaign set out to reach from the start. It’s also why both ruling class parties sought to discredit and smear the campaign – because to them, demonizing a campaign is easier than offering a program that meets the scale and urgency of the problems facing the working class. These parties spent hundreds of millions of dollars on attack ads, a new record for the state, rather than a positive platform.

This line isn’t new. Establishment politicians, party pundits , and corporate media echo this line every election cycle to shut down third-party candidates before a single vote is cast. It rests on a series of false assumptions — as if people’s votes are owned by one party or another, don’t have to be earned, and are directly transferable. But it’s a lie that has been repeated so often, it has been accepted as “common sense.” It’s no wonder 6 in 10 Americans worry a third-party vote would be “wasted,” or could “help elect the candidate they like least,” despite 62% saying a third-party is needed .

Levy’s campaign set out to challenge the system entirely, and promote a long-term vision of reorganizing society — a new socialist reconstruction. Working people face endless war, mass deportations, crippling debt, and wages that don’t cover rent and child care. Neither party offers answers to these problems, because they answer to the same entities that produce them and benefit from them. The Democrats’ structural inability to deliver, despite their lofty promises each election cycle, is what has opened the door to far-right reaction.

To end this cycle, Levy’s campaign spoke to the fundamental questions of who holds power and what a socialist transformation can look like. The “spoiler” charge only serves to scare people from running independently and telling the truth. Roughly 95,000 Ohioans voted to show their agreement that the work to break this cycle has to start somewhere.

Two decades prior to the abolition of slavery, the country’s first antislavery party faced the same charge. Abolitionists founded the Liberty Party to break with the two parties that both answered to the slaveholders. The 1844 election laid this bare. The Democrat, James Polk, supported the immediate annexation of Texas as a slave state. The Whig, Henry Clay, owned slaves himself and waffled on the question of annexation. Liberty Party voters refused to pick the lesser evil, so they ran their own candidate. When Polk narrowly carried New York, and with it, the presidency, Liberty Party voters were blamed, and even accused of giving slavery a new “life lease.” But their answer was simple – if you want antislavery votes, run antislavery candidates. The Liberty Party’s influence far outlived that moment. By refusing to choose between the least guilty of two slaveholders, they helped force the question of slavery into the center of American electoral politics. The party’s platform and leaders, including Ohio’s own Salmon P. Chase, served as the foundation for the radical Republican coalition that then came along and broke the duopoly of its time.

Today, the “spoiler” charge still serves the same function: to normalize the system as it exists, and to protect the ruling class. It tells people to be governed by fear, and tells parties with radically different ideas to take themselves out of the fight before it even starts. The PSL’s Levy campaign showed a different path: a campaign that stands on principle, and puts forward real solutions, can resonate with workers of all types, and everywhere, including in places the mainstream media says socialists can never reach.

The Party for Socialism and Liberation is comprised of leaders and activists, workers and students, of all backgrounds. Organized in branches across the country, our mission is to link the everyday struggles of oppressed and exploited people to the fight for a new world. Interested in joining? Click here!

scraped.h1: New Socialist Roundtable: From the polls to the streets!
scraped.body_text:
Socialist candidates Andre Easton, Greg Levy and Joe Tache join Karina Garcia to discuss the road ahead after tens of millions handed a crushing defeat to Donald Trump and the Republican Party this midterm season.

While voters sought to punish the right wing and its billionaire agenda, they were also dreaming of peace, justice and good jobs — a dream that the capitalist system will not deliver. With the Democratic Party claiming victory, workers are left to wonder how we can win the promises made and the rights we deserve.

Tune in for this discussion in which Andre, Greg, Joe and Karina discuss how Election Day was never really the finish line — we must take the fight from the polls to the streets!

scraped.h1: Solidarity Statement with the South African Communist Party (SACP)
scraped.body_text:
The Party for Socialism and Liberation (PSL) congratulates and extends revolutionary greetings to the South African Communist Party (SACP) for its historic electoral gains.

In South Africa’s November 4 municipal elections, the SACP ran independently of the African National Congress (ANC) for the first time since the country’s first democratic elections in 1994. According to the final vote tally released on Sunday, November 8, the SACP won 271 seats in a hard-fought campaign.

The SACP’s bold decision to run independently, after more than thirty years of ANC-led rule and decades of concessions to capital that have only deepened the impoverishment of the Black majority and working class, has given momentum to the class struggle in South Africa. The SACP has rightly asserted that eradicating racial apartheid requires material transformation, and that such transformation is possible only when economic power is wrested from private capital and corporate power and placed in the hands of the working class and Black majority.

The SACP’s May “Conference of the Left” was a crucial step toward strengthening a left pole in South Africa and building a working-class movement capable of fighting both at the ballot box and in the streets for full emancipation.

Onward to victory, comrades!

scraped.title: Hakim Adi’s “Pan-Africanism and Communism”: A pro-Stalinist attempt to erase the Trotskyist alternative — Part Ten
scraped.description: This is the tenth part of an 11-part series reviewing British historian Hakim Adi’s book on the Communist International and Africa. It examines how the book erases Leon Trotsky’s role in founding the International and his theory of Permanent Revolution.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
[ Part One ] [ Part Two ] [ Part Three ] [ Part Four ] [ Part Five ] [ Part Six ] [ Part Seven ] [ Part Eight ] [ Part Nine ] [ Part Ten ] This is the tenth part of an 11-part series responding to British-based historian Hakim Adi’s recently republished book, Pan-Africanism and Communism: The Communist International, Africa, and the Diaspora, 1919–1939.

The most sickening feature of Adi’s book is his defence of the Moscow Trials and the Great Purges. This fact alone establishes Adi’s book as an exercise in crude Stalinist apologetics and historical falsification. Responding to unnamed critics who questioned his failure to address Stalinist repression in his first edition, Adi states in the introduction to the second edition:

Other reviewers lamented the fact that I did not say more about what they termed “Stalinist repression,”[!] events that occurred within the Soviet Union during the 1930s. The fact [is] there is much new literature on that period, some of it appearing in Russia, for those who are interested in such matters. With the rise of fascism internationally and the attempts of the imperialist systems states, headed by Britain and the United States, to encourage and direct this against the Soviet Union, as well as anti-government conspiracies and terrorism internally, it cannot be considered surprising that policing activities increased in the Soviet Union during this period. It is also well known that this situation was exploited by unscrupulous people, including very senior people, many of whom were later themselves arrested and made to answer for their crimes. In those tragic circumstances many innocent people as well as guilty ones lost their lives, including two members of the South African Communist Party who were of Latvian origin. [ 1 ]

This is a revolting falsification of history. Decades of historical scholarship have exposed the frame-ups, the manufactured Show Trials, and the systematic use of torture and mass executions which led to the physical annihilation of an entire generation of revolutionary Marxists. Nearly one million people were killed in this wave of counterrevolutionary violence.

As historian Vadim Rogovin established in Stalin’s Terror of 1937–1938: Political Genocide in the USSR , the repression was not indiscriminate. It was a politically directed campaign to exterminate socialist opposition to the Stalinist bureaucracy and destroy the generation that embodied the revolutionary traditions of October 1917. It dealt a devastating blow to the revolutionary consciousness of the Soviet and international working class, whose consequences have reverberated for generations.

Between 1936 and 1938, the Stalinist regime staged three public Moscow Trials in which much of the surviving leadership of the October Revolution faced outlandish accusations of terrorism, sabotage, espionage and collaboration with Nazi Germany and imperial Japan. At the first trial, in August 1936, all sixteen defendants were sentenced to death, including Grigory Zinoviev, introduced earlier by Adi as the first president of the Communist International. In the third trial, in March 1938, Bukharin—who also occupies an important place in Adi’s account, especially in the development of the Comintern’s policy towards South Africa—was also condemned and executed.

The Moscow Trials’ central target was Leon Trotsky. Although in exile, Trotsky was the principal accused, charged in absentia with organising a vast conspiracy of terrorism, sabotage and espionage against the Soviet Union. The trials and the campaign surrounding them also prepared the ground for Trotsky’s own assassination. On August 21, 1940, Trotsky was killed by Ramón Mercader, an agent of Stalin’s secret police. The murder was the most consequential political assassination of the 20th century.

Countless leading figures in the Comintern, the organisation that Adi’s book purports to examine, were killed in the Stalinist purges. Yet Adi passes over these events, falsely implying that Stalinist repression was limited to the Soviet Union.

Rogovin has documented how Stalin’s repression was directed “With no less fury … against revolutionary emigrants, members of the international communist movement.” He explains that “in the mid-1930s, several tens of thousands of foreign communists were living in the Soviet Union.” Some worked in the Comintern, Profintern and Communist Youth International, while others worked in Soviet institutions. Many non-party émigrés were granted asylum because they had been persecuted for defending workers, scientific activity, or participation in national-liberation struggles. He estimated that 80 percent of these people were repressed during the Great Purge. He notes that among the first arrested were founders of foreign Communist parties, participants in the early Comintern congresses, and former members of the left wing of the Second International. [ 2 ]

The scale of destruction wreaked on the Comintern was staggering. Approximately 4,600 German Communist political émigrés were living in the Soviet Union; around 3,000 disappeared during the terror, and by April 1938 some 70 percent of the German Communists in the USSR had been imprisoned. Twenty-five of the 26 leading Polish Comintern cadres in the Soviet Union died. Around 800 Yugoslav Communists were murdered. Hundreds of Austrian and Bulgarian Communists perished, while refugees and political émigrés from Greece, Italy, Hungary, the Baltic states and elsewhere were subjected to arrest, imprisonment and execution. The Comintern staff itself was reduced by approximately half, while more than 40 percent of a studied group of 375 leading Comintern cadres present in the USSR from 1936 onward were arrested. [ 3 ]

Among the victims was Osip Piatnitsky, one of the most important officials of the Communist International during the 1920s and early 1930s. Piatnitsky opposed the mass repression. He was arrested by the NKVD in October 1937, imprisoned for a year, summarily condemned and executed on October 30, 1938. Adi repeatedly cites Piatnitsky and describes his activities, but omits any reference to his horrible fate.

Leon Trotsky (1879-1940), was the co-leader of the 1917 Russian Revolution, socialist opponent of Joseph Stalin, founder of the Fourth International, and strategist of world socialist revolution.

The terror also struck directly at figures involved in the anti-colonial movement. Virendranath Chattopadhyaya, the Indian revolutionary and former secretary of the League Against Imperialism—an organisation to which Adi devotes extensive attention—was arrested and shot in 1937. Two other Indian revolutionaries who had made their way to the Soviet Union were likewise executed. [ 4 ]

For African and African American revolutionaries, Stalinist repression was anything but distant. The fate of Albert Nzula is particularly significant. Nzula was the first black general secretary of the Communist Party of South Africa and one of the most important African Communists of his generation. After arriving in Moscow in 1931, he worked in the orbit of the Comintern and Profintern, contributed to The Negro Worker and collaborated with Soviet Africanists on Forced Labour in Colonial Africa (1932).

His experience in the Soviet Union brought him into conflict with the Stalinist bureaucracy. Edwin Mofutsanyana, the veteran black South African Communist who was in Moscow with him, later recalled that Nzula expressed “Trotskyite and anti-Stalinist sentiments” and had questioned Stalin’s leadership. Comintern officials subjected him to disciplinary proceedings and decided he should not be allowed to return to South Africa because they feared he might “infect” the party with his political views.

Nzula died in Moscow in January 1934, before the Moscow Trials and before the Great Terror reached its height. Adi accepts the official explanation offered by Stalinist officials, remarking that Nzula “remained in Moscow until his death in 1934”. [ 5 ] In an accompanying footnote , he states that “Nzula suffered from alcoholism, which was a major contributory factor to his death of pneumonia.” [ 6 ]

Adi conceals the political controversy surrounding Nzula’s death. CLR James later reported, based on information attributed to Jomo Kenyatta, who was in Moscow at the time, that Soviet security officials had seized Nzula. George Padmore told South African then-Trotskyist Charlie van Gelderen that, shortly before Padmore’s own break with the Communist movement, Nzula had warned him not to come to Moscow. Paul Trewhela, a former South African Communist Party member, subsequently drew attention to these accounts and to the evidence of Nzula’s growing hostility toward Stalinism. [ 7 ]

The fate of one of the most important figures in African Communism is stripped of its political significance, with Adi taking it upon himself to shield the Stalinist bureaucracy from any scrutiny.

The fate of the African American Communist Lovett Fort-Whiteman is less ambiguous. Fort-Whiteman was a pioneer of Communist work among black workers in the US, helped establish the American Negro Labor Congress, participated in the Comintern and later lived in the Soviet Union. When the repression intensified, he tried to leave the USSR. But he was arrested in 1937, exiled and subsequently sentenced to forced labour in Kolyma, where the brutal conditions of imprisonment led to his death in January 1939.

Internal Communist documents denounced Fort-Whiteman for alleged Trotskyism. One mid-1930s report stated that he had “showed himself for Trotsky,” while in 1938, CPUSA Comintern representative Pat Toohey declared, “Whiteman is a Trotskyist.”

While Adi’s book heavily draws upon the life of Fort-Whiteman—he is cited more frequently than Trotsky and Stalin combined—he reduces the fate of this African American Communist to a single footnote: “Fort-Whiteman died in prison in the Soviet Union in 1939.” [ 8 ]

The mass purges extended directly into the Communist Party of South Africa. Lazar Bach and the brothers Paul and Maurice Richter were caught in the terror after travelling to the Soviet Union. The Richter brothers were executed in 1938, while Bach was imprisoned and died in a Soviet camp in 1941. More than fifty years later, at its Seventh Congress in 1989, the SACP posthumously reinstated all three after receiving information from the Soviet Communist Party that they had been convicted on the basis of “false evidence extracted from them by the Soviet security authorities.” [ 9 ]

For Africa, the terror’s consequences went far beyond the destruction of individual revolutionaries. Stalinist repression tore apart the institutional apparatus through which the Comintern had attempted to study Africa and educate African cadres to provide revolutionary leadership.

The African Department of the Communist University of the Toilers of the East and the African section of the Research Association for the Study of National and Colonial Problems were abolished in 1936–37. Georgy Danilov, a pioneer of African linguistic studies in Moscow, was expelled from the Communist Party on accusations of “Trotskyite propaganda,” arrested and shot in 1937. A. Z. Zusmanovich, who had collaborated with Nzula on Forced Labour in Colonial Africa (1932), was removed from his work, while I. I. Potekhin was also dismissed. Research on Africa in Moscow was effectively shattered.

A study by historians Hilary Lynd and Thom Loyd noted that, “Amid escalating terror, Soviet interest in Africa and the diaspora largely disappeared. Soviet Africanists and Comintern officials who had been interested in Africa faced repression because of their contacts with foreigners. Many were sent to camps; some perished there.” [ 10 ]

Stalinist counterrevolutionary violence also extended to the Caribbean. Sandalio Junco was an Afro-Cuban communist, a leading trade unionist, and the Cuban representative in the ITUCNW’s early work. Adi records Junco’s prominent intervention on the “Negro Question” at the founding congress of the Confederación Sindical Latinoamericana, his role liaising between the ITUCNW and the Latin American trade-union movement, and his appointment as vice-chair of the RILU Negro Bureau with responsibility for Latin America and the Francophone Caribbean. He acknowledges in a footnote that Junco later became “one of the leaders of Trotskyism in Cuba” and was expelled from the Cuban Communist Party after returning to the island in 1932.

But Adi refuses to explain that Junco was assassinated by Stalinist gunmen on May 8, 1942, at a meeting in Sancti Spíritus commemorating the revolutionary Antonio Guiteras. Armed Communist Party militants stormed the gathering and opened fire, killing Junco and two others. Junco’s assassination effectively decapitated the Trotskyist movement in Cuba, depriving the Caribbean of one of its most experienced revolutionary leaders. This weakened the revolutionary Marxist opposition in Cuba, with profound implications for the subsequent development of the island’s socialist movement, paving the way for the Stalinist alliance with Cuban petty-bourgeois guerrilla forces led by Fidel Castro that would emerge in the Cuban Revolution in 1959.

Perhaps the most repugnant aspect of Adi’s defence of the Moscow Trials and the Great Purges is his concluding recommendation: “There is much academic literature on the subject from historians such as J. Arch Getty and Grover Furr.” [ 11 ]

Furr is not a historian but a notorious Stalinist apologist whose writings are devoted to rehabilitating Stalin and vindicating the fraudulent Moscow Trials. Over the past 15 years, Furr has produced an extraordinary volume of Stalinist apologetics, publishing some 18 books, including Khrushchev Lied (2011), Trotsky’s Amalgams: Trotsky’s Lies, the Moscow Trials as Evidence, the Dewey Commission , Volume One (2015), Yezhov vs. Stalin (2016), Leon Trotsky’s Collaboration with Germany and Japan (2017), The Fraud of the Dewey Commission (2018), The Moscow Trials as Evidence (2018), Stalin: Waiting for ... the Truth! (2019), Trotsky’s Lies (2019), New Evidence of Trotsky’s Conspiracy (2020), Trotsky and the Military Conspiracy (2021), The Fraud of the Testament of Lenin (2022), Trotsky’s Comintern Conspiracy: The Case of Osip Pyatnitsky (2024), and Khristian Rakovsky: Trotsky’s Japanese Spy (2025). The depths of this scoundrel’s defence of Stalin are exposed in his declaration:

There is not now, nor has there ever been, any evidence that the Moscow Trials were dishonest – staged or fabricated. On the contrary: we have a great deal of evidence that they were honest, and that the defendants were guilty of at least the crimes to which they confessed. [ 12 ]

Adi’s recommendation of Grover Furr says far more about Adi’s own political outlook than it does about Furr himself. To recommend Furr as an authority on the Moscow Trials is an intellectual disgrace, comparable to directing students studying the Holocaust to the writings of David Irving, the notorious Holocaust denier.

Adi compounds this by placing Furr alongside J. Arch Getty, an established academic historian whose interpretations of Stalinism are themselves open to criticism but whose archival scholarship cannot be equated with Furr’s apologetics. This juxtaposition brazenly frames Furr’s views as part of a legitimate historical debate.

The consequences of the Stalinist terror for the future struggles of the African masses would be far-reaching. At precisely the moment when a young African proletariat was beginning to emerge and African and African American revolutionaries were being drawn toward Marxism by the immense authority of the October Revolution, Stalinism destroyed the cadres, institutions, and intellectual connections through which the revolutionary experiences of October might have been transmitted to them. Stalinism erased an entire line of political continuity.

One cannot understand the subsequent dominance of bourgeois nationalist movements and leaders in the post-war anti-colonial struggles without reckoning with the Stalinist counterrevolutionary terror. It does not lie outside the subject of a history of the Comintern on the “Negro Question”. It is central to it.

To be continued.

Op cit., p. XIX.

Vadim Z. Rogovin, Stalin’s Terror of 1937–1938: Political Genocide in the USSR , trans. Frederick S. Choate (Oak Park, MI: Mehring Books, 2009), pp. 303–307.

Katja Rippert, “The Stalinist Terror in the Communist International and Its Impact,” World Socialist Web Site , September 21, 2025.

Jonathan Derrick, Africa’s ‘Agitators’: Militant Anti-Colonialism in Africa and the West , 1918–1939 (London: Hurst & Company, 2008), p. 379.

Op. cit. p. 274.

Op. cit. p. 487, footnote nº 82.

Op. cit. p. 418, footnote nº 163.

Hilary Lynd and Thom Loyd, “Histories of Color: Blackness and Africanness in the Soviet Union,” Slavic Review 81, no. 2 (Summer 2022): 394–417. Available at: https://doi.org/10.1017/slr.2022.154

scraped.title: Workers Struggles: Europe, Middle East & Africa
scraped.description: Meat industry workers in Spain in five-day stoppage joining workers’ struggles and mass youth protests sweeping Europe; protests over social conditions continue across Iran by retirees and bus drivers in Yazd; judicial workers in Ghana continue national strike over pay
scraped.body_text:
The World Socialist Web Site invites workers and other readers to contribute to this regular feature.

Workers across Spain’s meat industry began a five-day strike November 9, after a breakdown in negotiations for a new national collective agreement. The stoppages, scheduled to run until November 13, affect approximately 126,000 workers in slaughterhouses, meat-processing plants, cutting rooms and associated services.

The CCOO and UGT union members demand annual wage increases of at least 4 percent, linked to inflation, with backdated payments and guarantees that increases will not be offset against other benefits. They are demand a reduction in annual working hours, payment for their 15-minute meal break, improved paid leave and better provisions for partial retirement.

The workers say production rates are being intensified in the strenuous environments of slaughterhouse and processing plants and demand measures to curb this, along with necessary improvements in health and safety.

This is one of a growing number of strikes, including a nationwide walkout November 11 of metalworkers in Murcia, teachers, doctors and rail workers, joining mass youth demonstrations in Spain and across Europe.

Around 30 nursery workers across six children’s nurseries in Barnsley, England walked out for the day on Monday. The stoppage included a rally outside the recently closed nursery in Grimethorpe.

The GMB union members, who voted unanimously for the action, are protesting the outsourcing of the nurseries by the far-right Reform UK-led Barnsley Metropolitan Borough Council to private provider, Limetree.

While it was agreed that the transferred workers would retain their current pay and conditions, it excluded access to the Local Government Pension Scheme. Instead, they were transferred to the company’s basic statutory pension scheme, meaning lower pension payouts and the loss of Death in Service entitlement.

Further one day stoppages are planned for November 18 and 26.

UK rail workers employed by outsourcing companies Bidvest Noonan and Rail Gourmet under contract to publicly owned TransPennineExpress (TPE) are set to walk out Friday. Bidvest Noonan provides cleaning services, while Rail Gourmet provides catering services. TPE runs passenger services across the north of England.

The Rail, Maritime and Rail (RMT) union members are protesting low pay and want access to improved sick pay and pension provision.

In a separate dispute, RMT members employed by outsourcing company Gate Solutions under contract to state-owned rail company LNER are scheduled to hold a 24-hour stoppage, also on Friday. It follows a previous 24-hour stoppage October 16.

They are protesting Gate stopping paying the Real Living Wage figure to its employees, instead paying a lower rate just above the legal minimum wage. The RMT also accuses LNER of racism. The union’s research shows “ethnic minority workers are four times more likely to be on one of LNER’s outsourcing contracts than directly employed.”

LNER runs mainline east coast services between Edinburgh and London. Picket lines will be set up at sites including London King’s Cross, Doncaster, Leeds and Edinburgh.

UK train managers working for Chiltern Railways are set to walk out Thursday in an ongoing dispute over plans by the company to introduce driver only operated (DOO) trains on its new proposed East West rail route. When completed, the new route will connect Oxford and Cambridge.

The RMT members oppose the planned use of DOO trains as it would abolish the safety critical role of the managers.

The walkout will disrupt services between Stratford-upon-Avon, Leamington Spa and Birmingham Moor Street. Picket lines are planned for stations at Birmingham Moor Street, Stourbridge Junction and Banbury Station.

Around 70 workers employed at the Royal Naval Armaments Depot in Coulport, Scotland began an overtime ban Monday after rejecting an inadequate pay offer. They are employed by ABL Alliance, which comprises AWE plc, Babcock Marine and Lockheed Martin to service the UK’s nuclear submarine fleet.

The Unite union members voted by an over 98 percent majority seeking an improved pay offer. The overtime ban will be followed by a three-day stoppage from November 16.

A strike by municipal bus drivers in the Iranian city of Yazd has entered its second week. The drivers are protesting the increasing costs of tyres, batteries, engine oil and spare parts, which have risen several multiple times over the course of a year.

Sunday saw protests by Social Security retirees in Ahvaz. They gathered outside the provincial General Directorate of Social Security, calling on the government to address their deteriorating living conditions.

Retired workers held protests in Shush and Haft Tappeh over water and power outages, accusing the government of being indifferent to their plight. Retirees of the state-owned Bank Saderat also held demonstrations to protest the rapid erosion of the value of their pensions resulting from high living costs and the impact of inflation.

Decades of US sanctions and the recent naval blockade has resulted in the devastation of the Iranian economy. The threat of further military attacks by the US continues in the aftermath of the midterm elections.

Judicial workers across Ghana are continuing their indefinite nationwide strike, begun November 2, over delayed salary reviews, unpaid arrears and worsening conditions of service. The Judicial Service Staff Association of Ghana (JUSAG) and the Judicial Service Staff Association of Ghana’s Union announced on November 9 that the stoppage would continue after the government failed to respond to their latest demands.

The unions submitted revised demands on November 5, following negotiations with government officials and Judicial Service management. They said they had already made concessions to accommodate the government’s financial constraints but received no official response. JUSAG General Secretary Abdulai Yakubu described the revised proposals as the unions’ final compromise, warning that workers would remain on strike unless an acceptable agreement was reached.

The stoppage has disrupted court proceedings across Ghana, delaying hearings and access to justice. A legal rights organisation estimated that more than 2,000 people arrested since the strike began have been unable to obtain judicial decisions on bail or remand.

Hundreds of garment workers demonstrated outside the Baby Coca/Hela factory in Alexandria, Egypt on November 1–2, after its sudden closure left around 1,400 employees without jobs or wages.

Workers arriving at the factory in the Abis district of the city on November 1 found the gates locked, and were informed by security guards that the plant had permanently closed. Management gave workers no prior notice, despite assurances that production would continue.

Workers said they had not received their October wages, severance payments or the documentation needed to seek alternative employment. They also discovered that the company failed to remit social insurance contributions for around a year, despite regularly deducting payments from their salaries. The factory, previously operated by a Chinese company, had most recently been run by Sri Lanka-based Hela Apparel Holdings. Around 1,200 Hela employees and 200 Baby Coca workers were affected.

Police intervened to disperse the protests, with the Egyptian Commission for Rights and Freedoms reporting that female workers were forcibly searched and assaulted by police officers. One elderly worker reportedly collapsed and suffered convulsions. The Center for Trade Union and Workers Services demanded payment of outstanding wages and negotiations with workers’ representatives.

Thousands of workers at Festive Chicken, a subsidiary of Astral Foods, are continuing an indefinite strike begun October 29 in Gauteng and Mpumalanga in South Africa.

More than 100 workers and supporters gathered outside Astral Foods’ Olifantsfontein processing plant on Tuesday, where strikers have maintained a picket line. They are demanding a monthly wage of R13,500, medical aid benefits and safer working conditions. The strike followed a wage deadlock at the Commission for Conciliation, Mediation and Arbitration (CCMA).

On October 30, the Labour Court ruled that the workers were entitled to take part in a protected strike and barred the company from disciplining or dismissing them. Festive Chicken is part of Astral, one of South Africa’s largest poultry producers, whose products supply KFC, Nando’s, Spur and Hungry Lion. The Olifantsfontein plant is central to its operations.

Take-home wages range from R5,400 to R6,500 a month for 45-hour weeks, below the roughly R7,300 earned by farm workers on 48-hour weeks. Dikeledi Rosina Mogwenya, who has worked in the hatchery since 2003, said her workload had nearly tripled, with the number of machines per worker rising from 12 to 35, while her pay barely moved. A single worker must count 35,000 chicks a day. “The cost of living is too high,” she said, listing school fees, rent and transport.

Nomasonto Ncwane, a 10-year employee, described the contempt of management. Workers are rewarded each September with free meals, only to be told at the end of October that the company is making a loss, while managers “make millions.”

Workers also report dust causing respiratory problems and long shifts in cold rooms without adequate protective clothing or extra allowances. Lawyers for Human Rights and the Casual Workers Advice Office have helped workers contest alleged intimidation and threats of dismissal.

Workers at five state-owned tertiary institutions in Taraba State, Nigeria, began a two-week warning strike November 9 over unpaid entitlements, salary deductions and the government’s failure to implement agreed allowances. The Joint Action Committee of Tertiary Institutions announced the action following more than four months of unsuccessful negotiations with the state government.

Other grievances include withheld union dues and savings contributions, and the failure to implement the N70,000 transport relief payment for public servants.

Public sector workers in Osun State, Nigeria, began a three-day strike on November 9 over the continued withholding of statutory allocations to local government councils. The Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC) called the stoppage in support of Nigeria Union of Local Government Employees members, who have suffered financial hardship as a result of the funding dispute. The strike was scheduled to continue until midnight on November 11.

Government offices throughout the state were shut on Monday, including the state secretariat and House of Assembly in Osogbo. Local council offices were also closed, while pupils at public schools were sent home as teachers joined the walkout. The NLC said the federal and state governments had failed to respond to a seven-day ultimatum demanding the release of funds, threatening workers’ allowances, pensions, gratuities and other entitlements.

Nurses in Zimbabwe have taken strike action over inadequate salaries, reduced allowances and worsening conditions in public hospitals. Many nurses reported receiving less pay than in previous months, despite the rising cost of living. The Zimbabwe Congress of Trade Unions issued a statement on November 5, supporting the action and demanding the government urgently address workers’ grievances.

The nurses are demanding substantial salary increases, improved housing and transport allowances, and free medical treatment at public hospitals, which many say they can no longer afford. They complain that government-provided buses do not accommodate their shift patterns, leaving workers struggling to travel to work. Chronic shortages of essential medical supplies and equipment, alongside inadequate staffing levels, are further undermining patient care.

Workers at Coca-Cola Beverages in Kenya won a court ruling November 10 allowing them to take strike action over unresolved employment disputes.

The Kenya Union of Commercial, Food and Allied Workers had issued a 21-day strike notice on May 26, threatening industrial action from June 16 over collective bargaining negotiations, job evaluations, medical benefits, outsourcing and the dismissal of 56 workers.

The company, which employs more than 1,500 workers, sought a court order prohibiting the strike.

The union accused management of failing to implement the Labour Ministry’s recommendations by withholding payments owed to dismissed workers and refusing medical coverage for employees’ spouses. It also opposes outsourcing arrangements that threaten existing jobs. A union shop steward was dismissed on June 5, allegedly for trade union activities.

On November 7, Kenya’s Employment and Labour Relations Court rejected the company’s request for a blanket strike ban, ruling that it had failed to demonstrate sufficient grounds for prohibiting any industrial action.

However, the court has barred strikes over all matters covered by existing collective bargaining agreement or already before the courts. It ordered Coca-Cola to provide a payment schedule for the 56 dismissed workers and any outstanding entitlements. The union retains the right to strike over unresolved disputes, although there is no confirmation that industrial action has begun.

scraped.body_text:
This examination and exposure of the inveterate opportunism of Savas Michael-Matsas, was originally published on August 11, 1989 and appeared in Volume 16, Nos. 3-4 of the Fourth International magazine. It was written by David North in response to the split between Gerry Healy, the long-time leader of the WRP, and Michael-Matsas, the national secretary of the Workers Internationalist League in Greece.

Michael-Matsas had previously supported Healy in 1985, defending his opportunist politics and betrayal of Trotskyism. He broke with the ICFI, refusing all discussion with other sections. He asserted that they had no authority to even meet without the permission of Healy. In 1989 Healy and Michael-Matsas came into conflict over tactical issues relating to their opportunist agendas, which led to a sudden and bitter collapse of their unprincipled collaboration.

Healy died five months later, on December 14, 1989. For a Marxist analysis of Healy's political career, see Gerry Healy and His Place in the History of the Fourth International by David North.

***

The split between Gerry Healy and Savas Michael brings to a shabby and pathetic end the squalid partnership of two opportunist renegades from Trotskyism and lackeys of the Soviet Stalinist bureaucracy.

In October 1985, Healy found in Savas Michael, who was then secretary of the Greek section of the International Committee of the Fourth International, the one man so devoid of political principles and personal integrity that he was prepared to justify and even eulogize the depraved practices and gross abuse of authority that had led to Healy’s expulsion from the Trotskyist movement. Michael lied to his own members about the circumstances of Healy’s expulsion, refused to permit the distribution of the documents of the International Committee, and split his organization from the ICFI. Finally, he sought to defraud the workers’ movement in Greece by presenting himself as the secretary of a bogus “International Committee.”

This entire miserable enterprise has come to the end it deserved. The self-styled secretary of the “ICFI” has been abandoned by Healy. Though he claims to have had the support of the majority of the party’s leadership, Michael has been tossed out of the premises of the Greek Workers Revolutionary Party and his name, without even the dignity of an official announcement, no longer appears in its press.

In a mimeographed English-language statement, dated July 1, 1989, the central committee of Michael’s faction of the Greek Workers Revolutionary Party gives the following account of the split (which, except for corrections in the spelling, is reproduced exactly as written):

“The Workers Revolutionary Party of Greece, affiliated until recently to the ‘ICFI’ led by G. Healy, became the target of a vicious attack and of the split activities of G. Healy himself and his tiny clique:

“Healy, presenting himself as more Gorbachevite than Gorbachev himself—in matter of fact he is well on the right of the Gorbachev group—tried to impose on the WRP, his pro-Stalinist line, forbidding any criticism to the policies of the official leadership of the CPSU. The WRP, although supporting Perestroika and Glasnost in the USSR, had and has a critical attitude, fighting for the independent Trotskyist analysis, programme and leadership of the developing political revolution.

“G. Healy clashed with the WRP, in November 1987, when S. Michael, the general secretary of the WRP, with the support of the Greek Trotskyist leadership, issued an ‘Open Letter to M. Gorbachev’ sharply criticizing the attacks on Trotsky and the historical truth incorporated in the official speech of the 70th anniversary of the October Revolution.

“This ‘Letter’ was, for Healy, an ‘unforgivable crime,’ as well as the support given by the WRP to Boris Yeltsin against his bureaucratic purge, which took place at the same period. Healy, not only accused Yeltsin for ‘ultra-leftism’ and openly supported his Stalinist opponent, Ligachev, but tried also to silence, with bureaucratic means, the criticisms of the WRP and S. Michael.

“As G. Healy himself said, from November 1987 he started to organize a split in the WRP through a secret tiny faction of supporters. As he could not have a majority in the elected leadership, Healy intervened, using all the cominternist methods to change the composition of the PC and the CC of the WRP, expelling elected members who politically disagree with his line and his unconstitutional actions.

“In a 2 days time, an ‘emergency congress’ of the Greek section was called by Healy and his ‘IC’—against all the rules of the constitution of the WRP and of the FI—in April 1-2, 1989. An orgy of bureaucratic purge escalated from the so-called ‘congress’ onwards continued afterwards with a campaign of expulsions, slanders and intimidation.

“The WRP was split by the actions of Healy. But the continuity of Trotskyism was not destroyed: the majority of the party leaders, cadres and members and all the youth organization the Young Socialists, fought back the liquidationist attack and defended the principles of Trotskyism against the pro-Stalinist revisionists.

“The WRP had its constitutionally held emergency congress in June 11th 1989, broke irrevocably with the revisionism developed by Healy in his decay, defended all the revolutionary heritage of Trotskyism, including the heritage of the first 10 congresses of the ICFI, and decided to fight, in the road of the world socialist revolution to build the Fourth International.”

Even if one were to accept this account of the split between Healy’s “Marxist Party” in Britain and the Greek Workers Revolutionary Party, it represents a devastating self-indictment of the unprincipled political activities of Savas Michael over the last four years.

It is the height of political cynicism for Michael to complain that the Greek WRP has been the victim of the unconstitutional activities of Gerry Healy. When Savas Michael split from the International Committee in October 1985, he did so in order to defend the personal and unchallengeable right of Healy to do whatever he pleased!

Michael refused to attend a duly-constituted emergency meeting of the ICFI, which had been called following the expulsion of Healy from the British Workers Revolutionary Party on October 19, 1985. The WRP Central Committee took this action on the basis of evidence that Healy had engaged systematically in the sexual abuse of female party members, many of whom were underage.

The ICFI scheduled a meeting for October 25, 1985. It recognized that the gross abuse of authority of which Healy was accused was inextricably linked to the opportunist degeneration in the political line and organizational methods of the British WRP over an extended period. This crisis had developed to such a point that the WRP leadership was on the verge of a devastating split and the entire organization threatened with a political collapse.

For this reason, the International Committee insisted that it intended to examine the evidence relating to the allegations against Healy and also to analyze the political issues underlying the crisis inside the Workers Revolutionary Party.

Michael, however, proclaimed that Healy was a “historic leader” with unchallengeable authority and who, therefore, was not subject to any constitutional procedures either within the WRP or the International Committee. He asserted that the WRP Central Committee did not have the power to expel Healy and that the International Committee could not hold a meeting unless it had been personally summoned and sanctioned by Healy!

The International Committee rejected this reactionary position, which had nothing to do with constitutional procedures based on the organizational principles of democratic centralism. It informed the Greek section that Michael could, as a delegate to the ICFI, oppose the expulsion of Healy and attempt to win the international movement over to his position. But, it insisted, Michael and the Greek Workers Internationalist League (as the organization was then known) could not defy the political discipline of the International Committee on the preposterous ground that Healy was some sort of Stalin-style infallible “historic leader.”

Michael ignored the instructions of the International Committee, the highest body within the Fourth International. Instead, Michael entered into a behind-the-scenes conspiracy with Healy and his supporters in a minority faction of the WRP headed by Sheila Torrance. He also established contact with the representative of the Spanish section of the ICFI, urged her to boycott the ICFI meeting, and then issued a “joint communiqué” rejecting the authority of the International Committee.

The International Committee meeting was held on October 25, 1985 as scheduled. Its delegates voted unanimously in favor of the expulsion of Healy based on irrefutable and uncontested evidence which confirmed the charges against him. At the same time—despite fierce opposition from the leaders of the WRP majority faction, Cliff Slaughter and Michael Banda—the ICFI adopted a procedure to resolve the crisis within the WRP on the basis of an exhaustive discussion of all issues of political perspective and program. This procedure required scrupulous respect for the rights of the pro-Healy minority faction led by Torrance.

The Torrance faction immediately rejected the independent intervention of the International Committee and officially split from the ICFI on the morning of October 26, 1985. They were case-hardened nationalists who believed that the ICFI had no business “interfering” in disputes inside the British WRP.

But it was the intervention of Savas Michael that provided them with a bogus “international” cover for their reactionary split from the International Committee. Moreover, Michael’s action rescued Healy and provided him with a new international forum for his opportunist activities. Without Michael’s defense of Healy’s supra-constitutional powers in 1985, this so-called historic leader would not have been in a position to organize inside the Greek WRP what Michael now denounces as an “orgy” of “expulsions, slanders and intimidation.”

Indeed, the International Committee foresaw the inevitable results of Michael’s unprincipled maneuvers and issued a clear warning to the Greek Workers Internationalist League. In a letter dated November 9, 1985, the International Committee told the Greek section that its rejection of international collaboration and discipline meant that “the WIL faces destruction as a Trotskyist party.” Noting that the WIL had disregarded the ICFI’s advice that it postpone its plan to “transform” itself into a mass-type revolutionary party pending the political clarification of the issues arising from the crisis inside the British WRP and the International Committee, the letter stated:

“Comrade Savas and the CC [of the WIL] know that there are gigantic destructive dangers in founding a party on the unprincipled foundation of a break with internationalism. The very best interpretation which can be placed on Comrade Savas and the Greek CC’s break from the IC is that they fear disruption of their work for the transformation into a party. Such a position, politically, means that internationalism, the foundation of our movement in every country, is rejected in favor of immediate national concerns as perceived by the WIL leadership.”

Not only did this letter anticipate the eventual collapse of Michael’s new “revolutionary party.” The ICFI was entirely correct in its evaluation of the nationalist opportunism which underlay Michael’s unprincipled support for Healy. He and his right-wing associates in the WIL anticipated that their split with the International Committee would liberate their activities in Greece from all international Marxist supervision. The new Greek Workers Revolutionary Party—as the organization was renamed in late November 1985—would be free to do whatever it liked in Greece.

Michael immediately hailed the split as an opportunity to repudiate all the fundamental political conceptions of the Fourth International. He denounced the International Committee’s uncompromising defense of the Marxist program as “the reactionary return to the practices of the period of the defeats and isolation of Trotskyism.” In opposition to the International Committee, which, due to its obsession with principles, “wanted to confine Trotskyism to small sects,” Michael discovered in unrestrained opportunism a new political panacea.

Thus, as soon as the split was consummated, the Greek Workers Revolutionary Party turned to popular front politics. Its work within Greece became centered on working out electoral alliances with the Greek Stalinists and various petty-bourgeois “progressive” forces. In municipal elections held in Piraeus in 1986, the WRP entered into discussions with the Stalinists and several small bourgeois parties with the aim of forming a political bloc. It attempted to justify its capitulation to popular frontism by proclaiming that “a broad collaboration of the progressive and left forces of Piraeus can become the key which will give to our municipality a capable and fighting municipal authority, which together with the people of Piraeus will struggle for a new political agreement for the people’s interest.”

Little more than one year later, the transformation of the WRP into an open agency of class collaborationist politics had reached the stage where it supported the election of the bourgeois politician Vassiliou to the presidency of Cyprus.

One does not know whether to laugh or retch upon reading Michael’s claim that Healy “tried to impose on the WRP his Stalinist line.” This absurd attempt to portray himself as the innocent victim of Healy’s political chicanery is contradicted by Michael’s own account of his relations with the “historic leader.” In another document, dated May-June 1989 and published in a magazine called Revolutionary Marxist Theory, Michael makes clear that he collaborated fully with Healy in the elaboration of their pro-Gorbachev line.

“In the summer of 1986, after the Congress of Soviet Cinematographers and the Soviet Writers’ Congress and after the speech of Gorbachev at Khabarovsk, at the same time G. Healy and S. Michael—who then and until 1987 collaborated closely and fruitfully, being in nearly daily telephone communication—reached the same conclusion that the turn to perestroika meant a leap in the political revolution against the Stalinist bureaucracy in the Soviet Union.”

On the basis of this Pabloite adaptation to the “reform wing” of the Stalinist bureaucracy, Michael gave full backing to Healy in the ensuing fight inside the Healy-Torrance faction of the British WRP. In opposition to Torrance, who objected to Healy’s support for Gorbachev, Michael wrote a “joint communiqué,” signed by Healy and himself on November 4,1986, which asserted, “The Trotskyist movement is not indifferent or neutral towards the changes in the Soviet Union. It must urgently and actively intervene into them supporting with a united front action every blow against the bureaucracy....”

Michael went along entirely with the pro-Gorbachev line worked out by Healy. From 1987 on, Socialist Change , the newspaper of the WRP, became the local Athens house-organ of the Gorbachev bureaucracy. There is ample reason to believe that Michael’s services to the Gorbachev regime were financially rewarded. Similar propaganda services rendered by Socialist Change to Middle Eastern regimes and bourgeois national movements had previously been offered by Michael in exchange for special subsidies of which the rank- and-file members were not informed. Indeed, in one of his own documents, Healy noted in passing that Michael “has close contact with the Libyans, the Soviet Embassy, the CP and the PLO. ”

At any rate, Michael became a specialist in providing cynical rationalizations for the counterrevolutionary politics of the Kremlin bureaucracy, as witnessed by his rapturous praise for the Soviet-US agreement on missiles in September 1987, in which he compared Gorbachev’s dealings with Reagan to the revolutionary diplomacy carried out by the Bolsheviks in the early years of the Soviet regime!

On the question of the economic policies of perestroika— whose essential aim is the restoration of capitalist property in the Soviet Union and its integration into the structure of world imperialism—Michael was, and remains, in agreement with the Gorbachev regime.

However, and this is where he apparently ran afoul of Healy, Michael insisted, though not too vigorously, on his right to occasionally criticize Gorbachev. To a great extent, this position arose from Michael’s need to maintain some small political justification for the continued existence of his petty-bourgeois group outside the ranks of the Greek Communist Party. However, this was not acceptable to Healy, who made it clear that he saw no need for the continued existence of Michael’s organization. At the third congress of the Greek WRP, according to Michael, “The greatest confusion was provoked as the membership of the WRP, thunderstruck, heard the historic leader of postwar Trotskyism, Gerry Healy, tell them that for the sake of the political revolution in the USSR, with a turn to the membership of the Communist Party of Greece and a United Front with it, the road was open for ‘a unified CP on a Trotskyist basis.’” ( Revolutionary Marxist Theory )

Once Healy arrived at this conclusion, he proceeded to organize the removal of Savas Michael and his supporters from the Workers Revolutionary Party.

The documents of the split provide further illustration of the grotesque character of Healy’s degeneration. He now operates as nothing more than a paid stooge of the Moscow bureaucracy. In October 1988, with the full support of Savas Michael, Healy’s bogus “International Committee’’ announced it was forming a united front with the Memorial Union in the USSR, an organization of a faction of the bureaucracy, including physicist Andrei Sakharov and academician Yuri Afanasyev, which explicitly supports the restoration of capitalism. A photograph of Healy and Vanessa Redgrave meeting with leaders of Memorial in the editorial offices of the Moscow News was prominently displayed in the April 1 issue of Socialist Change.

Like Healy’s previous “united fronts” with the Palestine Liberation Organization and the governments of Libya and Iraq, this one consists of providing “Trotskyist” support for a counterrevolutionary regime in exchange for money. The Soviet bureaucracy, whose intelligence agencies are intimately familiar with the circumstances surrounding the catastrophe which overtook Healy in 1985, know how easy it is to use and manipulate a man in his desperate political straits. Pathetically dependent upon the good graces of his Kremlin patrons and working under the supervision of whoever the KGB has assigned to “handle” him, Healy became frightened that Michael’s “unauthorized” letter to Gorbachev—which contained criticisms of the Soviet leader’s televised denunciation of Leon Trotsky on November 2, 1987—might undermine his “united front” with the Soviet government. He came to the conclusion that it was necessary to disband this organization.

First, he informed Michael that while his criticisms were correct, “the content was historically an error” and the letter should not have been sent because Gorbachev’s speech had also announced the Politburo’s decision to investigate Stalin’s crimes. While Michael submitted to Healy’s criticism, a new pretext was soon found to resume the offensive against the Greek WRP. Michael’s organization produced a 1989 calendar which apparently did not include a photograph of Trotsky and other martyrs of the Left Opposition. It is likely that Michael was simply trying to adapt himself to what he thought Healy wanted; for Vanessa Redgrave—Healy’s principal accomplice—regularly gives interviews in the Soviet press without mentioning the name of Leon Trotsky.

However, Healy pounced on Michael, intoning, “The calendar presented the forms of appearance which the political revolution takes without their historical content. Thus, it represented a continuation of the political error which took place in connection with the speech of November 2, 1987 by Gorbachev, on the 70th anniversary of the October Revolution. There was an attack on its form, a criticism against Trotsky, Bukharin and others, while the historical content, the [formation] by Gorbachev of a Committee of Investigation for the examination of the crimes of Stalin, was ignored.”

When Michael, at long last, refused to quietly accept the removal of all his supporters from the central committee and make the necessary “self-criticism,” Healy resorted to his special mystical language to explain the gravity of the issue:

“A leader who refuses to base his political analysis on the Thing-in-itself, counterposes to dialectical materialism self-constructed images which are a determinateness of his own Ego... The Egotist is incapable of correcting errors, given that he is limited only to self-constructed thought forms. Without the establishment of the ‘in-itself’ of the historical content of thought forms, it is impossible to correct errors. Without the negation of Being from the external world, where, within its unity of analysis and synthesis with historical materialism, not-Being emerges, it is not possible, for any historical content to exist. No ‘thing-in- itself’ content (not-Being) — no correction of errors. The individuals who, like Fichte, exceed their own Ego, generally speaking, turn to blaming others for the very mistakes which, in the name of the ‘excessive subject’ of their Ego, they made themselves. Egotism is the deadly enemy of the training of a collective Marxist leadership. It is the trademark of subjective idealist bourgeois ideology.”

It is not very hard to decipher this pseudophilosophical verbiage. One has only to understand that the real “thing-in-itself” with which Healy’s ego is preoccupied is his cash subsidy from Moscow.

The political outcome of Healy’s purge of Michael and his supporters from the Greek WRP has been clearly indicated by the recent change in the masthead of Socialist Change . It now carries the hammer and sickle—without the number four! This is a necessary symbolic preparation for the eventual liquidation of the WRP into the Stalinist party.

It should be noted that within weeks of the split, Socialist Change was able to complete its special fund on time, due to a sudden and miraculous last-minute infusion of three million drachma, nearly half the total of the entire fund!

Before the split of 1985, Healy’s political and personal opinion of Savas Michael was usually expressed in language which is unprintable. He spoke with contempt of Michael’s political spinelessness, indifference to principle, ignorance of history, and nationalist provincialism, and would refer with bitter sarcasm to evidence of his physical cowardice and petty-bourgeois vanity. Michael would seem to shrivel beneath the force of Healy’s withering and merciless denunciations. So brutal were Healy’s verbal onslaughts that even those on the International Committee who agreed with the gist of his criticisms could not help but feel sorry for the hapless Michael, whose eyes would grow red and watery during these terrible tirades.

That Michael and Healy would eventually emerge as allies in a common front against the International Committee would have seemed inconceivable even to an astute observer. But politics possesses an inexhaustible gift for irony; and the crisis which overtook the British Workers Revolutionary Party in 1985 brought about the unexpected reconciliation. There was, of course, a deeper logic at work. Without him being fully conscious of it, Healy’s protracted opportunist degeneration had drawn him closer to Michael over the years. In retrospect, it may well be that his often-apoplectic reaction to the mere physical presence of Michael may well have reflected Healy’s inner anxiety over what he himself was becoming.

Now that his marriage of convenience with Savas Michael has been terminated, Healy has produced a document, dated April 23, 1989, in which he recalls that Michael’s politics “contains the worst features of Greek nationalism.” He recalls that prior to the split of October 1985, Michael’s section “had to be expelled on account of a nationalist orientation .”

Despite the Greek organization’s subsequent readmission and its defense of Healy in October 1985, “bourgeois ideology remained deeply entrenched within the section.” Healy asserts, “In the objective conditions of Greek bourgeois nationalism, the number of cadres was reduced to a ‘hard core’ within which reactionary Greek bourgeois nationalism continued to develop. As the number of members fell after the founding congress of October 1985, so the nationalist orientation developed until it began to threaten the very existence of the Greek section of the ICFI.” This account is a devastating indictment of Healy. After all, how does he explain that his only international base of support in 1985 was provided by an organization based on Greek bourgeois nationalism? Of course, Healy will not attempt to answer this question.

Nor does Savas Michael help his own political cause with his account of the split. He writes the following about Healy’s organization of the split within the Greek WRP:

“The methods which they have employed to wound the party and its cadre have lacked nothing of the villainous, bankrupt and filthy methods of Stalinism: intrigues, unconstitutional dismissals of members of the Politburo on the order of Gerry Healy alone and only because they expressed differences, unconstitutional dismissals of members of the CC, splitting, the organizing of ‘congresses’ in two days in violation of the constitution and without discussion and informing members and closed to them. Slanders of the most vulgar police and Stalinist type.”

In other words, exactly the methods which Healy employed, with the full support of Savas Michael, against the International Committee.

What Michael does not attempt to explain is how his infallible “historic leader”—the peerless author of Studies in Dialectics, whose “dialectical materialist method of training” represents, in the words used by Michael in early 1986 to denounce the ICFI, “the highest creative contribution ... of Cde Gerry Healy to the world revolution”—has within such a short period of time been transformed into an out-and-out Stalinist gangster.

Michael cannot and will not answer this question because he himself shares essentially the same Pabloite perspective as Healy; and his differences with him, despite all the fighting and shouting, are essentially of a tactical character. Both Michael and Healy take as their theoretical point of departure the basic Pabloite conception that the political revolution will be realized through the initiative of one or another section of the bureaucracy.

Even as he is licking his wounds, Michael declares: “Against false charges, the CC of the WRP shows that it supports warmly and without conditions the political antibureaucratic revolution in the USSR, which is developing in the form of perestroika, while we give critical support to the leadership of Mikhail Gorbachev. We support every measure of Gorbachev which strikes against the bureaucracy and we exercise criticism of every practice or speech which delays the revolutionary process. We support the formation of a united front with the leadership of Gorbachev and much more so with the fighters of the left wing like Boris Yeltsin and the anti-Stalinist Memorial Union.”

If this is supposed to represent a break with the Stalinism of Healy, it is truly mutiny on one’s knees. In fact, to the extent that a genuine “programmatic” difference can be gleaned from this brawl between two Pabloite factions, it would appear that Michael is more openly aligned with that section of the bureaucracy—led by the Inter-Regional Group of Yeltsin, Afanasyev and Sakharov—who are emerging as the most militant procapitalist element within the Stalinist leadership. But even this difference should not be overstated, because Healy himself has already proclaimed these very individuals to be the “leaders” of the political revolution.

Less than four years after he claimed that his break from the “sectarians” of the International Committee would quickly transform the Greek WRP into a mass party, Michael now wanders around Athens without a press and without a party. Like all opportunists, he foresaw absolutely nothing. Having no understanding of the implications of the protracted struggle waged by the International Committee against Pabloite opportunism, he blindly pursued the same opportunist methods which have led so many times to political shipwreck. Michael stupidly believed that he could combine a purely platonic adherence to Trotskyism with practical support for the Stalinist bureaucracy.

Two years ago, this writer ridiculed Michael’s conception of “critical support” for Gorbachev and predicted its pathetic outcome:

“Savas Michael, dressed in a warrior’s toga, will fight alongside Gorbachev sword in hand as the Soviet leader combats the bureaucracy; but then, the moment Gorbachev and the bureaucracy attack the workers, Michael will deftly pivot to his left and hurl himself against Gorbachev. We can be sure that in the course of this complex and awkward maneuver, Savas Michael’s toga will become unraveled and this petty-bourgeois sophist will stand politically naked in front of the working class, exposed before one and all as a charlatan.” ( Fourth International, September 1987, pp. 11-12.)

And so it has come to pass.

There is one other feature of the Healy-Michael split of which we must take note. In the document of April 23, 1989, Healy makes a dark reference to the possibility of police penetration of the Greek WRP. “In a section plunging into debt to the usurers,” he writes, “the doors are wide open for the Greek state to work unhindered inside the party.” In October 1985, it was none other than Savas Michael who joined with Healy in making slanderous allegations, which they did not even attempt to substantiate in any way, that their opponents in the International Committee were police agents. How the wheel does turn!

The split between Healy and Michael is the final vindication of the struggle conducted by the International Committee of the Fourth International against all the revisionist tendencies that emerged out of the opportunist degeneration of the British Workers Revolutionary Party. Each of these tendencies refused to recognize the political authority of the International Committee, proclaimed its political demise, and, as in the case of Healy-Michael and Torrance, even went so far as to usurp the name of the ICFI for the purpose of endowing their own essentially nationalist activities with some historical legitimacy.

But in the course of less than four years, all of these opportunist formations have been politically shattered.

The WRP faction led by Cliff Slaughter, Michael Banda, and Bill Hunter has broken into approximately a dozen fragments. Michael Banda has denounced Trotskyism and proclaimed his allegiance to Stalinism. Cliff Slaughter and Bill Hunter, who following Banda’s desertion proposed to rebuild the Fourth International on the basis of an alliance with the Argentine Morenoites, came to blows over the failure of the WRP to consummate the alliance. Hunter is now the representative of the Morenoites in Britain.

The original Healy-Torrance faction of the WRP broke up within a year of the split—with Torrance preserving the name Workers Revolutionary Party, while Healy and Vanessa Redgrave formed their “Marxist Party.” Later, another leading member of the Torrance group, Richard Price, split with Torrance to form the Workers Internationalist League. And, finally, the Healy-Michael alliance has broken apart.

All of these bewildered and demoralized groups and individuals operate within a purely national framework. Not one of these organizations are related on the basis of a common program to any organization existing outside their own national boundaries. And, as with all radical petty-bourgeois organizations that operate on such a parochial foundation, their own national existence lacks all political stability.

On the other hand, the International Committee of the Fourth International has demonstrated astonishing strength and viability during this same period. Since its final split with the British WRP on February 8, 1986, the International Committee has developed an unbreakable unity between its sections. Not only have there been no splits between sections of the ICFI, not a single split has taken place within any of the ICFI sections.

This internal strength within an international movement that is active in North and South America, Europe, Asia and Australia is the expression of the profound political clarification that the International Committee has achieved on the basis of the unrelenting political, theoretical and organizational struggle it has conducted against Pabloite opportunism. This struggle is recorded in published books, articles and documents totaling thousands of pages.

The unity of the International Committee is not merely an organizational achievement. It reflects, if still only in embryonic form, the emerging political reunification of the vanguard of the international working class under the banner of Marxism. The Fourth International, under the leadership of its International Committee, is becoming the proletariat’s World Party of Socialist Revolution.

items.summary: Following an explosive political year, Minnesota Democrats dominated the midterm elections, but Minnesotans must remember that ICE was defeated by the people, not by the Democratic Party.
