scraped.title: Minnesotans Voted Blue, but Democrats Didn’t Defeat ICE - Left Voice
scraped.description: Following an explosive political year, Minnesota Democrats dominated the midterm elections, but Minnesotans must remember that ICE was defeated by the people, not by the Democratic Party. We need a party that represents the working class and our struggles, not the capitalists.
scraped.author: Charlotte White
scraped.body_text:
Following an explosive political year, Minnesota Democrats dominated the midterm elections, but Minnesotans must remember that ICE was defeated by the people, not by the Democratic Party. We need a party that represents the working class and our struggles, not the capitalists.

Charlotte White

Almost one year after Operation Metro Surge shook the Twin Cities, Minnesotans turned out to the polls in huge numbers — the state had the second-highest voter turnout in the nation behind Maine. Motivated by the cost-of-living crisis, rejection of the war in Iran, outrage at the ongoing genocide in Palestine, and their experience living through the ICE offensive of last winter, Minnesotans overwhelmingly chose Democrats over Republicans. Only in three rural farmland House districts did Republicans win their races; the Governor’s Mansion, a Senate seat, and five of the state’s eight House of Representatives seats went to Democrats.

While these results represent an enormous rejection of Trumpism, it is important for Minnesotans to remember that one of Trump’s biggest political defeats came not from the ballot box or the Democratic Party, but from the mass movement against ICE in the Twin Cities last winter. Our strength is not in which capitalist politician we elect, but in our own self-organized struggle. A blue wave won’t help us build our power and win our demands — we need a working-class party that fights for socialism.

In the Governor’s race, Democratic Senator Amy Klobuchar and Republican State Representative Lisa Demuth faced off for Tim Walz’s seat, which he announced he would leave earlier this year after a Medicare fraud scandal shook the state government. The clear frontrunner since the beginning, Klobuchar easily won the night, becoming the first woman to serve as Governor of Minnesota.

While Democrats have held the Governor’s Mansion since 2011, Klobuchar won by a larger margin than Walz ever did — he won his first election by 10 points and won re-election in 2022 by just over seven points; Klobuchar beat Demuth by over 13. Most notably, and reflective of the deep dissatisfaction with the Republican Party, Klobuchar gained more support in the rural farmlands than Democrats have in years.

Typically, Democrats win office in Minnesota based on the urban vote in Rochester, Duluth, and the Twin Cities, but Klobuchar won even typically Republican counties. Seven rural counties that voted strongly Republican in 2024 flipped parties to vote Klobuchar in this governor’s race, with some flipping by nearly 15 percentage points. Every single county in the state voted more strongly in favor of Democrats in this governor’s race than they did in the 2024 Presidential election. Voters cited the cost-of-living crisis, the war on Iran, attacks on immigrants, and “government corruption” as key issues in their vote this year, and overwhelmingly shifted away from the Republican Party as a result.

In the Senate, one seat was up for grabs, and Democrat Peggy Flanagan easily beat Republican Michele Tafoya by over 10 points. Neither candidate was incumbent as the seat was being vacated by retirement, but the seat has been strongly Democrat since 2009 and was expected to go to Flanagan. More left-leaning than Klobuchar, however, Flanagan was unable to capture the rural areas to the same extent.

Of the seven rural counties that Klobuchar flipped, Flanagan was only able to flip three, and while every county in the state voted more Democrat in the Governor’s race than they did last Presidential election, some counties actually voted more Republican in this race, with rural counties tending to favor Tafoya. Flanagan is aligned more with the progressive populist wing of the Democratic Party than the establishment wing, earning the support of Bernie Sanders early on and running with priorities like ICE abolition and an end to the genocide in Palestine — in her victory speech on Tuesday, she proudly shouted to the crowd that she plans to “rip ICE apart.”

These stances set Flanagan apart from more centrist Democrats in the state like Klobuchar and gave her less success in capturing the votes of Republican-turned-Democratic voters in rural areas. Nevertheless, she won her race and will join the senate as the first Indigenous woman to do so.

As predicted, the Democrats did best inMinnesota’s cities. The House districts around the Twin Cities went Democratic by even larger margins than in the last election. In the Second District, just south of the Twin Cities, Democrats won by 15 points, whereas the district only favored Harris in the 2024 presidential race by five points. In the Third District, northwest of the Twin Cities, they won by almost 30 points, up from Harris’s 21-point lead in 2024. Northeast of the Twin Cities, in the Fourth District, Democrats won by almost 47 points, whereas the incumbent won by around 35 points in the last election, and the district favored Harris by the same margin.

In the Fifth District, representing Minneapolis, Ilhan Omar won re-election by over 60 points. She won by just shy of 50 points last time, and the district voted for Harris by almost 62 points. Although she was not in danger of losing her seat, Omar — a progressive populist Democrat with a strong relationship to Democratic Socialists of America — has been the target of major attacks from the Trump Administration this year. A long-time Trump critic, Omar spoke strongly against Operation Metro Surge this winter, and the administration has targeted her with racist, anti-Muslim attacks in the lead-up to the midterms.

Accusing her of immigration fraud, Trump had her home raided by the FBI just a few weeks ago, a clear retaliation against her anti-Trump rhetoric and a warning to the entire state that humiliated the Trump Administration last winter. While the attacks stirred up anti-Somali racism in the rural areas, they were not enough to damage her lead, and she serve a fifth term.

Notably, in Omar’s race, independent Develle Jackson took over seven percent, not too far behind the Republican, who took 16. Jackson ran as an independent with a campaign built on self-determination for Palestine, increased taxes on the rich, free and universal healthcare, and enshrining abortion access into law. While ultimately unable to challenge Omar, his independent campaign was the most successful in Minnesota by a wide margin, and is indicative of a Twin Cities population that demands progressive politics but does not want to commit to the Democratic Party that Ilhan Omar remains within.

As more and more young people identify as independent, it is no surprise that an independent candidate would find such success amongst a politicized, anti-Trump voter base seeking alternatives to the two parties that disappointed them so deeply during the BLM Movement of 2020 and this year during Operation Metro Surge.

In the districts that stayed Republican, the margins were much less comfortable than in recent elections. In the Sixth District, incumbent Republican Tom Emmer won re-election by only 11 points, whereas in both the 2024 and 2022 elections, he won by 25 points. The district voted for Trump by almost 20 points in 2024. Even in the very strong Republican Seventh District, incumbent Michelle Fischbach kept her seat by 30 points — a huge lead to be sure, but down her previous two elections, where she won by closer to 40 points.

In the Eighth District, representing the Northeast, Republicans have historically held the seat but less comfortably, facing strong competition from Democrats in Duluth and the Boundary Waters region. The Republican incumbent Pete Stauber held his seat, but by just over six points. down from 16 in 2024 and 15 in 2022.

One race, though, is too close to call and will go to a recount: in House District 1, Democrats will very likely pull off a major upset. Incumbent Republican Brad Finstad currently trails by one-tenth of a point; less than 300 votes separate him from Democrat Jake Johnson. This is even more surprising considering Finstad won re-election in 2024 by over 17 points, and in 2022 he won by over 11 points. District 1 was not predicted to flip and no major news outlets were calling it a race to watch in the lead-up to the elections — the seat hasn’t gone to a Democrat since Tim Walz held it early in his political career.

The district favored Trump by 12 points in the 2024 Presidential race, and represents the corn and soybean farmlands of the Southern border. Although the district includes Rochester and Mankato, urban areas that tend to go Democrat, the farmlands truly decide the fate of the district, and this year the farmlands have rejected Republicans more than it has in recent history. Trump’s war with Iran has skyrocketed prices on fuel and fertilizer, and the higher cost of these farming necessities have destroyed farmers’ bottom line across the country.

The war has also exacerbated the broader cost-of-living crisis, which has hit working-class Americans hard everywhere, and rural workers are dissatisfied with Trump’s failure to address their economic needs. Losing the rural working class and farmers has spelled disaster for the Republicans this midterm, and the southernmost district in Minnesota exemplifies this. Although the race has not been certified for Johnson, he has publicly thanked his constituents for the win, and it seems unlikely that even a recount will save the Republican incumbent.

The Democrats defeated the Republicans at the polls in Minnesota, but the Far Right was defeated in Minnesota by the people who organized themselves to fight back this winter. This battle was not fought, and was not won, by any Democratic Party politician, but by the people of the state who took the fight into their own hands.

While the fight against ICE in Minnesota this winter focused on immigrants’ rights, it also organically connected to other struggles. It was commonplace to see Palestine flags at anti-ICE protests, for example, and signs often included anti-war slogans and denunciations of the ultra-rich “ Epstein class .” These protests emerged as a response to acute attacks from ICE, but they expressed a broader rejection of the Far Right, and people’s fighting rage came from a deep-seated hatred of the Trump administration and disgust with their warmongering abroad and attacks on immigrants at home.

It was this fighting spirit that led Minnesotans to organize themselves into Rapid Response groups to watch out for ICE and take direct action when ICE vehicles were spotted, and it was this fighting spirit that led Minnesotans to organize enormous mass mobilizations and economic blackouts in sub-zero temperatures to demand that ICE leave their cities. These enormous protests and economic blackouts forced the Trump Administration’s hand — they fired Border Patrol commander Greg Bovino and scaled back ICE presence in the Twin Cities significantly.

While ICE has not completely left the Twin Cities, this retreat from Trump put him in a very weak position and created one of the biggest humiliations of his political career. This victory did not come from Tim Walz or Jacob Frey; it didn’t come from even progressive Democrats like Ilhan Omar or Peggy Flanagan. It was won by the people, organized independently from below, who took matters into their own hands and used their power to shut the cities down not once, but twice.

The Minnesotans who led this fight went to the polls last week looking not only for economic relief or a “return to normal,” but with deeply political demands, including ICE abolition and an end to the genocide in Palestine. The people of Minnesota and across the nation deserve a party that will fight for these demands, which emerged organically from the social movements of the last few years. The Democratic Party is not that party.

Many are cautiously optimistic about the blue wave, hoping that they will be safe from attacks for now. This hope, though, is lukewarm — discontent with the Democratic Party is extremely high, and its victory was due much more to a rejection of Trumpism than faith in the Democrats. This shows us that there is space to build an alternative. We do not have to accept the disappointments of the Democratic Party. We can create a party of our own, by the working class and for the working class, that fights not only for reforms to the capitalist system, but also for an end to the capitalist system altogether.

A party of our own, independent of the capitalists, could help organize our struggles in the streets, uniting and strengthening them. It would also represent, and fight for, the demands of the people, running candidates who answer only to the working class and oppressed who elected them, making no allegiances and no concessions to the capitalists or their politicians. This does not have to be an abstract dream, postponed for some day in the future while we “vote blue no matter who.” The self-organized struggle of the Twin Cities this winter showed that this kind of party is possible.

In this post-midterm season, let’s not forget that the Democrats didn’t defeat ICE, we did, and a blue wave isn’t coming to save us — we have to save ourselves. In Minnesota and across the United States, it’s time for a party of our own. Let’s build a working-class party that fights for socialism.

scraped.description: A million signatures and a flood of angry calls show pressure building from below against Jeffries and Schumer — and against the idea that Democrats’ midterm sweep gave them a blank check.
scraped.author: Sou Mi
scraped.body_text:
A million signatures and a flood of angry calls show pressure building from below against Jeffries and Schumer — and against the idea that Democrats’ midterm sweep gave them a blank check.

Sou Mi

An online petition urging House Democrats not to elect Hakeem Jeffries as the next Speaker of the House has garnered over a million signatures. Similar backlash has also greeted Chuck Schumer and the possibility that he could become Senate majority leader.

Coming on the heels of the “ blue tsunami ,” in which Democrats secured a majority in both the House and the Senate, the revolt against both Jeffries and Schumer shows that there is still widespread discontent with one of the two major parties of capital and a desire for change. Far from being a mandate for the Democratic Party, the election results signaled a complete rejection of Donald Trump and his program which was predicated on tax cuts for the wealthy, attacks on immigrants and democratic rights, and the expansion of imperialist war abroad — all while working people faced rising inflation and higher cost of living. With inequality at its highest level in the country since the Federal Reserve began tracking the data in 1989, the midterms showed a deep desire for an end to austerity.

With the promise of “affordability,” the Democratic Party was able to capitalize on this discontent, but it now has to deliver at a moment when few trust it to. NBC’s final poll before the election found that the Democrats’ lead came mostly from anger at Trump and the GOP, not active support for Democrats. According to the survey, despite widespread enthusiasm at the polls and voters expressing they preferred a Democrat-controlled Congress, the party’s approval rating stood at just 29%, reflecting a continued wariness towards the party.

The backlash now, against two pillars of the Democratic Party’s establishment is perhaps the most salient example of this phenomenon. Both Jeffries and Schumer, who are currently the House and Senate minority leaders respectively, have dramatically low approval ratings across the board. Only 18% of voters view Jeffries favorably. Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats for over a decade, has an approval rating of a dismal 13%.

In addition to the petition’s million-plus signatures, Congressional Democrats say that they’ve received hundreds of calls since last Tuesday urging them not to elect Jeffries as Speaker or Schumer as Senate majority leader. At the center of this backlash are their records on Wall Street and Israel. Both are leading allies of financial capital in Congress and have long championed the Zionist state and its political aims.

Not only have they received millions in funding from AIPAC over the years, but Schumer and Jeffries have spent years treating opposition to Israel’s genocide in Palestine as a form of hate, even as millions across the country are increasingly souring to the Zionist state. Indeed, Israel’s favorability among Americans is now at a record low , compounded by the continuation of the genocide and the expansion of war in the region. A New York Times/Siena poll in May found that 74 percent of Democratic voters oppose military and economic aid to Israel. Years of livestreamed genocide have brought tens of thousands of students, workers, and anti-Zionist Jewish people into the streets. This, coupled with a continuing war that has made clear to many that there is always money for war and nothing for working people — even as costs rise — has helped turn opposition to Zionism from a fringe position into a mainstream one. It has pushed the Democratic Party’s own voters far to the left of its leaders on Israel. Yet just this year, both leading Democrats spoke at AIPAC’s donor summit in February, mere weeks before the United States and Israel attacked Iran. Any opposition Jeffries and Schumer have voiced to the subsequent war in Iran — an issue that fueled much of the anger expressed at the polls — has focused largely on whether Congress approved it.

Now, as calls to replace Schumer and Jeffries grow, the progressives who led the charge this midterm cycle, channeling this anger against Israel and Big Capital, are weighing their options. In the House, DSA-backed progressives like Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier from New York, Adam Hamawy from New Jersey, and Melat Kiros from Colorado have refused to commit to Jeffries so far. For her part, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who is increasingly a figurehead of the progressive movement, said that House Democrats were united behind Jeffries’s leadership.

In the Senate, Bernie Sanders, while maintaining his support for Jeffries, has said that he won’t be backing Chuck Schumer for majority leader, saying it is “time for change.” Among the incoming class, both Abdul El-Sayed from Michigan and Peggy Flanagan from Minnesota have indicated that they want Chris Van Hollen as majority leader. Van Hollen, who had initially said he didn’t want the job, has now said he’s in “listening mode.” Van Hollen, despite his criticism of Israel’s genocide and support for Medicare for All, is no outsider and has said he hopes the next leader will offer new plans and commitments without breaking with the party’s main donors. In plain speak? It means a friendlier face of the same party, one that is still answerable to Wall Street and the pro-Israel lobby—the very forces that have long run the Democratic Party and that millions just voted against.

Regardless of the outcome of the current struggle over Jeffries and Schumer, the growing debate shows that working people no longer want to go on as before. But reclaiming control over our lives can’t be tied to choosing different managers at the top, especially when they attempt to tie our fate to the interests of a capitalist, imperialist state.

History has already borne witness to this. In 2006, Democrats took control of Congress, riding on the widespread rejection of the Iraq war, only to continue funding it while in office. In 2008, in the face of the Great Recession where working people lost their jobs and homes, Democrats won a 257-seat majority in the House, along with the Presidency, which they used to rescue Wall Street.

A new generation is now awakening to political life, refusing to continue as before and demanding that the rich pay for the crises they’ve created. The fight against war and genocide, for healthcare for all, for housing, and for taxing the rich will not be resolved from above, by a party and a political caste beholden to the same interests that got us here. As Minnesotans showed earlier this year, when they mobilized in schools, neighborhoods, and workplaces to kick ICE out of their communities, we have to harness our anger and mobilize from below, uniting our struggles against imperialism and war with the fight for a different future so we can win each and every demand. And it will take building our own political, class-independent power: a party of our own, independent of the two parties of capital, and one that can organize the power of our class to fight every attack and for a socialist future.

Democratic Party

scraped.title: Trump’s Political Death - Left Voice
scraped.description: The results of the midterm elections were nothing short of catastrophic for Trump. But the Democrats will not shield us from right-wing attacks or new austerity measures — only independent, working-class mobilization is capable of doing that.
scraped.author: Carlos Buendía
scraped.body_text:
The results of the midterm elections were nothing short of catastrophic for Trump. But the Democrats will not shield us from right-wing attacks or new austerity measures — only independent, working-class mobilization is capable of doing that.

Carlos Buendía

Trump’s electoral defeat , as in Brazil , is the result of the democratic mobilization of broad sectors of youth and the working class against the Far Right. It is a defeat that emerges from the bottom up. This is his final political defeat, diminishing the GOP’s power in both chambers and ending his political legacy.

Among these movements from below, we have seen highly radicalized developments, such as the Minneapolis uprising, and the growth of DSA and the idea of socialism as a national political movement with significant influence among young people and sectors of the working class.

As a countertrend, a new political phenomenon appears to be emerging from the Democratic victory in Texas: a young political figure, James Talarico, who presents himself as a powerful centrist force, potentially capable of pulling the Democratic Party and the political establishment into his orbit in the lead-up to the next elections.

Although the election results strengthen for now the Democratic Party as a whole, the emergence of this young Texas senator introduces a “moderate” alternative. This shifts the balance of forces in the palace struggle, creating a tendency to move politics back toward the “center” and away from the poles represented by Trump and AOC.

While the Congressional Progressive Caucus added 25 new members, the “centrist” New Democrat Coalition added 39, and the conservative Blue Dog Coalition doubled its membership from ten to 20.

In this context, AOC’s role has changed. She is no longer the uncontested “left-wing presidential alternative” within the Democratic Party “movement.” With a renewed centrist tendency, she has considerably less political space than she did six months ago, when the field appeared to be wide open.

A few weeks before the elections, DSA caucuses aligned with Mamdani managed to push through a nationwide consultation within DSA on whether AOC should be promoted as a candidate in the Democratic presidential primaries. The vote was divided, although AOC won overall, with results in major chapters such as Boston showing a narrow 52% to 48% margin.

In Providence, Rhode Island, 75% of voters approved an ordinance to divest city funds from Israel on November 3. Rhode Island DSA’s independent candidate, Brittany Kubicek, won 23% of the vote in the general election, demonstrating that there is enormous political space to the left of the Democratic Party — space that must be won without hesitation or timidity.

In light of this, the premature and unnecessary attempt to tie DSA to the Democratic Party is far more a political maneuver aimed at demobilizing and demoralizing DSA and its left wing than an exercise in “realpolitik.”

This is precisely where the importance of the Rhode Island DSA chapter’s resistance to capitulating to the Democratic Party lies. Across the country, there is resistance within the DSA to the liquidationist orientation, which ultimately seeks to block the socialists’ path toward the working class.

The key to the political development of the advanced sectors of the youth and workers is the emergence of a new political force in the national arena, a party of the workers. This is the most important task of the moment for the whole workers’ movement. Any step further we can take in this struggle will become the post from which to fight the ruling class in the near future.

There’s a new generation of youth and workers who have nothing to lose, as their present is already shattered by capitalism. So they take to the streets. They did so in Minneapolis, but also in France, Italy, Germany, Spain, Portugal, Albania, Brazil, Argentina, India – and counting. Like in Minneapolis, the workers are fighting with their own methods. There was a general strike called in France on November 5 and one organized in Italy on November 11, part of a growing strike movement across Europe.

The next two years will see a lame duck president, but we shouldn’t expect the situation to be peaceful or calm.

The ruling classes will use chaos and disorder to push their reforms and austerity, and continue their attacks on working people around the world while polluting the globe at devastating scale. And the resistance will grow.

We have to learn to combat the maneuvers of the regime and keep our course steady. History is on our side.

¡Venceremos!

scraped.title: It Took 110 Years to Correct the Record
scraped.description: Guest Opinion. Jim Thorpe won. That is not a metaphor or a grievance. It is a measurement. At Stockholm in 1912, in the pentathlon and the decathlon — the two hardest all-around tests in sport — the Sac and Fox athlete from Oklahoma won by margins so wide that the King of Sweden is said […]
scraped.author: Elyse Wild
scraped.h1: It Took 110 Years to Correct the Record
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

Guest Opinion.

Jim Thorpe won. That is not a metaphor or a grievance. It is a measurement. At Stockholm in 1912, in the pentathlon and the decathlon — the two hardest all-around tests in sport — the Sac and Fox athlete from Oklahoma won by margins so wide that the King of Sweden is said to have told him, “You, sir, are the greatest athlete in the world.” The stopwatch said it. The tape said it. The record, for a few months, said it.

Then the record was changed — not because the measurement was wrong, but because a fact from another field was admitted as evidence against it. Thorpe had once been paid a few dollars to play summer baseball. A rule about amateurism, written for a different game, reached across and annulled an outcome it did not witness. In 1913, his medals were taken, his name struck, and the titles handed to the men who had finished behind him.

Your contribution is appreciated.

Notice who the rule protected. Not the competition — Thorpe’s excellence was the competition, and every man in those events knew where he stood relative to it. The rule protected the institution’s authority to define who is permitted to excel. When reality contradicted the rule, the institution did not amend the rule. It amended reality.

Every organization keeps a version of this case in a drawer: the result that was quietly rewritten because the rule mattered more than the outcome, the measurement subordinated to the definition. The Thorpe case is only the most documented one — and the most instructive, because of how long the correction took and who finally forced it.

The correction came in stages, and the stages are the lesson. In 1983, thirty years after Thorpe died in poverty, the IOC returned replica medals and listed him as co-champion — a correction that still shared his titles with the runners-up, as if the stopwatch had recorded a tie. The men listed beside him, to their credit, had always said the titles were Thorpe’s. The half-measure stood for another forty years.

What ended it was not the institution’s conscience. It was a campaign. Bright Path Strong — named for Wa-Tho-Huk, Bright Path, Thorpe’s own Sac and Fox name — gathered 75,000 signatures and pressed the case until Norway and Sweden, speaking for the athletes who had held the titles, agreed to give them back. On July 14, 2022, 110 years after Stockholm, the IOC restored Jim Thorpe as the sole champion of both events. The institution amended reality a second time — back toward the truth — because Native people and their allies refused, for over a century, to accept the first amendment.

There is a temptation to file this under history, as a wrong righted. Resist it. The mechanism that took Thorpe’s medals is not retired. It operates wherever a definition is valued above a measurement, wherever the keeper of the record would rather edit the outcome than examine the rule. The question the case puts to every institution is not whether its rules were followed. It is whether its rules still serve the purpose they claim to serve — or only the authority that enforces them.

And there is a second lesson, in the century it took. Records do not correct themselves. They are corrected by people who keep the true measurement in memory long after the official one has been printed — in this case, a family, a Nation whose flag still carries the Olympic rings, and a movement named for a bright path lit by lightning.

Jim Thorpe won. For 110 years, the record said otherwise. Now it doesn’t. The distance between those two sentences is the whole story — and it was closed by the people who never stopped measuring.

Joe Cozart is an author of forty books, including “The Distance Between,” and the founder of GMJoe™ Consulting in Grand Forks, North Dakota. During Native American Heritage Month he released a one-minute film on the Thorpe case, “The Clarity Algorithm at work: The Jim Thorpe Paradox.”

Elyse Wild is Senior Health Editor for Native News Online, where she leads coverage of health equity issues including mental health, environmental health, maternal mortality, and the overdose crisis in... More by Elyse Wild

scraped.description: On Tuesday, Nov. 10, the Seneca Nation swore in Tina Abrams as President, marking the first time in history the tribe has elected a woman to its highest office. Abrams was sworn in during the Nation’s Canvass Day ceremony, along with several other Executive, Council, and other candidates who won office in last week’s Seneca […]
scraped.author: Native News Online Staff
scraped.h1: Sixty Years After Granting Women the Right to Vote, Seneca Nation Swears in First Woman President
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

On Tuesday, Nov. 10, the Seneca Nation swore in Tina Abrams as President, marking the first time in history the tribe has elected a woman to its highest office.

Abrams was sworn in during the Nation’s Canvass Day ceremony, along with several other Executive, Council, and other candidates who won office in last week’s Seneca Nation elections.

Your contribution is appreciated.

“Our people went to the polls to choose a leader you believe in, a leader you can trust to lead our Nation with strength, honesty, vision and conviction,” Abrams told the large crowd gathered at Seneca Allegany Resort & Casino. “I am honored beyond words to stand before you as your choice, your President, and as the first woman to receive and accept that responsibility.”​

“I know that I bear a great responsibility to you – to all of you, all 8,500 Senecas,” she continued. “I will work every day to honor that responsibility and to live the words of the oath I take today. Yours will always be the voice that guides me.”

Abrams was first elected to the Seneca Nation Council in 2001 and was the first woman appointed co-chair in 2012. Earlier this year, she became the first Native American woman to be honored with the New York State Senate Woman of Distinction Award.

At Monday’s swearing-in ceremony, Abrams spoke of the many people who influenced her. She spoke of the Seneca Clan Mothers who, before the Nation adopted an elected form of government in 1848, chose the Nation’s chiefs. She also spoke of her family’s historic involvement with the Nation, including her grandfather, Morris Jimerson, and her father, Walden Jimerson, who both served on the Nation Council and fought to give women the right to vote in Nation elections.

The right to vote was secured in a 1964 referendum, followed by the right to hold elected office in 1966. President Abrams’ grandmother, Sybil Eels, was the fourth Seneca woman ever elected to a government position.

“Now, the same little girl from Cattaraugus who used to go to meetings with her father and fall asleep in the Council House; a proud mother and grandmother who raised her family here in Allegany; and a longtime voice for the Seneca people on Council, will lead our Nation for the next two years,” Abrams said.

scraped.h1: Quinault Nation Buys 11,000 Acres Within Its Own Reservation
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

The Quinault Nation has purchased more than 11,000 acres of ancestral land within its reservation from a logging company.

The land was one of the largest privately owned properties within the Quinault Indian Reservation, making up roughly half of the reservation’s privately owned fee lands, according to a press release from The Nature Conservancy. The land sits within the Olympic Rainforest and is largely in the Raft River watershed, home to salmon, steelhead trout, elk, and culturally significant gathering areas used by Quinault people.

Your contribution is appreciated.

President of the Quinault Indian Nation Guy Capoeman said the purchase allows the tribe to steward its ancestral lands cohesively, rather than parcel by parcel.

“This acquisition represents a vision in the making by our forebears,” Guy Capoeman, president of the Quinault Indian Nation, said in a press release. “This is making our ancestral land whole again and will allow future generations to strategically manage our culture and traditional land as our ancestors intended.”

The acquisition brings Quinault Indian Nation ownership within the Reservation from approximately 47% to more than 52%.

“Some of the most fractionated and disconnected land parcels exist on the Quinault Reservation, preventing meaningful forestry, fisheries, cultural and overall ecological resource regeneration,” Tyson Johnston, the 1 st councilperson on the Quinault Tribal Council’s business committee, said. “This historic acquisition represents one of the most meaningful milestones Quinault has seen to restore our land base, heal our forests, and ensure our children and descendants can preserve our way of life.”

The acquisition cost was $60 million, funded by $25 million through Washington’s Climate Commitment Act and its Natural Climate Solutions Account, approximately $20 million from the Quinault Indian Nation, and $15 million raised by The Nature Conservancy from private donors and foundations.

scraped.title: Flooding forces evacuation notice in Lil'wat First Nation
scraped.description: Evacuation orders have been issued for Lil'wat First Nation and parts of the Village of Pemberton, north of Vancouver.
scraped.author: The Canadian Press
scraped.h1: Shelter-in-place advisory issued near Squamish, B.C., due to flooding from heavy rain
scraped.body_text:
APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

Evacuation orders have been issued for parts of Vancouver Island, the Lil'wat First Nation in the central Interior, and parts of the Village of Pemberton, about 150 kilometres north of Vancouver. Photo: APTN.

A shelter-in-place advisory has been issued north of Vancouver, where roads have flooded due to dam run-off triggered by storms that have drenched parts of southern British Columbia with more than 300 millimetres of rain in 48 hours.

The rains that are forecast to ease Thursday before a weaker system arrives Friday have also forced evacuation orders for parts of Vancouver Island, the Lil’wat First Nation in the central Interior, and parts of the Village of Pemberton, about 150 kilometres north of Vancouver.

The entire Village of Pemberton is under an evacuation alert, while the District of Squamish about 90 kilometres to the south has told residents of Paradise Valley to shelter in place after dam discharge swamped local roads.

British Columbia’s emergency information system says residents in areas including Sunwolf Lodge and Cheekye Ranch should stay indoors if they can.

The District of Squamish says in a statement that the spill level from the Cheakamus Dam at Daisy Lake peaked at approximately 5 a.m. and was expected to decrease slowly throughout the day.

The district says the spill level decrease was to create room in the reservoir for another upcoming storm, as well as to eventually allow for roads to be re-opened.

It says a rainfall warning ended this morning and that heavy rain is no longer expected through Friday.

It also says river levels are expected to peak Thursday and begin to drop as rainfall from the storm works its way through the river system.

A string of weather systems has slammed southwestern B.C since last week, with 306 millimetres of rain falling at Port Mellon in the Howe Sound region since Tuesday.

The Village of Pemberton’s evacuation order covers properties on Airport Road, including the community’s airport, wastewater treatment facility, wildland fire management base and a public golf course due to flooding and “high-risk river levels.”

The B.C. Ministry of Transportation’s DriveBC website says Highway 99 east of Pemberton has been shut in both directions.

The Lilʼwat Nation has also expanded an evacuation order and alert for the area from Kwetsa7 along the Lillooet River corridor to Lillooet Lake.

Elsewhere, the Strathcona Regional District issued a water conservation notice for the village of Sayward on the northeast coast of Vancouver Island, as high flows in Newcastle Creek led to extra sediment in the water.

An evacuation order due to flooding and landslide risks remains in place for about 30 properties in the village of Zeballos on northwest Vancouver Island.

While rains have eased in parts of the province including Metro Vancouver, orange rainfall warnings remain in place for west and inland Vancouver Island, indicating severe storms that are likely to cause significant damage and disruption.

“A strong frontal system over the area will weaken today. Rain will continue to ease as the front weakens,” Environment Canada said Thursday.

A less-severe yellow rainfall warning is active for the Sunshine Coast and parts of east Vancouver Island.

Environment Canada says several locations reported more than 100 millimetres of rain in the last 48 hours, including Kennedy Lake on Vancouver Island (248 mm), Port Alberni (123 mm), Porteau Cove on the Sea to Sky Highway (140 mm), Whistler (138 mm), and Squamish (134 mm).

scraped.title: Report covering 10 years of prison life shows little has changed
scraped.description: The newest report from Canada’s correctional investigator says there has been “an absence of progress" over 10 years.
scraped.author: Emma Honeybun
scraped.h1: Newest report from correctional investigator says 10 year review of prison life shows little has changed
scraped.body_text:
APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

A hallway inside one of Canada's prisons. Photo: APTN File

The newest report from Canada’s federal prison watchdog says that despite 49 recommendations over 10 years, there has been “an absence of progress” in reducing the over-incarceration of Indigenous Peoples.

Valerie Phillips, who was the interim head of the Office of the Correctional Investigator (OCI) , wrote that findings indicated Correctional Services Canada (CSC) “remains predominantly risk-averse, security-driven, and institution-centred, with Indigenous-specific initiatives operating at the margins rather than as core system functions.”

“The central finding of this report is clear and consistent. A persistent gap remains between policy commitments and what is experienced on the ground,” she wrote. “This gap is the defining challenge of federal corrections.”

The OCI acts as a watchdog for the federal corrections system, taking complaints from prisoners and prison workers and visiting prisons to assess living conditions and trends, such as the over-incarceration of Indigenous Peoples.

Every year, the office releases an annual report which summarizes findings from the last year, paired with recommendations for Corrections Service Canada (CSC) to help address issues or gaps.

Phillips released the 2025-2026 annual report on Oct. 26, the first since former correctional investigator Ivan Zinger took his retirement in February.

This time, she wrote her report based on findings from the last decade.

In the 206-page document, she concluded that there is no behind-bars support that can replace community-based alternatives.

Indigenous Peoples remain over-represented throughout the entire legal system because of a lack of community-based supports, as well as risk assessment tools which advocates believe are rooted in outdated, colonial practices.

Sen. Kim Pate said she found the report “disheartening.”

“The situation keeps getting worse because we need the courage and the conviction to actually recognize that what has happened for decades has been not only ineffective, it’s been damaging and has made people who already have significant past trauma and histories of abuse in situations of more risk of not having their needs met,” she told APTN News.

“And until we do that and until we address those in the community and provide support to folks to have those, have their needs met, we will continue to see more of the same.”

Nicole Kief, the executive director of Prisoners’ Legal Services (PLS) , had a similar reaction and said the report didn’t “surprise her at all.”

PLS is a clinic operated by the Vancouver-based West Coast Justice Society, which offers prison-related legal aid to Indigenous and non-Indigenous clients.

“As I’m reading through these reports, I just find myself nodding and nodding and nodding and nodding, because this is all consistent with what we see in our own work,” Kief said.

From the perspective of an advocate who sees the barriers faced by people in incarceration on the day-to-day, she said what is often the biggest challenge is the “gap between policy and practice.

“That’s what stands out to me,” she said.

In the report’s section on Indigenous corrections, Phillips wrote that there have been gains when it comes to corrections officers being more culturally informed with the help of increased training introduced as recently as the fall of 2025.

For example, a higher number of Indigenous Peoples in incarceration had access to cultural resources because corrections officers were better equipped to recognize and place people in programs at an earlier stage than before.

For example, that year, 37 per cent of high-risk Indigenous offenders participated in the Pathways initiative , an Elder-driven cultural healing program for those preparing to transfer to a lower security facility.

In the 2022-2023 fiscal year, fewer than 10 per cent of Indigenous offenders accessed the program, which means there was almost a 30 per cent jump in two years.

However, the progress is undermined by risk assessment tools and written legislation that isn’t being changed, she continued.

In 2025-2026, the Pathways program only increased capacity from 350 to 366 people at one time, nationally, and 76 people “remained waitlisted despite operating at approximately 86 per cent capacity,” Phillips wrote.

The report said, “97 Indigenous offenders account for more than two-thirds of the population in the institutions where Pathways is offered, yet only a small proportion are able to access a Pathways bed.”

High-security assessment a result of unmet needs, says advocate

Ultimately, Phillips wrote, “while training on Indigenous Social History has expanded, guidance remains largely theoretical.

“As a result, statutory obligations to meaningfully consider systemic and background factors continue to be applied inconsistently.”

On this note, Phillips referred to the risk assessment process as a “long-standing systemic barrier.”

As of June 2026, “only 20.2 per cent of Indigenous men were classified as minimum- security,” according to the report, “while 58.6 per cent were classified as medium-security.”

Kief said PLS often deals with clients who are classified as high-security, and that they’re continually assessed for “adjustment,” meaning how well they can adapt to a prison environment.

This has become a barrier for many people who find the maximum-security environment quite triggering, she said.

“They have so much PTSD from prison officers, from police, from other state actors who have assaulted them,” she said. “And the highly secure environment, the very tense and confrontational culture, and the way it’s run. People are in that flight or flight, heightened modes all the time … and so they’re considered high-security, high institutional adjustment.”

But then, Kief added, she’ll read a report from an Elder about the same person, “They’re night and day.”

She said she believes many people in incarceration who have been assessed as high-risk may present themselves differently and show more success if they had access to supports which are only made available to medium-to-low-risk offenders.

“You respond to the environment that you’re in,” Kief said, “and if your environment involves guard patrols with weapons, metal slamming doors, being handcuffed everywhere you go, uses of force by guards, violence, and isolation, you are going to become a product of that environment.”

Healing lodges useful, but restricted

High-risk labels limit eligibility to supports such as healing lodges, which operate like Indigenous-based halfway houses for those reintegrating into communities.

There are currently 10 in Canada. Six are operated by Indigenous governments, with oversight from CSC, and the remaining four are operated entirely by CSC.

The lodges were established in direct response to Section 81 and 83 of the Corrections and Conditional Release Act, which state that,

According to Pate, the decision to use this legislation in the form of healing lodges was made to address a rising number of suicides among federally sentenced Indigenous women in particular.

From 1988 to 1992, seven women being held at the Prison for Women (P4W) facility in Kingston, Ont., died by suicide. Six of the women were First Nations.

Pate said the Indigenous Women’s Circle, co-chaired by the Native Women’s Association of Canada , had called for more healing approaches in response, and brought up the concept of a healing lodge for the Kingston facility, specifically, as the prisoners there were labeled as maximum-security and could not just be released.

Okimaw Ohci Healing Lodge, the first federally mandated healing lodge, was then established in Maple Creek, Sask. in 1995.

This first location included a safe lodge, Pate said, a secure area for maximum security prisoners.

“Ironically and horrifically, no woman classified as maximum security has ever, ever gone to a healing lodge, even though that was precisely who they were envisioned for,” she said.

According to Phillip’s report, healing lodges operated by Indigenous communities with CSC oversight remain “significantly underutilized” when compared to healing lodges entirely operated by the government. However, healing lodge occupancy as a whole was only 73 per cent over the fiscal year.

“In 2025-26, the six Section 81 [Indigenous-led] healing lodges collectively operated at 52.4% occupancy, with 110 of 210 beds vacant, even as CSC facilities retained individuals who met transfer criteria,” Phillips wrote. “As one Section 81 healing lodge reported, half of its beds remained empty while sending institutions continued to double-bunk minimum-security individuals, including those already approved for transfer.

“By contrast, CSC-run healing lodges reported near-full occupancy [90.9 per cent], underscoring a systemic preference for internal placements over community-based alternatives.”

Also contributing to the low occupancy rates is the fact that, initially, only minimum-security prisoners were allowed to go. However, the door has since been opened to medium-security prisoners on account of no Indigenous prisoners being able to access the resource, according to Pate.

Kief added that “there’s nothing” in the legislation which prohibits high-security prisoners from accessing healing lodges. Instead, eligibility is mandated only by CSC.

According to the OCI report, approximately 878 people expressed an interest in being moved to a healing lodge between 2021 and 2025, but only 307 releases were granted.

“Although CSC has indicated that not all expressions of interest translate into parole eligibility, the scale of this gap underscores ongoing systemic constraints,” Phillips wrote.

Pate had a similar point. She said the risk assessment and classification processes used by corrections have been challenged “as racist, sexist and ableist” in the Supreme Court of Canada.

“If you’re an Indigenous woman with past trauma, such as post-traumatic issues related to residential school or past abuse, then the chances of you being classified as higher security is very much linked to whatever needs you have and those being translated into risk factors by the Correctional Service of Canada,” she said.

In 2003, the Ontario Commission of Human Rights (OCHR) acknowledged this. In a report titled Paying the Price: the human cost of racial profiling , it recommended that, “with respect to Aboriginal persons, organizations or institutions involved in the delivery of services to the Aboriginal community [including corrections] should review their practices to ensure that they are adapted to the unique needs … and that their staff is properly trained in issues concerning the Aboriginal community.

“It is the Commission’s view that the evidence of the existence of racial profiling is incontrovertible; that this approach of denial does not work and only exacerbates tensions in our society,” the OCHR continued. “It is not conducive to either tackling racial profiling or to good community relations.”

Similarly, in 2019, several incarcerated women who were interviewed as part of the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls stated that, while CSC is required to conduct an “Aboriginal Social History report,” — also known as a Gladue report — to determine systemic harm prior to imprisonment, as a way to “identify and consider culturally appropriate options that could contribute to mitigating risk and may also inform placement in a facility like a healing lodge,” many still felt as though “their histories were used against them for security classification.”

In 2022, Pate helped work on the 12 Indigenous Women report, which outlined the 10 primary risk factors that contribute to imprisonment, including police bias and forced separation from their children, using interviews from 12 Indigenous women in incarceration.

In the report, she concluded that “Once the 12 Indigenous women were sentenced to federal prison, ill-suited and discriminatory risk assessment tools as well as Gladue reports chronicling their experiences of abuse and violence resulted in them being placed in higher security levels and viewed as security risks.”

Referencing the report, Pate said, “Although about half of the women serving federal sentences, particularly Indigenous women, were in for what were considered to be offences of personal violence, almost all of those were in response to violence, poverty, challenging circumstances that they were first subjected to, and it was their response to not having police protection, not having supportive community, not having the necessary resources that they were responding, and then they would often be criminalized.”

So, in the present day, it creates a system where there are potential supports for Indigenous Peoples, such as the aforementioned Pathways program, but they are not always accessible, and they do not address the issue of high-security profiling and over-representation which brings Indigenous Peoples to the federal prison system in the first place.

“The presumption being that they [Indigenous prisoners] will get access to [cultural] norms, they will get access to supports, they will get access to Elders. And then when that doesn’t happen because of the classification system, because the entire basis upon which the system rests is never addressed, we don’t build up a community,” Pate said. “We don’t provide support to First Nations, Métis and Inuit groups to provide meaningful support and assistance on the ground to prevent people from ending up in custody.

“But then we expect somehow to go into prison, come out, and still without adequate resources, do better. I mean, it’s a fool’s game to think that not investing in community first and foremost is in any way the way to go.”

‘Redirection of resources’

There are a few ways to move forward from here, including improved investment. However, the 2026 Federal Budget did not have anything that could “fundamentally change the inequities that exist in [Indigenous] communities,” Pate said.

Other changes could be rooted in policy.

“The fact that we don’t see clean water, housing, healthcare, as protected human rights is something that the Canadian government could change now,” she said. “Canada is a wealthy country in terms of human resources, in terms of natural resources, there is no excuse that everybody does not have access to clean water, housing, health care and social and economic supports.”

She said policies that address those issues would “actually lower crime rates; it would result in a better standard of living for everybody and would benefit all of us in ways that we would see very quickly.”

Kief said that, because PLS is not an Indigenous organization, it has been working with and learning from several Indigenous-led advocacy groups and governments, including the Assembly of First Nations (AFN) on a “redirection of resources.”

She said, when addressing the over-incarceration of Indigenous Peoples, funds that are currently being spent on in-facility supports and resources, such as bringing in Elders for the Pathways program, could be redirected to Indigenous communities or under-funded, community-based healing lodges.

“I think it has been kind of a lifeline for some people to have access to, say, an Elder or a cultural program,” Kief said. “But they’re way too limited, and few and far between and under-resourced … the whole thing seems backwards, right?

“Why do we have 99 per cent security, one per cent meaningful stuff, right? Wouldn’t it be better if we had 99 per cent meaningful stuff, and then we wouldn’t need all the security?”

APTN News contacted OCI and CSC, but interviews could not be organized before the deadline.

Emma is a Red River Métis with family roots in St. Malo, Manitoba. She graduated from RRC Polytech’s Creative Communications program in 2023 and went on to serve as a community journalist and photographer for the Free Press Community Review until she joined APTN in 2026. Equipped with a strong sense of justice, she enjoys covering stories in the central prairies for a larger audience. Her work has also appeared in Manitoba Inc. Magazine, the Free Press, and RRC Polytech’s student paper, The Projector.

scraped.title: First Nations Bank says federal budget ‘generational’ opportunity
scraped.description: Indigenous Service Canada Minister Mandy Gull-Masty agrees, saying FNBC CEO Bill Lomax is “right on the money”
scraped.author: Keelan Jacobs
scraped.h1: First Nations Bank CEO says federal budget is a ‘generational’ opportunity for First Nations
scraped.body_text:
APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

Bill Lomax, president and CEO, First Nations Bank of Canada, speaks during the luncheon at the Canadian Club Toronto on Nov. 4, 2026. Photo: Nathan Denette/The Canadian Press.

First Nations Bank of Canada (FNBC) president and CEO Bill Lomax says the federal budget offers a rare opening for First Nations to move from consultation into genuine ownership of the infrastructure and energy projects that will define Canada’s economy for decades.

Lomax framed the scale of planned investments in transportation, energy and electricity infrastructure as “a generational opportunity for First Nations to play a leading role in building Canada’s future.”

“When First Nations move beyond participation to become owners, we create lasting economic opportunities, build wealth for future generations and strengthen Canada’s economy as a whole. When First Nations succeed, Canada succeeds,” Lomax said in a statement following the budget.

“But we need to think beyond consultation, employment and contracting opportunities. While these remain important, First Nations must also be recognized as business partners and owners, with the ability to build businesses, acquire equity and participate directly in the long-term economic benefits these projects generate.”

The FNBC is Canada’s only Indigenous-owned chartered bank, founded in 1996, operates 22 branches and service centres across six provinces and three territories, manages more than $1.6 billion in assets, and through its subsidiary FNB Trust, administers approximately $5.5 billion.

The federal budget, tabled Nov. 5, commits more than $50 billion over 10 years to Indigenous programs and services. The largest single piece is $32 billion over a decade for First Nations housing and on-reserve infrastructure.

That includes the new First Nations On-Reserve Infrastructure Program, backed by $18.5 billion for infrastructure and $11 billion for housing that aims to maintain, renovate and build thousands of homes over 10 years.

“This budget is an opportunity to invest in who we are,” Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty told APTN News in an interview Tuesday. “It’s an opportunity to better define who we are. It’s an opportunity to have a strategic approach to what our financial position is going to be, and I think the greatest opportunity of all is to demonstrate to Canadians the fiscal impact that Indigenous people have on the Canadian economy.”

The budget also introduces the new Canada Growth Incentive (CGI) for Canadian entrepreneurs, investors and employees, which is also open to Indigenous business people. The goal of the CGI is to keep investment money in Canada.

It offers a new capital gains tax exemption for “Canadian builders” of up to $15 million earned from the Canadian businesses they invested in. To benefit, Canadians will have to reinvest and keep their money in Canada and Canadian businesses.

“The Canada Growth Incentive (CGI) will be one of the most significant incentives to attract and retain builders here in Canada by creating the path for entrepreneurs, investors, and employees to reinvest in Canada,” the budget said. “This represents a level shift in the attractiveness of firms, large and small, to invest-and reinvest-in Canada, and deliver lasting prosperity for all Canadians.”

The budget is also promising money for education, health, child welfare, policing and emergency management.

The budget also outlines the government’s support for the Indigenous Loan Program that loans money to First Nations for projects.

“I hope everybody listening or reading our interviews about the budget understands that I’m here to spend money; come to me with your proposals. I’m going to do everything I can to meet the needs, so work with me,” said Gull Masty.

Where’s the money?

Aaron Pete, chief of Chawathil First Nation in British Columbia, told APTN that he’s taking a cautious approach to the budget because the money “rarely finds its way to First Nation communities in a constructive way.”

“It [the budget] sounds promising, but again, my concern is that it gets stuck in Ottawa and doesn’t actually reach these communities,” he said.

Pete was a councillor in 2022 and became chief in 2025. He has a podcast where politicians of all stripes are invited to share their opinions on the state of the country and First Nations politics.

He acknowledged that many of the government’s stated priorities — clean running water, higher-quality infrastructure and support for First Nations — are the right ones, but flagged ongoing concerns.

“My big overarching concern that I continue to have is how Indigenous Services Canada has a very Ottawa-centric approach,” he said. “There are restrictions on how provinces use [money] and they have to go to Ottawa for approval on budget spending. I think there should be more regional support so they can make decisions on a case-by-case basis.

He said the government does have other programs that help First Nations financially, but isn’t sure everyone is getting assistance.

“We have the First Nations Finance Authority , we have the First Nations Financial Management Board , and we have the First Nations Tax Commission . There are experts in this area out there,” said Pete.

“Is that knowledge, is that capacity reaching the most vulnerable First Nations that are still far behind the poverty line and need that support?”

Major Projects ‘designated in the national interest’

Another way the government is bringing in First Nations to participate in the economy is through its proposed infrastructure projects.

It set up a Major Projects Office based in Calgary to oversee the development of the projects that are heavy in fossil fuels and gas.

Currently, three projects- Roberts Bank Terminal Expansion Project, LNG Canada Phase 2 in B.C., and the Pacific Link Pipeline from Alberta to Vancouver have been designated as “projects of national interest.”

Canada said it approached approximately 130 First Nations along the Pacific Link pipeline route and offered them a chance to invest in the project.

First Nation leaders complained the federal government came with little information about the project. It’s still not clear what the final investments or arrangements will be.

Pete said he’s optimistic about the shift toward economic partnership with Canada in major projects.

“We have moved a long way within First Nation communities and Indigenous communities more broadly to where we get to even be considered for equity ownership for an opportunity like this. Our ancestors were just trying to have a voice on where it would be placed and the impacts on the environment,” he said.

“To be able to reap financial benefits from something like this is a huge change. And I just hope that everybody is processing how monumental that is. Imagine if we had had some equity ownership in CN Rail or CP Rail. That is unthinkable. But the amount of revenue we would have produced had we been equity owners in that would have been incomprehensible.

“Our ancestors fought for us to have a seat at the table. And now we have one. And we get to reap some of the financial benefits from major projects moving forward. That’s a big deal from my perspective. And that should be celebrated.”

Read More:

Mississaugas of the Credit invests $15M million to become shareholder in First Nations Bank of Canada

Budget 2026 delivers $32B to First Nations, but Métis, Inuit largely left out

He also noted progress in the consultation process itself.

“With the major projects office being required to consult First Nations communities, First Nations get to play an instrumental role in shaping where the pipelines end up going. And that’s, again, a huge change of pace, even since the TMX pipeline, so the conversations have advanced so significantly that now we’re being consulted well before the project is finalized.

“They’re seeking our input on a planned project. And that’s another major step.”

Keelan is Anishinaabe from Walpole Island First Nation (Bkejwanong Territory). He graduated with an Honours B.A. In Political Science from the University of Toronto and follows the stories where power, money and public policy meet. Keelan has a strong interest in economics and finance, and is a lifelong hockey and sports fan.

scraped.title: smǝlqmíx Youth lead rally against greenlit Copper Mountain Mine expansion: ‘They don’t care that their decision makes us sick’
scraped.description: The province greenlit the mine’s expansion earlier this year — but young people are ‘united’ to protect the nearby Similkameen River
scraped.author: Aaron Hemens, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
scraped.h1: smǝlqmíx Youth lead rally against greenlit Copper Mountain Mine expansion: ‘They don’t care that their decision makes us sick’
scraped.body_text:
The province issued permits for the mine’s New Ingerbelle pit earlier this year — but young people are ‘united’ against the project, which they say threatens the Similkameen River

Aaron Hemens, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter

●

●

A group of smǝlqmíx (Similkameen) Youth are continuing calls to stop a controversial mine expansion project in their homelands after it was greenlit by the province earlier this year.

Members of the nmlqitkʷ (Similkameen River) Defenders, a group of syilx smǝlqmíx Youth “fighting for the water,” hosted an event on Sunday in the town of Keremeos, speaking about their “refusal” of the Copper Mountain Mine’s New Ingerbelle expansion.

More than 50 people of all ages and backgrounds were in attendance, with many displaying signs with messages that read “No to the Ingerbelle Mine Expansion.”

After years of deliberating, the “B.C.” government greenlit the New Ingerbelle expansion in February , issuing Mines Act and Environmental Management Act permits. The open pit gold and copper mine is located near “Princeton” in smǝlqmíx territory, which is about an hour northwest of Keremeos.

There have been years-long concerns from syilx communities and advocates about the impact that the expansion of the mine and its already towering tailings dam will have on the Similkameen River, which some worry could have “catastrophic impacts” on the valley.

The expansion will see the mine’s existing 192-metre tailings dam — roughly equivalent in height to a 58-storey building — increased by an additional 87 metres, according to the province’s Environmental Assessment Office (EAO) .

While acknowledging that she was “angry” and “upset” to have to stand up for the water; the land; and all the beings that rely on them, nmlqitkʷ defender Meadow Arcand said on Sunday that the Indigenous Youth “have a responsibility to do this work.”

“What we’re really looking out for is these young ones, the sacred ones that are going to come after us. Like our ancestors did before us, like our Elders did before us, like the old people did before us,” said Arcand.

“We’re standing here so people can’t say that we didn’t.”

She extended this same responsibility to anyone benefitting from Okanagan waters and territories – not just syilx smǝlqmíx people.

“We need people to care about our relationships with all life: with the water, with each other, and with the future generations,” she said.

“What we do here now matters. What our ancestors did matters.”

Older generations of the smǝlqmíx community also spoke on Sunday, denouncing the mine expansion and sharing their support for the Youth. The organizers left handouts to resources – such as their online petition and declaration – and other information bulletins on what’s happening with mining in their homelands.

They also brought with them the syilx Okanagan Nation’s siwɬkʷ (Water) Declaration .

The expansion project is set to see the century-old mining operation revive its old Ingerbelle open pit gold and copper mine site near the Similkameen River. The expansion will extend the mining’s operation until 2047, according to the province.

After the province greenlit the mine’s expansion project in February, leadership at both Upper and Lower Similkameen Indian Bands (USIB, LSIB) denounced the government’s decision , saying that “no consent” was given.

y̓ilmixʷm (Chief) kalʔlùpaɋʹn Keith Crow of LSIB told IndigiNews in 2022 that the Similkameen River is the lifeblood of the valley.

“If we lose that, we lose our identity. We lose who we are,” Crow said.

Meanwhile, the mine’s owner Hudbay Minerals issued a statement saying it “proactively engaged” with USIB and LSIB throughout the permitting process, and “finalized refreshed participation agreements” with both communities — “reinforcing the company’s commitment to strong Indigenous partnerships.”

“We want to thank the B.C. government, the USIB, the LSIB and our local communities for their open and efficient collaboration throughout the process,” said Robert Carter, Hudbay’s “Canadian” senior vice president, in the statement earlier this year.

“Through our strong commitment to responsible resource development and the expansion of copper production from Copper Mountain, we will be continuing to provide a metal that is vital for electrification and the global energy transition and supporting B.C.’s Critical Mineral Strategy.”

For decades, the Similkameen River’s water quality has been negatively impacted by mining operations and other industries. In the same month that B.C. greenlit the New Ingerbelle expansion, a province-wide council of outdoor recreationists declared the waterway among the province’s most endangered rivers – citing the mine’s expansion as a major threat.

At this week’s gathering – which organizers described as a “protection, not a protest” – Arcand reiterated that many people in the community “don’t want” this expansion to go through.

The gathering on Sunday, she highlighted, was the culmination of smǝlqmíx Youth discussing and coming together to plan for over a year now.

“Do we depend on this mine for life? No – lut,” she said, with “lut” being the nsyilxcen word for “no.”

“We depend on the water for everything, for all life. Not just as us, but all life depends on the water … All water is connected. So whatever we do in any watershed is going to impact the collective.”

Fellow organizer Madeline Terbasket said that the young people of the Similkameen are “united” in their cause to stand up for the water, the tmixʷ (wildlife) and the tmxʷulaxʷ (the land). They said that the Youth’s voices matter in these discussions, and that Copper Mountain Mine operators, Hudbay Minerals, “can not continue to ignore our loud lut.”

“We have not had meaningful consultation with the mine. The province greenlit this project too fast. There are going to be deathly consequences if the New Ingerbelle expansion continues moving forward,” said Terbasket.

“How do we dismantle something as grotesque as the mine wanting more, more, more? We need to find solutions together.”

For years, the impact that mining and other industries are having on the river “has been seriously affecting my mental health,” they added.

“I think it is weighing on all of our hearts in some way … I do mean when I say that we are playing with human lives here. Indigenous Youth face death and suicide at an alarming rate,” they said.

“By putting this in expansion, we would take away hope from so many young people.”

The river “is everything to me,” they continued.

“The province fast-tracked this project because they want the economic benefits. They don’t care that their decision makes us sick. Blood will be shed by many for the benefit of few.”

For generations — “since q’sapi (a long time ago)” — they said their family grew up along the river. They shared stories, from their lifetime and before theirs, of family members enjoying what the river had to offer — from fishing to swimming.

“‘Water is life’ is not just a slogan to me. Anytime I have a hard day, I pray to water. And I feel better after,” they said.

“I owe my life to this river. I must speak up. I must do something.”

LSIB Elder Eliza Terbasket shared her experiences “on that river, living off that river,” and the changes she’s seen to its waters in her lifetime.

From swimming in the water during the summer, to helping her brothers skate on it in the winter, there was even a time where she said her brothers would fish out of it.

Similar to proponents of the mine today, she said when she was younger, she saw mining as a way to bring jobs and economic revenue to the valley.

“I was very naive. I hadn’t realized how much our water was being affected,” she said.

As mining operations from “Hedley” to “Princeton” came and went throughout the later half of 20th century, she said she began to realize that the river was changing.

“Our animals are changing – they’re being affected by the poison in our waters,” said Terbasket.

“I imagine that all of us in this valley are already affected by the poisons in our waters. We just don’t know it.”

Her prayer, now and always, she said, is for “the ones that come after us” to be able to live a long and healthy life.

“How do we do that if our water is not good?” she said.

“I love how many people showed up today. I really appreciate each and every one of you. Because that gives me hope.”

Elder Larry Kenoras said that “hopefully,” his other relatives can stand up and support the Youth.

“So they don’t have to fight — we can sit down and talk like this in a good way,” said Kenoras.

Other syilx Nation members, Jennifer Lewis and Dixon Terbasket, also said they were also willing to stand by and support the Youth.

“It’s something that takes organization, it takes unified people. It’s about people standing up and holding hands, and deciding that water is the most critical thing,” said Dixon.

Lori Goldman from Seniors for Climate South Okanagan said that they are a group of seniors who support the Youth however they can, because “later is too late,” she said.

“We know what we need to do. And our leaders are not doing it,” said Goldman.

“We have the power, when we come together, to make our voices stronger and to make something happen. It is possible.”

Pauline Terbasket, the executive director of the Okanagan Nation Alliance and a member of LSIB, said that she is supporting the Youth because she believes they will “lead the way.”

“Let the Youth lead the way – they are leading the way. Like the salmon, they’ll lead a way; they’ll find a way – they already have,” said Terbasket.

Aaron Hemens, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter

Aaron Hemens is an award-winning photographer, journalist and visitor in unceded syilx Okanagan territory. He is Filipino on his mom’s side, and has both French and British roots on his dad’s. As a settler, he is committed to learning and unlearning in his role as Storyteller for the Okanagan region, and to accurately and respectfully tell stories of Indigenous Peoples throughout the area. Aaron’s work is supported in part with funding from the Local Journalism Initiative in partnership with The Discourse and APTN.

And yet, I have hope for journalism because of the work we’re doing at IndigiNews.

At IndigiNews, we embody tâpwêwin — the Cree value of integrity and responsibility in truth-telling. We are committed to our independent, Indigenous-led newsroom rooted in community, accountability, and relationality. We believe storytelling is a sacred fire that connects our pasts, presents, and futures through the storytellers in our Storytelling Lodge . IndigiNews creates space for Indigenous journalists, storytellers, Knowledge Keepers, and communities to gather, learn, and share stories that matter.

As a registered charity, we are building a fire that allows our work not just to ignite but to thrive. Rather than relying on advertising or corporate acquisition, IndigiNews is sustained by people like you who believe Indigenous stories are important for the future of our communities.

Your support is making a real difference.

Our community of supporters, our Firekeepers , make it possible to grow our newsroom, publish award-winning journalism, train emerging Indigenous journalists through initiatives like the ReFocus Photojournalism Fellowship, and publish trustworthy stories that serve our communities across the country. Every story we publish helps fill in gaps left by mainstream media and ensures Indigenous perspectives are represented with care, accuracy and respect.

But there is still more work to do.

As the media landscape becomes more and more uncertain, community support is as necessary and essential as it’s ever been. Every new Firekeeper helps protect the independence of our newsroom and strengthens journalism that is accountable to our many and varied communities over corporations.

That’s why we’re inviting you to become a Firekeeper.

Firekeepers tend to and protect the sacred fire. Your monthly contributions directly support IndigiNews’s Storytelling Lodge, helps sustain our independent, Indigenous-led newsroom, and ensures future generations of Indigenous storytellers have the resources they need to do the work.

As a registered Canadian charity, all eligible donations receive a charitable tax receipt.

If you believe Indigenous stories matter, if you value independent journalism, and if you want to help build a strong future for Indigenous media, we invite you to join our circle of Firekeepers today.

Together, we can keep the fire burning.

— Eden Fineday, Publisher, IndigiNews

Frey Blake-Pijogge, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter

●

●

Matt Simmons
