items.summary: President Donald Trump's administration wants to sell public lands to states, tribes and local governments The post Trump administration wants to sell public lands and shrink the federal estate appeared first on ICT. Matthew BrownAssociated Press BILLINGS, Mont. — President Donald Trump’s administration wants to sell public lands to states, tribes and local governments as part of an effort to “decrease the size of the federal estate,” according to a new plan presented by the Interior Departme...

scraped.title: Trump administration wants to sell public lands and shrink the federal estate - ICT
scraped.description: The Interior Department oversees about 20 percent of U.S. land, putting it at the center of a decades-long debate over whether the government controls too much land.
scraped.author: Associated Press
scraped.h1: Trump administration wants to sell public lands and shrink the federal estate
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Matthew Brown Associated Press

BILLINGS, Mont. — President Donald Trump’s administration wants to sell public lands to states, tribes and local governments as part of an effort to “decrease the size of the federal estate,” according to a new plan presented by the Interior Department.

Agency officials said the sale of federal property would allow the government to focus resources on “nationally significant” lands, which were not defined. They offered no details on what parcels could be sold, nor the scope or location of potential sales.

The proposal drew quick pushback from some lawmakers, including Trump’s former Interior secretary, Republican Rep. Ryan Zinke, showing it faces strong headwinds in Congress even before Democrats assume the majority in January.

The Interior Department’s five-year strategic plan also calls for land transfers and exchanges to support greater energy production, a centerpiece of the administration’s pro-fossil fuel policies. It reflects the Trump administration’s view of most public lands as assets to be used, rather than to be set aside for preservation.

The Interior Department oversees more than 750,000 square miles of land — an area greater than Texas and California combined — along with vast underground mineral reserves. That puts the agency at the center of a contentious, decades-long debate over whether the government controls too much land.

The Associated Press sent emails to Interior officials Wednesday requesting comment and further details.

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

Most public lands are in Western states. In some, the government controls the vast majority of land, protecting it from potential exploitation but also hindering growth. Nevada, for example, is almost 80 percent under federal control.

Interior officials said a portion of any land sale proceeds would be returned to the buyer for conservation purposes elsewhere.

Yet it’s uncertain if Interior Secretary Doug Burgum can achieve the administration’s goals without cooperation from Congress.

Federal law puts significant constraints on public land sales, said Mark Squillace, a professor of natural resources law at University of Colorado Law School.

Land cannot be sold if it’s under protected status. And before a sale can occur, it must be deemed appropriate under certain criteria. Those include cases of land that is uneconomic to manage or where a sale would “serve important public objectives, including but not limited to, expansion of communities and economic development.”

Zinke’s office said in a statement that he “remains firmly opposed to the sale or transfer of public lands.” It said Zinke would vote against any legislation on the issue if it happens before the lawmaker leaves Congress after this term.

The ranking Democrats on the House and Senate natural resources committee — buoyed by their party’s success in last week’s midterm elections — pledged to fight any land sales.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

Democratic New Mexico Sen. Martin Heinrich said federal lands “belong to the American people, not private interests looking to cash in.”

California Democratic Rep. Jared Huffman said Democrats would resist the move.

“Americans love their public lands and sent a clear message last week: the Trump administration’s schemes to auction off our treasured resources and silence opposition must stop now. Democrats in Congress are going to deliver,” Huffman said.

Some Western lawmakers last year sought to sell vast tracts of land in Utah and Nevada, saying that could generate revenue and ease growth pressures in booming cities. Among the proposals, Utah Republican Sen. Mike Lee suggested selling more than 2 million acres to states or other entities.

Those efforts failed amid bipartisan opposition.

The plan sets out a road map for the Interior Department’s priorities and actions between 2026 and 2030. Future administrations would not be bound by it.

The department regulates mining, drilling, grazing, recreation and other activities that many state and local officials want greater control over. Interior includes the Bureau of Land Management, National Park Service, Fish and Wildlife Service and Bureau of Indian Affairs.

The agency’s strategic plan was last updated four years ago under former Democratic President Joe Biden.

Burgum and Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner last year proposed using “underutilized” federal land for affordable housing. Turner said some 7 million homes were needed. Officials under Biden also sought to use public lands for affordable housing, although on a smaller scale.

scraped.h1: Midterm election results for judicial races with Native candidates
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Kevin Abourezk ICT

While many think of political positions when the midterms come around, there were also judicial positions up for election with Native candidates.

Fourteen Native candidates ran for seats in the judicial system with 10 of them winning or keeping their seats.

All 14 races were within a state, county, or municipal court system.

“I’m looking forward to getting back on the bench,” said Deborah Ann Begay, Diné, who won her race for Maricopa County Justice of the Peace on Nov. 3.

She encouraged Natives to get more involved in politics and civics.

“Don’t this moment pass you by,” she said. “Be a part of the change. Commit to making changes in your community, in your home, and in your life.”

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

Jennifer Jermaine, White Earth Nation, thanked her supporters after winning her race for Maricopa County Justice of the Peace.

“Thank you to all of our donors who enabled us to hire locally and support the next generation of community leaders,” she said on her Facebook page. “It takes a village to run a political campaign! I’ll be back in court tomorrow to continue as your San Marcos Justice of the Peace.”

Following is a list of candidates for judgeships across the country and whether they won those races during the 2026 election season.

scraped.title: ‘Birthplace of Native American Golf’ celebrates 50 years - ICT
scraped.description: The Mescalero Apaches’ Inn of the Mountain Gods reflects history, ancient and modern
scraped.author: Mark Wagner
scraped.h1: ‘Birthplace of Native American Golf’ celebrates 50 years
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Mark Wagner Special to ICT

MESCALERO, New Mexico — Skiing was clearly not a popular pastime for Apache tribal members in 1963.

As far as anyone can recall, not a single Apache tribal member even knew how to ski, said Sarah Kazhe, whose father served on the tribal council at the time.

Nevertheless, with the Mescalaro Apache Tribe facing heavy poverty and high unemployment, then-Tribal Chairman Wendell Chino convinced the oil man who built the nearby Sierra Blanca Ski Resort to sell the tribe the ski area at a considerable loss.

It was a move that steered the Mescaleros into the hospitality and tourism business in a way that no tribe had ventured before. Under Chino’s vision and leadership, the tribe had expanded by the mid-1970s with the Inn of the Mountain Gods, including a ski and hunting lodge, a recreational lake and groundbreaking golf course designed by Ted Robinson Sr. that is now known as the “Birthplace of Native American Golf.”

Against all odds, and despite the fact no Apache was known to have grown up skiing or playing golf at the time, the resort marked its 50th anniversary in 2025, with the golf course celebrating the anniversary this year of its completion in 1976.

Today, the Inn of the Mountain Gods Resort and Casino has nearly 300 rooms and suites, 38,000 square feet of gaming space and a convention or meeting capacity for up to 3,000, with the lake and championship golf course. The numbers of golfers and other visitors each year are not publicly available, but Ski Apache alone is reported to handle about 300,000 visitors per year.

‘A champion story’

The visionary Chino served as tribal chairman from 1955 to 1965 and then as president for more than 30 years, from 1965 until his death in 1998.

With the tribe’s purchase of the ski resort in 1963, Chino worked closely over the next decade with Kazhe’s father, Peter Khaze, and others, to develop plans for the ski and hunting lodge, golf course, hotel, convention center and casino. The tribe had a winter income from the ski operation, but officials wanted to bring in summer tourists as well.

The plans developed a hitch, however, after the tribe hired Ted Robinson Sr. to build a golf course to grace the hillsides and ponderosa forest of the Sacramento Mountains. Robinson was the “King of Waterscapes,” with designs known the world over for naturalistic and playable courses built around water features.

Chino and Robinson then came up with a new idea: Why not build a lake along with the golf course?

Mescalero Lake is now a 144-acre, man-made reservoir that physically centers the resort. Horse trails mark the bulwark trails to the east of the resort that dammed the water of Carrizo and Cienegita creeks. The water is stocked with trout for fishing, and kayaking is a recreational feature of the resort.

At night, the breathy and haunting calls of loons give voice to the night. During the day, gunshots from the nearby Apache Hunting Lodge startle the calls of the crows, some of which are as large as eagles.

“Our story has value in it,” Sarah Kazhe told ICT. “We still know how to fish and how to hunt. We know how to survive and persevere and live in an ever-changing world. We can do that and still hold onto our identity. Our story is a champion story.”

In addition to the traditional lifestyles of hunting and fishing, Kazhe notes, “We know how to sit around a campfire and tell stories. Those traditions are passed down. Yes, we need to evolve, but we also have not lost our identity.”

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

That identity thrives on what today is a territory in south-central New Mexico that covers about 463,000 acres.

‘Red Capitalism’

On any given night at the dinner hour, the Great Hall fills with travelers pulling travel bags and golf bags. Wendell’s, a restaurant named for Chino, bustles with folks prepared to dine on Indigenous-inspired foods. The late sunlight fills the valley with gold aspen and clear blue skies.

While the number of people who remember Chino and his visionary ways has steadily dwindled, Emmaline Botella, a tribal member who has worked at the resort for 35 years, remembers Chino well.

“There was something about him that made you listen,” she said. She herself went from being a waitress to holding many roles. She now works as a senior accountant for the resort, and her family’s history parallels the economic evolution of the tribe and feathers into Mescalero history in historic ways.

Hugh Chee, Botella’s great-grandfather, was a scout for Geronimo and served time with him and others imprisoned at Fort Sill. When they were released in 1913, the Chiricahua were invited to join the Apache in Mescalero. The Lipan Apache had joined the reservation in 1903.

While Geronimo would not make it back to the homeland, Botella’s grandparents did. They settled in Whitetail on the southern side of the territory, near the large tribal cattle ranch that still operates today. Botella grew up working at the resort.

“Some people talk, but it’s hard to listen to them,” she said. “Mr. Chino was someone you wanted to listen to.”

Sarah Kazhe also remembers Chino as having a drive and vision that live on today.

“Following Chino’s passing, my father created the Wendell Chino Golf Classic to honor him,” Kazhe said. “The tournament was later retired and replaced by the Mescalero Invitational Golf Tournament.” That tournament was eventually folded into other events at the golf course.

Chino coined the term “Red Capitalism” to reflect an Indigenous approach to building the economy. Kazhe said she understands the concept, and notes that his vision for full employment is still very much the tribe’s legacy.

She points to a comment Chino was fond of saying.

“The Navajos make rugs, the Pueblos make pottery, and the Mescaleros make money,” he would say.

Growing demand

Golfers are obsessed with origins. Like salmon, they swim upstream to find where things began.

Since 1975, the year Inn of the Mountain Gods opened, Native golf has gone through considerable growth. Today, about 70 tribes own and operate courses, and a number of Native players thrive at the professional and collegiate level.

Acclaimed Native golfer Notah Begay lll won the Wendell Chino Open tournament at a young age. Robert Komahcheet ll, Comanche, won the tournament when he was 23. And while these early Native tournaments and successes may have been seeded at the Inn of the Mountain Gods, Native golf and golfers have evolved beyond the Sacramento Mountains since 1975.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

Many other Native players have now reached a high level, including Steve McDonald, Potawatomi; Gene Webster Jr., Ojibwe, Oneida, and Navajo; Beans Factor, Chickasaw; Ricky Fowler, Navajo; and Skyesong Alexis, Sioux. This year, Gabby Barker, Shoshone-Paiute, had her first professional win and, like Aidan Thomas, Laguna Pueblo, is closing in on a tour card, a certification that allows play on a professional tour.

Begay — who recently won one of the highest honors in golf, the Payne Stewart Award — credits Inn of the Mountain Gods and Peter Kazhe in the growth.

“Pete Kazhe was an instrumental part of the Native American golf renaissance in the early 1980s,” Begay told ICT recently. “The first and maybe the biggest step took place when Wendell Chino took action to make the Inn of the Mountain Gods the first ‘true’ destination resort in Indian Country. But Pete was a consistent presence in promoting the game to Native communities and playing consistently himself. If not for people like Pete, there may not have been a place for a young NB3 to sharpen his game. I’m truly thankful to Pete’s commitment and inspiration.”

There are also now dozens of Native-owned, destination courses, designed by the best architects, and some, such as Circling Raven in Idaho and Wildhorse in Oregon, have developed relationships with the Ladies Professional Golf Association. All regularly hold successful Native and non-Native tournaments, and host travelers from around the world.

The Inn of the Mountain Gods golf course is discussed in hushed and reverent tones, developed well before gaming began to draw in the revenues necessary to design and run a golf course.

On a recent visit, having passed by the statue of the Spirit Dancers that guard the entrance, and coming through the Great Hall and glancing out at Mescalero Lake, a visitor’s eyes are drawn to the island green that punctuates the landscape.

Nestled beneath the gaze of Sierra Blanca and framed by the deep blue waters of the lake, the island balances the gold, blue and green colors in a way that speaks to one of the purest design features of golf course architecture — the feature of the risk and reward.

A bad shot is not just off the fairway, or short or long. It’s gone, into the water.

On a recent day, a gentleman from El Paso — which is a short, two-hour drive from the resort — had come with his wife to gamble and play golf.

He mentioned that during his last visit, three years earlier, he had been with his brother Larry, who has since died. The man said he’d never successfully made it over the water on the island green, but on this day he did — a soft line drive that carried over the broom grass and blue water.

“That was for Larry,” he said, with soft but considerable pride.

A sacred peak

The Apache call Sierra Blanca Dził Gais’ą́ní — the sacred mountain — and the bald, high peak guards the northern wall of the valley surrounding Mescalero Lake.

At certain times of year, with a light snow, the face of an elder appears on the northeast slope. It’s said to be the man who lives in the mountain to protect the Mescaleros, who have been living in the hills since before recorded time.

That same spirit is represented at the entrance to the Inn of the Mountain Gods — a dramatic statue of the five Ga’an dancers — the Crown Dancers, the mountain gods. At the cultural learning center, a visitor learns that of the five Crown Dancers, one is called the Clown, or Messenger. The Clown Dancer is considered the most powerful of the five, the “boss.” He is both fierce but can bring relief and laughter.

Bobby Jones — one of the finest golfers and course designers in history — famously said, “On the golf course, a man may be a dogged victim of inexorable fate, be struck down by an appalling stroke of tragedy, become the hero of an unbelievable melodrama, or the clown in a side-splitting comedy — any of these within a few hours, and all without having to bury a corpse or repair a tangled personality.”

Seems the game of golf at Inn of the Mountain Gods is ruled by gods who distribute a varied menu of fates, including comedy. Bobby Jones did not live long enough to play at Inn of the Mountain Gods, but if he had, the Clown Dancer might well have had a message or two for him.

The island green and its waters await all comers.

Dr. Mark Wagner is a golf historian and the founding director of the Binienda Center for Civic Engagement at Worcester State University in Massachusetts. His book, "Native Links, the Surprising History... More by Mark Wagner

scraped.title: As Peggy Scott prepares to say ‘I Do,’ the Black women who fought to tell her story deserve their flowers, too
scraped.description: Peggy Scott and “The Gilded Age” fanbase are preparing to celebrate her big day we unpack who has made it even possible.
scraped.author: Kay Wicker
scraped.h1: As Peggy Scott prepares to say ‘I Do,’ the Black women who fought to tell her story deserve their flowers, too
scraped.body_text:
Peggy Scott and “The Gilded Age” fanbase are preparing to celebrate her big day. We unpack who has made it even possible.

Brocade gowns, delicate overcoats, hats, gloves, and full skirts were on full display as some of New York’s finest gathered at the iconic Central Park Boathouse to celebrate a bride-to-be whose impending nuptials have become the talk of high society.

The guest of honor was none other than Peggy Scott, of course, an accomplished journalist who has managed to find love among New York’s Black elite, even if her future mother-in-law isn’t entirely sold on the match. But despite what the above description suggests, this wasn’t a bridal luncheon in 1880s Manhattan. No, it was modern-day New York.

On Monday, Nov. 9, HBO, in collaboration with Da Gild, the show’s official Black fan community founded by activist Brittany Packnett Cunningham, hosted a lavish bridal luncheon for the fictional bride-to-be in the network’s hit period drama “The Gilded Age.”

“Peggy’s getting married, so naturally, we made an afternoon of it,” began the caption of a post shared on the show’s official Instagram page .

Some 100 guests arrived dressed in their finest Gilded Age-esque attire and delighted in food, decadent cakes, drinks, and a special conversation featuring members of the show’s cast, including Denée Benton—who has brought Peggy to life since the first season—Cynthia Nixon, and Jessica Frances Dukes, alongside executive producers Sonja Warfield and Davita Scarlett, and historian Erica Armstrong Dunbar.

The afternoon also celebrated Black content creators and featured several Black-owned businesses, including Brooklyn Blooms, BCakeNY, The Oyster Lover, Pastry Box, and Gladys Bookshop, just to name a few. Guests were also treated to an advance screening of the third episode of the show’s fourth season and sent home with hardcover journals inspired by Peggy’s first novel, “Friends in These Times.”

“We were so honored to help celebrate this auspicious occasion!! Founder @mspackyetti and Parlor Talk co-host @slynnyoung led a most beautiful conversation with stars of stage and screen, and our beloved members of Da Gild did indeed, as one might say, show up, and show out!” the fan community shared in the comments.

A post shared by The Gilded Age (@gildedagehbo)

It’s not lost on many how this moment in Peggy’s evolution from shy, demure secretary and aspiring writer to an accomplished journalist and the future Mrs. Kirkland wouldn’t be possible without the Black women who have been fighting to bring Peggy to life in full color behind the scenes.

Among them have been Warfield, the writer and executive producer who has helped shape Peggy’s storyline; director and executive producer Salli Richardson-Whitfield, who has brought her world to life on the screen; Dunbar, whose historical expertise has worked to ensure her story is told with accuracy; and, of course, Benton, who has fought to give the character the same depth and opportunities as her white co-stars.

Peggy was initially envisioned as a domestic worker with a much smaller role in the series among the larger upstairs-downstairs of American society, but Benton and Dunbar pushed for a more expansive portrayal, including a career befitting her education and a life that extended well past the homes of wealthy white New Yorkers. Benton also advocated for Black women to have a greater say behind the scenes, helping bring Warfield into the writers’ room and elevate Richardson-Whitfield and Dunbar to executive producer roles.

“There are some things that I can’t mention, but there were parts of Peggy that were entrenched in limited white imagination and entrenched in stereotypes,” Benton told Harper’s Bazaar in 2022.

The result has been a character whose story has evolved rapidly since viewers first met her while she was working as a secretary for Agnes van Rhijn, played by Christine Baranski. Drawing inspiration from pioneering Black writers like Ida B. Wells and Julia C. Collins, Peggy has since become an accomplished journalist at the New York Globe, published her first novel, and navigated family tensions, heartbreak, and eventually a healthy love with Dr. William Kirkland, played by Jordan Donica.

Her journey has also given audiences a glimpse of the Black New York that existed outside the Van Rhijn household, from her parents’ prosperous Brooklyn home to the offices of the New York Globe and the families, professionals, and social circles that made up the city’s thriving Black upper class. Phylicia Rashad joined the series as Peggy’s now soon-to-be mother-in-law, bringing even more color and candor, especially as she disapproves of Peggy for everything from her complexion to her career and growing activism.

“These are stories that haven’t been told,” Warfield told the Los Angeles Times in 2022 , adding how her own family’s history of prosperity is among her inspiration.

As Peggy’s story has grown on the screen, so has the enthusiasm among Black viewers, who have embraced both her character and the rich history depicted through her experiences in droves. That affection has grown into an official fan community, Da Gild, and its companion podcast, “Parlor Talk.”

Because, truthfully, Peggy has been something of an unexpected invitation for Black viewers to recollect a chapter of American history rarely afforded such an elegant treatment on screen. For once, the Black characters in a major period drama aren’t simply colorblind additions to an otherwise white world, nor are their lives exclusively depicted through their oppression at the hands of their white counterparts. They have their own society, and plenty of drama to go around.

It’s an invitation to remember that while racism and oppression were very much about the everyday realities of the late 19th century, Black life wasn’t always defined by it. And with Peggy’s wedding on the horizon, it’s one invitation we’re more than happy to accept.

scraped.title: Morris Brown president celebrates anonymous $700,000 gift: ‘We needed this good news!’
scraped.description: Morris Brown College president Kevin E. James says an anonymous donor gave the Atlanta HBCU $700,000 as it continues its recovery.
scraped.author: Odafe Oghen
scraped.h1: Morris Brown president celebrates anonymous $700,000 gift: ‘We needed this good news!’
scraped.body_text:
President Kevin E. James announced the contribution, expressing gratitude as the Atlanta HBCU continues its institutional resurgence.

Morris Brown College has another reason to celebrate as the historic Atlanta HBCU continues its institutional comeback. The college has received a $700,000 donation from an anonymous benefactor, a contribution that President Dr. Kevin E. James says is welcome news for the institution.

“We needed this good news!” James wrote in a Facebook post on Wednesday, Nov. 11 . “To the anonymous person who just donated $700,000 to Morris Brown College — THANK YOU!!”

Journalist Philip Lewis also shared news of the contribution on X Thursday , noting that James had announced the anonymous gift to the Atlanta-based HBCU.

While the identity of the donor and the intended use of the funds have not been publicly disclosed, the contribution represents a significant show of support for an institution that has spent years working to rebuild.

Founded in 1881 by the African Methodist Episcopal Church, Morris Brown College was established to provide higher education opportunities for Black Americans at a time when access to colleges and universities was severely restricted.

The institution faced significant financial and administrative challenges that culminated in the loss of its accreditation in 2002. The setback left the college without access to federal financial aid for students and threatened its long-term survival.

After years of working toward recovery, Morris Brown achieved a major milestone in April 2022 when it regained accreditation through the Transnational Association of Christian Colleges and Schools. The achievement restored its eligibility for federal financial aid and marked a turning point in its comeback.

James, who became president in 2019, has helped lead the institution through its rebuilding efforts, emphasizing enrollment growth, financial stability and renewed investment in the college’s future.

The latest donation arrives as Morris Brown continues strengthening its position among the nation’s historically Black colleges and universities. Although the donor has chosen to remain anonymous, the $700,000 gift offers another encouraging sign of support for an institution that has served generations of Black students.

scraped.body_text:
Sneed says the station attributed his departure to revenue concerns, but the announcement comes days after his exchange with Tennessee Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn, prompting speculation online.

FOX13 Memphis reporter Rob Sneed is speaking out after being let go from his freelance anchor and reporting position, a decision that has prompted questions from viewers following his recent exchange with Tennessee Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn.

In a social media statement, Sneed announced that FOX13 management informed him of the decision on Nov. 5, saying the station attributed it to financial considerations.

“I did not know this was coming,” Sneed wrote. “I was told the decision ultimately came down to the station’s revenue.”

A post shared by Rob Sneed (@rob_sneed_)

The departure comes days after Sneed questioned Blackburn about how she plans to serve Black Tennesseans following her historic gubernatorial victory. As FOX13 reported in its coverage of Blackburn’s election-night remarks , the Republican said she wanted to work with residents across the state.

During the exchange, Sneed asked, “How are you going to be able to help the Black American community?” When Blackburn responded that she hoped members of the community would work with her, Sneed followed up with a simple question: “How?”

Blackburn subsequently pointed to issues including maternal health and education, adding that Black Tennesseans would find her administration’s door open.

As Atlanta Black Star reported , the timing of Sneed’s departure has prompted speculation online about whether the two events are connected.

A FOX13 representative reportedly told the publication Unapologetically Memphis that Sneed’s departure was an HR matter and declined further comment. A source familiar with the situation also reportedly told the outlet that the decision involved a private matter unrelated to his exchange with Blackburn.

In his statement, Sneed reflected on his experience in Memphis, saying he accepted the opportunity after spending a year away from television news and taking a position for significantly less than his experience warranted.

“I wasn’t chasing a paycheck. I was chasing a second chance,” he wrote.

Despite the unexpected departure, Sneed expressed gratitude to viewers who welcomed him into their homes and reaffirmed his commitment to his career.

He also made clear that he is open to opportunities in television news, communications and public relations.

“My story is far from over,” Sneed wrote.

scraped.title: Keisha Lance Bottoms Defends Tyler Perry On Her Transition Team
scraped.h1: Keisha Lance Bottoms Claps Back at Critics of Her Choice to Add Tyler Perry to Transition Team
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms has heard all the online chatter about adding Tyler Perry to her transition team. And now she’s opening up about her reasoning!

By

Shanelle Genai

Published

ATLANTA, GEORGIA – NOVEMBER 9:(L-R) Keisha Lance Bottoms and Tyler Perry attend Tyler Perry’s “The Gospel Of Christmas” Atlanta Premiere at Tabernacle on November 9, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Prince Williams/WireImage)

Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms is taking the time to silence critics of her choice to add media mogul Tyler Perry to her transition team. Now Perry himself is adding his two cents to the conversation.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

Bottoms shared her explanation during a new interview on The Streetz Morning Takeover, hosted by Yung Joc, clarifying that Perry is just one of 10 co-chairs on her team. She went on to say that the group includes people whose work has impacted various sectors of the community. Citing Perry’s business acumen and work to bring jobs to the state, Bottoms made it clear that the team will eventually expand to include at least 100 people.

“Tyler is, one, a great friend. He’s a great human being. He has a multi-billion-dollar business in the heart of Atlanta,” she explained on the show. “He does a lot on behalf of the community. He employs a lot of people; he supports a lot of small businesses over at his studios. So it makes sense that he would be a part of it.”

Related: Keisha Lance Bottoms Adds Tyler Perry to Transition Team

In a separate interview with Atlanta’s WSB-TV during the premiere of his new Netflix film, “The Gospel of Christmas,” Perry spoke about being a part of Bottoms’ team, adding that he was “honored” to be asked. He explained that his close relationship with her started during her time as mayor.

“For her to ask me to be a part of it, I was honored. And I absolutely want to do all I can to make sure that she is put in the best position to succeed because she is a brilliant woman, very smart with a heart and compassion,” Perry began.

He went on to share that he called Governor Kemp after Bottoms won to discuss continuing “the level of business” with the state and how they could both support Bottoms in her new role.

“I had a conversation with him because I’ve had a great relationship with them. I said, how do we continue the level of business and amazingness that you’ve done and to be able to give her all the tools she needs to make sure that all of Georgia thrives, everybody in Georgia, no matter what the race,” Perry said.

As we previously told you , in the November 2026 midterm elections, Bottoms made history by becoming the state’s first Black governor and the first Black woman governor in American history. She’s set to be sworn in January 2027.

scraped.title: Black Men Urged to Start Prostate Cancer Screening at 45
scraped.h1: American Cancer Society’s New Prostate Cancer Guidelines Urge Black Men to Start Screening at 45
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

The leading cancer organization wants Black men to begin annual prostate cancer screening at 45 in an effort to address racial disparities.

By

Shellie M. Scott

Published

Doctor and patient engage in a focused healthcare consultation.

One of America’s most trusted cancer organizations has released new prostate cancer screening guidelines, giving Black men a clearer directive for early detection. In a Nov. 12 press release , the American Cancer Society (ACS) recommended that Black men start testing at 45 and continue every year through age 69, regardless of family history. That’s five years earlier than the recommended starting age for non-Black men at average risk, who are advised to have a prostate-specific antigen (PSA) blood test every two years from ages 50 through 69.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

Previously, the ACS emphasized discussing screening at age 45 rather than recommending regular testing. The PSA blood test measures the level of a substance made by the prostate. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), a high result doesn’t necessarily mean cancer , but a PSA test can help detect cancer earlier.

The updated guidelines reflect what evidence has already revealed. Earlier research from the society estimated that Black men’s rates of developing and dying from the disease were 70% to 110% higher than those of white men. The ACS also reported that prostate cancer can be treated and “eradicated” when detected early.

In the new press release, Dr. William Dahut, chief scientific officer at the ACS, addressed the disparities for Black men, saying, “By making a direct recommendation for men to engage in screening and advocating for earlier and more frequent screening for Black men, our aim is also to help reduce prostate cancer disparities and ease the disease burden.”

RELATED: How Black Women Living With Breast Cancer Can Build a Powerful Support Circle

However, not all organizations recommend the same schedule. For example, the CDC’s screening page shares the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force’s advice that men ages 55 to 69 should talk with their doctor about whether to get a PSA test.

Still, screening isn’t perfect. ABC News reported that testing can sometimes lead to false-positive results, overdiagnosis and treatments that might be harmful. The ACS says clinicians should explain risks and benefits before starting screening.

scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

Rumi Carter’s shopping preferences have been revealed and folks on the internet can’t stop raving over how relatable they are! Let’s talk about it.

By

Shanelle Genai

Published

Screenshot: TikTok

It seems like every new detail we learn about Rumi Carter, Beyoncé and Jay-Z’s youngest daughter, makes the internet love her even more. And the latest reveal about her shopping preferences is further proof of that!

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

If you somehow missed it, Bey spoke about Rumi during a new interview for i-D Magazine. In it, she shared how excited she is to pass down her archival looks and wardrobe to the nine-year-old and her older sister, Blue Ivy, especially now that they’re developing their own sense of unique style. Speaking to her love of clothes and fashion, Bey then revealed that there are two stores, specifically, that Rumi loves to spend time in.

“Rumi’s favorite place to shop right now is Ross and TJ Maxx these days,” Bey said.

Related: 7 of Our Favorite Rumi Carter Looks

And you know what? We can do nothing but heap praise on her because if you take one scroll on TikTok and know anything about women and their “dilly-dallying” agendas, those two stores seem to always make the list.

So the fact that Rumi is already up on game and knows about the cool clothes and home goods found at those stores at this young age is truly impressive. No wonder why her outfits are already conversation starters! And it’s also no wonder why folks online were gushing over her and cracking hilarious jokes over this new reveal.

“Rumi knows her pieces!!!! Wait until she get up in HomeGoods,” wrote one user on X/Twitter.

“RUMI KNOW A GOOD DEAL WHEN SHE SEE IT YES NIECE,” said another.

One other user wrote : “This means there are beautiful and unnecessary ass household décor items with impossibly removable stickers on them somewhere inside Beyoncé and Jay-Z’s multi-million dollar home and I LOVE THIS.”

Added another: “I’ve always felt like Beyoncé was a frugal queen, and this just confirms it bc how Rumi know about the Maxx, chile.”

Another user noted , “Rumi could dilly dally with me lol because same, niece.”

TJMaxx also eventually entered the chat, saying in the comments section on a TikTok video : “Rumi’s Maxxinista era? We’re so here for it!”

scraped.title: 'That Was Not In the Script': Ice Cube Says Mike Epps’ Impromptu Joke May Have Cost Him the Oprah Moment of a Lifetime
scraped.description: Ice Cube thinks one joke Mike Epps made years ago may explain why he was the only ‘Barbershop’ star left off Oprah Winfrey’s show.
scraped.author: Sharmaine Johnson
scraped.h1: ‘That Was Not In the Script’: Ice Cube Says Mike Epps’ Impromptu Joke May Have Cost Him the Oprah Moment of a Lifetime
scraped.body_text:
Ice Cube thinks one joke Mike Epps made years ago may explain why he was the only ‘Barbershop’ star left off Oprah Winfrey’s show.

Mike Epps may have played a part in why Ice Cube missed out on an opportunity with Oprah Winfrey.

Epps and Cube have been friends for decades, co-starring in movies like “Next Friday” and “Friday After Next.”

But one unscripted joke in a separate film reportedly complicated things for Cube and his “Barbershop” cast mates.

During the Nov. 11 episode of “ Club Shay Shay ,” Shannon Sharpe spoke with Ice Cube and Epps about collaborations and their work over the years.

Sharpe asked Cube why he wasn’t included in a 2006 press stop on Oprah Winfrey’s self-titled talk show for “Barbershop.”

Despite his role in bringing the comedy to life, the N.W.A. founding member vividly remembers being excluded from Winfrey’s show.

He suggested that an unscripted joke in “All About the Benjamins” years earlier may have played a part in why he missed the opportunity.

Released on March 8, 2002, the film stars Cube as bounty hunter Bucum Jackson. Epps plays Reggie Wright, a small-time con artist who gets caught up in a diamond heist.

The two initially find themselves on opposite sides of the law before teaming up to track down the stolen diamonds.

Cube recalled a scene in which the pair search for a gun inside a fish tank filled with dangerous sea creatures. He also explained how Epps came up with the Oprah reference.

“You know when we was looking for the gun through the motherf—g thing with the sharks in there, the fish tank? I said, ‘Stick your hand in there,’ and he was like, ‘Man, it’s better, I might as well stick my, you know, in Oprah’s a—.’”

The official line from the scene was, “You trying to be funny. That’s like asking me to stick my tongue in Oprah Winfrey’s a—! I’m not f—g sticking my hand in there!”

Apparently, the West Coast native wasn’t expecting Epps to take the joke there. He clarified that Epps came up with the line himself.

“That was not in the script, homie. I got the script, bro. That was straight ad-lib. I wouldn’t even have thought of that line,” Ice Cube explained.

Epps immediately turned his attention to Oprah, jokingly asking why she was watching a movie with that kind of dialogue.

“Oprah, why are you watching movies like this?” he said.

Epps’ explanation also prompted a conversation about how much room actors typically have to improvise. He explained that he usually receives scripts with much of the dialogue already written.

Previously in the conversation, Ice Cube shared the 70/30 breakdown, explaining that about 70 percent of what audiences see is written, while the remaining 30 percent leaves room for improvisation.

That allowed Epps to add his own personality to the role, including the unexpected Oprah punchline.

“Yeah, man. I was like, that’s probably what did it,” he admitted.

The comedian eventually shifted into damage-control mode, making sure Oprah knew that he had nothing but love for her.

“Oprah, you know I love you. My mother always loved the Oprah show,” Epps said to the camera.

Cube wasn’t buying the sudden show of affection and accused his co-star of kissing up to the talk show legend. Epps laughed it off, adding, “No, I got to start reading these scripts better.”

Meanwhile, Cube and Epps have another project bringing them together. The longtime collaborators recently launched their podcast, “ Listen and Laugh ,” with its first episode premiering Nov. 6.

The inaugural episode featured fellow hip-hop legend Dr. Dre as their first guest, allowing fans to hear the trio share stories and conversations about music and entertainment.

The wider picture isn't any steadier. Newspaper ad revenue has fallen more than 80% since 2005, and local newsrooms are closing at a rate of roughly two a week nationwide. When outlets go under, it's rarely the ones built to center a Black perspective from the ground up that get to stick around.

scraped.title: Trump’s Attempt to Drag Obama Into Questions About His Growing Fortune Takes an Embarrassing Turn When Reporter Challenges His Claim
scraped.description: Trump tried to deflect questions about his family’s business dealings by dragging Obama into the conversation. He dragged Obama into a corruption discussion with a Netflix claim that a fact-check quickly shut down.
scraped.author: Yohance Kyles
scraped.h1: Trump’s Attempt to Drag Obama Into Questions About His Growing Fortune Takes an Embarrassing Turn When Reporter Challenges His Claim
scraped.body_text:
Trump tried to deflect questions about his family’s business dealings by dragging Obama into the conversation. He dragged Obama into a corruption discussion with a Netflix claim that a fact-check quickly shut down.

President Donald Trump suffered an embarrassing loss in the midterm elections.

But the egocentric billionaire still has former President Barack Obama on his mind after those defeats.

Trump, 80, watched MAGA Republicans get demolished across the nation. Obama, 65, saw his Democratic Party take control of the U.S. House and Senate as well as key governorships.

The sitting president gave his first sit-down interview since the electoral rout with “60 Minutes.”

CBS News correspondent Ross Douthat questioned the commander in chief about various topics.

In particular, Trump was asked about foreign entities investing in a private company run by the GOP leader’s son. Voters cited corruption as a top issue behind the so-called blue tsunami at the ballot box.

“Look, every president has a problem,” Trump insisted before going into a long diatribe about his staff, the media, George Washington, Wall Street and cryptocurrency.

Around two minutes later, Trump turned his attention to Obama by pushing a demonstrably false narrative about his White House predecessor.

“Look at Obama. Obama got from Netflix… How much did Obama get? Obama got $100 million to make a movie,” Trump claimed.

Douthat informed him, “Obama did that after his presidency.”

The current president jumped back in to wrongly declare, “No, he didn’t. He made the deal during his presidency.”

Trump’s falsehoods continued when he also said, “Obama got $100 million from Netflix during his presidency. And he made a movie afterward, and the movie made about three cents.”

Factcheck.org called Trump’s assertions “false.” Obama and his wife, former First Lady Michelle Obama, signed a multi-year deal with Netflix in 2018.

The couple’s Higher Ground Productions inked the contract with the streaming giant a year after Obama left the White House. He served from 2009 to 2017. The financial terms of the deal were not publicly disclosed.

Meanwhile, Trump has increased his estimated net worth by roughly $2.7 billion since winning the 2024 presidential election , according to Forbes.

His growing fortune has been fueled by cryptocurrency ventures, including meme coins, international real estate deals and licensing agreements.

First Lady Melania Trump also secured a lucrative entertainment deal ahead of her husband’s second inauguration.

In January 2025, Amazon reportedly agreed to pay $40 million to license a documentary about the former model and a related project.

Trump faced an avalanche of criticism. His attempt to tie his own questionable business connections while in office to Obama’s post-White House move into the entertainment business stirred controversy.

“When someone uses a whataboutism, they are admitting that they are guilty and are just trying to deflect,” suggested an Instagram user.

Another poster on the app wrote, “We are all exhausted from all this grift and corruption, hence the midterm blue trouncing! Read the room, Republicans.”

“What? He lied? What a surprise,” read one sarcastic comment. A second jokester predicted, “In the future, ‘Trumping’ is going to be slang for lying.”

Several people zeroed in on Trump constantly talking about Obama. Many observers believe that obsession stems from Obama making fun of Trump at the White House Correspondents’ Association Dinner in 2011.

“Talk about a guy living rent-free in his head,” joked a commenter about Trump’s one-sided fixation on Obama. Likewise, someone proclaimed, “He is so infatuated with Obama.”

The Obamas’ Higher Ground Productions has been behind several Netflix feature films, including “Fatherhood” and “Worth” in 2021, followed by “Rustin” and “Leave the World Behind” in 2023.

Their documentary film credits on Netflix include the Oscar-winning “American Factory” (2019), “Becoming” (2020), “American Symphony” (2023) and “Air Force Elite: Thunderbirds” (2025).

“We hope to cultivate and curate the talented, inspiring, creative voices who are able to promote greater empathy and understanding between peoples, and help them share their stories with the entire world,” Obama stated in a May 2018-dated press release from Netflix.

Michelle, 62, added, “Barack and I have always believed in the power of storytelling to inspire us, to make us think differently about the world around us, and to help us open our minds and hearts to others.”

scraped.title: Rubio Racked Up $1.2M Taxpayer Tab for Personal Trips and His Estimated Payback Is a Joke, But Leavitt’s Defense Takes the Cake
scraped.description: Marco Rubio’s trips to his son’s college town racked up a $1.2 million government flight bill. Karoline Leavitt’s defense only fueled the backlash.
scraped.author: ArLuther Lee
scraped.h1: Rubio Racked Up $1.2M Taxpayer Tab for Personal Trips and His Estimated Payback Is a Joke, But Leavitt’s Defense Takes the Cake
scraped.body_text:
Marco Rubio’s trips to his son’s college town racked up a $1.2 million government flight bill. Karoline Leavitt’s defense only fueled the backlash.

Marco Rubio has made it a point to attend his son’s college football games, even when it requires flying hundreds of miles from Washington on a government aircraft.

At a recent University of Florida Gators game, the secretary of state arrived at Gainesville Regional Airport aboard a military jet, where security officers and a convoy of SUVs were waiting to transport him to campus.

For most parents, following their children’s college sports careers can be an expensive commitment.

For Rubio, taxpayers have been footing much of the bill.

A Washington Post investigation found that Rubio has accumulated more than $1.2 million in government flight costs while traveling to Gainesville, Florida, where his son Anthony plays football for the University of Florida.

Although federal rules require Rubio to reimburse the government for personal travel, the estimated reimbursement based on commercial airfare would be about $18,000. Neither Rubio nor the State Department has disclosed how much he has actually repaid.

The State Department confirmed that Rubio has traveled to Gainesville aboard government aircraft at least 23 times since taking office last year. At least 10 trips coincided with Florida Gators football games, including five this fall.

The department classified 15 trips as “solely personal,” with estimated flight costs totaling approximately $770,600. Another seven trips combined personal and official travel, adding $443,900, according to the Post’s calculations using Defense Department flight rates.

The newspaper excluded Rubio’s most recent trip from its $1.2 million estimate because the State Department declined to answer questions about it.

Rubio primarily travels aboard Gulfstream C-37A and C-37B jets, which the Defense Department charges other federal agencies approximately $9,100 per flight hour to use, the Post reported. On three occasions, he traveled aboard a larger Boeing C-32A, an aircraft commonly used to transport the vice president and other senior government officials. Those flights cost approximately $18,600 per hour.

Security rules prohibit Rubio, the defense secretary, and the directors of the FBI and CIA from flying commercially. As a result, he must use government aircraft even for personal travel.

Federal rules require him to reimburse taxpayers only what an economy-class commercial ticket would have cost, rather than the actual expense of operating the aircraft.

The Post estimated that a round-trip commercial ticket between Washington and Gainesville on game days averaged $820. Applied to Rubio’s personal travel, that would put his estimated reimbursement at about $18,000—a small fraction of the $1.2 million government flight bill.

Rubio defended his travel in a statement to the newspaper, saying, “I have and will continue to try and make it to as many events that are important to me personally and to my family as possible.”

Assistant Secretary of State Dylan Johnson also defended Rubio’s use of government aircraft, saying they are necessary to “ensure continuity of operations, continuity of government and access to secure communications at all times. And he will continue to do so.”

But the frequency of Rubio’s personal trips has raised questions about whether following the rules is enough to satisfy a public official’s responsibility to taxpayers.

Cynthia Brown, senior ethics counsel at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, said federal rules may permit the trips, but they still raise concerns about how Rubio spends taxpayer money.

“If this travel becomes something that is undermining the integrity of your service, are you really taking care of taxpayer dollars the way that you’re obligated to as a public official?” Brown asked.

She described the issue as “more of an optics issue than a violation” but added that although it may not be “technically improper, it is something that I think is really important to shine the light on.”

The scrutiny also creates an uncomfortable contrast with Rubio’s own position on government travel before joining the Trump administration. In 2023, while serving as a Republican senator, he demanded an investigation into then-Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg’s use of government aircraft.

“American taxpayers deserve assurances that their tax dollars are not wasted by the government’s highest officials,” Rubio wrote at the time.

An inspector general ultimately found that Buttigieg complied with federal rules, with his government aircraft travel totaling $59,000.

Rubio’s football devotion is well established, according to the Post. His son Anthony, a walk-on running back who did not receive an athletic scholarship, is now a senior at Florida. He has appeared in only four games over four years, accumulating 75 yards and scoring one touchdown. Rubio has attended every game his son has played, along with several in which Anthony never smelled the field.

Rather than address the unanswered questions about the reimbursement, former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt took a different approach after the Post published its findings.

“Washington Post confirms Secretary Rubio is a great dad,” she wrote on X.

The response did not sit well with critics, who argued that being a supportive parent does not explain why taxpayers should shoulder the cost of repeated personal trips.

“His child is an adult,” one person said . “Most parents with a college athlete can’t afford to go to every game. But when @SecRubio does it on the tax payer dime, we’re supposed to applaud? I couldn’t afford to go to all my daughters competitions… so out of touch.”

Another critic questioned why ordinary taxpayers should subsidize the personal activities of Cabinet officials.

“He can go to his son’s game on his own dime. I’m sick of paying for Trump and his Cabinet officials entertainment. Greedy Pigs!”

A third reaction broadened the criticism beyond Rubio, pointing to a growing pattern of complaints about the administration’s use of public resources.

“Thank God voters showed up. We are sick and tired of the constant grift and corruption. Each one is worse than the one before.”

Outlets like ours get roughly 1% of the $170 billion spent on U.S. advertising each year, and that margin is shrinking further as advertisers walk back the DEI-linked commitments they made in 2020. The wider picture isn't any steadier. Newspaper ad revenue has fallen more than 80% since 2005, and local newsrooms are closing at a rate of roughly two a week nationwide. When outlets go under, it's rarely the ones built to center a Black perspective from the ground up that get to stick around.

scraped.title: How Black Organizers Overcame Alabama’s Latest Gerrymandering Effort
scraped.description: Years of organizing helped to overcome a redrawn map, but activists warn that this success doesn’t make the map any less discriminatory.
scraped.author: Brandon Tensley
scraped.h1: How Black Organizers Overcame Alabama’s Latest Gerrymandering Effort
scraped.body_text:
Capital B News

Read them in Seen & Heard, our free, twice-weekly newsletter.

The night U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures of Alabama learned that he had won reelection, history was in the room.

Walking to the stage to give his victory speech at Ravello Ristorante in Montgomery, Alabama, he passed Sheyann Webb-Christburg, 70, who was about 8 years old in 1965 when she joined activists on the Edmund Pettus Bridge on “Bloody Sunday” in their fight for voting rights.

Figures, a Democrat, told Capital B that he thought about his parents and other relatives who had shaped his life, as well as the sacrifices that his wife and children had made while he was on the campaign trail. But he also thought about people beyond his family who had paved a path for him.

“It’s those people that, you know, this victory meant more to than it ever could to me,” he said, referring to Webb-Christburg, whom Martin Luther King Jr. dubbed the “smallest freedom fighter.”

His triumph this month was, to many, an unexpected rebuke of Republican efforts to weaken Black voting power in Alabama, where activists had spent years fighting for fairer congressional representation. His win also reflected the strength of an organizing network that had prepped for political and legal setbacks long before the midterms. The results offered a lesson in how Black voters and activists could overcome a political landscape that had shifted dramatically right beneath their feet — even as they continued to challenge the fairness of the map.

“Black voters sent a resounding message that we cannot be silenced or counted out,” Janai Nelson, the president and director-counsel of the Legal Defense Fund, said of the Black voting strength that was on display in the South and beyond on election night. “Now, it is imperative that every eligible voter stays engaged and vigilant.”

The stakes couldn’t have been higher, particularly for those activists who had spent years struggling for a second heavily Black congressional district. In 2023, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld a lower court’s ruling that Alabama’s map had violated the Voting Rights Act of 1965 by giving Black voters control in only one district, or 14%, though Black voters make up roughly 27% of the state’s voting-age population. A new map subsequently gave them control in two districts, or 28%, clearing the way for Figures’ first win in 2024.

But that achievement came under threat in June of this year. Following the Supreme Court’s decision in April further eroding the Voting Rights Act, Alabama Republicans returned to an earlier map that reduces the Black voting-age population of Figures’ district from 49% to 40%. The change meant that Figures would have to compete for the support of voters who hadn’t previously been part of his constituency.

Figures’ Republican opponent, state Rep. Rhett Marques, suggested in May that the new map didn’t go far enough. “Alabamians deserve congressional representation that reflects who we are: a proudly conservative, red state. That means a 7-0 map, not 6-1,” he said .

Those gerrymandered boundaries didn’t stop Figures from winning the contest. He secured about 54% of the vote, according to the AP . Marques conceded before Figures’ campaign was ready to declare victory. Figures recalled a sense of relief that was quickly followed by deep gratitude for everyone who had given him another term.

“People had entrusted us once again to be able to do the work that we love to do — and on behalf of the people we love,” he said.

Evan Milligan was driving to a watch party in Montgomery when a friend texted him the news that Figures had won. He had to pull over and soak in the moment.

For Milligan — the named plaintiff in the case that led to the creation of Figures’ district — and other activists, the race’s outcome was the result of efforts they had begun long ago. This work stretched back at least to 2021, when activists began meeting regularly to prepare for the next round of redistricting and possible Republican gerrymandering.

Milligan recalled how various groups would connect every two weeks to coordinate their efforts. During those Zoom meetings, they would share updates, discuss legal strategies, and figure out which groups were working and in which parts of the state.

Those discussions, Milligan said, helped to establish relationships across groups that didn’t always agree on how to challenge Republican redistricting. Some favored pursuing claims under the Voting Rights Act, while others advocated for an approach that prioritized using the language of keeping counties intact. But those disagreements didn’t prevent them from sticking together. They ultimately forged a network that could respond swiftly when the political environment shifted.

“We evolve, we change, we have to be able to adapt,” Milligan, who was in a Berlin church when he received a text message in 2023 saying that he had won a major voting rights case against Alabama, told Capital B.

“The community’s ability to overcome a barrier doesn’t mean that the barrier was justified in the first place.”

Anneshia Hardy , Alabama Values executive director

That preparation proved to be essential when the Supreme Court in June allowed Alabama to revert to a map that reduced the Black voting-age population share of Figures’ district. Activists worked to identify communities needing additional outreach, harmonizing their efforts so that, as Milligan put it, “no corner [of the district] was left untouched.” The work included nonpartisan voter education as well as separate efforts by campaigns to persuade voters.

Anneshia Hardy, the executive director of Alabama Values, a nonprofit grassroots organization, was one of the activists leading these efforts. On election night, she spent 12 hours in an election protection operation in Montgomery, responding to reports of voting problems. Afterward, she joined relatives at her cousin’s house for a watch party. Her aunt, a cashier, was eager to hear Hardy’s debrief.

For Hardy, this engagement sprang from years of legal fights over voting rights. The litigation had created opportunities to reach voters who might not have been paying attention as the map battle played out. Some had testified during the proceedings and learned about the ramifications of redrawing boundaries. This participation, in turn, deepened their relationships with organizations working to protect Black access to the franchise.

After the latest Supreme Court decision, Hardy said, activists built on those preexisting relationships. In part, that organizing looked like establishing community hubs and working groups. But it also entailed reaching people in spaces not typically associated with politics, using the redistricting fight to shine a light on how decisions about voting boundaries could affect every facet of someone’s life: access to healthcare, the cost of living, and more.

But Hardy cautioned against buying into the narrative that Republicans’ gerrymandering efforts “didn’t work.” Black communities have long organized under unequal conditions, from the push against Jim Crow-era voter suppression to more recent legal battles over redistricting, she explained, and their success in overcoming obstacles shouldn’t be used to diminish the seriousness of those obstacles.

“The community’s ability to overcome a barrier doesn’t mean that the barrier was justified in the first place,” she told Capital B.

Some analysts have stressed that, without gerrymandering, Black voters would have still more seats in Congress. The lawmakers they helped to elect, they say, face a clear charge to bolster voting rights protections — for instance by passing the elusive John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act — so that Black political representation doesn’t hinge on overcoming gerrymandered maps.

For Figures, the altered boundaries required his campaign to expand to reach a different electorate. He explained that approximately 60% of the population in the new district had previously been represented by him. This meant that he had to be intentional about introducing himself to voters across a different geographic area.

But he maintained that the issues that mattered to residents — the cost of living, agriculture, rural hospitals, infrastructure — were largely unchanged.

“The message we were getting to people and how we were getting the message to people, none of that changed,” Figures said. “The only thing that changed is where we were getting that message to.”

Brandon Tensley is Capital B's national politics reporter. More by Brandon Tensley

scraped.title: Democrats Spent Millions to Win, Just Not in These Southern States
scraped.description: Close Senate losses in Louisiana and Florida reveal a split between the party’s voting rights message and its investment in Black political power in the South.
scraped.author: Adam Mahoney
scraped.h1: Democrats Spent Millions to Win, Just Not in These Southern States
scraped.body_text:
Capital B News

Read them in Seen & Heard, our free, twice-weekly newsletter.

BATON ROUGE, Louisiana — Walking through the bright blue and yellow doors of Ryan Elementary School to cast his first-ever ballot, 18-year-old Altori Doherty had never heard the name Jamie Davis, a Black Democrat running to be Louisiana’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.

Neither had 37-year-old Thedric Haney. Nor had 25-year-old Vivian Hayes.

Down the river in New Orleans’ Ninth Ward, 39-year-old Arlet Wylie was in the dark, too.

Ultimately, Davis lost the Senate race by 1.7 points to Republican challenger Julia Letlow. Some of that loss rests on a lack of investment by the national Democratic Party across the state, advocates and residents said.

In the weeks leading up to the election, the party and its affiliates spent nothing on ads there, according to AdImpact via Wesleyan Media Project.

It wasn’t just Louisiana. Florida and Mississippi’s lack of investment also stand out.

Four of the seven closest Senate races — South Carolina, Florida, Mississippi, and Louisiana — were in the South. Yet groups affiliated with the national Democratic Party spent $11.8 million on ads across those states in the weeks before the election. By comparison, the other states — Ohio, Alaska, and Iowa — received $81.7 million, roughly nine times as much per race.

For Black voters and organizers, the narrow margins in Florida, Louisiana, and Mississippi exposed a contradiction at the heart of Democrats’ midterm success. National Democrats made the fight over Black voting rights a rallying cry without making several of the states at the center of that fight a spending priority.

But the decisions played out differently across the three states. In Louisiana, Davis struggled to become known in a state national Democrats had largely written off. In Florida, senatorial candidate Angie Nixon’s supporters saw resistance not just to the state’s electoral prospects, but to her politics as a Democratic Socialist. In Mississippi, party leaders ignored signs that the senatorial race was winnable. There, the national calculation eventually changed, but the largest advertising commitments came late.

In interviews, advocates described a cycle in which national Democrats have treated Southern states as unwinnable, withholding the resources needed to reach voters, then leaving local organizers to overcome both the barriers to Black political participation and the belief that nothing will change.

At the national level, Black Southerners have “been overlooked and made not a priority for as long as I can remember,” said Ashley Shelton, a Baton Rouge resident and founder of the Power Coalition for Equity and Justice.

Shelton has fought for years for greater Black political participation and was a defendant in the congressional redistricting case trying to maintain equal Black representation in the state.

In Louisiana, many voters that Capital B met were unaware that their home was at the center of the largest voting rights struggle in generations.

In April, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the state’s 2024 congressional map, finding that the state had engaged in unconstitutional racial gerrymandering when it created a second majority-Black district. The decision weakened the guarantees for fair voting representation among minority voters nationwide.

In the weeks leading up to Nov. 3, Shelton saw map after map that “left out Florida, Louisiana, Texas, and Mississippi as winnable Senate races.”

The Democrats would go on to win Texas and are currently leading in the Mississippi race, but “if [the national party] would send us like 10% of what they’re willing to spend in a battleground state like Ohio, it would make a huge difference in states like Louisiana and Florida,” Shelton said.

In Louisiana, the investment gap was visible in a basic fact: Voters did not know the Democratic U.S. Senate candidate’s name.

More than half of the nearly two dozen voters Capital B interviewed on Election Day in Baton Rouge and New Orleans had never heard of Davis or knew little about his campaign. Davis himself told WAFB -TV that his campaign found roughly 35% to 40% of Louisiana voters still did not know who he was.

U.S. Rep. Troy Carter, a Black Democrat from New Orleans, said he sought $2 million from national Democrats for Davis during the campaign’s final three weeks, as polling suggested a tightening race. Carter said some money arrived, but “not nearly as much as we would have liked.”

Davis, a farmer, said that additional funding could have paid for door-knocking and an immediate response to a late attack advertisement that he said used artificial intelligence and misrepresented his positions.

In Florida, there were doubts about whether the national party wanted to invest in Nixon.

Erica Hall, a Florida food access advocate who spoke with hundreds of voters this year, said, “Too many party leaders treated her as a risky choice because she is a Democratic Socialist.”

Darius Jones, founder of the National Black Empowerment Council, also said he believed Nixon’s politics contributed to the party’s hesitation.

Nixon campaigned on Medicare for All, a $25 federal minimum wage, universal child care, stronger union protections, and a wealth tax on billionaires.

To Hall, the primary had already settled the question of whom the party should support.

“It was a diverse group of voters that chose her as a nominee, and the party had a responsibility to invest in her campaign and give her a real chance to compete,” she said.

Nixon ultimately fell about 3 percentage points short. In the final weeks before the election, she said she lacked enough money to run a single television advertisement. The Washington Post reported that the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee did not spend on her race.

In Mississippi, Scott Colom, who defeated the Republican incumbent after a prolonged ballot count, had early champions. U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock of Georgia helped raise money for voter registration and mobilization.

But when Warnock first urged donors in April at a Washington, D.C., fundraiser to take Mississippi seriously, members of the audience laughed, CNN reported.

By Labor Day, Democratic political action committees were encouraging donors and allied groups to consider the race as polling and the wider Senate map improved Democrats’ prospects.

The group announced its first Mississippi advertising campaign on Oct. 20, two weeks before Election Day, committing $1.2 million.

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee did not respond to Capital B’s requests for comment. A spokesperson for the Democratic National Committee said: “This midterm election’s historic results in the South proved our theory of the case: that when you invest and organize everywhere, you can win anywhere.”

The DNC sent between $17,500 and $22,500 a month to every Southern state chapter this year. (As of mid-2026, the DNC held roughly $18.5 million in debt against approximately $16.3 million in cash on hand, putting the committee more than $2 million in the red.)

“The DNC played an important role in expanding the map and flipping seats up and down the ballot,” the spokesperson added.

More money would not have guaranteed a victory. But the closeness of the races in Louisiana and Florida has sharpened a question Black organizers say the party can no longer avoid: How much of the South’s Republican dominance reflects voters’ preferences, and how much is sustained by decisions not to compete?

For many that Capital B spoke with, the lack of support exposed a party leadership too removed from the Black communities it counted on and from the economic pressures shaping their lives. Black candidates were left to compete without the resources they needed, while Black voters were asked to deliver victories without a meaningful say in where the party placed its bets.

Shelton said national leaders had neglected people “outside their own tax bracket,” even as those voters faced threats to health care and food assistance.

Hall saw a national party that expected Black women to deliver votes “without seeing them as real people.”

“Don’t just come to our neighborhood to get our votes and speak at a church,” she said. “That’s empty to me. This is the most engaged I’ve seen Black Florida in a long time, and it was without [national Democratic] support.”

Organizers say the missing investment means fewer opportunities to connect voters’ concerns about grocery prices, utility bills, healthcare, and schools to the candidates asking to represent them — and less support for the year-round work of building political power in communities whose votes the party depends on elsewhere.

Jones, of the National Black Empowerment Council, offered a more favorable assessment of the broader election results, arguing that victories by other Black candidates demonstrated a path to political power through coalition-building.

Across the historically Republican South this midterm election, Democrats won 63 congressional races compared to 92 Republican victories. There are still over 20 uncalled races.

About 9 in 10 Black voters supported the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race this year, up from about 8 in 10 who supported Kamala Harris’ presidential campaign in 2024. In Florida, 90% of Black voters supported Nixon.

The national Democratic Party’s “conversation about the Supreme Court’s efforts to roll back the Black vote … led to increased turnout,” Jones said, and even with losses in Louisiana and Florida, “that’s going to help make things better for Black people on the issues that are most important to our community.”

In the week since the election, Davis has said that he is weighing a run for governor next year and, if he does not enter that race, plans to run for Senate in 2028. Next time, he said, he would start campaigning earlier.

Nixon is unsure about running again. She questioned whether the party valued Black candidates’ leadership as much as the voters they mobilized. Two days after the election, she announced Never Scared PAC, an organization focused on civic engagement, developing local leaders, and building political power for working families. Its first announced task was training activists to press lawmakers about potential budget cuts and their effects on working families and seniors.

With the race in Mississippi still unresolved, the question was not only whether the late push would prove sufficient, but whether Democrats would approach the next campaign differently. Before the election, Colom had urged the party to invest in rebuilding its Southern strength.

Some Black organizers remain disappointed.

Gary Chambers, a former Senate candidate from Baton Rouge, said that in the week after the election, Black Louisianans “are doggishly proud of the work we have done here. We are ashamed of the party that has ignored us.”

“I see the consequences when communities are asked to organize, volunteer, and vote, but the resources and support don’t follow,” Hall added. “It’s disheartening, especially for people like me on the front lines that’s out here really doing the work. I’m not in an ivory tower talking. I’m out here on the ground every single day.”

Chambers took it a step forward: “So for every district that was won all over this country, you owe a debt to Baton Rouge,” he said. “You owe a debt to Louisiana because none of this would have been possible if it were not for the fighters here.”

Adam Mahoney is the climate and environment reporter at Capital B. He can be reached by email at adam.mahoney@capitalbnews.org, on Bluesky, and on X at @AdamLMahoney. More by Adam Mahoney
