scraped.title: Mississippi Elects Its First Black U.S. Senator in 150 Years
scraped.description: After a prolonged ballot count, the state joins the “blue wave” by electing a Democrat to serve in Washington.
scraped.author: Aallyah Wright
scraped.h1: Mississippi Elects Its First Black U.S. Senator in 150 Years
scraped.body_text:
Capital B News

Read them in Seen & Heard, our free, twice-weekly newsletter.

One week after nearly a million voters cast their ballots, the results are in. Mississippians picked a new U.S. senator: Scott Colom, the district attorney from Columbus.

Colom defeated incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become the first Black person the state has sent to the Senate in more than 150 years. He received 49% of the vote, leading Hyde-Smith by more than 4,500 votes.

“I’ve always said this campaign belongs to the people of Mississippi, and I’m incredibly proud of everyone who made their voice heard,” Colom wrote in a post on Nov. 9. “I’ll work every day in the U.S. Senate to build a future that generations of Mississippians can be just as proud to call home.”

Many voters who said they voted for Colom told Capital B he listened to their concerns, from farmers facing high diesel prices to funneling resources to keep rural hospitals open.

“What’s urgent to me is I see that the person that’s in office now is not looking out for everybody’s best interest,” said Vince Davis, 62. “What I see from Scott is that he is for all Mississippians because he’s for lower costs, he’s for higher wages, and he’s for healthcare. I don’t see that cause being uplifted from Cindy.”

Colom didn’t just win over Black voters. He also outperformed in Republican counties such as Forrest, Lafayette and Oktibbeha. He flipped at least 18 counties, according to a preliminary analysis by the Jackson newspaper Clarion Ledger.

The ballot counting process — and casting a vote on Election Day — didn’t go without hiccups. Many voters who didn’t know they had been marked inactive had to cast an affidavit, or provisional, ballot. They experienced long lines and were directed to travel to different locations to get their ballots corrected. Volunteers who observed the counting also reported challenges with accessing correct information about location and meeting times to be present while the election commissioners began counting.

The NAACP congratulated Mississippians for their historic participation in the midterms. The organization said voters had to overcome confusion at the ballot box and attempts of intimidation.

“They showed up for their communities, for their families, and for the future of their state. They reminded the nation that we the people have the power,” Derrick Johnson, NAACP president, said in a statement.

He praised the efforts of the Mississippi State Conference NAACP, which opened 11 field offices, knocked on more than 150,000 doors across half of counties, and registered more than 17,000 voters. The effort was part of the organization’s get-out-the-vote campaign.

“Our work didn’t stop when the polls closed. We doubled down, helping voters cure their ballots, observing the counting process, and ensuring all eligible votes were counted. Mississippi voters fought throughout this election, and we were proud to stand alongside them from registration to certification,” said Charles Taylor, president of the Mississippi chapter.

Neither campaign has stated if it will challenge the election results. Unlike other states, Mississippi does not have a recount law. However, a candidate can request to examine the ballot boxes within 12 days of the election. Either party still has the option to make a legal challenge.

scraped.title: US renews push to open Pacific marine protected area to fishing
scraped.description: Environmental science and conservation news
scraped.h1: US renews push to open Pacific marine protected area to fishing
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

The U.S. government has published proposed rules to allow commercial fishing in an area more than double the size of California inside a Pacific marine reserve that encompasses a network of islands, atolls, seamounts and coral reef systems.

The proposed rules, published Nov. 9 by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), or NOAA Fisheries, would lift fishing restrictions around Johnston Atoll, Wake Island, and Jarvis Island in the Pacific Islands Heritage Marine National Monument (PIH). Commercial fishing would be permitted between 50 and 200 nautical miles (93-185 kilometers) from these islands, while waters within 50 nmi would remain off-limits to protect species and habitats. The total affected area covers 1 million square kilometers (408,000 square miles).

In its proposal, NOAA says the rules would support the “long-term sustainability of U.S. fisheries,” and align with previous directives from the Trump administration to increase fishing in the Pacific, including a presidential proclamation in April calling for the “unleashing” of commercial fishing in the PIH . At the same time, NOAA also says fishing in the PIH may only have a “minor” beneficial impact on fisheries operations and management.

The proposed rules are open for public comment until Dec. 9.

Activists have criticized the proposal and NOAA Fisheries’ characterization of the potential harm to cultural resources and protected species as “negligible.”

“The ocean has always been a place of connection for Pacific peoples, and the Pacific Islands Heritage Marine National Monument has important historical and cultural ties,” William Aila, a Native Hawaiian fisherman and former chair of the Hawaiʻi Department of Land and Natural Resources, said in a statement. “These same waters provide threatened and endangered wildlife a rare refuge where they can feed, breed, and recover. Many Pacific Islander descendants have answered the call to protect this special area, and we are hopeful that their comments will allow us to protect this place for generations to come.”

The PIH has 5,000-year-old coral reef systems, 165 known seamounts that serve as biodiversity hotspots, and hosts threatened species such as seabirds, sharks, rays, whales, and sea turtles, according to the Pacific Islands Heritage Coalition.

This isn’t the first time the government has attempted to allow commercial fishing in the PIH. In April 2025, NOAA Fisheries issued a letter calling for the authorization of fishing in parts of the protected area. However, U.S. conservation groups represented by environmental law organization Earthjustice won a lawsuit to stop it from moving forward. Now, David Henkin, an attorney at Earthjustice, says the group is prepared to sue again.

“We prevailed in court the last time this happened,” he said in a statement , “and we’ll head back to court again to defend the pristine waters of the Pacific Islands Heritage Marine National Monument.”

Banner image: Coral at Jarvis Island in the Pacific Islands Heritage Marine National Monument. Image by USFWS/Jim Maragos via Flickr ( CC BY 2.0 ).

scraped.title: After years of speculation, Suriname evicts Mennonites farming in the Amazon
scraped.description: Environmental science and conservation news
scraped.h1: After years of speculation, Suriname evicts Mennonites farming in the Amazon
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

More than 50 Mennonites have been deported from Suriname following years of controversy over plans to establish agricultural settlements for large-scale farming in the Amazon Rainforest.

Authorities removed the Mennonites, members of a conservative Christian group that rejects modern technology, from state land in Suriname’s Sipaliwini district. They had been staying in the area with expired residency permits, according to a statement from the president’s office. On Oct. 31, they were reportedly flown to Bolivia, from where they originally came.

“The point is essentially that the primary Amazon Rainforest is not being cut down for large-scale agriculture. I am opposed to that,” Suriname President Jennifer Geerlings-Simons told local media in an Oct. 4 interview, per a statement published by her office.

In 2023 and 2024, Mongabay exposed plans to transfer hundreds of thousands of hectares of rainforest to Suriname’s Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock and Fisheries (LVV). The plan involved relocating Mennonites from other areas in Latin America, including Belize and Bolivia, to Suriname to help develop large-scale farming projects that could boost the country’s domestic food production.

Mennonites have a track record of rapid, profitable agribusiness development across the Americas — but often at the expense of forests. In some cases, their expansion has resulted in illegal deforestation.

Roughly 93% of Suriname is covered in forest. Some of the Mennonite agriculture projects were cancelled following backlash over protecting the country’s forest cover and net-negative carbon emissions status. But in 2024, one of the projects continued through a public-private partnership between the agriculture ministry and Suriname Green Energy Agriculture N.V., a private company working in agriculture and bioenergy.

Representatives for Suriname Green Energy Agriculture N.V. asked a court to stop the Mennonites’ recent deportation, arguing the government had agreed to work toward providing them with permits so the company could develop agricultural land and produce biofuel.

“The expulsion of the foreign workers will have serious consequences for the business activities of the [company],” a court summary said.

The court rejected the claim on Oct. 29, saying the Mennonites must follow residency and work permit regulations.

Also in October, authorities used drones to track down and remove more than 63 Mennonites who had arrived from Bolivia and Mexico. The operation was part of a task force to remove illegal settlements in the rainforest, announced in August by Geerlings-Simons.

On Oct. 31, at least 55 Mennonites were reportedly returned to Bolivia on a charter flight and banned from entering Suriname for one year. The other eight evicted Mennonites weren’t sent to Bolivia because they’re Mexican nationals.

It’s unclear how many more Mennonites remain in Suriname or whether they have permits to live and work there.

Banner image: An illegal road is visible in Suriname’s Amazon Rainforest. Image by AP Photo/Ivan Valencia.

scraped.title: Smallholder farmers struggle on El Niño frontline; will the world help?
scraped.description: Environmental science and conservation news
scraped.author: Glenn Scherer
scraped.h1: Smallholder farmers struggle on El Niño frontline; will the world help?
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

Smallholder farmers across the globe are bracing for, or already feeling, the effects of a historically strong El Niño. This event — forecast to peak in December with lasting impacts deep into 2027 — has brought warnings of shocks to global food prices and food security .

The record-breaking 2026-2027 El Niño could drive an additional 49 million people into acute hunger, according to the United Nations , with southern Africa and Central America likely hardest hit. Expectations are that supplies of key staples such as rice and corn and commodities like cocoa, coffee and palm oil will be deeply reduced.

Millions of smallholder farmers who grow the food we consume are on the frontline of these impacts, experts say.

Palm oil suppliers in Indonesia, for example, are already reporting losses due to a prolonged El Niño-linked drought , while in Sudan long delayed rains are raising risk of widespread famine .

In Central America, Guatemalan farmers are seeing sharp reductions in crops meant for home food consumption. The governments of El Salvador, Honduras and Panama have all issued El Niño emergency declarations, as have Bolivia and Peru in South America.

“Fairtrade producers that we’re talking to are already seeing impacts,” Amanda Archila, CEO of Fairtrade America, told Mongabay in a video interview. “You’re already seeing clear signs of a dramatic increase in the number of food insecure smallholders.” Key cash crops could be far more deeply impacted over the coming months.

The current El Niño is exposing a fundamental weakness in global food systems, according to Sumit Roy, assistant general manager of the palm oil programme at Solidaridad , an international NGO. “Climate risks are concentrated at the farm level, while the resources to manage them remain concentrated further downstream,” Roy told Mongabay in a video Interview. As a result, “smallholders are facing the maximum brunt with limited access to finance, resources or technical support.”

“There has been a lot of talk over the last 20 years of risks to the future of cocoa and coffee and bananas and other tropical commodities,” Archila said. “We are actually seeing that be borne out in real time.”

The smallholder harms likely to come from the current record El Niño can be roughly extrapolated from past events . The most recent El Niño of 2023-2024, for example, brought a prolonged drought to southern Africa , which hammered maize production — a crucial crop linked to food security across the region. Smallholder farms there are predominantly rain fed; when those rains didn’t come, it triggered mass crop failures.

In Zambia, the 2023-2024 drought led to harvest reductions of around 1.76 million metric tons , with more than one million farming households impacted. “Zambia recorded over 40% crop failure,” said Agrey Wapamesa, a consultant at the International Water Management Institute, a research organization.

“The impacts of El Niño have been extremely devastating in the region,” agreed Hambulo Ngoma, a researcher with the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center. He believes that this year’s El Niño — dubbed a “super” and “Godzilla event” by the world’s media — could be worse than those in the past. 2027 projections already point to a large scale regional drought across southern Africa .

“I wish the preparation [for the current El Niño] actually began long ago, because when we speak of the 2023-2024 El Niño, it was a disaster,” for Zambia and other southern African countries, Wapamesa told Mongabay in a phone interview.

A threat to Latin America’s smallholders also looms. Carlos Isaza, head of Solidaridad’s coffee program in Colombia, recalls the effects of the 1997-1998 El Niño, which brought crop yield declines of up to 60%. “That year was terrible economically and socially here in Colombia’s coffee region,” Isaza told Mongabay in a video interview.

The 2015-2016 El Niño also reduced Colombia’s coffee harvests by around 50%, he noted. His team’s surveys suggest losses of around 20-30% so far this year, with more bad news expected in the coming months.

The mechanisms for crop failures are clear: Increased temperatures and drought due to escalating climate change, and intensified every few years by naturally occurring El Niños, harm both the coffee plants and the beans, reducing their quality, while also driving a proliferation of pests. “Farmers suffer a lot,” Isaza said.

As in past years, the 2026-2027 El Niño will bring heightened health risks for smallholder farmers and their families, threats that include prolonged working hours in dangerous extreme heat; limited access to clean, drinkable water; as well as increased infectious disease .

Byomkesh Talukdar, assistant professor in the Department of Global Health at Florida International University in the U.S., warns that, based on past events, the El Niño now unfolding will not only bring food insecurity, but also exposure to disease, including malaria and dengue. “It is going to have impacts overall on farmers’ health, especially those who are living in tropical countries, and also to some extent subtropical countries,” Talukdar said.

“Governments should take [this year’s event] seriously.” Talukdar said. “If governments don’t take any immediate action, [this El Niño] could trigger a cascading effect of consecutive crop failures. And that can impact farmers’ health, and also farmers’ communities, and also children’s health.”

Vulnerable groups — including women-led households, people with disabilities and poorer farm communities — are among the hardest hit, Wapamesa said. “When you look at their productive assets, their finances, and social protection services, they were highly affected,” Wapamesa said, referencing the 2023-2024 event in Zambia.

Climate change and the extreme weather it brings lead to economic deprivation, which in turn can trigger increased child labor and workers’ rights violations. Research by UNICEF, for example, found that in 2024 El Niño’s heat waves and flooding led to school closures, leaving children vulnerable to child labor.

“Whether it’s palm oil, whether it’s other crops, when there is a climatic event happening, when there are extreme events happening, it exposes … social challenges and issues,” Roy said.

Reducing El Niño harm requires both short-term preparations to support smallholders and long-term adaptation in the face of escalating climate change, experts say.

Ngoma highlights the need to improve El Niño early-warning systems that prepare farmers for looming drought or other extremes. He was part of a trial project that reached more than one million farmers across southern Africa with a digital campaign to disseminate information ahead of the 2023-2024 event. That, he said, helped farmers plan which crops to plant based on expected meteorological conditions.

Another key preparation: Nations and transnational companies can support smallholders via crop diversification efforts, both by helping them plant alternative drought-resistant crops and by exploring and incentivizing alternative revenue streams. Ngoma said that this sort of aid should come alongside early warnings. His research on El Niño crop impacts in Zambia found maize, legumes and oil seeds like soy were the most drought effected there and required aid.

For some commodity crops — like coffee and cacao — employing longer-range agroforestry techniques, such as the planting of hardy shade trees, can be beneficial, experts said. Solidaridad’s Isaza noted that shade trees substantially reduce yield losses on coffee farms, based on research in Colombia. In the short term, mulch application can help maintain soil moisture, while utilization of beneficial bacteria can protect bananas.

“Investing in climate-proofing … [for] small horticultural systems in particular is very important,” Ngoma said. This includes investments in irrigation systems and rainwater harvesting.

Both Ngoma and Wapamesa urged that governments and food commodities companies shift from a reactive response to an anticipatory response as climate change escalates and El Niños intensify. “I think a lot more needs to be done beyond just the usual talk of ‘there’s an El Niño coming and you have to prepare,’” Ngoma said. “A lot more support” is needed.

That support must not only come during El Niño years, but over the long-term to help smallholders prepare for an evolving climate, experts said. Farmers often understand “how to improve soil health, manage their crops, [and] adapt to changing weather patterns, but they don’t have the resources to do it,” Archila said.

For the time being, “the cost of managing these climate crises are completely borne by smallholder producers, with … that risk [largely invisible to] big consumer goods companies,” she added.

Roy pointed to a recent report that called on agrifood companies to invest in solutions like regenerative and climate-smart farming to help smallholders adapt to climate change, an effort that would also cut carbon emissions across commodity supply chains.

“We are asking companies to invest in reducing their Scope Three emissions, [those that occur in a company’s value chain], and invest in the smallholder farmers, so that mitigation measures reach them,” Roy said. “Climate finance … doesn’t reach the smallholder at all. Both the mitigation finance and adaptation finance [don’t] reach them.”

Experts offer a pragmatic rationale for the urgency expressed in their pleas to act in support of smallholders: In a recent opinion piece in The New York Times , author and journalist David Wallace-Wells warned that our current “monster El Niño will give us … a brief preview of a hotter and more chaotic world,” one likely to permanently arrive by 2035. The current event, he wrote, “will also offer a test of how well prepared and adapted [we are for] that future.”

Banner image: Farmers tend cropland in Mozambique. The 2015-2016 El Niño brought prolonged drought to southern Africa, reducing crop yields and impacting food security for millions of people. As climate change-induced drought intensifies, repeated annual crop losses lead to long-term economic hardships, impacting mental health including depression and anxiety, a set of conditions that has led to higher suicide rates among farmers in southern Africa. Image by Leopoldino Jeronimo/Kepa via Flickr ( CC BY-NC 2.0 ).

Citation:

Wapamesa, A., Sichalwe, D., & Ukwiremye, C. (2026). From the 2023/2024 drought disaster to 2026/2027 El Nino preparedness: Lessons for strengthening smallholder farmer resilience in Zambia. doi: 10.2139/ssrn.7022138

items.title: ¿Se puede recoger agua de lluvia en Estados Unidos?
items.summary: Lo que debes saber antes de instalar un barril o cisterna

scraped.title: ¿Se puede recoger agua de lluvia en Estados Unidos? » Yale Climate Connections
scraped.description: Yale Climate Connections is a nonpartisan, multimedia service providing daily broadcast radio programming and original web-based reporting, commentary, and analysis on the issue of climate change.
scraped.author: Johani Carolina Ponce
scraped.h1: ¿Se puede recoger agua de lluvia en Estados Unidos?
scraped.body_text:
Yale Climate Connections

En el jardín de Mario Ríos, el cambio se notó primero en las orquídeas. Después de analizar el agua de pozo que utilizaba para regar y descubrir que presentaba intrusión de sodio, este residente del condado de Broward, en el sur de Florida, decidió instalar dos barriles para recoger la lluvia. “Después de comenzar a usar el agua de lluvia, vi una gran diferencia en la salud de mis plantas, especialmente de mis orquídeas”, relató.

Ríos obtuvo los depósitos después de completar una clase sobre el uso y la instalación de barriles de lluvia. El Programa de Voluntarios Master Gardener de la Universidad de Florida enseña jardinería a personas que luego, como voluntarias, educan a la comunidad de Broward County. La capacitación busca que las personas que reciben los barriles sepan cómo utilizarlos y puedan instalarlos conectados a las canaletas o colocarlos al aire libre. Al terminarla, Ríos pudo obtener sus dos barriles mediante el programa local. “Cada barril almacena 55 galones de agua de lluvia”, explicó. En conjunto, pueden guardar hasta 110 galones para regar sus plantas.

La experiencia de Ríos muestra, a escala doméstica, el potencial de esta práctica ante un clima marcado por lluvias extremas y períodos secos que presionan el abastecimiento de agua. La Quinta Evaluación Nacional del Clima de Estados Unidos, publicada en 2023, indica que, entre 1958 y 2021, la cantidad total de precipitación caída durante el 1 % de los días más lluviosos aumentó 60 % en el noreste y 45 % en el medio oeste, las dos regiones con los mayores incrementos del país. Sin embargo, el potencial de la cosecha de lluvia y las normas que la regulan varían de un estado a otro.

El cambio climático contribuye a intensificar este fenómeno. A medida que aumentan las temperaturas, se intensifica la evaporación, lo que incrementa la humedad disponible en la atmósfera y puede alimentar tormentas con precipitaciones más fuertes. Según l a Agencia de Protección Ambiental de Estados Unidos, el calentamiento causado por las actividades humanas ha contribuido al aumento de estos episodios en el país.

Valoramos mucho tus perspectivas, por lo tanto, queremos que nos mandes tus preguntas sobre el cambio climático y sus efectos.

Sin embargo, recibir una gran cantidad de lluvia en pocas horas no significa que el agua estará disponible cuando se necesite. El sur de Florida vivió un ejemplo reciente de ese contraste: después de varios meses de sequía, el 26 de octubre de 2025 cayeron hasta 10 pulgadas de lluvia en apenas tres horas en el noreste de Broward y el sureste de Palm Beach. Las precipitaciones inundaron viviendas, dejaron más de 100 vehículos varados y generaron decenas de llamadas de rescate. Según el Servicio Meteorológico Nacional, las lluvias de finales de octubre de 2025 pusieron fin temporalmente a la sequía en la región, pero las condiciones de sequía moderada regresaron a mediados de noviembre del mismo año.

Frente a ese contraste, la cosecha de lluvia permite reservar parte del agua de los aguaceros para utilizarla durante los períodos secos. “La cosecha de agua de lluvia definitivamente puede ayudar a los hogares a soportar períodos secos, y es aquí donde pueden ayudar los episodios de lluvia intensa”, explicó Adriana Zúñiga-Terán, profesora asociada de la Escuela de Geografía, Desarrollo y Medioambiente de la Universidad de Arizona. “Durante un solo episodio de lluvia intensa se pueden llenar cisternas o tanques muy grandes, o cualquier mecanismo de almacenamiento que se tenga instalado”.

Los sistemas más sencillos, como el de Ríos, recogen el agua que baja de los techos y la almacenan en barriles para regar jardines y plantas. Las cisternas tienen mayor capacidad y pueden atender otros usos que no requieren agua potable, dependiendo del tratamiento y de las normas locales. La EPA incluye ambos sistemas entre las formas de infraestructura verde destinadas a retener y reutilizar el agua de lluvia.

La decisión entre un barril y una cisterna depende de la cantidad de agua que se quiera almacenar y del espacio disponible. “Un barril de lluvia es generalmente un recipiente pequeño conectado a una bajante, mientras que una cisterna es un tanque de almacenamiento más grande que puede instalarse sobre o bajo tierra”, señaló Lorna Bravo, agente de Horticultura Urbana de Broward County Parks and Recreation.

¡No podemos hacer este trabajo sin ti! Aproximadamente el 83 % de cada dólar que donas se destina directamente a pagar a nuestro equipo de reporteros, editores, meteorólogos y productores de radio. El otro 17 % cubre este sitio web, computadoras portátiles, un sistema de nómina y otros gastos similares necesarios para nuestro trabajo.

Durante una tormenta, estos depósitos también pueden reducir temporalmente la cantidad de agua que corre por los techos, aceras y calles hasta llegar a los drenajes. Ese flujo se conoce como escorrentía: es el agua que no se infiltra en el suelo y se desplaza sobre la superficie, donde puede recoger patógenos, nutrientes, sedimentos, metales y otros contaminantes antes de llegar a canales, ríos o zonas costeras.

El agua almacenada puede reducir el uso de agua potable en el exterior de las viviendas. “Los propietarios pueden reducir de manera realista su consumo de agua, y esto puede ayudar a los municipios a continuar suministrando agua durante los períodos secos”, señaló Zúñiga-Terán. “Pueden mantener vivas sus plantas y árboles durante la escasez de agua sin utilizar agua potable”.

El potencial de recolección puede ser considerable. Como regla general, una pulgada de lluvia sobre un pie cuadrado de superficie produce aproximadamente 0.62 galones. Eso significa que una pulgada sobre un techo de 1,000 pies cuadrados podría generar alrededor de 620 galones, antes de descontar las pérdidas del sistema. Sin embargo, un barril doméstico típico almacena apenas entre 50 y 60 galones. Recoger una porción importante de un aguacero requiere varios depósitos o una cisterna de mayor capacidad.

El volumen que puede recoger una vivienda depende principalmente de las dimensiones del techo, la cantidad de lluvia y la capacidad del depósito. “Como ejemplo general de UF/IFAS, recoger 1,000 galones de una lluvia de dos pulgadas requeriría aproximadamente 1,200 pies cuadrados de superficie de captación”, dijo Bravo. “Eso demuestra tanto el potencial de la escorrentía del techo como la importancia de ajustar la capacidad de almacenamiento al techo y al uso previsto”.

Para la mayoría de los hogares, un barril funciona como una fuente complementaria para regar plantas en macetas, huertos, plantas recién sembradas y áreas pequeñas del jardín. Una cisterna puede proporcionar una cantidad mayor para riego y otros usos exteriores, pero puede requerir una bomba o permisos locales, especialmente si estará enterrada, conectada a la plomería o unida estructuralmente a la vivienda.

El clima está cambiando y nuestros periodistas están aquí para ayudarte a comprender lo que está pasando. ¡Suscríbete a nuestro boletín informativo y nunca te pierdas una historia!

La cantidad que puede almacenarse también está condicionada por el espacio disponible. “Otra limitación es el espacio que ocupa: mientras más grande sea la cisterna, mayor será el volumen de agua almacenada y más espacio ocupará”, explicó Zúñiga-Terán. “Además, se necesita gravedad o una bomba para acceder al agua almacenada, pero los sistemas de cosecha de lluvia generalmente tienen esto resuelto”.

El peso del agua obliga a escoger cuidadosamente dónde colocar el depósito. “Un barril de lluvia lleno de 55 galones puede pesar aproximadamente entre 460 y 485 libras, incluido el barril, por lo que debe colocarse sobre una base firme y nivelada capaz de soportar al menos 500 libras”, advirtió Bravo. Las cisternas más grandes, agregó, “deben diseñarse e instalarse cuidadosamente para evitar hundimientos, grietas, filtraciones y riesgos para la seguridad”.

El desbordamiento debe dirigirse lejos de los cimientos de la vivienda y de las propiedades vecinas. El depósito también debe colocarse lejos de posibles fuentes de contaminación, como las tuberías de aguas residuales. Antes de excavar para instalar una cisterna subterránea o las tuberías correspondientes, se debe llamar al 811 para localizar los servicios públicos enterrados.

El agua que llega al depósito no debe considerarse automáticamente apta para el consumo humano. “La principal limitación es que no es agua potable. No se puede cocinar con ella ni beberla”, indicó Zúñiga-Terán. “El agua almacenada necesitaría tratamiento para convertirse en agua potable”.

En su recorrido por el techo, el agua puede recoger polvo, residuos procedentes del material del techo y excrementos de aves o pequeños animales. Por eso, los sistemas pueden incorporar mallas para detener hojas y un dispositivo de primera descarga, que desvía el agua inicial del aguacero, generalmente la que contiene más contaminantes. El agua recogida puede utilizarse para fines no potables, pero beberla o cocinar con ella requiere tratamiento y análisis adecuados.

El mantenimiento es necesario para conservar la calidad del agua y evitar la reproducción de mosquitos. “El tanque debe tener una tapa que cierre herméticamente y todas las aberturas, incluidas las de entrada y desbordamiento, deben cubrirse con una malla fina para mantener fuera a los mosquitos, los residuos y los animales pequeños”, dijo Bravo. Los propietarios, añadió, “deben inspeccionar regularmente los barriles y las cisternas, reparar rápidamente las mallas o tapas dañadas y asegurarse de que el agua no se acumule en canaletas, bandejas o áreas de desbordamiento cercanas”.

La mayoría de los estados permite recoger sin restricciones el agua que cae sobre las propiedades, pero Colorado y otros 18 estados fijan algún tipo de límite sobre quién puede hacerlo y cómo puede utilizarse. También pueden intervenir los códigos locales de construcción y plomería y las restricciones de las asociaciones de propietarios.

El costo y el espacio pueden dificultar la adopción de estos sistemas entre las familias con menos recursos. “Las comunidades de bajos ingresos suelen tener viviendas más pequeñas con patios más pequeños, lo que hace que la limitación de espacio sea todavía más significativa. Una cisterna puede ocupar la mayor parte del patio”, explicó Zúñiga-Terán. “Si no existen programas municipales para llegar a los residentes de bajos ingresos, el costo del sistema puede ser una barrera para su adopción”.

Los inquilinos pueden enfrentar otra dificultad: algunos programas de ayuda económica están diseñados exclusivamente para dueños de viviendas. Esa condición puede dejar fuera a personas interesadas que no tienen una propiedad.

Sigue nuestro canal de WhatsApp y suscríbete a nuestro canal de Youtube .

Antes de instalar el sistema, “los propietarios deben revisar las restricciones de la asociación de propietarios o de la escritura y los requisitos locales de mantenimiento de la propiedad”, recomendó Bravo. En el caso de cisternas grandes, particularmente las instaladas bajo tierra o conectadas a bombas o tuberías, “los propietarios deben comunicarse con el departamento local de construcción antes de la compra o instalación para determinar si se aplican permisos, inspecciones, distancias mínimas o medidas para localizar los servicios públicos”.

Colorado muestra cómo los derechos históricos sobre el agua pueden influir en una práctica doméstica. Desde 2016, el estado permite recoger agua de techos residenciales en un máximo de dos barriles con una capacidad combinada de hasta 110 galones. El agua debe utilizarse en la propiedad donde fue recogida y únicamente para fines exteriores, como regar jardines o césped. La ley permite restringir la captación si se determina que perjudica materialmente derechos de agua existentes.

Texas ofrece un contraste porque sus leyes buscan impulsar la cosecha de lluvia. El Estado exime del impuesto sobre las ventas los equipos utilizados para esta práctica e impide que las asociaciones de propietarios la prohíban de manera general. Además, exige incorporar esta tecnología en el diseño de determinados edificios estatales nuevos. Por su parte, algunos gobiernos locales y proveedores de agua de Texas promueven esta práctica mediante incentivos, como descuentos en barriles de lluvia y reembolsos por la instalación de sistemas de almacenamiento.

Los incentivos adquieren mayor importancia entre los hogares que no pueden asumir por sí solos el costo de la instalación. Sin embargo, “los programas que existen para ayudar a los residentes de bajos ingresos a adoptar sistemas de cosecha de lluvia suelen excluir a los inquilinos, ya que están dirigidos principalmente a los propietarios”, señaló Zúñiga-Terán.

En Miami-Dade, los residentes que completen un taller, compren un barril que reúna los requisitos y lo instalen correctamente pueden solicitar un reembolso de 50 dólares. El programa permite hasta dos reembolsos por propiedad y exige que los barriles tengan una capacidad mínima de 50 galones, un grifo y una junta que evite filtraciones.

La lluvia estacional de Florida obliga a mantener expectativas realistas. “Una cisterna más grande puede proporcionar un suministro más significativo para el riego no potable y los usos exteriores, especialmente durante la temporada de lluvias”, explicó Bravo. “Sin embargo, las precipitaciones de Florida son estacionales y el agua almacenada puede ser limitada durante períodos secos prolongados”.

La capacidad de estos sistemas para controlar inundaciones también tiene límites . Un barril que permanece lleno no puede recibir agua de la siguiente tormenta: el propietario debe utilizar su contenido para recuperar espacio de almacenamiento. Además, un depósito pequeño no puede contener el volumen producido por un aguacero extremo. Su aporte es mayor frente a lluvias pequeñas y frecuentes.

Por eso, la cosecha de lluvia no debe verse como una solución aislada. “La cosecha de agua de lluvia funciona mejor como parte de una estrategia general de conservación”, señaló Bravo.

items.title: October 2026: Earth’s warmest October on record
items.summary: The year 2026 is expected to be Earth's 2nd-warmest year on record, with 2027 likely to be the warmest.

scraped.title: October 2026: Earth's warmest October on record » Yale Climate Connections
scraped.description: The year 2026 is expected to be Earth's 2nd-warmest year on record, with 2027 likely to be the warmest.
scraped.author: Jeff Masters, Bob Henson
scraped.h1: October 2026: Earth’s warmest October on record
scraped.body_text:
Yale Climate Connections

October 2026 was the planet’s warmest October since modern record-keeping began in 1850, NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information , or NCEI, reported on November 12. NASA and the European Copernicus Climate Change Service also rated it as the warmest October. The global average temperature for January-October 2026 was the second-highest on record, trailing only 2024.

Global ocean surface temperatures set their fifth consecutive monthly record in October, and the month produced the highest departure from ocean-temperature average for any month in 177 years of analysis. Global land temperatures were the third highest on record for any October. It was the third-warmest October on record for global temperatures estimated by satellite through the lowest few miles of the atmosphere (the lower troposphere).

According to the European Copernicus Climate Change Service , 2026 will most likely be the second-warmest year on record (about 80% probability), with about a 20% chance of tying or exceeding 2024 as the warmest year on record. Climate scientist Zeke Hausfather and NASA both project that 2026 will be the first or second-warmest year on record, behind 2024, with 2027 likely to run away with the record. (Strong El Niño events normally peak in northern winter, and global temperature is typically higher in the second calendar year of the event than in the first one because of El Niño’s massive release of heat from ocean to atmosphere.)

With 10 months of the year now in, 2026 as a whole is on track to see the second warmest year on record in ERA5. And with a record-setting El Nino we are very likely to see a record warm 2027:

Get news for people who love the planet. Sign up for our newsletters for the latest weather updates, tips, and inspiring stories

The 48 contiguous United States racked up the fourth-warmest average temperature for any U.S. October in data going back to 1895, behind only 1963, 2024, and 1947. The nation’s year-to-date average temperature (Jan.-Oct.) was easily the warmest on record (see the Bluesky posts by climatologist Brian Brettschneider below). Unless the Nov.-Dec. period is substantially colder than the average from recent decades, the calendar year 2026 will end up as the warmest in U.S. history ( see our writeup from Nov. 9 ).

Jan-Oct 2026 temperature classification compared to the 1991-2020 normal for the Contiguous U.S. 0.0% was record cold (since 1940). 0.0% was much below normal. 0.00% was below normal. 4.75% was near normal. 95.25% was above normal. 78.4% was much above normal. 41.9% was record warm (since 1940).

Here is the January-October 2026 temperature ranking compared to all January-October periods since 1895 using PRISM data. Nationwide, it is easily the warmest January-October on record. 🔥🔥🔥

An El Niño advisory continues in the Eastern Pacific, NOAA reported in its November 12 monthly discussion of the state of the El Niño/Southern Oscillation, or ENSO. Sea surface temperatures in the benchmark Niño 3.4 region for the period August-September-October (the Oceanic Niño Index, or ONI) were at 2.5°C above average , the first time on record that the Aug.-Oct. value has been above 2°C. The monthly anomaly for October exceeded 3°C, as shown in the Bluesky graphic embedded below.

NOAA’s newer Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI), which adjusts the three-month value based on warmth throughout the global tropics, was at +2.0°C for Aug.-Oct. 2026, slightly below the record-setting +2.1°C from Aug.-Oct. 1997. Whether we use ONI or RONI, we have already reached the threshold of 2.0°C above average that is used to define “super” (i.e., very strong) El Niño conditions. See our writeup from November 11 on more on these indices and on how this El Niño event may shape the coming winter across the U.S. Gulf Coast and East Coast states.

NEW – ‘Simply staggering’: Rapidly developing ‘super El Niño’ on track to peak in December ✍️ Written by @ceciliakeating.carbonbrief.org💬 With comments from @zekehausfather.com Read here ➡️ buff.ly/Iw1PU6H

According to official probabilities from the NOAA Climate Prediction Center issued on October 19 using the RONI index, it is essentially certain (100% chance) that El Niño conditions will continue through January-February-March 2027. By April-May-June, neutral conditions become the most likely outcome (61% chance, with a 38% chance of El Niño and a 1% chance of La Niña). The odds of neutral conditions are also at 61% for June-July-August, but with a mere 6% chance of El Niño and a 33% chance of La Niña. It’s worth noting that a strong El Niño event is often ( though not always! ) followed by a La Niña event by the subsequent fall and winter, which in this case would be 2027-28.

According to the National Snow and Ice Data Center , Arctic sea ice extent during October 2026 was the 12th-lowest in the 48-year satellite record. The Arctic experienced its fifth-warmest October on record.

Antarctic sea ice extent in October 2026 was the second-lowest on record, nearly tied with 2023 for the lowest amount. The Antarctic region had its second-warmest October on record.

Weather records expert Maximiliano Herrera has documented the records listed below in October. Follow him on Bluesky: @extremetemps.bsky.social or X: @extremetemps . (November’s tally may be even more impressive: In just the first six days of November, according to Herrera, stations in 152 countries reported the warmest daily minimum ever measured at any location in that country.)

items.summary: The organization created the Reforestation Hub tool to help people understand which land is suitable for reforestation and how planting trees can benefit the climate.

scraped.title: The Nature Conservancy wants to bring back forests » Yale Climate Connections
scraped.description: The organization created the Reforestation Hub tool to help people understand which land is suitable for reforestation and how planting trees can benefit the climate.
scraped.author: YCC Team
scraped.h1: The Nature Conservancy wants to bring back forests
scraped.body_text:
Yale Climate Connections

Transcript:

Before European settlement, forests blanketed about a billion acres of what is now the continental U.S. But large swaths of those forests were later cleared for farming or to build cities and towns.

Jason Milks of The Nature Conservancy says replanting trees in some of those areas could help reduce climate change.

Milks: “Restoring forests where they have occurred historically … is one of the most powerful tools we have to sequester carbon out of the atmosphere.”

It’s not possible everywhere.

Milks: “We need productive agriculture. We live in cities and communities that aren’t going to have full forest coverage.”

But in many areas – like unused pastures, flood-prone fields, river banks, and sprawling lawns – people could plant trees without interfering with other important land uses.

So the Nature Conservancy developed a free online tool called the Reforestation Hub .

On an interactive map of the U.S., users can zoom in on any county or tract of land.

In each area, they can see how many acres are suitable for planting trees and how much carbon dioxide those trees could pull from the atmosphere each year.

So the data can help identify opportunities for reforestation, one area at a time.

Reporting credit: Sarah Kennedy / ChavoBart Digital Media

scraped.title: COP31: How Ed Miliband answered Carbon Brief readers’ questions - Carbon Brief
scraped.description: UK foreign secretary and COP veteran Ed Miliband in Antalya spoke with Carbon Brief earlier today at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, to answer readers’ questions.
scraped.author: Simon Evans
scraped.h1: COP31: How Ed Miliband answered Carbon Brief readers’ questions
scraped.body_text:
UK foreign secretary and COP veteran Ed Miliband spoke with Carbon Brief earlier today at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, to answer readers’ questions.

Carbon Brief readers submitted questions via CB Connect on topics including the UK’s “climate leadership”, the COP31 electrification target, as well as the roadmaps on deforestation and fossil fuels .

Membership

Despite recent criticism over the approval of the Jackdaw gas field, Miliband argued that the UK is still seen as a climate leader, due to its “ambitious targets on net-zero”.

Pushing back on a question about COP reform, Miliband explained how he is “quite pro the institution of the COP”, given its role in bringing countries together for climate action.

He emphasised the importance of action on methane and the UK’s “support” for the “35×35” electrification pledge .

Carbon Brief: Well, thanks very much for joining us. I know you’re very busy and we’ve got some reader questions. It’s great that you’ve got time to answer some.

Ed Miliband: Can I just say how much I love Carbon Brief?

CB: Thanks. Lovely to hear.

EM: Like, comment and subscribe!

CB: How, in your experience at COP31 so far, has the UK’s decision to approve the Jackdaw gas field and the rumoured rollback of its EV targets affected the UK’s standing as a climate leader?

EM: People see us as showing leadership. People don’t see us as rolling back, and I think what people see is a government that is driving the agenda on electrification and clean power. Because after all, we have a clean power 2030 target, which is world-leading.

[We] have the most ambitious targets on net-zero, the [ nationally determined contributions ] NDCs, of frankly, any country in the world. [We] are legislating for no new oil and gas licences.

And what I’m trying to do here is also bring a new dimension to this, which is the whole national security dimension. Because I think, if you’re serious about national security, you need to be serious about climate. And those parties – and those people – who aren’t serious about climate, I don’t think they’re serious about national security. Because this is a national security issue for, I think – frankly – every government across the world.

So I think, look, people see British leadership. People are looking forward to our [presidency of the] G20 [in 2027], where climate resilience [and] debt development will be central to the agenda as well.

CB: Are you confident that the UK can still meet its 2030 NDC target [to cut emissions 68% below 1990 levels]?

EM: Absolutely, we’re going to go all out to meet it. I think that’s so important, and that is the whole principle of the NDCs, is [that] you drive towards seeking to meet them. Obviously, it’s stretching. We inherited, from 2024, a difficult situation from the previous government, but we’re going to go all out to do what we can.

CB: Great. With the UK and other developed countries facing increasing fiscal pressures, how can you go about ensuring developing countries receive the financial and technical support that they need?

EM: Look, I think the biggest thing we need to do, cognisant of those fiscal pressures and the situation facing developing countries, is multilateral development bank (MDB) reform. So making sure that the MDBs work to the maximum for developing countries.

There’s lots of evidence out there and I was speaking about this at the World Bank annual meetings about the fact that the MDBs could do more to leverage their balance sheets. You know, potentially hundreds of billions of pounds – dollars – more that could be helping developing countries. Helping developing countries with climate resilience, helping them with relieving the debt burden in terms of the financing of the debt.

And, you know, one of the things that we’re going to be doing as part of our G20 is convening those MDBs to, in a friendly way, you know, point to the best practice of some of them, push the others to do more. I feel from our discussions that this is absolutely possible – for us to do more.

So yes, there are more fiscal constraints in developed countries, including in Britain , but it doesn’t mean we can’t make a difference. And I think it’s really, really important to say to your viewers: we are serious about, not just our national leadership on climate, but our international leadership as well, and we believe we can make a difference.

CB: It’s become part of the narrative that the COP process has run its course, and that people should focus more on mini-coalitions, groups of middle powers. What would you say to that, and how would you like to see the COP process reformed?

EM: I mean, I’m quite pro the COP process – not the process, but I’m quite pro the institution of the COP – and I’d say that in two respects.

One, if you look at the sweep of history, I was at the Copenhagen COP of 2009, [which] ended in acrimony. We were heading for a 4C world back then. Now, we’re heading for a 2.5C, 2.6C world, according to the latest UNEP emissions gap report – one of my favourite publications.

And look, 2.6C is bad, right? And we’ve got to do a lot more as a world, but we have made progress. And why? Because of multilateralism, because of the institution, being part of the COP, driving people forward.

That’s one part of it. The second part of it is [that the COP is] a place where these “coalitions of the willing” are formed. If I think about what I’ve done while I’ve been here [in Antalya] – I was at an event on forests, coalitions of the willing acting on the forest leaders’ partnership, acting to protect the forest. An event on electrification, a big focus of the Turkish presidency. An event on industrial policy, green industrial policy. Countries working together. An event this morning on methane, really crucial. We’re trying to, with a coalition of the willing, get it onto the COP agenda. And then, an event on climate security.

So that gives people, your viewers, a sense of why I think this [COP process] matters. You know, it’s not simply a talking shop. I think it is also a place where action happens.

CB: You mentioned the electrification pledge put forward by the Turkish presidency. Is the UK a signatory to that yet?

EM: We support the electrification pledge, absolutely, and you know we want to drive forward. It’s stretching for the UK, but we think it’s the right thing to do. And why? Because – it’s really important to say this – because electrification is a way of getting off the fossil-fuel rollercoaster. Clean-energy electrification is the way I think about it.

[Three hours after Carbon Brief’s interview with Ed Miliband, the UK government confirmed its endorsement of the 35×35 electrification pledge.]

And if there’s one lesson we’ve got to learn from these two wars that we’ve seen – Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the Iran war – it’s [that] you can’t have security on the basis of fossil fuels. It’s not even – even [for a] country like America, a massive fossil-fuel producer is affected by higher prices. But for fossil-fuel importers, covering 75% of the world’s population [including the UK], we are price takers. And you know the fossil-fuel rollercoaster is terrible for the cost of living. That’s why clean energy, clean electrification, is the answer. Electrify now!

CB: The UN climate convention and the Paris Agreement both commit countries, including the UK, to implement “climate-change education, training, public awareness and participation”. Why doesn’t the UK have a national programme on this, particularly given the flood of misinformation in this area?

EM: We need to do more. You’re completely right. Look, I am always ambitious to do more, and more climate education – well, more public information – is important.

I did the first annual climate and nature statement in 2025. It was repeated in 2026 by [environment secretary] Mary Creagh. I was in the House of Commons for that, and that whole institution was part of me believing, as energy secretary, that it was important to find ways to inform the public.

And I fully acknowledge we need to do more. We need to do more. But we need to do more to both tell people about what is happening, in terms of climate and nature, but also say there are answers, because it can’t just be a council of despair. It’s also got to be a council of hope – not false hope – but a council of honesty, but also hope.

CB: Great. How would you like to see the Brazilian roadmaps on fossil fuels and deforestation taken forward? Are you keen to see those as part of the formal negotiated outcome [at COP31]?

EM: I think what’s interesting about this goes back to your question about the coalition of the willing. Look, there’s obviously no secret that there are countries that are obstacles to the fossil-fuel roadmap being part of – central – to the COP decision. And we took a decision last year that there was a big enough coalition of the willing – I think there are 80 countries or more – to drive this forward.

I think the Brazilians are to be incredibly commended for having produced this fossil-fuel roadmap. I think we should now be thinking, as individual countries, how can we build on that work ourselves? Because it’s doing exactly what I hoped it would do, which is to grapple with the important issues that we face.

I think we have to accept there are some countries – in a world where you have to operate by consensus – where not every decision is going to get into the COP decision. But it doesn’t mean we can’t make progress on it, and I think that’s really true in this case.

CB: Great. One final question from my end, if I may. What’s an outcome that you’re going to be looking for at the end of this COP, that you’re going to be happy to take home to the UK?

EM: I think the most important thing is action to drive forward the climate agenda, and that’s what I want to see. You know, it goes back to the point about the cost. Some of it is about the formal decision-making, but a lot of it is about the real, tangible outcomes that have happened over a couple of weeks.

And if I think about what I’ve done here, you know, if we can get methane and the importance of methane – which, as you know, and as your viewers will know – is such an important short-term difference we can make in terms of preventing the rise in temperatures, and we can get that onto the agenda of the COP. If we can show progress on other aspects of the real economy – what’s happening in the real economy – all of those things are going to be important.

I think there’s something else, though, which is, these events of countries coming together. They contradict those people who say, you know, people are giving up on climate. Because you’ve got more than 190 countries that are coming together [at the COP], reaffirming their belief in the Paris Agreement, reaffirming their belief that they need to make efforts, as part of the Paris Agreement, to meet the climate goals – and working together on these issues.

It doesn’t mean they aren’t hard, but it does show that there is really important global commitment, which I’ve been hearing, to this agenda.

CB: Brilliant. Thanks very much, Ed.

EM: Thank you.

This interview was conducted by Dr Simon Evans at the COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, on 12 November 2026. Filming by Josh Gabbatiss and Daisy Dunne, with editing by Joe Goodman.

scraped.title: Analysis: Climate-finance pledges fall 70% as countries meet at COP31 - Carbon Brief
scraped.description: The amount of public funding pledged to help developing countries tackle climate change has dropped by more than 70% in 2026, according to Carbon Brief analysis.
scraped.author: Josh Gabbatiss
scraped.h1: Analysis: Climate-finance pledges fall 70% as countries meet at COP31
scraped.body_text:
The amount of public funding pledged to help developing countries tackle climate change has dropped by more than 70% in 2026, according to Carbon Brief analysis.

Developed countries are required under UN climate treaties to provide “ climate finance ” and have traditionally announced multi-year pledges to feed into their global commitments.

Most of these pledges expired in 2025 and, since then, the US has withdrawn from international climate efforts and many European aid budgets have been cut.

A civil-society tracker shows that only five nations have announced new multi-year pledges, including just one major donor – the UK.

Germany, France and Japan are among the key contributors that have so far failed to set out plans for new climate finance, while none is expected from the US.

As a result, the total amount of public climate finance pledged over the next few years amounts to just $11.7bn a year in spending, down from recent levels of around $40bn.

Experts tell Carbon Brief that global conflict, fiscal constraints and the rise of the far right are all making it harder for developed-country governments to pledge new funds.

As the COP31 summit in Turkey gets underway, developing countries are stressing their urgent need for new finance, after nations agreed to a new global target just two years ago.

Under the Paris Agreement , developed countries are obliged to provide climate finance to help developing countries cut their emissions and prepare for climate disasters.

This financial assistance can be channelled through multilateral development banks , UN climate funds and investments “mobilised” from the private sector.

But a large chunk is also expected to come directly from the public coffers of developed countries – primarily their foreign-aid budgets. This public spending has made up roughly a third of climate finance flowing to developing countries in recent years.

The EU, the US and others agreed just two years ago that they would “take the lead” on scaling up annual climate finance from $100bn in the early 2020s to $300bn by 2035.

Donor countries have traditionally supported such goals by announcing multi-year targets that indicate how much they plan to spend on climate finance.

Nearly all of these pledges expired in 2025 – and hardly any major donors have announced new ones to replace them, covering the period out to 2030.

This lack of new commitments is captured in a tracker of old and new financial commitments by climate NGOs NRDC and E3G .

Carbon Brief analysis of this data, based on an annualised breakdown of targets, shows that developed countries had previously pledged around £42bn a year in public finance.

As the chart below shows, based on current pledges, this has fallen by around 71% to £11.8bn, on average, over the remainder of the 2020s.

Not all contributors announced public climate-finance pledges in advance for the pre-2026 period. Some did not hit their stated targets, while others exceeded them.

While official data for 2025 is not yet available, bilateral public finance reached £43.9bn in 2024, broadly in line with the amount pledged by developed countries.

International climate finance has been consistently dominated by five nations – Japan, Germany, France, the US and the UK.

These countries – together with the EU – have provided around 90% of all the bilateral, public climate finance going to developing countries in recent years.

Of these key players, only the UK has announced a new pledge, committing £6bn ($8bn) of aid between 2026-27 and 2028-29, plus £6.7bn ($8.9bn) from outside its aid budget.

This accounts for half of all the annual funds pledged from 2026 onwards – averaging $5.7bn a year.

The European Commission makes up most of the remainder, with an average annual contribution of $4.5bn promised out to 2027.

Rather than a new pledge, this is due to the commission promising to spend €28bn ($31.8bn) over its 2021-2027 budget period. Its post-2027 contribution is currently being discussed as part of wider EU budget negotiations.

Canada has promised to spend CA$5.3bn ($4.1bn) by 2030, averaging $860m a year. The Netherlands , Switzerland and Belgium have also pledged relatively small sums.

Overall, despite developed countries committing to scale up climate finance, these new pledges are either less ambitious – or only slightly more ambitious – than previous ones. This can be seen in the chart below.

The UK’s pledge appears more ambitious, but this is because the government has changed how it counts climate finance to include $8.9bn in “additional” public finance. When only the like-for-like aid components are compared, the new pledge amounts to a drop in ambition. (For more details, see the methodology.)

The most significant absence is the US, which committed to reaching $11.4bn in annual support by 2024 under the Biden administration.

Since president Donald Trump took power, the US has – for the second time – withdrawn from the Paris Agreement and shrunk its aid budget. It will not provide any official climate finance in the coming years.

Another notable absence is Australia, which is jointly hosting the upcoming COP31 summit, alongside Turkey. Josie Lee , policy and advocacy lead at Oxfam Australia , tells Carbon Brief:

“If Australia fails to announce a climate-finance pledge as president of negotiations, it would send a problematic message to those resisting action on climate change that might serve to embolden their agenda.”

Japan is the largest overall contributor of public climate finance, but it has not traditionally announced targets for this type of spending. Instead, the government set out overall goals that also bundle in finance “mobilised” from the private sector.

As a result, its public-finance ambitions have not been included in this analysis.

So far, the Japanese government has not announced any new multi-year climate-finance pledges, from either the public or the private sector.

Europe provides the majority of international climate finance, but European governments have massively cut their aid spending in recent years, citing economic strain and defence spending needs.

Germany and France, the two largest European climate-finance contributors, both pledged to reach €6bn ($6.8bn) per year by 2025. Neither has committed to anything beyond that.

Both nations have slashed their aid budgets in recent years, including funding for climate programmes. Germany missed its 2025 climate-finance goal due to these cuts.

Dr Anja Carolin Gebel , a senior policy advisor at Germanwatch , tells Carbon Brief that this issue has become more politically fraught since the centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) won the 2025 election and began leading a coalition government:

“The issue of climate change – and, subsequently, climate finance – has taken a back seat in the current government coalition.”

There has also been a political shift in France, Gaïa Febvre , international policy coordinator at Réseau Action Climat , tells Carbon Brief. She adds:

“The upcoming presidential election and the growing influence of the far right are likely to make new international financial commitments politically more difficult.”

Other significant European donors are also undergoing political turmoil.

Spain’s centre-left government has triggered a snap election for the end of November, making a new climate-finance pledge during COP31 less likely.

Following a narrow election win, a centre-left bloc in Sweden is still in the process of trying to form a new coalition government.

Some nations have signalled that their climate finance will continue flowing, even though they have not officially set out specific new pledges.

The Dutch government, for example, has said it will provide “at least” €300m ($334m) of specific climate funding annually out to 2031. However, it has also indicated that its total public climate finance is likely to be considerably higher in both 2026 and 2027.

To highlight the lack of new pledges, developing countries are championing a “climate-finance work programme” at COP31, which could provide a space to discuss scaling up public climate finance from developed countries.

In response, the EU has stressed that its member states are the “largest providers” of public climate finance and called on developing countries to submit overdue plans for cutting emissions. The EU and its member states provided a record €32.3bn ($40bn) in 2025.

Membership

Against this backdrop, EU climate chief Wopke Hoekstra recently told Bloomberg that “any conversation on new fresh money is dead in the water”.

Joe Thwaites , international climate finance director at NRDC, who runs the commitment tracker, tells Carbon Brief that “developed countries would be wise to show how they are continuing to lead on climate finance”. He says:

“The lack of new announcements is making the finance negotiations tougher than they need to be. The debate around the climate-finance work programme is arising because developing countries have little clarity about how much public climate finance there will be in coming years.”

This analysis is based on the climate-finance commitments tracker , run by the NGOs NRDC and E3G, supplemented with additional research.

Only the 23 “developed” countries that are obliged to provide climate finance are considered in this analysis, plus the EU. This includes western Europe, the US, Australia, Canada and New Zealand. Japan and Norway both provide substantial sums of climate finance, but have not announced specific public-finance pledges and therefore are not included.

Carbon Brief converted multi-year pledges into single years, with 2025 used as the baseline “pre-2026” year. Some countries committed to reaching a certain amount “by 2025”, in which case that value is used. Others said they would provide a total amount over several years, in which case the average value per year is used. Belgium, Switzerland and the US only set initial targets as far as 2024, so their 2024 values were used instead of 2025.

These values were compared with the average annual contribution for the remainder of the 2020s, based on the new pledges from the UK, Canada, Belgium, Switzerland and the Netherlands. Some climate finance has been committed by the Netherlands, but this is not expected to be its total contribution. The EU, Portugal and Greece have earlier pledges that extend into the latter half of the 2020s, although the latter two make very small contributions.

NRDC and E3G include all the UK’s newly pledged public finance in their tracker, including $8.9bn in “additional” public finance, which covers “equity, debt, guarantees, insurance and export credit” to mobilise private finance.

In previous Carbon Brief analysis comparing the UK’s new climate-finance target to its old one, this funding was not included. This is because the government did not previously count these funds towards its climate-finance goals, instead focusing exclusively on aid spending.

This analysis does not include pledges that some countries, including Germany and France, have made to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF). However, these pledges would not substantially change the main finding, shifting the overall reduction from 71% to 70%.

scraped.h1: The GOP lost its iron grip on Ohio. What’s the outlook for clean energy?
scraped.body_text:

Canary Media

12 November 2026

Democrats have finally managed to gain footing in Ohio’s halls of power — a shift that bodes well for clean energy in a state that’s become particularly hostile toward solar and wind.

Last week, voters ended Republicans’ 15 -year-long trifecta in Ohio, picking Democrat Amy Acton to be their next governor (and the first woman elected to that office). While the GOP still controls the state House and Senate, Democrats won enough seats to break Republicans’ supermajority in the House, meaning the party can no longer unilaterally override the governor’s vetoes.

From 2011 until now, Republican control of all three branches of state government has increasingly favored the oil and gas industry while limiting the growth of renewable power and scaling back energy-efficiency standards.

Acton campaigned on a different vision. Her affordability plan pledged to promote ​ “ the lowest-cost and cleanest sources of energy readily available” and to reinstate energy efficiency measures, renewable portfolio standards, and demand response programs, which incentivize customers to reduce or shift their energy consumption when the grid is strained.

In a Substack post last month, Acton wrote, ​ “ Ohio politicians have made it nearly impossible to advance zero marginal cost generation such as wind and solar,” so most of the state’s electricity comes from higher-cost fossil-fuels. ​ “ I will reexamine these obstacles that, in the long run, hit Ohio families in their pocketbooks.”

The question is what Acton can actually do to move the needle.

The main obstacle to utility-scale solar over the past five years has been a 2021 law, Senate Bill 52 , that lets counties ban almost all such new projects within their territories. Even without an outright ban, counties can block most projects before a developer can proceed with a permit application at the state level. SB 52 also applies to wind farms of 5 megawatts or more, though almost all proposals for large-scale wind projects stopped after a 2014 budget law more than doubled the distance that turbines must be from neighboring property lines.

Over a third of Ohio counties have now designated large swaths of land as off-limits to renewables under SB 52 . Acton can’t change that law and others on her own, since doing so requires legislative action.

Still, clean energy advocates are optimistic that the new governor will be able to knock down some roadblocks.

“ It’s a brand-new day here,” said Neil Waggoner, Midwest manager for the Sierra Club’s Beyond Coal campaign, who’s based in central Ohio.

Very soon, Acton will choose leaders for various regulatory agencies, subject to confirmation by the Ohio Senate. Those include the directors of the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency and the departments that deal with health, natural resources, agriculture, and development. The Ohio EPA handles permits for fossil-fuel plants and other polluting facilities, while the Ohio Department of Natural Resources decides matters dealing with hydraulic fracturing, injection wells, and coal mining.

Most notably for energy, those five agency directors will make up a majority of the voting members of the Ohio Power Siting Board, which issues permits for electric generation projections and other energy infrastructure. The board has seven standing voting members; the other two are the chair of the Public Utility Commission of Ohio and a member that represents the public.

Acton will eventually get to pick those last two members, too. The utility commission’s current chair, Jenifer French, can stay on as a regulator there until 2029 , but the governor can at any time designate a different chair, who will then also head up the Power Siting Board. The term for the current public member ends in 2030 .

Those personnel swaps could make Ohio friendlier to clean energy developers. In recent years, the siting board and its staff have mainly deferred to local governments on whether a solar or wind project is in the public interest . That has allowed the mere existence of local government opposition to derail projects, even when objections lack factual support or have been addressed by the developer.

Miranda Leppla, who heads the environmental law clinic at Case Western Reserve University School of Law, said she hopes the new board will take a genuinely broad view of the public interest, including a more critical examination of energy projects’ health and environmental impacts and the costs of climate change.

Acton will also appoint at least four of the Public Utilities Commission’s five members during her term, as their tenures come to an end. That agency is tasked with making sure Ohioans have reliable, affordable utility service. Leppla said new members could push utilities to embrace energy efficiency and demand response and pursue more equitable service across their territories.

While Acton cannot enact laws on her own, her election could force Republicans in the legislature to compromise more on energy policy.

“ The majorities in the House and Senate are going to have to work with the governor,” Waggoner said. ​ “ That’s a good thing. That’s the way government is supposed to work.”

Democratic Rep. Tristan Rader, ranking minority member on the current House Energy Committee, said he expects there will be some cooperation and actual movement toward the ​ “ all-of-the-above strategy that at least Republicans have given lip service to these last couple of years.” Otherwise, nothing would get done.

Even if the legislature won’t abolish SB 52 ’s terms for letting counties ban solar and wind, Republicans will no longer be able to unilaterally override Acton if she vetoes bills to further restrict solar, wind, or energy efficiency.

“ It would be fantastic to make sure we can’t go further down the path of promoting fossil fuels at the expense of different types of clean energy that could save Ohioans money and could do wonders for the impacts of climate change,” Leppla said.

However, there’s still the lame-duck session to get through.

One proposal, House Bill 1024 , would shift authority for review of thousands of agency rules and processes from the governor to lawmakers — essentially letting them undo regulations without having to amend the law or risk Acton’s veto. Republican Rep. Jamie Callender introduced the bill last month, shortly before the election; he was also a primary sponsor of 2019 ’s House Bill 6 , the coal and nuclear bailout law that gutted Ohio’s clean energy standards and is at the heart of the state’s ongoing utility-corruption saga.

Another gambit, House Joint Resolution 11 , proposes making the governor’s veto power meaningless by letting simple majorities override it. Introduced days after Acton’s election, it would place the issue before voters as a constitutional amendment next year.

Meanwhile, lawmakers could try to ram through some energy bills before the new year. Senate Bill 294 , which the Ohio Senate passed in June, may make building solar and wind even more difficult by specifying a minimum capacity factor of 50 % . Capacity factor refers to the ratio between actual electricity production and maximum output if a source runs continuously. Federal data shows the average capacity factor is around 24 % for U.S. solar farms and 34 % for wind, meaning Ohio’s law could essentially force developers to add batteries — along with costs and complexity — to their projects to meet the 50 % threshold

Another proposal, House Bill 862 , would let utilities own nuclear plants — and possibly stick consumers with part of the costs. That would run counter to a 2025 law that generally bars regulated electric utilities from owning generation and passing costs on to customers in what is supposed to be a competitive market.

Other draft bill language circulated this week would also keep coal plants open , even if the owner has signed a contract agreeing to close a facility or convert it to natural gas. Most imminently, that could force a large unit at the Cardinal power plant in eastern Ohio to stay open, even though the group that runs it is bound to shutter the facility by 2028 under a 2015 settlement deal prior owner American Electric Power made with the Sierra Club.

Much then could depend not only on Acton’s plans for next year, but also on what happens between now and New Year’s Eve, when the legislative session ends. Nonetheless, Rader is optimistic that the election results will lead to more renewables coming online in Ohio.

“ Let’s put all energy on an equal footing,” he said.

scraped.body_text:

Canary Media

12 November 2026

San Francisco Bay Area regulators have finalized a long-awaited rule that limits pollution from residential water heaters.

In 2023 , the Bay Area Air District board passed first-in-the-nation regulations setting zero-nitrogen-oxides ( NO x ) emissions standards on new home water heaters and space-heating systems sold in the region.

Last week, board members voted on final amendments for the water-heater measure, ensuring it will now take effect in 2028 — one year later than planned. The regulation includes several exemptions to address affordability concerns; about half of Bay Area installations are expected to qualify. Rules regarding the sale of home heating systems have yet to be finalized.

“ The vote is an enormous victory for clean air and the climate in the Bay Area — and really, for the nation,” said Sam Fishman, senior sustainability and resilience policy manager at the nonprofit San Francisco Bay Area Planning and Urban Research Association. The regulations put forward ​ “ a new model for how to transition the market away from polluting equipment in our buildings to clean equipment in a way that ensures a smooth, affordable, and equitable implementation.”

With the water-heater rules now firmly moving forward, ​ “ there’s no additional opportunity to roll them back,” Fishman noted.

The Bay Area’s newly cemented measure could guide other regulators in crafting clean-appliance rules, including those in California , Maryland , and a handful of other states that are exploring similar standards.

In the Bay Area, home to more than 7 million people, gas appliances emit more smog- and particulate-forming NO x pollution than the region’s passenger vehicles, according to the district. The bulk of those home emissions come from their fossil-fueled furnaces and water heaters.

Their pollution causes up to 85 premature deaths and 15 , 000 asthma attacks in the region annually, and eliminating it would deliver health benefits valued at $ 1 . 1 billion per year, according to Greg Nudd, deputy executive officer of policy at the air district. Space heating is responsible for the vast majority of the emissions.

Cost remains the main drag on heat-pump water heater adoption. On average, replacing an old gas water heater with a new gas model is about $ 3 , 600 , the district says, while switching to a heat-pump option is around $ 7 , 100 . Homeowners may also need to pay for changes to their property, like running an electrical line or remodeling a utility space, in order to accommodate the heat-pump water heater.

To address these economic barriers, regulators decided to allow certain property owners to continue to install gas water heaters: low-income households, owners of small water heaters for which heat-pump options don’t exist, and those with space or electrical constraints. Multifamily-building owners, who may need to plan system upgrades years in advance, won’t need to make the switch until 2033 .
