Costs could decline as the technology matures and policy support builds, however. For example, home-electrification startup Jetson Home told Canary Media that next year it expects the average Bay Area installation cost of a 50 -gallon unit will be about $ 4 , 500 . Plus, California has incentives worth hundreds to thousands of dollars for qualified homeowners, including 0 % state-backed financing , which can make a heat-pump version the cheapest option.

Once a water heater is paid off, the air district expects that a household will save $ 40 to $ 50 per year on its utility bills. Clean energy think tank RMI has estimated far higher average savings for the majority of households: $ 360 per year . The nonprofit attributes the difference to its analysis’ inclusion of a change to California’s electricity rate structure that makes electrification more cost-effective, especially for low-income customers.

Several industry and property-owner groups opposed the water-heater regulation, including the Silicon Valley Business Alliance, the National Association of Residential Property Managers, and the Business and Housing Network. Fossil-fuel corporations also fought the rule. A political action committee funded by Chevron, PBF Energy Western Region, Phillips 66 , and Marathon Petroleum spent about $ 60 , 000 toward the mayoral reelection of an air district board member who opposed the zero-emission standard, El Cerrito Mayor Gabe Quinto. (Quinto was not reelected.)

“ Landlords do not have an endless well of money,” said a concerned property owner from Pacifica at last week’s air district board meeting. ​ “ How are we expected to pay for these upgrades while keeping rents low?”

Opposition groups and affordability concerns have delayed similar rules in Southern California from being adopted, although that air district has implemented a pioneering clean-heat rule for light-industrial and commercial heaters.

In the Bay Area, city leaders from across the region spoke out in support of the water-heater measure at the meeting, including those from Berkeley, Oakland, Palo Alto, and San Jose. Joining them were high schoolers , physicians, and representatives of environmental groups, public health nonprofits, and the state’s air regulator, the California Air Resources Board.

“ I’ve had asthma my entire life,” said one proponent, a recent college grad. ​ “ The cost of some of my emergency room visits have been over $ 50 , 000 before insurance. I even had to withdraw from a semester in college because I developed bronchitis. … I implore you to reject the continued use of gas appliances in homes so other Bay Areans don’t have to deal with the physical, emotional, and financial impacts I’ve dealt with.”

After a motion to delay further action on the zero-emissions rule and one to hold a vote to repeal it entirely both failed, 15 of the 17 board members present voted in support of the amended rule, with one abstaining.

Next month, the board will convene to discuss the space-heating rule.

“ In 2023 , the board made a commitment to Bay Area residents: We would stop letting the appliances in our homes be one of the largest sources of NO x pollution in our region,” Joelle Gallagher, Napa County supervisor and air district board member, said at the meeting. ​ “ That pollution doesn’t stay in the garage or the utility closet. It forms fine particulate matter that settles across every county, every neighborhood, and every child’s lungs.”

scraped.body_text:

Canary Media

11 November 2026

North America’s first small modular reactor project is running into two familiar challenges for the nuclear industry: timing and cost.

Ontario Power Generation said in a Tuesday earnings release that the first BWRX- 300 unit at its Darlington site will not come online by its October 2030 target and will blow past its budget of $ 7 . 7 billion Canadian ($ 5 . 4 billion U.S.). The utility didn’t share new targets — it’s working on a revised assessment of cost and schedule that it expects ​ “ to be substantially completed by mid- 2027 .” It is the project’s second slip: When Ontario Power announced the design in late 2021 , it said the reactor could be completed as early as 2028 .

The Darlington project, located east of Toronto, is the first new nuclear build in Canada in more than three decades. It’s also the first test of a small modular reactor design that is being pursued by developers in the U.S. and beyond. The Tennessee Valley Authority received a construction permit for a BWRX- 300 from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission in September. Developer Blue Energy has also started the NRC application process to build a BWRX- 300 in Texas.

Unlike other next-gen nuclear designs recently greenlit for construction in the U.S., GE Vernova Hitachi’s BWRX- 300 uses the same light-water technology that undergirds most of the world’s existing nuclear fleet today. It’s designed to produce 300 megawatts of carbon-free electricity — a substantial amount, but far less than a conventional large-scale reactor.

Timeline and cost overruns have plagued North American nuclear projects and help explain why reactor construction has been anemic in recent decades. Just look at the latest nuclear power plants to be completed in the U.S.: Georgia Power’s Vogtle units 3 and 4 , both large-scale AP- 1000 reactors that came online in 2023 and 2024 , took an extra seven years and $ 17 billion to wrap up .

Nevertheless, nuclear energy is seeing resurgent financial and policy support in North America and elsewhere as demand for electricity — especially carbon-free electricity — rises.

The Darlington project is part of that wave. In total, Ontario Power Generation plans to build four units at a cost of $ 20 . 9 billion Canadian , and federal and provincial investment funds have since committed up to $ 3 billion Canadian for minority stakes in the project. In the U.S., the Biden administration backed nuclear power as an anchor for an emissions-free grid, and both Trump administrations have embraced it under the banner of ​ “ energy dominance.”

Proponents of SMRs argue that smaller, repeatable designs like the BWRX will be cheaper and faster to build than large-scale reactors. The idea is that mass manufacturing and construction of these reactors will create a sort of learning-curve effect, so even if the first unit is expensive to make, the 100 th unit will be far cheaper. But right now, this is only a hypothesis. Just two SMR plants are operating commercially worldwide, in Russia and China, and some in the nuclear industry argue that it’s more economical to stick with big reactors.

Given that the Darlington project is the first attempt at building a BWRX- 300 , some budget and timeline overruns aren’t surprising. Ontario Power Generation itself said that the update ​ “ reflects GE Vernova Hitachi ( GEVH ) Nuclear Energy’s ongoing engineering for its first-of-a-kind SMR , which has impacts on construction execution and supply chain performance.”

“ GE Vernova Hitachi is committed to working closely with Ontario Power Generation ( OPG ) and our partners to deliver the Western world’s first commercial SMR ,” a GE Vernova Hitachi spokesperson told Canary Media in an emailed statement. ​ “ While engineering and design maturity are important considerations, as OPG ’s update recognizes, there are multiple interconnected contributions across engineering, procurement and construction, as well as evolving market conditions, including inflation and geopolitical risks.”

While overruns are expected for a first-of-its-kind project, their scale matters. If costs or timelines balloon by too much, it could have a chilling effect on the other efforts to develop BWRX- 300 reactors. Vogtle offers a cautionary precedent. Even though its second new reactor was 30 % cheaper to build than its first, what’s remembered is the project’s enormous overall price tag.

scraped.h1: Coalition of Nonprofits Files Landmark Lawsuit to Stop Development of Advanced AI Systems at Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI, and SpaceXSI that Proliferate Bioweapons and Cyberattacks
scraped.body_text:

Daily news & progressive opinion—funded by the people, not the corporations—delivered straight to your inbox.

A project of Common Dreams

The lawsuit seeks to protect public safety and freeze the development of advanced AI systems before catastrophe strikes

Today, Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen , Heat Initiative, and The Alliance for Secure AI filed a lawsuit seeking to freeze the development of increasingly advanced AI models at Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI, and SpaceXSI that can escape human control, including fueling the proliferation of bioweapons and cyberattacks. The lawsuit, filed in Superior Court of California, County of San Francisco, alleges that even the executives developing this technology have warned that advanced AI systems pose imminent and catastrophic risks to humanity. The plaintiffs are asking the court to intervene before disaster strikes and assert that a freeze on the development of the most advanced AI systems is necessary to protect public safety.

The lawsuit details how existing, less powerful AI systems have already bypassed safeguards, accessed outside computer systems without authorization, empowered terrorists and other bad actors, and taken harmful actions their developers did not intend. Some of these attacks included AI agents hacking private companies, gaining unauthorized access to government databases, and submitting a false police report, all while acting without human control. AI experts—including leaders of AI companies—have warned that the inability to control advanced AI systems is likely to cause devastating harm and could even result in human extinction .

“Even as experts inside of AI companies warn of imminent disaster, the people closest to AI’s harms—parents, teachers, workers , and young people—are already sounding the alarm. AI is changing how people do their jobs, how kids learn, and what families pay to keep the lights on. Most Americans feel like they’ve lost control over their lives and livelihoods and are demanding accountability,” said Phil Aroneanu, Founder and Executive Director of Irreplaceable Education Fund . “We must freeze frontier AI development until the technology is under control and the American people have a say and a stake in its future, instead of leaving it to a handful of billionaire Big Tech CEOs.”

“Despite endless warnings about the grave risks their products pose to public safety and even civilization itself, AI company executives are rushing to develop and deploy ever-more advanced AI systems. We the People should not simply stand by and tolerate AI executives’ unhinged risk-taking at the public’s expense. Our lawsuit asks the court to apply existing law and find the AI corporations’ reckless practices unlawful and freeze further AI development,” said Robert Weissman, co-president of Public Citizen .

“Children have already paid the price for Big Tech prioritizing profit over safety. We’ve watched chatbots push kids toward suicide and AI tools turn their ordinary photos into AI-generated child sexual abuse material,” said Brooke Istook, CEO of Heat Initiative . “Now these companies are racing to build AI systems they admit they may not be able to control. If that happens, the protections we’ve spent years fighting for won’t be enough. Heat Initiative joined this lawsuit not just to protect children from dangerous technology, but to protect their entire future. We refuse to wait until there’s nothing left to protect.”

“For years, the executives building these systems have warned us that their own frontier models pose catastrophic risks,” said Brendan Steinhauser, CEO of The Alliance for Secure AI. “Yet they keep racing to develop and market increasingly powerful AI that they admit they cannot reliably control, and are now handing over AI research and development to AI itself. We hold every other industry accountable when its products threaten public safety, and AI companies should be no different. Today, we’re asking the court to hold AI companies to that same standard and protect the public from the threats posed by these powerful models.”

The plaintiffs are invoking California’s Unfair Competition Law to challenge practices they allege threaten public health , safety, and property.

“It is patently illegal for companies to develop and release products they know are unsafe in any respect, let alone have the potential to exterminate the human race,” said Former New Jersey Attorney General Matthew Platkin , who filed the complaint on behalf of the plaintiffs. “We are asking the court to intervene before the risks AI executives have warned us about cause devastating and irreversible harm. AI companies are causing a public nuisance by knowingly developing and deploying AI systems that pose catastrophic risk. These companies must match their rhetoric with action and stop developing dangerous AI systems that can escape human control before a tragedy occurs.”

The plaintiffs assert that AI companies should not be permitted to develop or release AI systems that their executives admit can cause significant harm, such as by enabling the development of bioweapons and catastrophic cyberattacks. Rather than wait for a mass casualty event to occur, the plaintiffs believe California law enables them to seek a freeze on the development of the most dangerous AI systems now.

Public Citizen is a nonprofit consumer advocacy organization that champions the public interest in the halls of power. We defend democracy, resist corporate power and work to ensure that government works for the people - not for big corporations. Founded in 1971, we now have 500,000 members and supporters throughout the country.

A series of analyses released in the lead-up to the summit—including the United Nations Environment Program's " Limiting Overshoot " publication from September, the UNEP's " The Emissions Gap Report 2026: The Point of Return " from October, and the World Meteorological Organization's " State of the Climate: Update for COP31 " from last week—have all sounded the alarm about at least temporarily surpassing 1.5°C, the Paris Agreement's global temperature rise limit for this century.

American-made bombs appeared to have been used in an Israeli strike on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, Gaza on Thursday, in which at least six people, including a surgeon and at least one child, were killed and at least 28 more were injured.

Trevor Ball, an analyst with Armament Research Services, told The New York Times that Associated Press footage of the aftermath of the bombing showed two 250-pound precision-guided aerial bombs that were manufactured in the US.

During the interview, the Michigan Democrat explained why he would like to see Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) replace current Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) as head of the caucus when the party takes the majority in the upper congressional chamber next year.

"If every Democrat was talking like Chris Van Hollen," said one peace advocate, "we'd be just weeks away from ending this war."

As leading Democrats express hesitation about using an upcoming fight over government funding to cut off money for President Donald Trump's illegal Iran war, Sen. Chris Van Hollen and Rep. Ro Khanna are pushing their party to act boldly against a conflict that spurred massive backlash against the GOP at the ballot box last week.

The Washington Sun reported Wednesday that Van Hollen (D-Md.) and Khanna's (D-Calif.) call for Democrats to withhold their support for any government funding package unless it excludes money for the Iran war is "hitting resistance from senior members of the party." The outlet cited several top Democrats, including Rep. Adam Smith of Washington , Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware, Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia , and other lawmakers who have voiced skepticism about potentially sparking a government shutdown over war funding just weeks after the midterms.

Mark Warner of Virginia , and other lawmakers who have voiced skepticism about potentially sparking a government shutdown over war funding just weeks after the midterms.

The monsters of late-stage MAGA-ism.

In the hopeful, chaotic aftermath of the biggest blue wave in 50 years, the inept “cartoon ghoul of a man” who fomented the carnage and his foul minions - Miller, Hegseth, Unholy Mike, the wrong Dana White - are scrambling like “pigs in the mire” to grasp some thorny new realities. To wit: Accountability is neither revenge nor crime, their once-vaunted “leader” is a dead clown walking, and hundreds of flipped state and federal seats mean their sleazy party is over.

This week we got the first giddy sightings of new Congressional Democrats, who auspiciously look much like diverse America, arriving at the Capitol for orientation. Fresh from their historic wins - flipping 549 legislative seats, ending 13 GOP supermajorities, creating at least six new Democratic trifectas, taking control of the House and Senate - they will now govern three quarters of Americans even as the Republican Party , per one online wiseacre, devolves into the Donner Party. Amidst the lame finger-pointing and precipitous shattering of GOP control, Mike Johnson blindly insisted “voters made the wrong choice" and smarmy Josh Hawley called for Christians to meet the “shocking and historic” election with a (notably modest) hour-long fast on Dec. 15 at the Capitol. Cheap thoughts and prayers: Go for it.

Because nobody ever claimed those who don't learn from history are doomed to repeat it, MAGA world has simply tripled down on their unequivocally rejected folly. First, led by a fragile narcissist snugly embedded in his alternate reality, flaccid calls of a rigged election slowly emerged . "Here we go," noted weary America. “Lather, rinse, repeat." "Does anybody really believe this "Election" was honest?" Trump whined, devising some "creative math" to falsely argue, "The Alaska Race is OVER. Dan Sullivan WON, BY A LOT!" MAGA idiots chimed in . Pillow Guy's "cybersecurity team" vowed to reveal vague "matching algorithmic patterns across multiple states," Alex Jones weirdly declared Trump "the ultimate Democrat sleeper cell," one Christo-fascist announced a Jan. 3 "Million Crusader March - Bring your cross!" SAD. Even evil Megyn Kelly was fed up: "Just stop."

But cults, by definition, don't. Instead, hell-bent on more losing, Trump gave voters a teeny stubby middle finger and chose to boost some of his most abject zealots, all tied to hated and calamitous policies: Stephen Miller , aka Pee Wee German, a literal Nazi with " blood on his hands" whose despised deportation machine moved Hispanics to help turn Texas blue; Pete Kegsbreath, a widely loathed, utterly inept asshole and war criminal whose bungled Iran war has made life unaffordable for vast swathes of America; and Gym Jordan, a buffoonish loyalist and former assistant wrestling coach known for long ignoring an infamous sexual abuse scandal with thousands of victims - there's even a movie - that creepily echoes the regime's ongoing cover-up of Epstein's boundless, Trump-adjacent atrocities. Heckuva job, Donnie et al.

Above all, like cornered animals clinging to the heroic memory of Nixon's refusal to accept any responsibility for his crimes - “When the president does it, it's not illegal” - the MAGA reponse to its glaring failures and looming accountability for them is to cry mean wolf and argue enforcing the law and embracing the constitutional task of Congressional oversight is, in fact, a crime, even months before the fact. Trump's already shrieking Dem "SLEAZEBAGS should go to jail for what they are doing," ie their job, which as an uber grifter he can only weirdly see as "extortion." "They are threatening a lot of people because they happen to be Republicans ," he wailed, a scaredy-cat Mob bully pathetically melting down into his usual feeble projection. "There are no impeachable acts committed, or even thought of, by the victims of this illegal process."

His toadies have predictably mobilized to back him up - first, with bonkers threats. White House Counsel Will Scharf sent a mob-like, "legally repulsive" letter to incoming Oversight Chair Robert Garcia warning that Democrats undertaking their constitutionally mandated Congressional oversight "may cross the line into blatant criminality," resulting in, umm, imprisonment. Citing no criminal statute 'cause it doesn't exist, he snarled, "We are monitoring the abusive and capricious threats (to) harass and aggrandize, rather than to advance any legitimate legislative end,” a rebuke one lawyer called "a total bluff” given Dems have that "for miles." Other experts mocked "a ham-fisted stab at intimidation" that "will be Exhibit 1" in a self-own giving Dems "ammo to go straight to subpoenas." Said one, “Get D-team lawyers, win D-team prizes.”

Attorney General (sic) Todd Blanche, who as America's top law enforcement official "clearly doesn’t have the slightest clue what the rule of law is," went on both CNN and Fox to also suggest Dems were committing crimes; when asked what those might be, viewers noted he looked worried - or "scargry," a blend of scared and angry - before he pivoted to, "I'm not interested in explaining." He babbled about Dems' "extremely troubling rhetoric, no basis, no facts, just everyone running around...You have to draw the line, we have to wake up in this country, that's not governing, that's a disappointment." And yes of course it's his job to represent Goebbels and "everyone else...Every A.G. in history actively defends executive members of an administration." In other words, "Trump's former personal lawyer is still Trump's personal lawyer."

Despite MAGA’s bravado - and cleaning house of flunkies who may have receipts - they continue to be “led” by a fumbling clown - caravans, "Afghanistan jungles," "perceived loss," "chartered the human ginome" - who lately ends speeches with, “By the way, I was not on the ballot.” On 60 Minutes, even right-wing Ross Douthat nailed him for his poors-are-dumb retort to $3 billion in grift and corruption : “I have a son who watches over money...Every president has a problem (going) back to George Washington .” And there was his inane Press Secretary choice of “the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior” who'd maybe bring some UFC fighters “though not from our Country, to defend us against the Lunatic Left.” He said he was “just kidding” after people realized he had the wrong Dana White, who alas is Black - other suggested Whites: Vanna, Betty, Walter - but he dragged his White to a bizarre presser anyway.

Amidst the tomfoolery, pundits point out the mid-term avalanche was the biggest rejection of any party since Watergate; its 13% net gain was the largest margin of victory since 1926, a "once-in-a century margin." "Everything is coming," says one. "It's going to be an entirely new day." Thanks to another GOP own goal, Dems will hit the ground running: They've been building investigative staffs from a large pool of former career prosecutors purged by Trump who know where the bodies are: "You cannot shred institutional memory - they just changed employers." Dems are working to reverse disastrous cuts in Medicaid , SNAP , other benefits. They're probing Susie Wiles' work with Kremlin-connected lobbyists and Marco Rubio's $1.2 million spent on military flights to Florida to watch his son (occasionally) play college football on our dime.

A judge made a D.C. golf course lawsuit the Caddyshack-like " surprise contender " for a belated legal showdown over feds' defiance of court orders, with a special master appointed to investigate "ethical violations” in the case. In Mississippi, Scott Colom just ousted Cindy Hyde-Smith to become the state's first Black U.S. senator since 1874, flipping the Dems' eighth Senate seat. Thomas Massie's resolute move to impeach "dangerously incompetent" Pete Hegseth for war crimes failed despite Hegseth's low-rent, lie-filled, "just following orders" hissy fit presser: "When he’s attacked, he hides behind the troops.” He squeaked through this time - "Tick tock get ready" - but John Oliver spoke for many when he urged, "Remove this fucking asshole." And Massie just got enough signatures to finally force a House vote to release millions of Epstein files. Garcia: “Our work is just getting started.”

Meanwhile, the guy whose lamentable victory Trump celebrated as "the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot" again proved what a " warrior ethos jerk" he remains - on Veterans ' Day yet - at an event at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, the country's most sacred war memorial. Because "everything is a show or photo op" to the empty buffoon with the make-up studio, Hegseth and his clueless coterie stood on the steps of the memorial for a "truly abhorrent " picture ; as they turned away, one of them loudly laughed, prompting a guard to furiously bark at them, as mandated, “ALL VISITORS WILL MAINTAIN AN ATMOSPHERE OF SILENCE AND RESPECT AT ALL TIMES." Online, a gazillion horrified people called Pete an oblivious asshat; many recalled visiting the site as middle-school kids who even then knew better, so what's his fucking problem.

At Arlington Trump was likewise insufferable. He compared his illegal 48-hour kidnapping stunt in Venezuela to America's endless, obscene tragedies in Vietnam , Iraq, Afghanistan, hideously argued "we got very little from any of those wars,” and gloated, "We’re taking out billions and billions of dollars of oil...To the victor belong the spoils." What a grotesquerie. Now the knives are out for him. For Veterans' Day, the Secret Handshake erected a new Bone Spurs tribute on the National Mall. Dubbed "The Foot Soldier," it features a golden Trump sitting on a pedestal rubbing a sore foot. Two plaques bear quotes. One from a 2013 photo in his Military Academy uniform: "I can be very military.” The other: "We honor the sacrifice (of) a soldier in spirit who marched to the front lines of dodging the draft, armed with a perfect diagnosis of bone spurs.”

With Democrats already infighting as the lame duck waddles amidst his crimes, lies, hate and question he'll never answer, The Bulwark entreats us to remember "There are no deals to be had." Our sole mission: "Destroy all monsters." In Unpopular Front, John Ganz proffers a similar but darker ultimatum: Eternal torment. He recalls 60 Minutes' Douthat asking Trump, "Do you think you're going to heaven?" Reply: "I hope so." Citing Christian forgiveness of your enemies, he asks if the smallest man on Earth can do that. Nope, he says: "I hate my enemies and I always will." In Dante's Inferno , Ganz notes, Dante and Virgil stop to talk to souls " stuck like animated friezes, repeating their state of sinfulness, the perpetual fate of the Wrathful...already pigs in the mire in this life." Thus is Trump's hatred "the entire substance of his being, the product of his disordered love for himself," and "relinquishing it would be an intolerable loss of self." So, inevitably, will he be "solidified into eternal bronzer."

"He was an arrogant person in the world/No goodness adorns his memory."

scraped.title: Palestinian Opinions Are Divided as Elections Are Now Postponed Until 2027
scraped.description: Although some in Gaza welcomed the prospect of elections, many are looking for solutions to more urgent problems.
scraped.author: Qassam Muaddi
scraped.h1: Palestinian Opinions Are Divided as Elections Are Now Postponed Until 2027
scraped.body_text:
Although some in Gaza welcomed the prospect of elections, many are looking for solutions to more urgent problems.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

On October 10, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas issued a presidential decree postponing the legislative and presidential elections from November 2026, the original scheduled date, until September 2027.

Amid obstacles imposed by the Israeli occupation, the postponement was justified by a need to create appropriate political, security, and on-the-ground conditions for free, fair, and inclusive elections.

According to the official Palestinian news agency WAFA , the decree aims to allow for comprehensive national dialogue to strengthen Palestinian unity, preserve Palestinian territory, safeguard the political system, address challenges that the electoral process is facing, and ensure the participation of Palestinians in Jerusalem, the West Bank, and the Gaza Strip while protecting their political and constitutional rights.

While some expected the postponement, in light of the cancellation of Palestinian elections in 2021, it nevertheless came as a surprise to observers.

In the Gaza Strip, reactions to the decision have been divided. Some consider it to be in the national interest, arguing that the current conditions in Gaza do not permit elections. Others believe that postponing the vote, after more than 20 years without elections, undermines the national democratic process and marginalizes the role of Gaza’s residents in determining their political future.

Fadi al-Sheikh Youssef, head of a youth-led electoral list that had been preparing to contest the elections, described the postponement as an unjust and direct denial of the Palestinian people’s democratic right.

“The elections should have continued after nearly 20 years of freezing the democratic process in Palestine,” he said. “If the Israeli occupation has imposed obstacles, the elections should have become a political battle fought by all parties against the occupation. This electoral process should have been a new opportunity to expose the occupation to the world and reveal the falsity of its claims about democratic practices and its supposed respect for freedom of expression and Palestinians’ right to political participation.”

He added that the postponement appeared to reflect an agreement among political parties to reproduce the same political landscape.

“Unfortunately, we see this postponement as part of an effort by the parties to recreate the same political scene. Even the justification of national consensus does not reflect the real wishes of the Palestinian people. If there had truly been national consensus, it should have been achieved over the past 20 years, not now, as the political landscape is being reshaped through a democratic process,” he said.

Al-Sheikh Youssef described the decision as deeply unjust and ill-suited to the current political landscape, arguing that it excluded new groups and political actors seeking to enter the arena and defend what remains of people’s dignity.

In a statement, Hamas said it viewed the decision to postpone the elections until next year as a step in the right direction, given the absence of the political, security, and on-the-ground conditions necessary for free and fair elections throughout the occupied Palestinian territories, including Jerusalem.

Hamas said the postponement should lead to comprehensive, serious and productive national dialogue. It also expressed its readiness to participate in discussions aimed at reaching clear and binding agreements for all parties, including mechanisms to reorganize Palestinian political institutions, particularly the Palestinian National Council and the Palestinian Legislative Council.

Furthermore, some Palestinian political analysts and academics offered a broader assessment of the political calculations behind the postponement and its potential consequences for the Palestinian political system.

Political analyst Adel Shadid told Mondoweiss that “despite the Palestinian demands and European pressure on the Palestinian Authority to hold elections, the PA are afraid of elections, because they know its officials know that there are real possibilities of losing, and despite that, I was surprised by the postponement of elections.”

According to Shadid, the elections were postponed in an unexpected manner. “I expected the Palestinian president Mahmoud Abbas to unilaterally call off the elections, like in 2021, but I didn’t expect all the Palestinian factions to meet in Cairo and then come out with a joint statement to call off the elections together,” he said.

Shadid pointed out that although the alliance of Hamas, the Palestinian Islamic Jihad, and the dissident Fatah currents led by Mohammad Dahlan and Nasser Al Qudwah had a very high chance of winning, these factions knew that there was still uncertainty regarding Israeli attempts to block Palestinians from voting in east Jerusalem. This would have given the PA the possibility of calling off elections by blaming the decision on Israel, exposing their unwillingness to relinquish control, while the factions wanted to make it clear that it was a Palestinian decision. Shadid also said that “the result of this decision will be that the Palestinian political scene will remain at the current stagnation, which prolongs the overall Palestinian incapacity to face the Israeli offensive.”

Shadid, who twenty years ago ran the elections campaign for Fatah in Hebron, the West Bank’s largest city, today believes that all factions, including the leadership of Fatah in the PA, act on narrow political calculations rather than the overall national interest.

“During the revolutionary years of the PLO, when it was based in exile, political legitimacy came from the role played in the struggle, or as the saying goes, from the barrel of the gun,” Shadid explained. “But since the PA was established as an embryo for a Palestinian state, legitimacy comes from a popular vote, but this transition wasn’t fully and properly made, which has created a rift between the leadership and the people.”

Despite the uncertainty, he remains hopeful for the next generation of Palestinian leaders. “The international solidarity movement today finds more Palestinian partners in civil society, where they can find more Palestinians from the young generations with whom they can cooperate, and eventually, a new Palestinian leadership will emerge and channel all this potential towards Palestinian liberation,” Shadid said.

For Palestinian analyst and academic Akram Atallah, all factions feared the elections, because their performance in the past years, especially during the Gaza genocide, was very poor. This meant that despite the wide opposition alliance, the voting rate would have shown that the popularity of all of them has fallen back.

“I wasn’t surprised by the postponement of elections, because in my opinion, president Abbas believed that Hamas, his main opponent, had lost much of its popularity and capacity of influence, but the formation of the wide opposition alliance changed his calculations, therefore, it was expected from him to postpone elections,” he told Mondoweiss .

Atallah believes that the consequences of calling off elections will be paid by the Palestinian people in general. “Elections for Palestinians meant the possibility to renew their leadership in order to counter the Israeli genocidal and expansionist project, and calling elections off means to remain in the same political weakness experienced by the Palestinian people,” he said.

For Atallah, the entire Palestinian political system is in crisis, from the PA losing influence to Hamas losing capacity to present an opposition, resulting in all factions becoming more concerned with “their share in the political pie” rather than a renewed leadership for Palestine.

Despite this, he insists that “the Palestinian people will produce new leadership, and Palestinians will continue their struggle and resilience despite the political stagnation.”

On the streets of Gaza, opinions remain divided between those who support the postponement and those who oppose it.

Mahmoud al-Dhahir, 41, originally from Rafah and now displaced in Khan Younis, said President Abbas had made the right decision, given the instability of the Gaza Strip’s political and security situation. According to al-Dhahir, people in Gaza are already struggling with severe problems related to food and shelter, leaving them in no position to focus on elections or think clearly about which candidates could meet their needs.

“We are now living in just 30 percent of the Gaza Strip. If elections are to be held, we at least want to be able to return to all parts of Gaza and move freely. Only then can we think about who will serve the interests of the Palestinian people and go to the ballot boxes,” he said.

Al-Dhahir had voted in the 2006 elections, hoping that conditions would improve. However, after Palestinians chose their representatives through the ballot box and Hamas’s list won, he said, Israel imposed a tighter blockade on Gaza and deprived its residents of their rights.

He argued that conditions in the West Bank might be more conducive to elections because its residents are not facing a genocide, but that the situation in Gaza is entirely different.

“The Palestinian people in Gaza have been living through a genocide that has continued for three years and has not yet ended,” he said. “It would be better to look for solutions to end this genocide before thinking about another vote or another election.”

Although some people in Gaza had welcomed the prospect of elections as a democratic process through which residents could choose their representatives, the conditions they face have left many looking for solutions to more urgent problems.

Bassem al-Masri, 51, who was displaced from Beit Hanoun and is now living in Deir al-Balah, said he was delighted when the elections were announced for a near-future date, viewing them as a long-overdue democratic right for the Palestinian people. At the same time, he said the current circumstances in Gaza were not conducive to holding elections.

More pressing priorities include enabling displaced people to return to their homes and rebuilding the houses they have lost. All of this, he argued, requires Palestinian leaders to unite before elections take place.

“Palestinian factions and leaders who want to unite and consolidate their political decisions into a single position should have taken this step to help the Palestinians devastated in Gaza, rather than doing so merely to take part in elections,” al-Masri said.

scraped.body_text:
Karp, who gave $1 million to MAGA Inc. in 2024, said after the midterms that he’s been a Democrat his “whole life.”

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation .

As Democrats prepare for their sweeping campaign to investigate corporate abuses during the upcoming Congress, Palantir CEO Alex Karp claimed this week that he and his company — a massive Trump administration collaborator — are actually “progressive” now.

Karp, who gave $1 million to MAGA Inc. in 2024 and another million for Donald Trump’s inauguration, told Politico Playbook on Wednesday that he’s always been a Democrat.

“I’ve been a Democrat my whole life. I grew up in a far left environment. I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir — all of our products are essentially progressive,” he told Politico , speaking of his company that has a $30 million contract with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to aid Trump’s mass deportation campaign.

Far from being progressive, Karp and his company have helped to accelerate the Trump administration’s descent into fascism while wooing Trump in order to gain favor with the government.

Just in April, Palantir landed in hot water for posting a far right, 22-point manifesto that it said was a summary of Karp’s 2025 book, The Technological Republic . Critics described the X post as technofascist, as it espoused a pro-war, pro-policing ideology, lamented the post-Holocaust “neutering” of Nazi Germany and Japan, and said that cultures that have “produced vital advances” are superior to those that are “dysfunctional and regressive.”

The tech CEO has been on the record many times branding himself and Palantir as undertaking a far right effort, with Karp calling his company “anti-woke” and praising the Trump administration’s anti-immigration measures.

But in the Politico interview, Karp claimed that he was happy that Trump acknowledged that “we kinda went too far” on immigration — a misrepresentation of Trump’s words earlier this week. Karp used the word “progressive” eight times to describe his political philosophy, despite the fact that progressivism is typically known for being antiwar, pro-immigrant, and opposed to tech companies like Palantir .

On top of Karp’s contributions to Trump, Palantir was recently revealed to have donated $10 million to Trump’s East Wing ballroom project. In exchange for these gifts, the Trump administration has helped to propel Palantir to being one of the top recipients of federal contracts, embedding its AI systems in the military and recruiting the company to mine Americans’ data to help monitor and build cases against people targeted by Trump’s deportation campaign.

Karp also appears to have given Republican House candidate Jay Obernolte $7,000 in January, federal disclosures show, though he listed his employer as “Plantatir Technologies” — making it so that his company wouldn’t come up in database search queries for Palantir, spelled correctly.

Karp’s comments represent what is likely a naked attempt to woo Democrats before they take control of Congress in January.

Some Democratic committees have already looked into Palantir for its dealings with the Trump administration and its work in building out mass surveillance systems for the federal government. This has spurred Palantir to hire former Democratic Sen. Jon Tester this week, in preparation for the new Congress. Palantir and other tech firms have also donated to House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York), who is poised to become speaker of the Democratically-controlled House.

scraped.title: Refugee Groups Sue to Stop Canada From Handing Over Asylum Seekers to ICE
scraped.description: The lawsuit says handing asylum seekers over to the abuse-perpetrating US is a violation of Canada’s constitution.
scraped.author: Jillian Kestler-D’Amours
scraped.h1: Refugee Groups Sue to Stop Canada From Handing Over Asylum Seekers to ICE
scraped.body_text:
The lawsuit says handing asylum seekers over to the abuse-perpetrating US is a violation of Canada’s constitution.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Canada is violating its own constitution by turning asylum seekers away at the border with the United States, where they face serious threats under U.S. President Donald Trump, Canadian legal experts and rights advocates say .

Amnesty International Canada, the Canadian Council for Refugees, and the Canadian Council of Churches are in court this week to challenge a decades-old pact that allows Canadian officials to summarily send most refugees back at the U.S. border.

People rallied in Toronto and Montreal, the two largest cities in Canada, on Monday to show support for the case and call on the Canadian government to rip up the Safe Third Country Agreement (STCA).

In Montreal, dozens of protesters held posters that read, “Canada must protect, not send back” and “Humanity has no borders.”

“If Canadians don’t feel safe in the United States, we can be sure that refugees aren’t safe either,” Lauren Lallemand, co-executive director of the Canadian Council for Refugees, told the crowd.

“The asylum system in the U.S. is failing, and those who flee in search of safety deserve to be protected.”

The Agreement

The Safe Third Country Agreement, which came into force in 2004, is premised on the idea that Canada and the U.S. each offer people access to a robust refugee protection system.

In practice, it means that asylum seekers can seek protection in the first country they arrive in, but not both: someone in the U.S. cannot apply for asylum in Canada, or vice versa.

For years, the restriction applied to asylum claims made at official crossings along the border.

But if people entered Canada irregularly between ports of entry (via farmers’ fields or rural roads, for example), they could circumvent the pact — and as Trump began to crack down on immigration during his first term, tens of thousands of people made dangerous crossings into Canada to request protection.

In 2023, amid public and political pressure to crack down on immigration, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and President Joe Biden closed the loophole, extending the Safe Third Country Agreement to the entire 5,525-mile border.

Now, only people who meet specific conditions — such as unaccompanied minors or individuals with relatives who are already in Canada — are exempt from being turned away under the Safe Third Country Agreement.

“Extremely Urgent, Harmful”

The lawsuit being heard in Federal Court in Toronto this week argues that the Safe Third Country Agreement violates equality rights under Section 15 of Canada’s constitution, known as the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

According to the complainants, that’s because the pact disproportionately harms racialized asylum seekers, including women fleeing gender-based violence, children, and members of the LGBTQ+ community.

Julia Sande, a lawyer at Amnesty International Canada, explained that Section 15 applies to everyone who is physically in the country, including refugee claimants.

“Canada cannot deport people to face torture, harm [and] persecution in another country,” she said. “It would be a violation of their Charter rights, even if it’s another country doing the harm, because it’s Canada’s decision to send them out … [and] to put them in [harm’s way] when harm is reasonably foreseeable.”

While conditions for asylum seekers and refugees in the U.S. have been concerning for a long time, Sande said the situation has deteriorated dramatically under the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump.

She pointed to the expansion of immigration detention as one example. “Things are obviously extremely urgent and extremely harmful,” she said.

“We all act in horror at what’s unfolding in the United States. You hear Canadian citizens talking about being afraid to go there, being afraid of ICE.”

“We all act in horror at what’s unfolding in the United States. You hear Canadian citizens talking about being afraid to go there, being afraid of ICE,” she told Truthout.

“I have a hard time believing that you could find anyone here who would say, ‘Yeah I’d really like my government to hand a child over to ICE to be thrown in detention … and ultimately sent back to a country where they fled gang violence.’”

Government Defends Pact

Canada’s federal immigration ministry — Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada — told Truthout in an email that it can’t comment on matters before the courts.

But it said the Safe Third Country Agreement “is designed to keep the Canada–U.S. border safe and well-managed,” adding: “It helps avoid sudden spikes in asylum claims that could overwhelm border crossings, housing, and processing systems. This means Canada can keep the border orderly while continuing to offer protection to people who need it.”

The government also says on its website that, “only countries that respect human rights and offer a high degree of protection to asylum seekers may be designated as safe third countries.”

But Yael Schacher, head of the Americas program at humanitarian group Refugees International, said the U.S. “absolutely” does not meet that threshold.

“The U.S. does not have fair procedures for asylum seekers anymore,” she said.

“We have a situation here where people that — by Canadian standards — should be entitled to asylum, entitled to protection, are having their rights violated all the time in the United States in many, many ways.”

“Canada Should Be Thinking Twice”

Schacher told Truthout that the Trump administration is not effectively screening asylum seekers for harm they would face should they be deported from the U.S. It also has purged judges who may have been favorable to asylum cases from U.S. immigration courts, effectively transforming them into “deportation courts.”

At the same time, the U.S. government is detaining people in dire conditions as it pushes to deport them to their home countries or to third countries where they face myriad dangers, including torture and imprisonment.

She described a recent case in which a Haitian man agreed to be deported to Haiti’s capital Port-au-Prince — which has been ravaged by deadly gang-related violence — after eight months in U.S. detention because he could not get sufficient insulin to manage his diabetes.

“He gave up his right to an asylum hearing on the merits because he couldn’t take the detention conditions anymore. He was afraid he was going to die,” Schacher said.

She said there have been cases in which people handed over to U.S. immigration authorities by Canada at the border have been detained and deported without a fair assessment of their asylum claims.

“‘Turning away’ is a way too euphemistic way of describing what Canada is doing, which is giving people to the U.S. immigration authorities, who are then putting them in prison and deporting them,” Schacher said, adding that Canada needs to rethink the STCA altogether.

“The U.S. doesn’t provide asylum anymore, and Canada — like Mexico — needs to rethink how it relates to the United States as a result.”

“The U.S. doesn’t provide asylum anymore, and Canada — like Mexico — needs to rethink how it relates to the United States as a result.”

That was echoed by Sande at Amnesty International Canada, who said that while she expects the legal challenge to the Safe Third Country Agreement to be a long process, the Canadian government “has the power to end this at any time.”

“If you survey people on the street and ask them, based on what you’ve seen unfolding in the United States, do you think the United States is safe for refugees? I think most people would say no,” Sande said.

“A government does not need a court to tell them what is abundantly obvious. They could stop sending people back to the U.S. today.”

scraped.title: Top intelligence Democrat says GOP should renew spy program before Democrats take over
scraped.description: Rep. Jim Himes evidently doesn’t think his fellow Democrats are big enough fans of warrantless surveillance.
scraped.author: Sophie Hurwitz
scraped.h1: Top Intelligence Democrat Says GOP Should Renew Spy Program Before Democrats Take Over
scraped.body_text:
“Americans across the political spectrum have good reason to distrust unchecked executive branch surveillance power,” civil liberties watchdog groups said. Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty

On Wednesday, the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, Rep. Jim Himes (D–Conn.), urged Republicans to “take the win” and renew President Donald Trump’s warrantless mass surveillance powers during the lame duck session.

Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA)—a provision used by US intelligence agencies to spy on the electronic communications of thousands of people outside the United States without a warrant—lapsed in June. Privacy advocates and civil libertarians have long decried the law as unconstitutional, and earlier this year, seven Republicans defied Trump and voted against renewing it .

But Himes, an intelligence hawk, is one of Section 702’s most vocal defenders—even if that means handing warrantless spying powers to the man he once called a “dictator.” With Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate, Himes is suggesting that his Republican colleagues “get this thing done in the lame-duck because it’s, you know, it’s going to be a very different 702 that gets reauthorized in the first quarter of next year,” as The Hill reported.

Trump opposed Section 702 during the Biden administration, but now that he’s back in office, he thinks the program is crucial for national security. And while congressional support for the program has largely hewed to partisan lines, Himes sounds more at ease with warrantless surveillance than most of his Democratic colleagues. He has called Section 702, even under the Trump administration, the country’s “ most rigorously overseen ” surveillance program and told WIRED he’s seen “zero evidence of abuse.” (Last year, the FBI closed an office that monitored for Section 702 abuses.) In April, Himes was the sole member of his state’s congressional delegation to back the program’s renewal, objecting only when Trump briefly placed Federal Housing Finance Agency hatchetman Bill Pulte in charge of national intelligence .

Come January, Himes will take the reins as chair of the House Intelligence Committee. In Wednesday interviews with The New York Times and The Washington Post , he set out his agenda for “aggressive” oversight of the Trump administration’s intelligence activities, including scrutinizing the CIA’s covert overseas operations. Himes also told reporters that the committee plans to “examine donations” made by defense contractors to Trump construction projects and “investigate whether intelligence analysts have been pressured to write reports that align with the objectives of senior officials in the Trump administration.”

But as Himes positions himself as a watchdog, civil liberties groups are condemning his final-hour effort to renew Section 702. On Thursday, a coalition including Demand Progress, the American Civil Liberties Union, and others sent a letter urging congressional leaders to keep FISA reauthorization off the table until the next Congress, noting that Section 702 has been used in recent years to spy on protesters , elected officials, and journalists.

“Americans across the political spectrum have good reason to distrust unchecked executive branch surveillance power,” the letter states. “No member of Congress knows who will occupy the White House in the years ahead, and constitutional protections should not depend on who is president.”

“Jim Himes has betrayed his own party and the American people,” Demand Progress senior policy advisor Hajar Hammado said in a statement. “After seeing a blowout election where Americans overwhelmingly rejected Trump and sided with the Democrats, Himes’s first instinct was to urge Republicans to use the little time they have left to hand Donald Trump and Stephen Miller the mass surveillance powers that they’re asking for.”

scraped.title: Alex Karp wants to be friends with Democrats again
scraped.description: The “arsenal of the broligarchy” is trying to ride the blue wave.
scraped.author: Sophie Hurwitz
scraped.h1: Alex Karp Wants to Be Friends With Democrats Again
scraped.body_text:
Palantir CEO Alex Karp is feeling blue. Mother Jones; Benedikt Von Loebell/Avalon/ZUMA

The surveillance tech giant Palantir’s products have always been “essentially progressive,” its founder Alex Karp said Wednesday.

Karp’s company won hundreds of millions of dollars in contracts under Donald Trump’s second term, soaring past the billion-dollar quarterly revenue mark by working with ICE to monitor immigrants and building AI systems for the US military. Karp has been known to praise Trump’s entrepreneurial instincts and crow about how Palantir’s technology “ disrupts humanities-trained, largely Democratic voters , and makes their economic power less.” But in a Politico Playbook interview today, he appeared to change his tune, pitching himself as the right weapons-tech oligarch to surf the blue wave.

“I’ve been a Democrat my whole life,” Karp said. “I grew up in a far-left environment. I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir—all of our products are essentially progressive.”

It is true that Karp has traditionally supported Democrats— he backed Kamala Harris in 2024. But after Trump’s reelection, Karp allied himself with the “anti-woke” right , and profited immensely by doing so.

Military contracting has always been a bipartisan business. But the Silicon Valley contractors who surged to power under Trump—Karp and Peter Thiel, as well as Elon Musk and Anduril’s Palmer Luckey —haven’t been shy about declaring their allegiances with the president’s party.

But now they’re nervous. The $1.5 trillion defense budget proposed by Pete Hegseth may be cut down in the 120th Congress. “A $1.1 trillion dollar budget will require them to make some trade-offs,” as government budget expert Mark Cancian of the Center for Strategic and International Studies put it in an article published Monday on the “tough choices, uncertainty, and scrutiny” defense contractors may now face: Companies could also be inundated with anti-corruption inquiries come January.

Karp’s pivot is emblematic of an industry positioning itself to stay in power, no matter which party controls the government. I spoke to defense and security reporter Sharon Weinberger, whose new book, Valley of Death , tracks the rise of the “arsenal of the broligarchy,” about what we can expect from Silicon Valley’s armorers as electoral power shifts in America.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

So, this assertion by Alex Karp that Palantir’s products are now “essentially progressive”—what do you make of that?

It’s not at all surprising for me, both for Palantir and probably what you’re going to see out of other companies going forward. Palantir, even going back to its early days, has tried to thread the needle on politics, so they have both portrayed themselves as an all-seeing surveillance system—in the sense that they’re named after palantiri , these all-seeing stones that actually have ominous connotations—but at the same time, since pretty early on, they have made this argument that they themselves are not actually a surveillance system, because they are not collecting the data, but allowing the data to be integrated.

I don’t take a side in that debate. I just think it’s very interesting that they want to portray themselves as all-powerful, but at the same time they don’t want to be portrayed as a surveillance system that violates privacy. And they’ve tried under every administration, under different eras, like the post-Snowden concerns about privacy and surveillance , to kind of have it, I would say, both ways.

Alex Karp is always a bit of a chameleon. He’s also a master of narrative. He has long identified as a Democrat, and if you look at his political donations, he—like other people involved in defense—actually kind of sprinkles the money around, because they have to survive in both Democratic and Republican administrations.

But he was always positioning himself ultimately as a Democrat for a long time, up until December 2024, at the Reagan National Defense Forum, which is the major bipartisan defense forum that’s held every year at the Reagan Library in California. He gets up as part of his panel, as part of his talk, and starts blasting the Democrats for their, quote, “woke pagan ideology.” It was sort of unprecedented for the CEO of a major defense contractor to attack a political party, either political party.

Given that, do you expect the results of last week’s midterms to affect the “arsenal of the broligarchy” that you write about?

What I’ve long argued is that people have real beliefs. I don’t doubt that Alex Karp has real beliefs. Peter Thiel certainly has real beliefs about the Antichrist and many other things.

But as companies, they have to survive in Democratic and Republican administrations, and they’re going to do that by maneuvering in their language and their narrative. They’re going to do that by the people they hire, which will be from both administrations, and the lobbyists they hire. But what is so different and a little bit dangerous about some of these new wave of defense companies like Palantir is that they have broken the norms of being bipartisan, where defense has long been a bipartisan issue.

So it’s not just whether they go from Democrat to Republican. And another pivot that’s worth mentioning—in fact, it’s I would say it’s a triple pivot for Karp—in the book, I have this picture of him in his Haverford College yearbook photo, draped in a keffiyeh.

I was going to ask you about the keffiyeh photo!

Karp may be just a little bit older than me. I don’t believe the same things I believed 20 or 30 years ago. I don’t criticize him personally for going through a political transformation, but after the October 7 attacks and then the expansion of the war in Gaza, he became a very vocal critic of some of the college campus protests.

That gives me pause for two reasons. We don’t really want the heads of our defense contractors to be commenting on domestic political speech. It’s a norm issue, not whether I agree or disagree with what he is saying, but also it reflects this amazing chameleon-like transformation that he’s made. And he’s making it again, if you look at some of his most recent remarks, because after October 7, it was “we stand with Israel.”

Now in some recent remarks, he’s a little bit backing away from that, just as you’re seeing with his remarks on ICE and immigration about going too far. The guy is a master of narrative. I give him credit on that. My biggest problem is not what he believes or doesn’t believe, but the way that we have traditionally expected our defense companies to stay out of politics.

Another major Silicon Valley contractor that I have on the mind right now is Elon Musk, who spent something like $400 million supporting losing candidates in the midterms . Do you expect to see any kind of similar pivot now from him?

Musk is the more extreme case. My issues with Musk are not his personal views or his political views, but again, the norm-breaking. He’s going to have a tougher time clawing back. But he’s also in a little bit of a different position because SpaceX has a de facto monopoly on military space launch.

That being said, business-wise, he’s not suicidal. I think it’ll be really interesting to watch what he does. He has certainly been influenced by the fact that Tesla has connections in China , and he has always backed away from making major criticisms of China. I suspect he will learn to like, if not love, a Democratic Congress.

This also depends on what happens with the next administration in two years. I suspect that we are also going to see some—I don’t know if moderation is the right word—but I wouldn’t be surprised if he shifts, if not his political position, then certainly his involvement in politics. I would not be surprised at all.

I think what he’ll see is that his dalliances, both with DOGE and his very right-wing stance , could be a detriment to his business. And I think he cares about his business above anything else. I’m not sure that he’s going to go and start embracing Democrats right away. But I do think that he is not going to try to fight a prevailing administration or Congress.

Any chance we’ll see a Silicon Valley version of the 1993 Pentagon Last Supper , when the Department of Defense warned weapons-makers that the government’s weapons-buying budget would shrink?

I mean, when the stock market bubble eventually collapses—we now have dozens, if not hundreds, of startups—you will see consolidation. Venture capitalists will tell you this. There is going to be a vast consolidation of these new startups, but that’s separate from the politics. Elon Musk has really notched successes with SpaceX in space launch, but the others have not proved themselves.

The question I raise is, if Silicon Valley companies become the new prime [contractors], are they going to be any better, faster, cheaper, or more innovative than the old primes?

scraped.title: RFK Jr. promotes activist who called abortion pill ‘high-risk’
scraped.description: The move is yet another sign that a Trump administration crackdown on mifepristone is coming.
scraped.author: Nina Martin
scraped.h1: RFK Jr. Promotes Activist Who Called Abortion Pill ‘High-Risk’
scraped.body_text:
Natalie Dodson receives an award from her boss, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., for her work on Moms.gov. Deptartment of Health and Human Services

This article has been republished from Autonomy News , a worker-owned publication covering reproductive rights and justice. Follow Autonomy News on Instagram , Bluesky , TikTok , Threads , and LinkedIn .

An anti-abortion operative is moving up the ranks at the Department of Health and Human Services. Natalie Dodson, a contributor to Project 2025, was promoted in October to counselor in the Immediate Office of the Secretary, according to her LinkedIn profile . That means she is in a position to advise HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. directly on programs and policy.

Researchers and abortion providers told Autonomy News they’re worried about the move. “The promotion of Natalie Dodson to a senior position advising the HHS Secretary is very concerning given her history of spreading scientific and health-related misinformation,” Daniel Grossman, an OB-GYN and director of Advancing New Standards in Reproductive Health at the University of California San Francisco, said in a statement.

Dodson previously worked at a far-right think tank, where she railed against the abortion drug mifepristone. During her time at HHS, she won an award for her work on a pronatalist website . She also serves as the acting deputy assistant secretary for population affairs, a position she has held since October of last year. That’s the HHS division that oversees Title X, the federal family planning program that the Trump administration has overhauled exactly as Project 2025 laid out . Dodson seems to have a friendly relationship with Kennedy—a post on her now-private Instagram profile shows them participating in falconry together.

HHS did not respond to a request for comment by publication time.

Dodson’s promotion comes at a critical moment. Though Democrats have retaken the House and Senate and promised to aggressively investigate Donald Trump and his allies, the White House still has plenty of levers to pull to restrict abortion access. Trump remains in control of federal agencies, which could swiftly impose new limits on medication abortion across the country. Congress would have little power to intervene.

The first attack came within days after the midterm elections: On Friday, the Department of Justice signaled that it would intervene in a Texas lawsuit that, if successful, has the potential to bankrupt Planned Parenthood .

“It is easy to read between the lines of her promotion: The Trump administration will continue to support any and all efforts to make abortion harder to access.”

In the months leading up to the midterms, administration officials certainly gave the impression that a post-election crackdown was on the way. Attorney General Todd Blanche said he would revisit the federal government’s interpretation of the Comstock Act, an 1873 obscenity law the anti-abortion movement argues should be enforced as a nationwide abortion ban. On a private call, Blanche also promised “ permanent solutions ” to the availability of abortion pills by mail. In a Congressional hearing, FBI Director Kash Patel said he was open to investigating abortion pill manufacturers.

Of all these looming threats, the most immediate is likely the Food and Drug Administration’s ongoing “ review ” of mifepristone’s safety, which is set to be completed early next year . Recent comments from FDA attorneys suggest that, at the very least, the agency is poised to reinstate old restrictions on mifepristone, which could require patients to make an unnecessary in-person visit to a clinic to get the drug, banning its availability via telehealth. Project 2025 called for the agency to revoke its approval of the drug entirely, which Kennedy has the power to do .

Trump’s latest pick to lead the FDA—Heidi Overton, a physician who has called abortion pills “dangerous” —will almost certainly be confirmed by the outgoing Republican Senate majority before the end of the year.

Prior to HHS, Dodson worked at the far-right Ethics and Public Policy Center (EPPC), an organization backed by megadonor Leonard Leo, who also serves on its board . Leo-backed groups spent millions to move the federal judiciary to the right , and have continued to pump money into anti-abortion causes since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade with its decision in Dobbs . The post- Dobbs effort to challenge the FDA’s approval of mifepristone in court has been led by Leo-funded organizations .

In fact, it was a report released by the EPPC that kicked off the FDA’s mifepristone review. In April 2025, the EPPC published a paper on its website purporting to show that mifepristone is much more dangerous than current FDA data would suggest. The report was deeply flawed—it wasn’t peer reviewed, and experts questioned its methods .

However, anti-abortion groups and lawmakers took the questionable paper and ran with it: Missouri Senator Josh Hawley sent a letter to the FDA the same day the report was published, demanding the agency “restore critical safeguards on the use of mifepristone.” Responding to Hawley in a Senate hearing a few weeks later, Kennedy called the report “alarming” and said its findings “indicate the label needs to be changed.” On June 2, then-FDA Commissioner Marty Makary pledged to conduct a review of mifepristone’s safety.

Though there’s no indication Dodson was involved with the paper, she worked at EPPC when it was published, according to her LinkedIn. And her views on medication abortion are clear: At a 2024 rally outside the Supreme Court, Dodson said she was there to ask the justices “to hold the FDA accountable for its reckless and unreasoned decision to remove important safeguards from high-risk abortion drugs.”

Dodson’s “statements about medication abortion do not reflect the large body of scientific evidence confirming the treatment’s safety,” Grossman said.

Ashley Jeanlus, another OB-GYN and a reproductive health advocacy fellow with Physicians for Reproductive Health, agreed.

“It just shows you how deep the anti-abortion roots go” within HHS, and how people like Dodson “really are the ones behind all of the policies that we see.”

“Dodson didn’t come to HHS with a background in medicine or science. She came from an anti-abortion think tank and contributed to Project 2025, and has a long history of prioritizing so-called ‘fetal personhood’ over the health and well-being of pregnant patients in the United States,” Jeanlus said in a statement to Autonomy News . “As the FDA continues its politically motivated review of mifepristone, it is easy to read between the lines of her promotion: The Trump administration will continue to support any and all efforts to make abortion harder to access, and it is being strategic and intentional in waiting until after the midterms to take more meaningful action.”

Liz McCaman Taylor, senior federal policy counsel at the Center for Reproductive Rights, put it simply: “It’s pretty outrageous.”

“It just shows you how deep the anti-abortion roots go” within HHS, and how people like Dodson “really are the ones behind all of the policies that we see,” she added.

While at EPPC, Dodson also contributed to a report promoting “restorative reproductive medicine” (RRM), which conservative groups and the Make America Healthy Again movement have framed as an alternative to in vitro fertilization. The approach involves using fertility awareness to help promote pregnancy as well as surgical interventions and other treatments that the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists says can actually delay pregnancy. “People struggling with infertility deserve every evidence-based option, not a narrowed menu shaped by politics that can cost them time they don’t have,” Jeanlus said.

The EPPC’s report on RRM was co-produced with the Heritage Foundation, which created Project 2025. Another contributor to that report: Marguerite Duane, an anti-abortion physician whom HHS recently awarded $8.4 million in grants, as Autonomy News exclusively reported. “It seems quite convenient, doesn’t it, that your partner in promoting this policy is now in a place where they are in charge of funding to continue promoting that policy,” McCaman Taylor said.

“It’s clear from the recent election that the public is tired of corrupt cronyism,” Grossman said. “We deserve to have qualified experts advising our nation’s leaders.”

According to LinkedIn, Dodson received an extraordinary achievement award from Kennedy for her work on Moms.gov , a federal government website debuted in May that directs pregnant people to anti-abortion crisis pregnancy centers . She also represents HHS at the United Nations, where she participates in efforts to get other countries to sign on to the Geneva Consensus Declaration , an anti-abortion pledge the Trump administration created during his first term.

“Personnel is policy,” McCaman Taylor said. “Putting people into these positions where they can even quietly make changes to how our federal dollars are spent is really influential, and will take a long time to undo, even if they’re not shouting about it.”
